Hyperdeterminant wavefunctions

Guan-Lin Lin Affiliation: Department of Physics, Boston College, Chestnut Hill, Massachusetts 02467, USA    Di Xiao Affiliation: Department of Materials Science and Engineering, University of Washington, Seattle, WA 98195, USA    Ying Ran Affiliation: Department of Physics, Boston College, Chestnut Hill, Massachusetts 02467, USA
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We systematically introduce hyperdeterminant wavefunctions as a variational-wavefunction-based theoretical framework for strongly correlated quantum states of matter, together with practical numerical simulation algorithms. This framework generalizes previously known fermionic parton constructions, yields reliable microscopics with intuitive physical pictures, and allows direct access to the fractionalized degrees of freedom together with associated microscopic effective field theories. We demonstrate the applications of this framework to fractional Chern insulators and quantum spin liquids. We comment that the hyperdeterminant states belong to a more general class of variational wavefunctions: the fused Gaussian states.

I Introduction

This long paper aims at developing a new theoretical framework to microscopically investigate strongly correlated quantum states of matter, particularly when fractionalized degrees of freedom (d.o.f.) are relevant, e.g., in the context of fractional Chern insulators[122, 119, 93, 117, 108, 142, 17, 95] or quantum spin liquids[6, 81, 12, 148]. In generic quantum systems, microscopic investigations usually require numerical simulations, often extensive ones. In the past, various numerical techniques have been developed in this field, including exact diagonalization (ED)[79, 139, 102], density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG)[138, 116], tensor-network (TN) methods[128, 94, 45, 47], quantum Monte Carlo(QMC)[25, 115, 10, 144], Gutzwiller-projected wavefunctions[49, 145, 44], and recently developed methods[22, 99, 58, 85, 124] based on machine learning.

In these microscopic techniques, one often faces a trade-off: we hope to capture microscopic energetics accurately while also having intuitive physical pictures for fractionalized d.o.f. Unfortunately, these two goals, in many cases, cannot be achieved together within one framework. This issue becomes somewhat urgent, particularly given the experimental discovery of the fractional quantum anomalous Hall states[21, 96, 146, 143, 84], where intuitive physical pictures would be very helpful for interactions between theoretical and experimental efforts.

The goal of an intuitive picture is to obtain a mean-field-like description of the quantum states under investigation. When fractionalized d.o.f. are present, we want to be able to access them directly. For example, when anyons[82, 140, 54, 9], or composite particles like composite fermions[68, 70, 53, 118] are present in the quantum state, we hope to directly compute their band structures. However, since these are fractionalized d.o.f. carrying gauge charges, they cannot be directly seen in the many-body spectra of the electrons. On the other hand, most modern, accurate microscopic methods (e.g., ED, DMRG, TN, QMC) only have direct access to the electrons. Reading out the microscopics of the fractionalized d.o.f., although still possible[40, 64], becomes highly nontrivial.

This paper may be viewed as an attempt to identify a sweet spot where both goals can be achieved within the same framework. We introduce the concept of hyperdeterminant (Hdet) wavefunctions with the locality structure, which generalizes the previously known fermionic parton constructions[15, 3, 69, 133, 80] for exotic states of matter. In some sense, Hdet wavefunctions are the natural generalization of Slater determinants, but for the situations when fractionalized d.o.f. are present. Namely, the Hdet wavefunctions are constructed from the fractionalized d.o.f., thereby allowing direct access to them.

As a class of variational wavefunctions, a crucial conceptual issue is the associated effective theories. Without knowing the associated effective theories, one may not directly know the quantum phase described by the variational wavefunctions. For this purpose, we develop a framework named the variational manifold path integral (VMPI). Applied to the Hdet wavefunctions, VMPI provides microscopic effective theories that capture physics from the lattice scale to the long distance, allowing one to sharply identify the quantum state of matter described by the Hdet wavefunction, as well as the collective mode dispersions. In simple terms, VMPI generalizes the time-dependent Hartree-Fock method of Slater determinants to Hdet wavefunctions, in a path-integral fashion.

Numerically simulating Hdet wavefunctions reliably is another challenge. Drastically different from the Slater determinants, simulating generic Hdet wavefunctions exactly is NP-hard. In the simplest limit, Hdet wavefunctions become products of determinants (e.g., a Laughlin wavefunction), which can be simulated by Monte Carlo. However, as we will see, deviating from this simplest limit is generally unavoidable if one wants to capture many important quantum phases at the microscopic level. To tackle this challenge, we develop a general method to approximately simulate Hdet wavefunctions: the projective expansion (PE), which allows one to systematically improve the approximation, order by order. The zeroth-order PE corresponds to a version of the mean-field approximation. Together with VMPI, PE allows one to compute the ground-state properties as well as the dynamical properties.

Hdet wavefunctions, the central topic of this paper, belong to an even larger class of variational wavefunctions, which we term the fused Gaussian states (FGS). FGS can capture more correlated quantum phases beyond the Hdet states, e.g., the FCI version of the ν=52\nu=\frac{5}{2} nonabelian state[90, 43], as well as correlated superconducting states. We will comment on FGS at the end of this paper. Crucially, as Hdet states, the FGS-based framework can also achieve both goals: reliable microscopics together with intuitive physical pictures. Many of the methods developed here, including VMPI and PE, can be applied to FGS.

This paper is organized as follows. In Sec.II, we introduce the definition of Hdet wavefunctions and their basic mathematical properties. However, not all Hdet wavefunctions are reasonable for low energy physics. In Sec.III, we introduce the concept of the locality-structure of Hdet wavefunctions. Hdet wavefunctions admitting a locality structure become physically reasonable. To motivate the locality-structure, we first present explicit calculation results for the Hdet states in traditional FQH systems in Sec.III.1. Readers may skip Sec.III.1 if one wants to directly see the definition of the locality-structure in Sec.III.2.5. In Sec.IV, we outline two types of model systems relevant for Hdet states: Type-(A) models featuring the full real-space d.o.f., and Type-(B) models confined within a topological band. Different model types lead to technical differences in the effective theory studies and simulation techniques presented afterward.

In Sec.V we present the effective theories for Hdet wavefunctions, by first introducing the general VMPI technique in Sec.V.1 as a path integral version of the time-dependent variational principle. Before applying to Hdet states, we apply VMPI to Slater determinants in Sec.V.2. The motivation is two-fold. First, since the time-dependent Hartree-Fock(TDHF) is well known, this subsection may help readers quickly follow the VMPI formalism. Second, in order to have a general discussion of effective theories for Hdet states, we have to introduce a collection of somewhat abstract mathematical objects. It turns out that essentially the same mathematical objects will be present when VMPI is applied to Slater determinants, and it is much easier to introduce them there. In the only appendix of this paper, Appendix A, we explicitly demonstrate these mathematical objects with a simple, concrete TDHF calculation. In Sec.V.3, we apply VMPI to Hdet states, identifying the Ward identities for the gauge fluctuations. The benefit of keeping the discussion general is that, the calculation of the VMPI actions and the collective mode dispersions outlined in Sec.V.3 can be viewed as well-defined algorithms. Together with PE, the microscopic effective theories for Hdet states can be computed directly.

In Sec.VI, we first describe the projective-expansion technique as a general method to approximately simulate Hdet states in Sec.VI.1. In Sec.VI.2 we present the mathematical structure of PE with closed-form formulas, together with algorithms. For readers not interested in technical details/algorithms, this subsection can be skipped. To demonstrate its capabilities, we present benchmark results in Sec.VI.3 for various quantum states and model systems. For instance, as advertised, the present framework allows direct access to the fractionalized d.o.f., and one may look into the parton band structures computed via the zeroth-order PE in FCI models in Fig.15. Finally, in Sec.VII, we comment on the generalization of Hdet states: FGS, as well as future research directions.

II Definition of Hdet wavefunctions and their mathematical properties

II.1 Definition of Hdet wavefunctions

Mathematically, the hyperdeterminant (Hdet) of a cubic tensor[24, 39] is a natural generalization of the determinant for a square matrix. Here, by a cubic tensor, we mean a rank-rr tensor Ti1,i2,…​irT_{i_{1},i_{2},...i_{r}} with identical dimensions for all indices: ik=1,2,…,Ni_{k}=1,2,...,N, ∀k=1,2,…​r\forall k=1,2,...r. Similar to the determinant of a rank-2 tensor (square matrix) Ai​jA_{ij}, the (combinatorial) hyperdeterminant of a general cubic tensor TT is defined as:

rank-2: det​(Ai​j)≡∑P∈SN(−1)P​A1​P​(1)​A2​P​(2)​…​AN​P​(N)\displaystyle\text{det}(A_{ij})\equiv\sum_{P\in S_{N}}(-1)^{P}A_{1P(1)}A_{2P(2)}...A_{NP(N)}
rank-3: Hdet​(Ti​j​k)≡∑P,Q∈SN(−1)P​(−1)Q​T1​P​(1)​Q​(1)​T2​P​(2)​Q​(2)​…​TN​P​(N)​Q​(N)\displaystyle\text{Hdet}(T_{ijk})\equiv\sum_{P,Q\in S_{N}}(-1)^{P}(-1)^{Q}T_{1P(1)Q(1)}T_{2P(2)Q(2)}...T_{NP(N)Q(N)}
rank-4: Hdet​(Ti​j​k​l)≡∑P,Q,R∈SN(−1)P​(−1)Q​(−1)R​T1​P​(1)​Q​(1)​R​(1)​T2​P​(2)​Q​(2)​R​(2)​…​TN​P​(N)​Q​(N)​R​(N)\displaystyle\text{Hdet}(T_{ijkl})\equiv\sum_{P,Q,R\in S_{N}}(-1)^{P}(-1)^{Q}(-1)^{R}T_{1P(1)Q(1)R(1)}T_{2P(2)Q(2)R(2)}...T_{NP(N)Q(N)R(N)}
rank-rr: Hdet​(T)≡∑σ2,…​σr∈SN∏α=2r(−1)σα​∏i=1NTi​σ2​(i)​…​σr​(i)\displaystyle\text{Hdet}(T)\equiv\sum_{\sigma_{2},...\sigma_{r}\in S_{N}}\prod_{\alpha=2}^{r}(-1)^{\sigma_{\alpha}}\prod_{i=1}^{N}T_{i\sigma_{2}(i)...\sigma_{r}(i)} (1)

We know that Slater determinants play a fundamental role in investigating conventional quantum states of matter of electrons. Before defining an Hdet many-body wavefunction, we would like to bring the readers’ attention to the following specific viewpoint of a Slater determinant many-body wavefunction.

For a free-electron quantum many-body state, we define the overlap matrix AA as:

Ai​j≡⟨ψi(e)|ϕj(e)⟩.\displaystyle A_{ij}\equiv\langle\psi_{i}^{(e)}|\phi_{j}^{(e)}\rangle. (2)

Here, |ψi(e)⟩|\psi_{i}^{(e)}\rangle labels a complete basis in the electron’s single-particle Hilbert space ℋ(e)\mathcal{H}^{(e)}: i=1,2,…,dim​ℋ(e)i=1,2,...,\text{dim}\mathcal{H}^{(e)}. |ϕj(e)⟩|\phi_{j}^{(e)}\rangle, however, labels the NeN_{e} (total electron number) filled single-particle states in ℋ(e)\mathcal{H}^{(e)}: j=1,2,…,Nej=1,2,...,N_{e}. Note that AA is a rectangular matrix, whose row-dimension could be much larger than the column-dimension. The quantum many-body state |Ψ(e)⟩|\Psi^{(e)}\rangle is well-defined as long as its overlap with an arbitrary many-body basis state |ψi1(e)​ψi2(e)​…​ψiNe(e)⟩|\psi_{i_{1}}^{(e)}\psi_{i_{2}}^{(e)}...\psi_{i_{N_{e}}}^{(e)}\rangle is defined. Here, we define

|ψi1(e)​ψi2(e)​…​ψiNe(e)⟩≡|ψi1(e)⟩​|ψi2(e)⟩​…​|ψiNe(e)⟩\displaystyle|\psi_{i_{1}}^{(e)}\psi_{i_{2}}^{(e)}...\psi_{i_{N_{e}}}^{(e)}\rangle\equiv|\psi_{i_{1}}^{(e)}\rangle|\psi_{i_{2}}^{(e)}\rangle...|\psi_{i_{N_{e}}}^{(e)}\rangle (3)

to be the simple direct product of single-particle states, which is not antisymmetrized.

The Slater-determinant wavefunction |Ψ(e)⟩|\Psi^{(e)}\rangle associated with AA is defined as:

Slater-det: ⟨ψi1(e)ψi2(e)…ψiNe(e)|Ψ(e)⟩≡det(Asub),\displaystyle\text{Slater-det: }\langle\psi_{i_{1}}^{(e)}\psi_{i_{2}}^{(e)}...\psi_{i_{N_{e}}}^{(e)}|\Psi^{(e)}\rangle\equiv\text{det}(A^{\text{sub}}), (4)

where AsubA^{\text{sub}} is the square submatrix obtained by stacking i1,i2,…,iNei_{1},i_{2},...,i_{N_{e}} rows of the rectangular matrix AA (see Fig.1(a) for an illustration). Crucially, the exponentially-sized many-body state |Ψ(e)⟩|\Psi^{(e)}\rangle is fully characterized by a polynomial-sized matrix AA.

Next, consider a general fermionic parton construction, in which an electron is split into a few species of fermionic partons. For instance, one may have e∼f(1)⋅f(2)e\sim f^{(1)}\cdot f^{(2)} for a bosonic electron, and e∼f(1)⋅f(2)⋅f(3)e\sim f^{(1)}\cdot f^{(2)}\cdot f^{(3)} for a fermionic electron. In the past, different versions of fermionic parton constructions have been introduced in the context of fractionalized quantum states of matter (e.g., quantum spin liquids, fractional quantum Hall states), from either the real-space viewpoints[15, 3, 69, 133, 136, 80], or from the tensor-product Hilbert space viewpoints[97, 92, 62]. Regardless of which version one uses, the basic idea remains the same: by transitioning to an enlarged Hilbert space of partons, one can construct exotic, fractionalized states with intuitive, mean-field-like physical pictures. In a previous work involving some of us[62], the core object for a general parton construction is identified: the tensor of fusion amplitudes. For instance,

e∼f(1)⋅f(2):Ti​j​k≡\displaystyle e\sim f^{(1)}\cdot f^{(2)}:\;\;T_{ijk}\equiv ⟨ψi(e)|∘​|ϕj(1)⟩|ϕk(2)⟩,\displaystyle\langle\psi_{i}^{(e)}|\mkern-1.0mu\mathord{\circ}\mkern-1.0mu|\phi^{(1)}_{j}\rangle|\phi^{(2)}_{k}\rangle,
e∼f(1)⋅f(2)⋅f(3):Ti​j​k​l≡\displaystyle e\sim f^{(1)}\cdot f^{(2)}\cdot f^{(3)}:\;\;T_{ijkl}\equiv ⟨ψi(e)|∘​|ϕj(1)⟩​|ϕk(2)⟩|ϕl(3)⟩.\displaystyle\langle\psi_{i}^{(e)}|\mkern-1.0mu\mathord{\circ}\mkern-1.0mu|\phi^{(1)}_{j}\rangle|\phi^{(2)}_{k}\rangle|\phi^{(3)}_{l}\rangle. (5)

Here, similar to the Slater-determinant case, |ψi(e)⟩|\psi_{i}^{(e)}\rangle labels a complete basis in the electron’s single-particle Hilbert space ℋ(e)\mathcal{H}^{(e)}: i=1,2,…,dim​ℋ(e)i=1,2,...,\text{dim}\mathcal{H}^{(e)}. |ϕj(1)⟩,|ϕk(2)⟩,|ϕl(3)⟩|\phi_{j}^{(1)}\rangle,|\phi_{k}^{(2)}\rangle,|\phi_{l}^{(3)}\rangle, on the other hand, labels the NeN_{e} (total electron number) filled single-particle states for each parton species: j,k,l=1,2,…,Nej,k,l=1,2,...,N_{e}. We also introduced an operator "∘""\circ" representing the fusion, which acts between ℋ(e)\mathcal{H}^{(e)} and ⊗pℋ(p)\otimes_{p}\mathcal{H}^{(p)} (p=1,2,3..p=1,2,3..). Note that despite one electron being split into a few species of partons, the total number of partons in each species is still equal to the total number of electrons.

The fusion tensor TT defines how to ”glue” the partons back into electrons in a general sense, and should be viewed as a rectangular-shaped tensor because the first index ii’s dimension, i.e., dim​ℋ(e)\text{dim}\mathcal{H}^{(e)}, is generically larger than NeN_{e}. The key observation of Ref[62] is that the (either bosonic or fermionic) electron many-body wavefunction in such parton constructions is really an Hdet wavefunction:

Hdet: ⟨ψi1(e)ψi2(e)…ψiNe(e)|Ψ(e)⟩≡Hdet(Tsub),\displaystyle\text{Hdet: }\langle\psi_{i_{1}}^{(e)}\psi_{i_{2}}^{(e)}...\psi_{i_{N_{e}}}^{(e)}|\Psi^{(e)}\rangle\equiv\text{Hdet}(T^{\text{sub}}), (6)

where the cubic subtensor TsubT^{\text{sub}} is obtained by stacking i1,i2,…,iNei_{1},i_{2},...,i_{N_{e}} slices of the rectangular tensor TT (see Fig.1(b) for an illustration). Again, we define the many-body basis as in Eq.(3), and the exponentially-sized many-body state |Ψ(e)⟩|\Psi^{(e)}\rangle is fully characterized by a polynomial-sized tensor TT.

II.2 Mathematical properties of Hdet wavefunctions

Before proceeding to physics, we list a few essential mathematical properties of the Hdet wavefunctions.

II.2.1 Statistics theorem

For an even-rank (odd-rank) tensor TT, the Hdet electronic wavefunction defined as Eq.(6) is automatically a fermionic (bosonic) many-body state.

Proof: This is a direct consequence of the definition of the combinatorial hyperdeterminant in Eq.(1). Consider a permutation π∈SN\pi\in S_{N}. Comparing with Eq.(6), the overlap of |Ψ(e)⟩|\Psi^{(e)}\rangle with the permuted many-body basis |ψiπ​(1)(e)​ψiπ​(2)(e)​…​ψiπ⁡(Ne)(e)⟩|\psi_{i_{\pi}(1)}^{(e)}\psi_{i_{\pi}(2)}^{(e)}...\psi_{i_{\pi(N_{e})}}^{(e)}\rangle is the hyperdeterminant of the cubic subtensor T~sub\tilde{T}^{\text{sub}} that can be obtained from TsubT^{\text{sub}} via permuting the first index by π\pi.

=\displaystyle= ∑σ2,…​σr∈SN∏α=2r(−1)σα​∏i=1NTπ⁡(i)​σ2​(i)​…​σr​(i)\displaystyle\sum_{\sigma_{2},...\sigma_{r}\in S_{N}}\prod_{\alpha=2}^{r}(-1)^{\sigma_{\alpha}}\prod_{i=1}^{N}T_{\pi(i)\sigma_{2}(i)...\sigma_{r}(i)}
=\displaystyle= ((−1)π)r−1​∑σ~2,…​σ~r∈SN∏α=2r(−1)σ~α​∏k=1NTk​σ~2​(k)​…​σ~r​(k)\displaystyle((-1)^{\pi})^{r-1}\sum_{\tilde{\sigma}_{2},...\tilde{\sigma}_{r}\in S_{N}}\prod_{\alpha=2}^{r}(-1)^{\tilde{\sigma}_{\alpha}}\prod_{k=1}^{N}T_{k\tilde{\sigma}_{2}(k)...\tilde{\sigma}_{r}(k)}

where we have defined k≡π⁡(i)k\equiv\pi(i) (so i=π−1​(k)i=\pi^{-1}(k)) σ~α=σα⋅π−1\tilde{\sigma}_{\alpha}=\sigma_{\alpha}\cdot\pi^{-1}, and consequently (−1)σ~α=(−1)π⋅(−1)σα(-1)^{\tilde{\sigma}_{\alpha}}=(-1)^{\pi}\cdot(-1)^{\sigma_{\alpha}}. Therefore, if rr is odd(even), the Hdet wavefunction is permutation symmetric(antisymmetric).

II.2.2 Basis-independence theorem

The fusion tensor TT defined in Eq.(5) is dependent on the basis-choice for both the electron and the partons. The natural question is whether the many-body Hdet wavefunction in Eq.(6) depends on these basis choices or not. Here we show that the Hdet wavefunction is basis choice independent.

First, the filled-parton single-particle states {|ϕk(p)⟩}\{|\phi_{k}^{(p)}\rangle\} (which do not need to be orthonormal) span a sub-Hilbert space for the parton species-pp. One may choose a different basis {|ϕ~k(p)⟩}\{|\tilde{\phi}_{k}^{(p)}\rangle\} that spans the same sub-Hilbert space. Namely, we may perform a transformation of basis for the parton species-pp:

|ϕ~k(p)⟩=∑l=1NeMk​l​|ϕl(p)⟩,\displaystyle|\tilde{\phi}_{k}^{(p)}\rangle=\sum_{l=1}^{N_{e}}M_{kl}|\phi_{l}^{(p)}\rangle, (8)

with an invertible Ne×NeN_{e}\times N_{e} matrix MM. For instance, if there are three species of partons, and p=1p=1, the corresponding rank-4 fusion tensor is transformed as:

Ti​j​k​l→T~i​j​k​l≡∑j′=1NeMj​j′​Ti​j′​k​l\displaystyle T_{ijkl}\rightarrow\tilde{T}_{ijkl}\equiv\sum_{j^{\prime}=1}^{N_{e}}M_{jj^{\prime}}T_{ij^{\prime}kl} (9)

Graphically, T~\tilde{T} is obtained from TT by contracting the matrix MM with the parton-leg-pp (see Fig.2 for illustration). In this case, one can straightforwardly show that the Hdet wavefunction defined by TT or T~\tilde{T} only differs by an overall constant factor det​(M)\text{det}(M). Namely, the many-body wavefunction is independent of the parton-basis choice.

Second, one may choose an arbitrary set of NeN_{e} electronic orbitals {|ψ~α(e)⟩}\{|\tilde{\psi}_{\alpha}^{(e)}\rangle\} (α=1,2,…,Ne\alpha=1,2,...,N_{e}, which again do not need to be an orthonormal set), that are linear superpositions of the basis {|ψi(e)⟩}\{|\psi_{i}^{(e)}\rangle\}:

|ψ~α(e)⟩=∑i=1dim​ℋ(e)Sα​i​|ψi(e)⟩,\displaystyle|\tilde{\psi}_{\alpha}^{(e)}\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{\text{dim}\mathcal{H}^{(e)}}S_{\alpha i}|\psi_{i}^{(e)}\rangle, (10)

characterized by a rectangular Ne×dim​ℋ(e)N_{e}\times\text{dim}\mathcal{H}^{(e)} matrix SS. According to Eq.(6), to compute the overlap between |ψ~1(e)​ψ~2(e)​…​ψ~Ne(e)⟩|\tilde{\psi}_{1}^{(e)}\tilde{\psi}_{2}^{(e)}...\tilde{\psi}_{N_{e}}^{(e)}\rangle with the many-body state |Ψ(e)⟩|\Psi^{(e)}\rangle, we only need to compute the hyperdeterminant of the cubic tensor 𝐓\mathbf{T} obtained from TT by contracting the electron-leg with the matrix S∗S^{*}:

⟨ψ~1(e)​ψ~2(e)​…​ψ~Ne(e)|Ψ(e)⟩=Hdet​(𝐓),\displaystyle\langle\tilde{\psi}_{1}^{(e)}\tilde{\psi}_{2}^{(e)}...\tilde{\psi}_{N_{e}}^{(e)}|\Psi^{(e)}\rangle=\text{Hdet}(\mathbf{T}), (11)

where

𝐓α​j​k​…≡∑i=1dim​ℋ(e)Sα​i∗​Ti​j​k​….\displaystyle\mathbf{T}_{\alpha jk...}\equiv\sum_{i=1}^{\text{dim}\mathcal{H}^{(e)}}S^{*}_{\alpha i}T_{ijk...}. (12)

The question is whether Eq.(11) is consistent with the definition Eq.(6). The answer is positive.

The simplest way to see this is to consider the definition Eq.(1), where the first index (i.e., electron-leg) is not permuted. Consequently, one can straightforwardly show that:

Hdet​(𝐓)\displaystyle\text{Hdet}(\mathbf{T})
=\displaystyle= ∑i1,i2,…​iNe=1dim​ℋ(e)S1,i1∗​S2,i2∗​…​SN,iNe∗​⟨ψi1(e)​ψi2(e)​…​ψiNe(e)|Ψ(e)⟩.\displaystyle\sum_{i_{1},i_{2},...i_{N_{e}}=1}^{\text{dim}\mathcal{H}^{(e)}}S^{*}_{1,i_{1}}S^{*}_{2,i_{2}}...S^{*}_{N,i_{N_{e}}}\langle\psi_{i_{1}}^{(e)}\psi_{i_{2}}^{(e)}...\psi_{i_{N_{e}}}^{(e)}|\Psi^{(e)}\rangle. (13)

Namely, based on the definition Eq.(3), Eq.(11) is consistent with Eq.(6). Therefore, the Hdet wavefunction is also independent of the basis-choice for the electron.

II.2.3 Second-quantized formulation

So far we have been using the first-quantized formulation to discuss Hdet wavefunctions. It may be helpful to translate the construction into the second-quantized formulation as well. For this purpose, one may define the fusion operator 𝐅^\hat{\mathbf{F}} as:

e∼f(1)​f(2):𝐅^=\displaystyle e\sim f^{(1)}f^{(2)}:\;\hat{\mathbf{F}}= ∑i​j​kTi​j​k​bi†​fj(1)​fk(2)\displaystyle\sum_{ijk}T_{ijk}b_{i}^{\dagger}f_{j}^{(1)}f_{k}^{(2)}
e∼f(1)​f(2)​f(3):𝐅^=\displaystyle e\sim f^{(1)}f^{(2)}f^{(3)}:\;\hat{\mathbf{F}}= ∑i​j​k​lTi​j​k​l​ci†​fj(1)​fk(2)​fl(3)\displaystyle\sum_{ijkl}T_{ijkl}c_{i}^{\dagger}f_{j}^{(1)}f_{k}^{(2)}f_{l}^{(3)}
\displaystyle... (14)

Only in this subsection, for simplicity, we assume that the single particle states |ψi(e)⟩|\psi_{i}^{(e)}\rangle, |ϕj(1)⟩|\phi_{j}^{(1)}\rangle, |ϕk(2)⟩|\phi_{k}^{(2)}\rangle, etc, are orthonormal in their own Hilbert spaces, respectively. The second-quantized operator fk(p)f_{k}^{(p)} is the fermionic annihilation operator associated with |ϕk(p)⟩|\phi_{k}^{(p)}\rangle. The electron creation operator, bi†b_{i}^{\dagger} for bosonic electron (rank-odd TT) and ci†c_{i}^{\dagger} for fermionic electron (rank-even TT), is associated with |ψi(e)⟩|\psi_{i}^{(e)}\rangle. The fusion operator "∘""\circ" in Eq.(5) can be exactly interpreted as 𝐅^\hat{\mathbf{F}}:

∘=𝐅^.\displaystyle\circ=\hat{\mathbf{F}}. (15)

One can check that the unsymmetrized overlap with an identical-particle state in the Fock space is equal to a second-quantized overlap:

⟨ψi1(e)​ψi2(e)​…​ψiNe(e)|Ψ(e)⟩=1Ne!​⟨0|eiNe​…​ei2​ei1|Ψ(e)⟩,\displaystyle\langle\psi_{i_{1}}^{(e)}\psi_{i_{2}}^{(e)}...\psi_{i_{N_{e}}}^{(e)}|\Psi^{(e)}\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{e}!}}\langle 0|e_{i_{N_{e}}}...e_{i_{2}}e_{i_{1}}|\Psi^{(e)}\rangle, (16)

where ei≡cie_{i}\equiv c_{i} (ei≡bie_{i}\equiv b_{i}) for fermionic(bosonic) electrons (even if more than one bosons fill the same single-particle level in the latter case). From this, it is easy to show that the electron many-body wavefunction in Eq.(6) can be obtained by:

|Ψ(e)⟩=1Ne!​𝐅^Ne​|Ψ(1)⟩​|Ψ(2)⟩​…,\displaystyle|\Psi^{(e)}\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{e}!}}\hat{\mathbf{F}}^{N_{e}}|\Psi^{(1)}\rangle|\Psi^{(2)}\rangle..., (17)

where the many-body state |Ψ(p)⟩|\Psi^{(p)}\rangle for parton species-pp is nothing but a single Slater-determinant state:

|Ψ(p)⟩=∏k=1Nefk(p)†|0⟩.\displaystyle|\Psi^{(p)}\rangle=\prod_{k=1}^{N_{e}}f^{(p)\dagger}_{k}|0\rangle. (18)

II.2.4 Relation to products of determinants and CPD

Previously, it is known that a fractionalized quantum state can often be written as a product of determinants. One seminal example is the FQH Laughlin wavefunctions at filling ν=1m\nu=\frac{1}{m}. In the disk geometry with symmetric gauge, ΨLaughlin=∏i<j(zi−zj)m​e−∑i|zi|24​le2\Psi_{\text{Laughlin}}=\prod_{i<j}(z_{i}-z_{j})^{m}e^{-\frac{\sum_{i}|z_{i}|^{2}}{4l_{e}^{2}}}, which can be viewed as the mm-th power of a Slater determinant (i.e., the ν=1\nu=1 integer quantum Hall state).

The product of determinants is a very special limit of the general Hdet wavefunctions. It is straightforward to show that, based on the definition Eq.(1), if a cubic tensor TT can be written as the product of square matrices in the following sense, then the hyperdeterminant of TT is the product of the determinants of the matrices:

If Ti​j​k=Ai​j⋅Bi​k, then: Hdet(T)=det(A)det(B),\displaystyle\text{If }T_{ijk}=A_{ij}\cdot B_{ik},\text{ then: }\text{Hdet}(T)=\text{det}(A)\text{det}(B), (19)

and similarly:

If Ti​j​k​l=Ai​j⋅Bi​k⋅Ci​l,\displaystyle T_{ijkl}=A_{ij}\cdot B_{ik}\cdot C_{il},
then: Hdet​(T)=det​(A)​det​(B)​det​(C).\displaystyle\text{Hdet}(T)=\text{det}(A)\text{det}(B)\text{det}(C). (20)

In Sec.III.1 we will show that the tensor TT for the Laughlin state can indeed be written as the product of matrices, but only after choosing a specific basis for the electron (the overcomplete real-space coherent-state basis {|z⟩}\{|z\rangle\} inside LLL). Clearly, whether the tensor can be written as a product of matrices crucially depends on the basis choice of the electron {|ψi(e)⟩}\{|\psi_{i}^{(e)}\rangle\}; but it does not depend on the basis choice for partons, which only rotates the matrices A,B​…A,B.... For example, if one wants to write down the same Laughlin state using the electron’s momentum-space Bloch basis (e.g., in the Landau gauge), TT will not be a product of the matrices. Consequently, Laughlin states are not products of determinants in the momentum-space basis. But from the bases-independence theorem, they are still always hyperdeterminants.

A natural question is: under what condition can the tensor TT be written as a product of matrices? This is an important question because, in practice, one can easily simulate a product of determinants using the Monte Carlo algorithm, which is why Laughlin states have been accurately investigated numerically. To answer this question, it is instructive to consider the two-parton construction for bosonic electrons in Eq.(19). After fixing the index ii, Ti​j​k=Ai​j​Bi​kT_{ijk}=A_{ij}B_{ik} can be interpreted as a singular value decomposition (SVD) of the matrix Tj​k​(i)≡Ti​j​kT_{jk}(i)\equiv T_{ijk}. Defining Aj​(i)≡Ai​jA_{j}(i)\equiv A_{ij} and Bk​(i)≡Bi​kB_{k}(i)\equiv B_{ik}, one finds:

Ti​j​k=Ai​j​Bi​k⟺Tj​k​(i)=Aj​(i)​Bk​(i).\displaystyle T_{ijk}=A_{ij}B_{ik}\Longleftrightarrow T_{jk}(i)=A_{j}(i)B_{k}(i). (21)

Namely, the square matrix Tj​k​(i)T_{jk}(i) is a product of two vectors, i.e., has only one nonzero singular value. Moving on to the three-parton construction for fermionic electrons in Eq.(20), the corresponding relation is:

Ti​j​k​l=Ai​j​Bi​k​Ci​l⟺Tj​k​l​(i)=Aj​(i)​Bk​(i)​Cl​(i).\displaystyle T_{ijkl}=A_{ij}B_{ik}C_{il}\Longleftrightarrow T_{jkl}(i)=A_{j}(i)B_{k}(i)C_{l}(i). (22)

This is a generalization of SVD to the rank-3 tensor T⁡(i)T(i): the Canonical Polyadic Decomposition (CPD)[23, 55, 74] of the rank-3 tensor Tj​k​l​(i)T_{jkl}(i). For a general rank-rr tensor 𝒜\mathcal{A}, the CPD is defined as:

𝒜i1,i2​…,ir=∑α=1Rλα⋅xα,i1(1)​xα,i2(2)​…​xα,ir(r),\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{i_{1},i_{2}...,i_{r}}=\sum_{\alpha=1}^{R}\lambda_{\alpha}\cdot x^{(1)}_{\alpha,i_{1}}x^{(2)}_{\alpha,i_{2}}...x^{(r)}_{\alpha,i_{r}}, (23)

where the minimal integer RR for this decomposition, for historical reasons, is called the CPD-rank of the tensor 𝒜\mathcal{A} (to avoid confusion of terminology, we warn the reader that the CPD-rank and the rank (i.e., rr) of a tensor have no direct relation). Mathematically, one may always absorb the CPD-values λα\lambda_{\alpha} into the CPD-vectors xx’s, which we will not do due to physical reasons that will become clear in Sec.III.

Eq.(22) means the CPD-rank of the rank-3 tensor Tj​k​l​(i)T_{jkl}(i) is one – a very special tensor. As already mentioned, the CPD-rank does not depend on the parton-basis choice, which only rotates the CPD-vectors xx’s. The CPD-rank only depends on the choice of the electron state |ψi(e)⟩|\psi_{i}^{(e)}\rangle participating in the fusion tensor. The question now becomes: given a fusion tensor TT, which defines Tj​k..​(i~)≡⟨ψi~(e)|∘​|ϕj(1)⟩|ϕk(2)⟩​…T_{jk..}(\tilde{i})\equiv\langle\psi_{\tilde{i}}^{(e)}|\mkern-1.0mu\mathord{\circ}\mkern-1.0mu|\phi^{(1)}_{j}\rangle|\phi^{(2)}_{k}\rangle... (∀|ψi~(e)⟩∈ℋ(e)\forall|\psi_{\tilde{i}}^{(e)}\rangle\in\mathcal{H}^{(e)}), is it always possible to choose one electron state |ψi~(e)⟩|\psi_{\tilde{i}}^{(e)}\rangle such that T⁡(i~)T(\tilde{i})’s CPD-rank is one?

The answer is negative. We will show in Sec.III.1 that, even for the next FQH state in the Jain’s composite-fermion sequence with n=2n=2, the CPD-rank of T⁡(i~)T(\tilde{i}) is larger than one for whatever choice of |ψi~(e)⟩|\psi_{\tilde{i}}^{(e)}\rangle. For bosonic (fermionic) electrons, Jain’s sequence is at filling fractions ν=nn⁡(2​s−1)+1\nu=\frac{n}{n(2s-1)+1} (ν=n2​n​s+1\nu=\frac{n}{2ns+1}), where the integer s=1,2,..s=1,2,.. characterizes the degrees of flux attachment. n=1n=1 cases recover the Laughlin states. One can consider the state at s=1s=1 and n=2n=2 (ν=23\nu=\frac{2}{3} for bosonic electrons, and ν=25\nu=\frac{2}{5} for fermionic electrons). It turns out that, even after choosing the optimal |ψi~(e)⟩|\psi_{\tilde{i}}^{(e)}\rangle minimizing the CPD-rank, for ν=23\nu=\frac{2}{3} bosonic case, the CPD-rank of T⁡(i~)T(\tilde{i}) is three. And for ν=25\nu=\frac{2}{5} fermionic case, the CPD-rank of T⁡(i~)T(\tilde{i}) is four. Already in these traditional FQH systems, the many-body wavefunctions cannot be written as a product of determinants. But, as pointed out in Ref.[62], these are still hyperdeterminants.

II.2.5 Exact Hdet is NP-hard

Drastically different from computing the determinant of a matrix, exactly computing Hdet of a tensor is generally NP-hard[60]. The Gaussian Elimination Algorithm, allowing a polynomial complexity for computing the determinant, is no longer applicable for (rank>2>2) tensors. One simple way to see the hardness of the Hdet is to consider another special limit of a rank-3 cubic tensor: Ti​j​k=Ai​j​δj​kT_{ijk}=A_{ij}\delta_{jk}. In this limit, the permutations in Eq.(1) must satisfy P=QP=Q for a nonzero contribution, and consequently Hdet​(T)=perm​(A)\text{Hdet}(T)=\text{perm}(A). Here, we introduced the permanent of the square matrix AA, which is an analog of the determinant but without the permutation sign. Permanent is related to the many-body wavefunctions of free bosons and is well-known to be NP-hard to compute[127, 1].

From a different perspective, one may consider the CPD structure of a fusion tensor TT. For instance, we will show in Sec.III.1 that, after choosing the (overcomplete) coherent state basis for the electron, which is CPD-optimal, the fusion tensor TT for the bosonic ν=23\nu=\frac{2}{3} Jain’s composite-fermion state satisfies:

Tz​j​kν=23=⟨z(e)|∘​|ϕj(1)⟩|ϕk(2)⟩=∑α=13λα​Aα,z​j​Bα,z​k,∀z.\displaystyle T^{\nu=\frac{2}{3}}_{zjk}=\langle z^{(e)}|\mkern-1.0mu\mathord{\circ}\mkern-1.0mu|\phi_{j}^{(1)}\rangle|\phi^{(2)}_{k}\rangle=\sum_{\alpha=1}^{3}\lambda_{\alpha}A_{\alpha,zj}B_{\alpha,zk},\;\;\forall z. (24)

Here the complex real-space coordinate zz labels the electron’s coherent states |z(e)⟩|z^{(e)}\rangle that can be obtained after projecting the delta-function at zz into the LLL. Note that the equation above should be viewed as the CPD of the rank-2 tensor Tj​k​(z)≡Tz​j​kν=23T_{jk}(z)\equiv T^{\nu=\frac{2}{3}}_{zjk}. A priori, both the CPD-rank R=3R=3 and the CPD-values λα\lambda_{\alpha} may depend on zz, but the Galilean invariance in the system dictates that they will not.

After inserting into the definition Eq.(1), one finds that the real-space wavefunctions for these systems are a summation of exponentially many products of determinants:

⟨z1​z2​…​zNe|Ψν=23(e)⟩=∑P,Q∈SNe(−1)P​(−1)Q​∑α1λα1​Aα1,z1​P​(1)​Bα1,z1​Q​(1)​…​∑αNeλαNe​AαNe,zNe​P​(Ne)​BαNe,zNe​Q​(Ne)\displaystyle\langle z_{1}z_{2}...z_{N_{e}}|\Psi^{(e)}_{\nu=\frac{2}{3}}\rangle=\sum_{P,Q\in S_{N_{e}}}(-1)^{P}(-1)^{Q}\sum_{\alpha_{1}}\lambda_{\alpha_{1}}A_{\alpha_{1},z_{1}P(1)}B_{\alpha_{1},z_{1}Q(1)}...\sum_{\alpha_{N_{e}}}\lambda_{\alpha_{N_{e}}}A_{\alpha_{N_{e}},z_{N_{e}}P(N_{e})}B_{\alpha_{N_{e}},z_{N_{e}}Q(N_{e})}
=\displaystyle= ∑{αi}∏i=1Neλαi​[∑P∈SNe(−1)P​Aα1,z1​P​(1)​…​AαNe,zNe​P​(Ne)]​[∑Q∈SNe(−1)Q​Bα1,z1​Q​(1)​…​BαNe,zNe​Q​(Ne)]\displaystyle\sum_{\{\alpha_{i}\}}\prod_{i=1}^{N_{e}}\lambda_{\alpha_{i}}\left[\sum_{P\in S_{N_{e}}}(-1)^{P}A_{\alpha_{1},z_{1}P(1)}...A_{\alpha_{N_{e}},z_{N_{e}}P(N_{e})}\right]\left[\sum_{Q\in S_{N_{e}}}(-1)^{Q}B_{\alpha_{1},z_{1}Q(1)}...B_{\alpha_{N_{e}},z_{N_{e}}Q(N_{e})}\right]
=\displaystyle= ∑{αi=1,2,3}∏i=1Neλαi⋅det​(𝐀⁡[α1,α2,…​αNe])⋅det​(𝐁⁡[α1,α2,…​αNe]).\displaystyle\sum_{\{\alpha_{i}=1,2,3\}}\prod_{i=1}^{N_{e}}\lambda_{\alpha_{i}}\cdot\text{det}(\mathbf{A}[\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},...\alpha_{N_{e}}])\cdot\text{det}(\mathbf{B}[\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},...\alpha_{N_{e}}]). (25)

Here, if we consider Aα,zi​jA_{\alpha,z_{i}j} as three matrices A⁡(α)A(\alpha) with α=1,2,3\alpha=1,2,3 and ii(jj) labeling rows(columns), the matrices 𝐀⁡[α1,α2,…​αNe]\mathbf{A}[\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},...\alpha_{N_{e}}] (and similarly 𝐁⁡[α1,α2,…​αNe]\mathbf{B}[\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},...\alpha_{N_{e}}]) are formed by choosing rows among three A⁡(α)A(\alpha) matrices according to α1,α2,…​αNe\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},...\alpha_{N_{e}}. This is a summation of 3Ne3^{N_{e}} products of two determinants.

Similarly, for the fermionic ν=25\nu=\frac{2}{5} Jain’s state, we will show:

Tz​j​k​lν=25=∑α=14λα​Aα,z​j​Bα,z​k​Cα,z​l,∀z.\displaystyle T^{\nu=\frac{2}{5}}_{zjkl}=\sum_{\alpha=1}^{4}\lambda_{\alpha}A_{\alpha,zj}B_{\alpha,zk}C_{\alpha,zl},\;\;\forall z. (26)

Its real-space many-body wavefunction is a summation of 4Ne4^{N_{e}} products of three determinants.

From this analysis, the importance of the CPD structure of the fusion tensor becomes clear. At this point, we introduce the concept of fusion channels. If the fusion tensor T⁡(i)T(i) has CPD-rank RR:

Tj​k​…​(i)≡⟨ψi(e)|∘​|ϕj(1)⟩|ϕk(2)⟩​…=∑α=1Rλα​Aα,i​j(1)​Aα,i​k(2)​…\displaystyle T_{jk...}(i)\equiv\langle\psi_{i}^{(e)}|\mkern-1.0mu\mathord{\circ}\mkern-1.0mu|\phi^{(1)}_{j}\rangle|\phi^{(2)}_{k}\rangle...=\sum_{\alpha=1}^{R}\lambda_{\alpha}A^{(1)}_{\alpha,ij}A^{(2)}_{\alpha,ik}... (27)

we say there are RR fusion channels to the electron state |ψi(e)⟩|\psi_{i}^{(e)}\rangle. We also say that the corresponding coefficient λα\lambda_{\alpha} is the fusion-amplitude for the fusion-channel α\alpha. The ”…” indicates there may be more than two species of partons. Throughout this paper, the superscripts (1), (2) are reserved to denote the parton species. In the next section, we will explore the physical meanings of the fusion channels.

II.2.6 About uniqueness of the fusion-tensor TT

Due to the bases-independence theorem, WLOG, in this subsection, we assume the electronic single-particle basis {|ϕi(e)⟩}\{|\phi_{i}^{(e)}\rangle\} is orthonormal.

Suppose a many-body state |ΨSlater(e)⟩|\Psi^{(e)}_{\text{Slater}}\rangle is a Slater-determinant wavefunction associated with some overlap matrix Ai​jA_{ij} (see Eq.(2)). Even if one does not know AA, conceptually, it is straightforward to read it out from the many-body state |ΨSlater(e)⟩|\Psi^{(e)}_{\text{Slater}}\rangle itself, up to a unitary transformation among the filled states: A~i​j=∑j′Ai​j′​Uj′​j\tilde{A}_{ij}=\sum_{j^{\prime}}A_{ij^{\prime}}U_{j^{\prime}j}. For example, one can compute the single-body correlation matrix ρi​i′=⟨ΨSlater(e)|ci′†​ci|ΨSlater(e)⟩\rho_{ii^{\prime}}=\langle\Psi^{(e)}_{\text{Slater}}|c^{\dagger}_{i^{\prime}}c_{i}|\Psi^{(e)}_{\text{Slater}}\rangle. In terms of matrices ρ=A⋅A†\rho=A\cdot A^{\dagger}. After diagonalizing ρ\rho, AA can be found. This means that the matrix AA is physical up to the expected unitary gauge redundancy UU.

What happens for an Hdet wavefunction |Ψ(e)⟩|\Psi^{(e)}\rangle defined via a fusion tensor Ti​j​k​…T_{ijk...} as in Eq.(6)? Can one read out TT from |Ψ(e)⟩|\Psi^{(e)}\rangle up to expected gauge redundancies? As mentioned in the bases-independence theorem, any G​L​(Ne,𝒞)GL(N_{e},\mathcal{C}) (i.e., an invertible Ne×NeN_{e}\times N_{e} complex matrix) transformation on a parton-index (i.e., j,k,…j,k,...) does not change the electronic state |Ψ(e)⟩|\Psi^{(e)}\rangle. In addition, obviously, any permutation between the parton indices, e.g., j↔kj\leftrightarrow k, does not change the electronic state as well. If we denote the number of parton species to be npn_{\text{p}}, we have the expected G​L​(Ne,𝒞)npGL(N_{e},\mathcal{C})^{n_{\text{p}}} and SnpS_{n_{\text{p}}} (SS is the permutation group) gauge redundancies.

This question is important because it tells us whether or not the fusion tensor TT in an Hdet wavefunction is as physical as the overlap matrix AA in a Slater-determinant wavefunction. At this point, we do not have rigorous mathematical results on this issue. However, it appears to us that generically TT should be fully fixed by |Ψ(e)⟩|\Psi^{(e)}\rangle up to the expected gauge redundancies above.

III The locality-structure of Hdet wavefunctions

So far, we have defined the Hdet wavefunctions mathematically. From the pure math viewpoint, one does not necessarily attach any physical meaning to the tensor TT as a fusion tensor, as defined in Eq.(5). One can even write down an arbitrary tensor TT, which nevertheless well defines a quantum many-body wavefunction according to Eq.(6). However, not all tensors TT’s are relevant to low-energy quantum many-body physics. A quantum Hamiltonian needs a notion of locality even to define the spatial dimension in a physical sense, and the same is true for its low-energy states.

For instance, for the ground state of a gapped local Hamiltonian, the connected correlators of local observables should have an exponential decay[56]. Although a general sharp statement for the ground state of a gapless local Hamiltonian is not known to the authors’ best knowledge, physical intuition indicates that the connected correlator of local observables should have a power-law decay, which cannot be too slow. In unitary conformal field theories, the bounds for the exponents of these power laws are known[87, 112].

This raises an important question: what kind of fusion tensors TT’s (and the associated Hdet wavefunctions) can be viewed as physically reasonable for low-energy physics? For a Slater-determinant wavefunction, which appears in various mean-field analyses of electron systems, it is usually not a problem since one typically first writes down a physical parent free-fermion Hamiltonian. For Hdet wavefunctions describing strongly correlated, possibly fractionalized quantum phases of matter, we need a prescription to encode locality in the fusion tensor TT, which we call the locality-structure of TT and define in Sec.III.2. Namely, only an Hdet wavefunction whose fusion tensor TT admits the locality-structure is a physically reasonable low-energy wavefunction. This locality-structure immediately leads to an effective field theory description of the Hdet wavefunctions discussed in Sec.V.3.

III.1 Fusion tensors for composite-fermion states in FQH

To explore the locality structure of fusion tensors, we will start by introducing explicit analytical results from a concrete parton construction in the context of traditional FQH states as a demonstration. Already in the early development of the composite-fermion approach, Jain pointed out that a real-space parton construction can obtain his composite-fermion wavefunctions[69, 70]. This parton construction was later further developed to describe more general FQH states, both abelian and nonabelian[133, 18, 135, 13].

In this real-space parton construction, one first identifies the electron operator as a product of a few species of real-space parton operators. As a demonstration, for simplicity, we will focus on the s=1s=1 composite fermion states (but nn can be a general positive integer, including the composite Fermi liquid state corresponding to n→∞n\rightarrow\infty.) For bosonic (fermionic) electrons, s=1s=1 means that there are two (three) species of partons:

b𝐫†=\displaystyle b_{\mathbf{r}}^{\dagger}= f𝐫(1)†f𝐫(2)†\displaystyle f_{\mathbf{r}}^{(1)\dagger}f_{\mathbf{r}}^{(2)\dagger}
c𝐫†=\displaystyle c_{\mathbf{r}}^{\dagger}= f𝐫(1)†f𝐫(2)†f𝐫(3)†\displaystyle f_{\mathbf{r}}^{(1)\dagger}f_{\mathbf{r}}^{(2)\dagger}f_{\mathbf{r}}^{(3)\dagger} (28)

If one assigns the electron’s charge to be unity q(e)=1q^{(e)}=1, then each parton species-pp should carry a fractional charge q(p)q^{(p)}, so that the total charge is the electron’s charge: ∑pq(p)=1\sum_{p}q^{(p)}=1. For instance, for the bosonic Jain’s FQH sequence at filling ν=nn+1\nu=\frac{n}{n+1}, q(1)=nn+1q^{(1)}=\frac{n}{n+1} and q(2)=1n+1q^{(2)}=\frac{1}{n+1}. And for the fermionic Jain’s FQH sequence at filling ν=n2​n+1\nu=\frac{n}{2n+1}, q(1)=q(2)=n2​n+1q^{(1)}=q^{(2)}=\frac{n}{2n+1} and q(3)=12​n+1q^{(3)}=\frac{1}{2n+1}.

Because each parton has a fractional charge, it sees a fractional strength of the magnetic field: the magnetic length of parton species-pp becomes lp≡leq(p)l_{p}\equiv\frac{l_{e}}{\sqrt{q^{(p)}}}. But note that the total number of partons for a given species is the same as the number of electrons. Consequently, each parton species is at an integer filling fraction: for the bosonic (fermionic) Jain’s FQH sequence: ν(1)=1\nu^{(1)}=1 and ν(2)=n\nu^{(2)}=n (ν(1)=ν(2)=1\nu^{(1)}=\nu^{(2)}=1 and ν(3)=n\nu^{(3)}=n). At the mean-field level, these partons are treated as non-interacting and simply form gapped Slater-determinant states. This is the basic idea behind all parton constructions. By enlarging the Hilbert space via introducing partons, one can obtain an intuitive description of a fractionalized quantum state in terms of free-parton states.

If one denotes a Slater-determinant parton-state by its integer filling fraction, the electron wavefunction is obtained simply by gluing all species of partons together in real space. For instance, for the bosonic Jain’s sequence: Ψ~(e)​(𝐫1,…​𝐫N)≡Ψν=1(1)​(𝐫1,…​𝐫N)⋅Ψν=n(2)​(𝐫1,…​𝐫N)\tilde{\Psi}^{(e)}(\mathbf{r}_{1},...\mathbf{r}_{N})\equiv\Psi^{(1)}_{\nu=1}(\mathbf{r}_{1},...\mathbf{r}_{N})\cdot\Psi^{(2)}_{\nu=n}(\mathbf{r}_{1},...\mathbf{r}_{N}), which we will abbreviate as

bosonic Jain’s states: Ψ~(e)≡Ψν=1⋅Ψν=n.\displaystyle\text{bosonic Jain's states: }\tilde{\Psi}^{(e)}\equiv\Psi_{\nu=1}\cdot\Psi_{\nu=n}. (29)

And similarly,

fermionic Jain’s states: Ψ~(e)≡Ψ2ν=1⋅Ψν=n.\displaystyle\text{fermionic Jain's states: }\tilde{\Psi}^{(e)}\equiv\Psi^{2}_{\nu=1}\cdot\Psi_{\nu=n}. (30)

When n→∞n\rightarrow\infty, the last parton species carries zero electric charge and sees no magnetic field. A natural choice for Ψν=n→∞=ΨF​L\Psi_{\nu=n\rightarrow\infty}=\Psi_{FL} is a Fermi liquid state with a circular fermi surface, leading to the composite Fermi liquid state for ν=1\nu=1 (ν=12\nu=\frac{1}{2}) for the bosonic (fermionic) case.

Note that Ψ~(e)\tilde{\Psi}^{(e)} is a product of Slater determinants. When n=1n=1, it recovers the Laughlin state successfully. A problem emerges when n>1n>1: the wavefunction Ψ~(e)\tilde{\Psi}^{(e)} is no longer inside the LLL. A wavefunction in the LLL should be holomorphic (up to the Gaussian factor), but the parton wavefunction Ψν=n>1\Psi_{\nu=n>1} contains antiholomorphic coordinates z¯i\bar{z}_{i}. This problem originates from the construction Eq.(28) at the very beginning, which explicitly relies on a real-space that goes outside the LLL. Physically, it is well known that a Chern band (e.g., LLL) cannot be Wannier-localized [125, 19, 107]. Inside the LLL, instead of the standard notation of real-space, the guiding center coordinates do not commute – leading to a noncommutative space[41, 97, 120].

If we view the gluing procedure from Eq.(28) as the first projection from the parton Hilbert spaces to the electron Hilbert space, to obtain a wavefunction inside the LLL for n>1n>1, it is crucial to perform a second projection: 𝒫L​L​L\mathcal{P}_{LLL}, which simply eliminates all components of an electron wavefunction outside the LLL:

Ψ(e)≡𝒫L​L​L​Ψ~(e).\displaystyle\Psi^{(e)}\equiv\mathcal{P}_{LLL}\tilde{\Psi}^{(e)}. (31)

Exactly what 𝒫L​L​L\mathcal{P}_{LLL} does to the many-body wavefunction has been a puzzle. On the numerical side, once 𝒫L​L​L\mathcal{P}_{LLL} is exactly implemented for n>1n>1 states, it is practically known that Ψ(e)\Psi^{(e)} becomes exponentially hard to compute, and no general analytical results are known. This difficulty prompted the development of an approximation scheme by Jain and Kamilla[67] in which Ψ(e)\Psi^{(e)} is approximated as a single determinant of a matrix whose elements are many-body wavefunctions, though whether this approximation is under control remains unclear.

On the conceptual side, it is not even clear whether 𝒫L​L​L\mathcal{P}_{LLL} changes the long-distance universal physics of the many-body state. Without 𝒫L​L​L\mathcal{P}_{LLL}, the topological field theory (Chern-Simons theory) in the standard commutative real-space describing the long-distance physics of Ψ~(e)\tilde{\Psi}^{(e)} can be obtained through a prescription developed by Wen and Zee[135]. However, in the presence of 𝒫L​L​L\mathcal{P}_{LLL}, it has been emphasized that noncommutative field theory needs to be used[121, 101, 57, 35, 31]. While significant progress has been made toward a noncommutative field-theoretic description of the bosonic Jain states[42], a similar description for the fermionic Jain states remains an open problem.

Ref.[62] pointed out that it is exactly 𝒫L​L​L\mathcal{P}_{LLL} that changes the product of determinant Ψ~(e)\tilde{\Psi}^{(e)} into a hyperdeterminant Ψ(e)\Psi^{(e)}. The fusion amplitude in Eq.(5) between partons and an electronic orbital |ψi(e)⟩|\psi_{i}^{(e)}\rangle inside the LLL, according to the real-space construction Eq.(28), is nothing but:

Ti​j​k​=el.boson\displaystyle T_{ijk}\underset{\text{el.}}{\overset{\text{boson}}{=}} ∫d​𝐫​⟨ψi(e)|𝐫(e)⟩​⟨𝐫(1)|ϕj(1)⟩​⟨𝐫(2)|ϕk(2)⟩,\displaystyle\int d\mathbf{r}\langle\psi^{(e)}_{i}|\mathbf{r}^{(e)}\rangle\langle\mathbf{r}^{(1)}|\phi^{(1)}_{j}\rangle\langle\mathbf{r}^{(2)}|\phi^{(2)}_{k}\rangle,
Ti​j​k​l​=el.fermi\displaystyle T_{ijkl}\underset{\text{el.}}{\overset{\text{fermi}}{=}} ∫d​𝐫​⟨ψi(e)|𝐫(e)⟩​⟨𝐫(1)|ϕj(1)⟩​⟨𝐫(2)|ϕk(2)⟩​⟨𝐫(3)|ϕl(3)⟩,\displaystyle\int d\mathbf{r}\langle\psi^{(e)}_{i}|\mathbf{r}^{(e)}\rangle\langle\mathbf{r}^{(1)}|\phi^{(1)}_{j}\rangle\langle\mathbf{r}^{(2)}|\phi^{(2)}_{k}\rangle\langle\mathbf{r}^{(3)}|\phi^{(3)}_{l}\rangle, (32)

which consequently defines the Hdet many-body wavefunction |Ψ(e)⟩|\Psi^{(e)}\rangle. In the present work, we will demonstrate the general analytical form for this fusion tensor TT, which will be shown useful even beyond the FQH context.

III.1.1 Showcase: bosonic electron with two-parton fusion rule

Here, we present the general fusion tensor for the real-space parton construction e∼f(1)​f(2)e\sim f^{(1)}f^{(2)} Eq.(28) in the following format. Assuming a filled single-particle state |ϕa​L​L(1)⟩|\phi^{(1)}_{aLL}\rangle for parton species-11 is in its aath-LL and a filled state |ϕb​L​L(2)⟩|\phi^{(2)}_{bLL}\rangle for parton species-22 is in its bbth-LL (a,b=0,1,2,…a,b=0,1,2,...) (both the parton fractional charges q(1),q(2)q^{(1)},q^{(2)} are nonzero and ∑pq(p)=1\sum_{p}q^{(p)}=1), then the fusion amplitude to an electron’s coherent state |z(e)⟩|z^{(e)}\rangle turns out to be:

⟨z(e)|∘​|ϕa​L​L(1)⟩|ϕb​L​L(2)⟩=(−1)a​[q(1)]b2​[q(2)]a+b2​Ca+ba​∑l=0a+b(−1)l​Ca+bl​(q(1)q(2))l2​⟨z(a+b−l)(1)|ϕa​L​L(1)⟩​⟨z(l)(2)|ϕb​L​L(2)⟩,\displaystyle\langle z^{(e)}|\mkern-1.0mu\mathord{\circ}\mkern-1.0mu|\phi^{(1)}_{aLL}\rangle|\phi^{(2)}_{bLL}\rangle=(-1)^{a}[q^{(1)}]^{\frac{b}{2}}[q^{(2)}]^{a+\frac{b}{2}}\sqrt{C^{a}_{a+b}}\sum_{l=0}^{a+b}(-1)^{l}\sqrt{C^{l}_{a+b}}\left(\frac{q^{(1)}}{q^{(2)}}\right)^{\frac{l}{2}}\langle z^{(1)}_{(a+b-l)}|\phi^{(1)}_{aLL}\rangle\langle z^{(2)}_{(l)}|\phi^{(2)}_{bLL}\rangle, (33)

where Cnl=n!(n−l)!​l!C^{l}_{n}=\frac{n!}{(n-l)!l!} is the binomial coefficient. Note that, by using the electron’s coherent state, the projection 𝒫L​L​L\mathcal{P}_{LLL} is already implemented. Also note that we allow both parton-11 and parton-22 to fill higher LLs. This is because, later, we will use these fusion amplitudes to describe states beyond the traditional FQH systems, e.g. those in FCI systems.

As a quick remark, there is a more symmetric and systematic way (e.g., easily generalizable to more parton species) to express the same fusion tensor in Eq.(33):

⟨z(e)|∘|ϕa​L​L(1)⟩|ϕb​L​L(2)⟩=∑k,l\displaystyle\langle z^{(e)}|\mkern-1.0mu\mathord{\circ}\mkern-1.0mu|\phi^{(1)}_{aLL}\rangle|\phi^{(2)}_{bLL}\rangle=\sum_{k,l} k!​l!a!​b!​(q(1))a−k2​(q(2))b−l2​Xk​l\displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{k!l!}{a!b!}}(q^{(1)})^{\frac{a-k}{2}}(q^{(2)})^{\frac{b-l}{2}}X_{kl}
⋅⟨z(k)(1)|ϕa​L​L(1)⟩​⟨z(l)(2)|ϕb​L​L(2)⟩,\displaystyle\cdot\langle z^{(1)}_{(k)}|\phi^{(1)}_{aLL}\rangle\langle z^{(2)}_{(l)}|\phi^{(2)}_{bLL}\rangle, (34)

where k,lk,l are nonnegative integers satisfying k+l=a+bk+l=a+b, and Xk​lX_{kl} is defined via the following binomial expansion:

∑k,lXk​l​Ak​Bl\displaystyle\sum_{k,l}X_{kl}A^{k}B^{l}
≡\displaystyle\equiv [(q(1)−1)​A+q(2)​B]a​[q(1)​A+(q(2)−1)​B]b.\displaystyle[(q^{(1)}-1)A+q^{(2)}B]^{a}[q^{(1)}A+(q^{(2)}-1)B]^{b}. (35)

On the RHS of Eq.(33), we have introduced the generalized coherent states in the nnth LL for partons: |z(m)⟩n​L​L|z_{(m)}\rangle_{nLL} (m,n=0,1,2​…m,n=0,1,2...). To explain its definition, we need to have a brief discussion on the well-known guiding-center and cyclotron degrees of freedom for a single charged particle moving in a uniform magnetic field. With the canonical momentum 𝚷=𝐩+q​𝐀\bm{\Pi}=\mathbf{p}+q\mathbf{A}, the cyclotron coordinate 𝜼\bm{\eta} and the guiding-center coordinate 𝐑\mathbf{R} are defined as:

𝜼≡\displaystyle\bm{\eta}\equiv l2ℏ​z^×𝚷,\displaystyle\frac{l^{2}}{\hbar}\hat{z}\times\bm{\Pi}, 𝐑≡\displaystyle\mathbf{R}\equiv 𝐫−𝜼,\displaystyle\mathbf{r}-\bm{\eta}, (36)

where ll is the magnetic length. 𝜼\bm{\eta} and 𝐑\mathbf{R} commute with each other, but

[η^x,η^y]=\displaystyle[\hat{\eta}_{x},\hat{\eta}_{y}]= i​l2,\displaystyle il^{2}, [R^x,R^y]=−i​l2.\displaystyle[\hat{R}_{x},\hat{R}_{y}]=-il^{2}. (37)

Namely, the single-particle Hilbert space can be decomposed as ℋ=ℋ𝐑⊗ℋ𝜼\mathcal{H}=\mathcal{H}_{\mathbf{R}}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{\bm{\eta}}. While 𝜼\bm{\eta} is the d.o.f. between different LLs, 𝐑\mathbf{R} is the d.o.f. within each LL. The commutation relation above allows one to construct the harmonic oscillator ladder operators:

a^𝐑≡\displaystyle\hat{a}_{\mathbf{R}}\equiv R^x−i​R^y2​l,\displaystyle\frac{\hat{R}_{x}-i\hat{R}_{y}}{\sqrt{2}l}, a^𝐑†=\displaystyle\hat{a}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{R}}= R^x+i​R^y2​l,\displaystyle\frac{\hat{R}_{x}+i\hat{R}_{y}}{\sqrt{2}l},
a^𝜼≡\displaystyle\hat{a}_{\bm{\eta}}\equiv η^x+i​η^y2​l,\displaystyle\frac{\hat{\eta}_{x}+i\hat{\eta}_{y}}{\sqrt{2}l}, a^𝜼†=\displaystyle\hat{a}^{\dagger}_{\bm{\eta}}= η^x−i​η^y2​l.\displaystyle\frac{\hat{\eta}_{x}-i\hat{\eta}_{y}}{\sqrt{2}l}. (38)

The magnetic translation along a vector (x,y)(x,y) only acts in the guiding-center subspace:

D^𝐑​(z≡x+i​y)≡exp⁡[il2​(−y​R^x+x​R^y)],\displaystyle\hat{D}_{\mathbf{R}}(z\equiv x+iy)\equiv\exp\Big[\frac{i}{l^{2}}(-y\hat{R}_{x}+x\hat{R}_{y})\Big], (39)

which satisfies the Girvin-MacDonald-Platzman (GMP) algebra[41]

D^𝐑​(α)​D^𝐑​(β)=exp⁡[α¯​β−α​β¯2​l2]​D^𝐑​(β)​D^𝐑​(α).\displaystyle\hat{D}_{\mathbf{R}}(\alpha)\hat{D}_{\mathbf{R}}(\beta)=\exp\Big[\frac{\bar{\alpha}\beta-\alpha\bar{\beta}}{2l^{2}}\Big]\hat{D}_{\mathbf{R}}(\beta)\hat{D}_{\mathbf{R}}(\alpha). (40)

The generalized coherent state |z(m)⟩n​L​L|z_{(m)}\rangle_{nLL} is defined as:

|z(m)⟩n​L​L≡(D^𝐑​(z)​|m⟩𝐑)⊗|n⟩𝜼\displaystyle|z_{(m)}\rangle_{nLL}\equiv\big(\hat{D}_{\mathbf{R}}(z)|m\rangle_{\mathbf{R}}\big)\otimes|n\rangle_{\bm{\eta}} (41)

where |0⟩𝐑|0\rangle_{\mathbf{R}} (|0⟩𝜼|0\rangle_{\bm{\eta}}) is the vacuum of the ladder operator a^𝐑\hat{a}_{\mathbf{R}} (a^𝜼\hat{a}_{\bm{\eta}}), and |m⟩𝐑≡a^𝐑†mm!​|0⟩𝐑|m\rangle_{\mathbf{R}}\equiv\frac{\hat{a}_{\mathbf{R}}^{\dagger m}}{\sqrt{m!}}|0\rangle_{\mathbf{R}} (|n⟩𝜼≡a^𝜼†nn!​|0⟩𝜼|n\rangle_{\bm{\eta}}\equiv\frac{\hat{a}_{\bm{\eta}}^{\dagger n}}{\sqrt{n!}}|0\rangle_{\bm{\eta}}).

The electron’s coherent state |z(e)⟩∈ℋ(e)|z^{(e)}\rangle\in\mathcal{H}^{(e)} in the LLL on the LHS of Eq.(33) is exactly the generalized coherent state when n=m=0n=m=0, with the electron’s magnetic length l=lel=l_{e}. The parton generalized coherent state |z(a+b−l)(1)⟩a​L​L∈ℋ(1)|z^{(1)}_{(a+b-l)}\rangle_{aLL}\in\mathcal{H}^{(1)} ( |z(l)(2)⟩b​L​L∈ℋ(2)|z^{(2)}_{(l)}\rangle_{bLL}\in\mathcal{H}^{(2)}) on the RHS of Eq.(33), is for m=(a+b−l),n=am=(a+b-l),n=a (m=l,n=bm=l,n=b) with the parton magnetic length l=l(1)l=l^{(1)} (l=l(2)l=l^{(2)}). Note that, to save notation, we neglect the subscripts aLL and bLL for the generalized coherent states in Eq.(33). And throughout this paper, the superscripts (1), (2) are reserved to denote the parton species.

Below, we work within the symmetric gauge. One can show that

|z(n)⟩n​L​L=(−1)n⋅𝒫n​L​L​|𝐫z⟩,\displaystyle|z_{(n)}\rangle_{nLL}=(-1)^{n}\cdot\mathcal{P}_{nLL}|\mathbf{r}_{z}\rangle, (42)

where 𝐫z=(Re​[z],Im​[z])\mathbf{r}_{z}=(\text{Re}[z],\text{Im}[z]), and |𝐫z⟩|\mathbf{r}_{z}\rangle’s wavefunction is 2​π​l⋅δ⁡(𝐫−𝐫z)\sqrt{2\pi}\;l\cdot\delta(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_{z}) (the normalization factor is chosen to simplify the expressions here). 𝒫n​L​L=|n⟩𝜼⋅𝜼⟨n|\mathcal{P}_{nLL}=|n\rangle_{\bm{\eta}}\cdot_{\bm{\eta}}\langle n| in this single-particle case.

The wavefunction of the generalized coherent state |z(m)⟩n​L​L|z_{(m)}\rangle_{nLL} can be written down, together with their overlaps within the same LL:

⟨𝐫ω|z(m)⟩n​L​L=\displaystyle\langle\mathbf{r}_{\omega}|z_{(m)}\rangle_{nLL}= (−1)n​m!n!​e−|ω|2+|z|2−2​z¯​ω4​l2​(z¯−ω¯2​l)n−m​Lm(n−m)​(|ω−z|22​l2), if ​n≥m,\displaystyle(-1)^{n}\sqrt{\frac{m!}{n!}}\,e^{-\frac{|\omega|^{2}+|z|^{2}-2\bar{z}\omega}{4l^{2}}}\left(\frac{\bar{z}-\bar{\omega}}{\sqrt{2}l}\right)^{n-m}L_{m}^{(n-m)}\left(\frac{|\omega-z|^{2}}{2l^{2}}\right),\text{ if }n\geq m,
⟨𝐫ω|z(m)⟩n​L​L=\displaystyle\langle\mathbf{r}_{\omega}|z_{(m)}\rangle_{nLL}= (−1)n​n!m!​e−|ω|2+|z|2−2​z¯​ω4​l2​(ω−z2​l)m−n​Ln(m−n)​(|ω−z|22​l2), if ​m≥n,\displaystyle(-1)^{n}\sqrt{\frac{n!}{m!}}\,e^{-\frac{|\omega|^{2}+|z|^{2}-2\bar{z}\omega}{4l^{2}}}\left(\frac{\omega-z}{\sqrt{2}l}\right)^{m-n}L_{n}^{(m-n)}\left(\frac{|\omega-z|^{2}}{2l^{2}}\right),\text{ if }m\geq n,
⟨ω(n)|z(m)⟩a​L​L=\displaystyle\langle\omega_{(n)}|z_{(m)}\rangle_{aLL}= m!n!​e−|ω|2+|z|2−2​z¯​ω4​l2​(z¯−ω¯2​l)n−m​Lm(n−m)​(|ω−z|22​l2), if ​n≥m,\displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{m!}{n!}}\,e^{-\frac{|\omega|^{2}+|z|^{2}-2\bar{z}\omega}{4l^{2}}}\left(\frac{\bar{z}-\bar{\omega}}{\sqrt{2}l}\right)^{n-m}L_{m}^{(n-m)}\left(\frac{|\omega-z|^{2}}{2l^{2}}\right),\text{ if }n\geq m,
⟨ω(n)|z(m)⟩a​L​L=\displaystyle\langle\omega_{(n)}|z_{(m)}\rangle_{aLL}= n!m!​e−|ω|2+|z|2−2​z¯​ω4​l2​(ω−z2​l)m−n​Ln(m−n)​(|ω−z|22​l2), if ​m≥n,\displaystyle\sqrt{\frac{n!}{m!}}\,e^{-\frac{|\omega|^{2}+|z|^{2}-2\bar{z}\omega}{4l^{2}}}\left(\frac{\omega-z}{\sqrt{2}l}\right)^{m-n}L_{n}^{(m-n)}\left(\frac{|\omega-z|^{2}}{2l^{2}}\right),\text{ if }m\geq n,

where Lnα​(x)=x−α​exn!​dnd​xn​(xn+α​e−x)L^{\alpha}_{n}(x)=\frac{x^{-\alpha}e^{x}}{n!}\frac{d^{n}}{dx^{n}}(x^{n+\alpha}e^{-x}) is the generalized Laguerre polynomials. Despite the similarity between the expressions of the wavefunctions and overlaps, conceptually they are very different objects: the nn-index in the wavefunctions labels the LL, while the nn-index in the overlaps labels the generalized coherent state in the bra. The crucial points are: (1) these wavefunctions are exponentially localized at zz by the magnetic length ll. (2) |z(m)⟩n​L​L|z_{(m)}\rangle_{nLL} carries zz-centered magnetic rotation angular momentum L=m−nL=m-n.

With these results, we can have a physical interpretation for the fusion amplitude Eq.(33). To be concrete, we list a few special cases: a=b=0a=b=0, a=0,b=1a=0,b=1 and a=b=1a=b=1.

⟨z(e)|∘​|ϕ0​L​L(1)⟩|ϕ0​L​L(2)⟩=Ξ0000,\displaystyle\langle z^{(e)}|\mkern-1.0mu\mathord{\circ}\mkern-1.0mu|\phi^{(1)}_{0LL}\rangle|\phi^{(2)}_{0LL}\rangle=\Xi^{00}_{00},
⟨z(e)|∘​|ϕ0​L​L(1)⟩|ϕ1​L​L(2)⟩=[q(1)​q(2)]12​Ξ1001−q(1)​Ξ0101,\displaystyle\langle z^{(e)}|\mkern-1.0mu\mathord{\circ}\mkern-1.0mu|\phi^{(1)}_{0LL}\rangle|\phi^{(2)}_{1LL}\rangle=[q^{(1)}q^{(2)}]^{\frac{1}{2}}\Xi^{01}_{10}-q^{(1)}\Xi^{01}_{01},
⟨z(e)|∘​|ϕ1​L​L(1)⟩|ϕ1​L​L(2)⟩=−2​[q(1)]12​[q(2)]32​Ξ2011\displaystyle\langle z^{(e)}|\mkern-1.0mu\mathord{\circ}\mkern-1.0mu|\phi^{(1)}_{1LL}\rangle|\phi^{(2)}_{1LL}\rangle=-\sqrt{2}\,[q^{(1)}]^{\frac{1}{2}}[q^{(2)}]^{\frac{3}{2}}\Xi^{11}_{20}
+2​q(1)​q(2)​Ξ1111−2​[q(1)]32​[q(2)]12​Ξ0211,\displaystyle+2q^{(1)}q^{(2)}\Xi^{11}_{11}-\sqrt{2}[q^{(1)}]^{\frac{3}{2}}[q^{(2)}]^{\frac{1}{2}}\Xi^{11}_{02}, (44)

where we defined a shorthand notation:

Ξk​la​b≡⟨z(k)(1)|ϕa​L​L(1)⟩​⟨z(l)(2)|ϕb​L​L(2)⟩.\displaystyle\Xi^{ab}_{kl}\equiv\langle z^{(1)}_{(k)}|\phi^{(1)}_{aLL}\rangle\langle z^{(2)}_{(l)}|\phi^{(2)}_{bLL}\rangle. (45)

Note that the parton states |ϕ(1)⟩|\phi^{(1)}\rangle and |ϕ(2)⟩|\phi^{(2)}\rangle can be any orbitals in their LLs. If one replaces |ϕ(1)⟩→|ϕj(1)⟩|\phi^{(1)}\rangle\rightarrow|\phi_{j}^{(1)}\rangle and |ϕ(2)⟩→|ϕk(2)⟩|\phi^{(2)}\rangle\rightarrow|\phi_{k}^{(2)}\rangle, these expressions in Eq.(44) are exactly the CPD structure Eq.(27) of the fusion tensor! Note that, although the analytical result Eq.(33) is obtained using the disk geometry, because the generalized coherent states are exponentially localized, on a finite-size system (e.g., finite-size torus), this fusion tensor is exponentially accurate when the system size is much larger than the involved parton magnetic lengths.

In the simplest case, a=b=0a=b=0, there is only one fusion channel (i.e., CPD-rank =1=1). But when the parton fills higher LLs, the number of fusion channels increases. Generally, the number of fusion channels:

Ra​b=a+b+1.\displaystyle R_{ab}=a+b+1. (46)

For instance, for the ν=23\nu=\frac{2}{3} Jain’s state, parton-11 has q(1)=23q^{(1)}=\frac{2}{3}, filling the LLL. Parton-22 has q(2)=13q^{(2)}=\frac{1}{3}, filling both the LLL and the 1st LL. The results here show that, after choosing the electron’s coherent state basis, there will be one fusion channel involving parton-22 in the LLL, and two fusion channels involving parton-22 in the 1st LL, so a total of three fusion channels (i.e., CPD-rank is three).

One may ask the opposite question: which electron basis should one choose so that the number of fusion channels is minimal (i.e., CPD-rank optimal)? Although we do not have analytical proof at this point, our numerical simulation shows that the CPD-rank-optimal basis for electrons is indeed the coherent-state basis for FQH composite fermion states. For example, for ν=23\nu=\frac{2}{3} Jain’s state, the fusion tensor for an electron’s complete basis (e.g., the Bloch basis in the LLL) Ti​j​kT_{ijk} can be easily computed on a torus, where i=1,2,…​32​Nei=1,2,...\frac{3}{2}N_{e}, j,k=1,2,…,Nej,k=1,2,...,N_{e}. Then one can numerically compute the fusion tensor (a square matrix) Tj​k​(i~)T_{jk}(\tilde{i}) for an arbitrary state |ψi~(e)⟩∈H(e)|\psi_{\tilde{i}}^{(e)}\rangle\in H^{(e)} according to the bases-independence theorem. We find that numerically minimizing the CPD-rank (i.e., SVD-rank in the present case) of Tj​k​(i~)T_{jk}(\tilde{i}) always leads to a coherent state |ψi~(e)⟩∝|z(e)⟩|\psi_{\tilde{i}}^{(e)}\rangle\propto|z^{(e)}\rangle at some position zz.

Suppose we interpret the overlaps on the RHS as the parton propagation in Eq.(33), clearly, a parton always needs to propagate to parton orbitals localized near the electron’s position in order to fuse into an electron, which we will call the locality structure for the fusion tensor Eq.(33). Motivated by this, we will soon define the locality structure for general fusion tensors.

Next, let’s further understand the physical meaning of the locality structure here. If a=b=0a=b=0, both partons propagate to the most localized state at the electron’s position zz: the coherent state |z(0)(p)⟩|z_{(0)}^{(p)}\rangle for parton species-pp in their LLL. If partons fill higher LLs, the generalized coherent state |z(m)(p)⟩n​L​L|z_{(m)}^{(p)}\rangle_{nLL} appears in their fusion rule. Pictorially, the orbital |z(m)(p)⟩n​L​L|z_{(m)}^{(p)}\rangle_{nLL} is most localized in nnth LL if m=0m=0, and more extended as mm increases. Physically, one may interpret it as a parton propagating to guiding-center orbitals in the vicinity of zz. The generalized coherent state |z(m)(p)⟩n​L​L|z_{(m)}^{(p)}\rangle_{nLL} is nothing but the angular-momentum expansion of such guiding-center orbitals.

Before proceeding, to save notation, we introduce the abbreviation for the generalized coherent states |z(m)(p)⟩n​L​L|z^{(p)}_{(m)}\rangle_{nLL}:

|z;𝐦(p)⟩≡|z(m)(p)⟩n​L​L.\displaystyle|z;\mathbf{m}^{(p)}\rangle\equiv|z^{(p)}_{(m)}\rangle_{nLL}. (47)

Namely, the bold-font 𝐦\bf m can be viewed as the combination of the indices (m) and nLL.

In fact, one can obtain both the form and coefficients (up to an overall factor) in the CPD structure Eq.(33) based on the locality structure and the Galilean invariance, without resorting to sophisticated calculations.

To see this, it is convenient to introduce another viewpoint on the locality structure – the local-fusion operator. The fusion tensor in Eq.(33), (after adding subscripts for partons) Tz​j​kT_{zjk} has a locality structure, which can be written as:

⟨z(e)|∘|ϕj(1)⟩|ϕk(2)⟩=∑α=1Rλα⟨z;𝐦α(1)|ϕj(1)⟩⟨z;𝐦α(2)|ϕk(2)⟩,\displaystyle\langle z^{(e)}|\mkern-1.0mu\mathord{\circ}\mkern-1.0mu|\phi^{(1)}_{j}\rangle|\phi^{(2)}_{k}\rangle=\sum_{\alpha=1}^{R}\lambda_{\alpha}\langle z;\mathbf{m}_{\alpha}^{(1)}|\phi^{(1)}_{j}\rangle\langle z;\mathbf{m}_{\alpha}^{(2)}|\phi^{(2)}_{k}\rangle, (48)

where |z;𝐦α(p)⟩|z;\mathbf{m}_{\alpha}^{(p)}\rangle are the generalized coherent states participating in the fusion tensor Eq.(33) for the fusion-channel α\alpha, and λα\lambda_{\alpha} are the rather complicated coefficients involving Ca+bk\sqrt{C_{a+b}^{k}}. In principle, the fusion-amplitude λα=λα​(z)\lambda_{\alpha}=\lambda_{\alpha}(z) may depend on zz, but at least in this showcase example, it is not after a proper gauge for the parton and electron states is chosen. We then define a local-fusion operator:

F^z≡|z(e)⟩⋅[∑α=1Rλα⟨z;𝐦α(1)|⟨z;𝐦α(2)|]\displaystyle\hat{F}_{z}\equiv|z^{(e)}\rangle\cdot\Big[\sum_{\alpha=1}^{R}\lambda_{\alpha}\langle z;\mathbf{m}_{\alpha}^{(1)}|\langle z;\mathbf{m}_{\alpha}^{(2)}|\Big] (49)

and define the integer RR as the number of local fusion channels. Note that F^z\hat{F}_{z} is an operator mapping a quantum state in the parton Hilbert space ℋ(1)⊗ℋ(2)\mathcal{H}^{(1)}\otimes\mathcal{H}^{(2)} to a quantum state in the electron’s single-particle Hilbert space ℋ(e)\mathcal{H}^{(e)}. (to avoid confusion with the bold-font many-body fusion operator 𝐅^\hat{\mathbf{F}} in Eq.(14) acting in the Fock spaces, we use regular font F^z\hat{F}_{z} here.) The fusion tensor can also be compactly expressed as:

⟨z(e)|∘​|ϕj(1)⟩|ϕk(2)⟩=⟨z(e)|F^z​|ϕj(1)⟩|ϕk(2)⟩.\displaystyle\langle z^{(e)}|\mkern-1.0mu\mathord{\circ}\mkern-1.0mu|\phi^{(1)}_{j}\rangle|\phi^{(2)}_{k}\rangle=\langle z^{(e)}|\hat{F}_{z}|\phi^{(1)}_{j}\rangle|\phi^{(2)}_{k}\rangle. (50)

Namely, F^z\hat{F}_{z} fully specifies how the partons are glued into the electron coherent state |z(e)⟩|z^{(e)}\rangle.

From this viewpoint, one may think of the state in the parton Hilbert space: [∑α=1Rλα∗|z;𝐦α(1)⟩|z;𝐦α(2)⟩]\Big[\sum_{\alpha=1}^{R}\lambda^{*}_{\alpha}|z;\mathbf{m}^{(1)}_{\alpha}\rangle|z;\mathbf{m}^{(2)}_{\alpha}\rangle\Big] as the ”parton-image-state” of the electron local orbital |z(e)⟩|z^{(e)}\rangle. If there is only one fusion channel, then the parton-image-state is a product state formed by different parton species. When the number of fusion channels increases, it indicates that the parton-image-state is an entangled quantum state between different parton species. The CPD-rank can be viewed as a measure for the entanglement between the parton species. Precisely, for the current two-parton fusion, the CPD-rank (i.e. SVD-rank) is directly related to the well-known 0th-order Renyi entanglement entropy: S0=log⁡(SVD-rank)S_{0}=\log(\text{SVD-rank}). For more-parton fusion, the CPD-rank is associated with the so-called Schmidt measure in the context of quantum information theory[33].

Now we show that the local fusion operator F^z\hat{F}_{z} for the fusion tensor Eq.(33) can be obtained via the Galilean invariance. First, the combination of ⟨z(a+b−l)(1)|a​L​L{}_{aLL}\langle z^{(1)}_{(a+b-l)}| and ⟨z(l)(2)|b​L​L{}_{bLL}\langle z^{(2)}_{(l)}| for the generalized coherent states on the RHS is simply a consequence of the zz-centered angular momentum conservation: the first orbital carries L(1)=b−lL^{(1)}=b-l, and the second orbital carries L(2)=l−bL^{(2)}=l-b. Their summation must be zero because the electron coherent state carries L(e)=0L^{(e)}=0.

Second, the coefficients λα\lambda_{\alpha} can also be obtained (up to an overall factor). The electron’s wavefunction in the LLL must be a holomorphic function (up to Gaussian factors), and cannot depend on z¯\bar{z}. Using the identity for the overlap between two generalized coherent states (special case of Eq.()):

⟨z(m)|ω(0)⟩n​L​L=1m!​(ω¯−z¯2​l)m​e−|ω|2+|z|24​l2+z​ω¯2​l2,\displaystyle\langle z_{(m)}|\omega_{(0)}\rangle_{nLL}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{m!}}\Big(\frac{\bar{\omega}-\bar{z}}{\sqrt{2}l}\Big)^{m}e^{-\frac{|\omega|^{2}+|z|^{2}}{4l^{2}}+\frac{z\bar{\omega}}{2l^{2}}}, (51)

we know that, if one plugs in |ϕa​L​L(1)⟩→|ω(0)(1)⟩a​L​L|\phi^{(1)}_{aLL}\rangle\rightarrow|\omega_{(0)}^{(1)}\rangle_{aLL}, |ϕb​L​L(2)⟩→|ζ(0)(2)⟩b​L​L|\phi^{(2)}_{bLL}\rangle\rightarrow|\zeta_{(0)}^{(2)}\rangle_{bLL}, the RHS of Eq.(33) becomes a multinomial of z¯,ω¯,ζ¯\bar{z},\bar{\omega},\bar{\zeta} together with Gaussian factors. Each term of the multinomial is ∝(ω¯−z¯)a+b−l​(ζ¯−z¯)l\propto(\bar{\omega}-\bar{z})^{a+b-l}(\bar{\zeta}-\bar{z})^{l}. The binomial coefficients in λα\lambda_{\alpha} are exactly such that the z¯\bar{z}-dependence all cancels out so that the multinomial ∝[(ω¯−z¯)−(ζ¯−z¯)]a+b=(ω¯−ζ¯)a+b\propto[(\bar{\omega}-\bar{z})-(\bar{\zeta}-\bar{z})]^{a+b}=(\bar{\omega}-\bar{\zeta})^{a+b}. In addition, it is easy to show that there is only one solution of λα\lambda_{\alpha} (up to an overall factor) such that the z¯\bar{z}-dependence in Eq.(33) cancels out.

We have shown that the number of local fusion channels increases as the partons fill higher LLs. Precisely, in the ν=nn+1\nu=\frac{n}{n+1} bosonic Jain’s sequence, the number of local fusion channels is 1+2+…+n=n⁡(n+1)21+2+...+n=\frac{n(n+1)}{2} (even in the thermodynamic limit). What would happen for the bosonic ν=1\nu=1 composite Fermi liquid corresponding to n→∞n\rightarrow\infty? The number of local fusion channels would go to infinity in the thermodynamic limit for sure. On the other hand, for any finite-size system, the number of local fusion channels should be finite based on physical intuition. How does the number of local fusion channels depend on the system size for ν=1\nu=1?

Here, we list the two-parton fusion tensor for the case q(1)=1q^{(1)}=1 and q(2)=0q^{(2)}=0, as in the case of bosonic ν=1\nu=1 composite Fermi liquid:

⟨z(e)|∘​|ϕa​L​L(1)⟩|ϕ(2)⟩=∫d​α2​π​le2​∫d​β​Cα​βa​L​L​(z)⋅⟨(z+α)(0)(1)|ϕa​L​L(1)⟩​⟨(z+β)(2)|ϕ(2)⟩,\displaystyle\langle z^{(e)}|\mkern-1.0mu\mathord{\circ}\mkern-1.0mu|\phi^{(1)}_{aLL}\rangle|\phi^{(2)}\rangle=\int\frac{d\alpha}{2\pi l_{e}^{2}}\int d\beta\;C^{aLL}_{\alpha\beta}(z)\cdot\langle(z+\alpha)^{(1)}_{(0)}|\phi^{(1)}_{aLL}\rangle\langle(z+\beta)^{(2)}|\phi^{(2)}\rangle,
where ​Cα​βa​L​L​(z)≡12​π​le2​⟨z(e)|(z+β)(e)⟩​⟨𝐫(z+β)(1)|(z+α)(0)(1)⟩a​L​L=12​π​le2​e−|β|24​le2⋅⟨β(0)(1)|α(0)(1)⟩a​L​L⋅eα¯​z−z¯​α4​le2\displaystyle\text{where }C^{aLL}_{\alpha\beta}(z)\equiv\frac{1}{2\pi l_{e}^{2}}\langle z^{(e)}|(z+\beta)^{(e)}\rangle\langle\mathbf{r}^{(1)}_{(z+\beta)}|(z+\alpha)^{(1)}_{(0)}\rangle_{aLL}=\frac{1}{2\pi l_{e}^{2}}e^{-\frac{|\beta|^{2}}{4l_{e}^{2}}}\cdot\langle\beta_{(0)}^{(1)}|\alpha^{(1)}_{(0)}\rangle_{aLL}\cdot e^{\frac{\bar{\alpha}z-\bar{z}\alpha}{4l_{e}^{2}}} (52)

A few remarks are in order. First, this result, obtained using the disk geometry, expresses the fusion rule as an integral over complex coordinates α\alpha and β\beta, describing local parton orbitals’ spatial deviations from the electron’s position. The crucial point for the local fusion tensor Cα​βa​L​L​(z)C^{aLL}_{\alpha\beta}(z) is that it exponentially decays as either α\alpha or β\beta is much larger than the electron’s magnetic length. Therefore, this fusion tensor still has the locality structure. Second, for parton-11, we use the coherent state |(z+α)(0)⟩a​L​L|(z+\alpha)_{(0)}\rangle_{aLL} to describe the local parton orbital. For parton-22, however, since it does not see a magnetic field, we use the real-space δ\delta-wavefunction: δ⁡(𝐫−(z+β))\delta(\mathbf{r}-(z+\beta)), i.e., |(z+β)(2)⟩|(z+\beta)^{(2)}\rangle to describe its local parton orbital. Finally, we allow parton-11 to fill its higher LL. This is because, later, we will use this fusion tensor to describe states beyond traditional FQH systems, e.g., in FCI systems.

Although it appears that one needs to perform a continuous integral over α,β\alpha,\beta, it turns out that, on a finite-size torus, the integral can be replaced by a double summation over discrete lattices (see Sec.III.2.1 for α\alpha-lattice. For β\beta-lattice of the charge neutral parton-22, the simplest way to see this is to consider a related construction in which β\beta d.o.f. is obtained by the tensor-product of the electron’s and parton-11’s cyclotron d.o.f., as shown in Ref.[62]). Up to the exponential tail, one needs ∼Ns(e)\sim N_{s}^{(e)} (the number of flux quanta through the sample) lattice points for α\alpha and also ∼Ns(e)\sim N_{s}^{(e)} lattice points for β\beta. As a matrix, the local fusion tensor Cα​βa​L​L​(z)C^{aLL}_{\alpha\beta}(z)’s size is ∼Ns(e)×Ns(e)\sim N_{s}^{(e)}\times N_{s}^{(e)}. After bringing this matrix to the diagonal form as in the local fusion operator Eq.(49), one finds that, on a finite size system, up to the exponential tail, the local fusion tensor CC in Eq.(52) has ∼Ns(e)\sim N_{s}^{(e)} local fusion channels.

The fact that the number of fusion channels RR scales as a power law with the system size indicates that partons are highly entangled in the CFL state within the LLL. (On the other hand, if one constructs a CFL state in a lattice model outside a Chern band, RR could be a finite value even in the thermodynamic limit.)

III.1.2 Showcase: fermionic electron with three-parton fusion rule

Here, we briefly present the general fusion tensor for the real-space parton construction e∼f(1)​f(2)​f(3)e\sim f^{(1)}f^{(2)}f^{(3)} Eq.(28) in the same format as the previous section.

Assuming we have filled single-particle states |ϕa​L​L(1)⟩,|ϕb​L​L(2)⟩,|ϕc​L​L(3)⟩|\phi^{(1)}_{aLL}\rangle,|\phi^{(2)}_{bLL}\rangle,|\phi^{(3)}_{cLL}\rangle for parton species-1,2,31,2,3 respectively (the parton fractional charges q(1),q(2),q(3)q^{(1)},q^{(2)},q^{(3)} are all nonzero and ∑pq(p)=1\sum_{p}q^{(p)}=1), from direct calculation, the fusion amplitude to an electron’s coherent state |z(e)⟩|z^{(e)}\rangle turns out to be:

⟨z(e)|∘​|ϕa​L​L(1)⟩​|ϕb​L​L(2)⟩|ϕc​L​L(3)⟩\displaystyle\langle z^{(e)}|\mkern-1.0mu\mathord{\circ}\mkern-1.0mu|\phi^{(1)}_{aLL}\rangle|\phi^{(2)}_{bLL}\rangle|\phi^{(3)}_{cLL}\rangle
=\displaystyle= ∑k,l,mk!​l!​m!a!​b!​c!​(q(1))a−k2​(q(2))b−l2​(q(3))c−m2⋅Xk​l​m\displaystyle\sum_{k,l,m}\sqrt{\frac{k!l!m!}{a!b!c!}}(q^{(1)})^{\frac{a-k}{2}}(q^{(2)})^{\frac{b-l}{2}}(q^{(3)})^{\frac{c-m}{2}}\cdot X_{klm}

where k,l,mk,l,m are non-negative integers satisfying k+l+m=a+b+ck+l+m=a+b+c, and Xk​l​mX_{klm} is the following multinomial coefficient:

∑k​l​mXk​l​m​Ak​Bl​Cm≡[(q(1)−1)​A+q(2)​B+q(3)​C]a⋅[q(1)​A+(q(2)−1)​B+q(3)​C]b⋅[q(1)​A+q(2)​B+(q(3)−1)​C]c.\displaystyle\sum_{klm}X_{klm}A^{k}B^{l}C^{m}\equiv[(q^{(1)}-1)A+q^{(2)}B+q^{(3)}C]^{a}\cdot[q^{(1)}A+(q^{(2)}-1)B+q^{(3)}C]^{b}\cdot[q^{(1)}A+q^{(2)}B+(q^{(3)}-1)C]^{c}. (54)

As concrete examples:

⟨z(e)|∘​|ϕ0​L​L(1)⟩​|ϕ0​L​L(2)⟩|ϕ0​L​L(3)⟩=Ξ000000,\displaystyle\quad\langle z^{(e)}|\mkern-1.0mu\mathord{\circ}\mkern-1.0mu|\phi^{(1)}_{0LL}\rangle|\phi^{(2)}_{0LL}\rangle|\phi^{(3)}_{0LL}\rangle=\Xi^{000}_{000},

=[q(1)​q(3)]12​Ξ100001+[q(2)​q(3)]12​Ξ010001−(q(1)+q(2))​Ξ001001,\displaystyle=[q^{(1)}q^{(3)}]^{\frac{1}{2}}\Xi^{001}_{100}+[q^{(2)}q^{(3)}]^{\frac{1}{2}}\,\Xi^{001}_{010}-(q^{(1)}+q^{(2)})\Xi^{001}_{001},

where we defined:

Ra​b​c=Ca+b+c+22=(a+b+c+1)​(a+b+c+2)2.\displaystyle R_{abc}=C^{2}_{a+b+c+2}=\frac{(a+b+c+1)(a+b+c+2)}{2}. (57)

⟨z(e)|∘​|ϕj(1)⟩​|ϕk(2)⟩|ϕl(3)⟩=\displaystyle\langle z^{(e)}|\mkern-1.0mu\mathord{\circ}\mkern-1.0mu|\phi^{(1)}_{j}\rangle|\phi^{(2)}_{k}\rangle|\phi^{(3)}_{l}\rangle=
=\displaystyle= ∑α=1Rλα⟨z;𝐦α(1)|ϕj(1)⟩⟨z;𝐦α(2)|ϕk(2)⟩⟨z;𝐦α(3)|ϕl(3)⟩,\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha=1}^{R}\lambda_{\alpha}\langle z;\mathbf{m}^{(1)}_{\alpha}|\phi^{(1)}_{j}\rangle\langle z;\mathbf{m}^{(2)}_{\alpha}|\phi^{(2)}_{k}\rangle\langle z;\mathbf{m}_{\alpha}^{(3)}|\phi^{(3)}_{l}\rangle, (58)

where |z;𝐦α(p)⟩|z;\mathbf{m}_{\alpha}^{(p)}\rangle are the generalized coherent states participating in the fusion tensor Eq.(53). The corresponding local-fusion operator is:

F^z≡|z(e)⟩⋅[∑α=1Rλα⟨z;𝐦α(1)|⟨z;𝐦α(2)|⟨z;𝐦α(3)|]\displaystyle\hat{F}_{z}\equiv|z^{(e)}\rangle\cdot\Big[\sum_{\alpha=1}^{R}\lambda_{\alpha}\langle z;\mathbf{m}^{(1)}_{\alpha}|\langle z;\mathbf{m}^{(2)}_{\alpha}|\langle z;\mathbf{m}^{(3)}_{\alpha}|\Big] (59)

where ​Cα​β​γa,b​(z)≡12​π​le2​⟨z(e)|(z+γ)(e)⟩​⟨𝐫(z+γ)(1)|(z+α)(0)(1)⟩a​L​L​⟨𝐫(z+γ)(2)|(z+β)(0)(2)⟩b​L​L\displaystyle\text{where }C^{a,b}_{\alpha\beta\gamma}(z)\equiv\frac{1}{2\pi l_{e}^{2}}\langle z^{(e)}|(z+\gamma)^{(e)}\rangle\langle\mathbf{r}^{(1)}_{(z+\gamma)}|(z+\alpha)^{(1)}_{(0)}\rangle_{aLL}\langle\mathbf{r}^{(2)}_{(z+\gamma)}|(z+\beta)^{(2)}_{(0)}\rangle_{bLL} (60)

Again, the fusion amplitude above admits the locality structure: local fusion tensor Cα​β​γa,b​(z)C^{a,b}_{\alpha\beta\gamma}(z) is exponentially suppressed when either α,β,γ\alpha,\beta,\gamma is larger than the magnetic length. The apparent integral of α,β,γ\alpha,\beta,\gamma over the length scale ∼le\sim l_{e} can be replaced by a finite summation over discrete lattices (each variable ∼Ns(e)\sim N_{s}^{(e)}), up to exponentially small tails.

III.2 The locality-structure of the fusion tensor

Here, we will present the definition for the locality-structure for the fusion tensor of a general Hdet wavefunction. Before that, we need to examine further the locality structure in the FQH showcase examples presented in the previous section to motivate the definition.

III.2.1 Overcomplete discrete-coherent-state basis within a Chern band

We first comment on the electronic coherent state |z(e)⟩|z^{(e)}\rangle participating in the local fusion tensors Eq.(48,58).

Very often, the electron coherent state basis {|z(e)⟩}\{|z^{(e)}\rangle\} is discussed as if zz is treated as a continuous variable. For instance, the usual many-body wavefunction of a FQH state indeed can be viewed as the overlap between the electron state with the continuous-coherent-state many-body basis: Ψ(e)(z1,z2,…,zNe)=⟨z1(e),z2(e),…,zNe(e)|Ψ(e)⟩\Psi^{(e)}(z_{1},z_{2},...,z_{N_{e}})=\langle z^{(e)}_{1},z^{(e)}_{2},...,z^{(e)}_{N_{e}}|\Psi^{(e)}\rangle. However, in a finite-size system, it is physically unnecessary to introduce an infinite number of orbitals to capture the many-body state. Instead, one should be able to limit zz on a lattice, which we call a Fine-Grid, so that the corresponding discrete-coherent-states {|z(e)⟩,z∈Fine-Grid}\{|z^{(e)}\rangle,z\in\text{Fine-Grid}\} are still enough to form a good basis (with resolution of identity, etc). In fact, a recent work[129] has exactly demonstrated that one only needs the Fine-Grid on a finite torus whose size is Ns(e)×Ns(e)N_{s}^{(e)}\times N_{s}^{(e)}. Namely, this Fine-Grid is generated by the minimally allowed magnetic translations 𝐚1FG,𝐚2FG\mathbf{a}_{1}^{\rm FG},\mathbf{a}_{2}^{\rm FG} along the two periodic directions on the finite torus. (See Fig.3 for an illustration of the Fine-Grid.) It is easy to show that, by the fact that the magnetic translations form a complete algebra, the discrete coherent states on the Fine-Grid feature the resolution of the identity:

∑z∈Fine-Grid|z(e)⟩​⟨z(e)|=Ns(e)⋅𝟏.\displaystyle\sum_{z\in\text{Fine-Grid}}|z^{(e)}\rangle\langle z^{(e)}|=N_{s}^{(e)}\cdot\mathbf{1}. (61)

We will denote {|z(e)⟩,z∈Fine-Grid}\{|z^{(e)}\rangle,z\in\text{Fine-Grid}\} as the discrete-coherent-state basis for the electrons in the LLL.

Note that this basis formed by (Ns(e))2(N_{s}^{(e)})^{2} states is overcomplete, since the dimension of the electron single-particle Hilbert space is only dim​ℋ(e)=Ns(e)\text{dim}\mathcal{H}^{(e)}=N_{s}^{(e)}. The overcompleteness is intrinsically related to the fact that we are working within the electron’s LLL in the showcase examples, which is a Chern band. On the one hand, a Chern band cannot be Wannier-localized[125, 19, 107]. Namely, there is no localized and orthonormal basis in the LLL. On the other hand, to expose the locality-structure of Hdet wavefunctions, we want to work with a set of localized electronic orbitals, even if they are overcomplete.

In general, one may start with a lattice tight-binding model and identify an isolated Chern band whose Chern number CC may or may not be ±1\pm 1 (e.g., C=±2C=\pm 2). Partially filling this Chern band may lead to FCI states that can be captured by Hdet wavefunctions. In this case, one can still work explicitly within the Chern band to discuss the locality-structure of the fusion tensor. To this end, one also needs to introduce the corresponding electronic discrete-coherent-state basis in this Chern band, which we require to be exponentially localized, overcomplete, and feature the standard resolution of the identity. Here, one straightforward prescription to generate the discrete-coherent-state basis is simply to project the original real-space orbitals in the tight-binding model into the Chern band. For instance, let’s say there are no​r​bn_{orb} electronic orbitals per real-space unit cell, denoted by {|𝐫u​c,i⟩}\{|\mathbf{r}_{uc},i\rangle\}, where 𝐫u​c\mathbf{r}_{uc} is the discrete unit-cell real-space position and i=1,2,…,no​r​bi=1,2,...,n_{orb} labels the orbital within the unit-cell. One natural definition of a discrete-coherent-state basis is {𝒫C​B|𝐫u​c,i⟩}\{\mathcal{P}_{CB}|\mathbf{r}_{uc},i\rangle\}, where 𝒫C​B\mathcal{P}_{CB} is the single-particle projection into the Chern band.

In summary, whenever we work within a Chern band, to expose the locality-structure for the fusion tensor, we will give up the orthonormal basis and proceed with the overcomplete discrete-coherent-state basis. If one works within a topologically trivial band, or one works within a complete tight-binding model, however, one could simply use the orthonormal Wannier basis to discuss the locality-structure for the fusion tensor.

III.2.2 A change of viewpoint for |z;𝐦(p)⟩|z;\mathbf{m}^{(p)}\rangle and |z(e)⟩|z^{(e)}\rangle

In the showcase examples, we already see that a parton-pp will always propagate to a parton orbital, some generalized coherent state |z;𝐦(p)⟩|z;\mathbf{m}^{(p)}\rangle at the electron’s position zz, to fuse into the electron.
