For fusion-channel α\alpha, this propagation is captured by the overlap ⟨z;𝐦α(p)|ϕ(p)⟩\langle z;\mathbf{m}_{\alpha}^{(p)}|\phi^{(p)}\rangle in Eq.(48,58).

These generalized coherent states are also not orthonormal. If we follow the original interpretation of ⟨z;𝐦(p)|ϕ(p)⟩\langle z;\mathbf{m}^{(p)}|\phi^{(p)}\rangle, these non-orthogonal properties of the orbitals may lead to extra (unnecessary) complications in interpreting the Hdet wavefunctions.

Here, we introduce a new viewpoint for the overlap ⟨z;𝐦(p)|ϕ(p)⟩\langle z;\mathbf{m}^{(p)}|\phi^{(p)}\rangle. From our Hdet construction, it is evident that the only important object is the value of the fusion tensor TT. Therefore, one may re-interpret ⟨z;𝐦(p)|ϕ(p)⟩\langle z;\mathbf{m}^{(p)}|\phi^{(p)}\rangle as long as its value is unchanged.

In this new viewpoint, we interpret the collection of all the parton localized orbitals as an orthonormal real-space basis for parton-pp: {|z;𝐦(p)⟩,z∈Fine-Grid,∀𝐦}\{|z;\mathbf{m}^{(p)}\rangle,z\in\text{Fine-Grid},\forall\mathbf{m}\}. The state |ϕ(p)⟩|\phi^{(p)}\rangle is then considered as a linear superposition of this orthonormal basis:

|ϕ(p)⟩=∑z∈Fine-Grid,𝐦⟨z;𝐦(p)|ϕ(p)⟩⋅|z;𝐦(p)⟩.\displaystyle|\phi^{(p)}\rangle=\sum_{z\in\text{Fine-Grid},\mathbf{m}}\langle z;\mathbf{m}^{(p)}|\phi^{(p)}\rangle\cdot|z;\mathbf{m}^{(p)}\rangle. (62)

For instance, one may choose |ϕ(p)⟩|\phi^{(p)}\rangle to be |ϕ𝐤(p)⟩a​L​L|\phi^{(p)}_{\mathbf{k}}\rangle_{aLL}, the Bloch state at a momentum point 𝐤\mathbf{k} in the aa-th LL. Here, to define the Bloch basis, one needs to introduce two commuting magnetic translations T^1,T^2\hat{T}_{1},\hat{T}_{2}, whose corresponding real-space unit cell area encloses one parton flux quantum. There will be many parton real-space orbitals {|z;𝐦(p)⟩,z∈Fine-Grid,𝐦∈aLL}\{|z;\mathbf{m}^{(p)}\rangle,z\in\text{Fine-Grid},\mathbf{m}\in aLL\} per unit cell (precisely, there are Ns(e)q(p)\frac{N_{s}^{(e)}}{q^{(p)}} parton orbitals per 𝐦\mathbf{m} per unit cell). In this new viewpoint, as one tunes 𝐤\mathbf{k}, |ϕ𝐤(p)⟩a​L​L|\phi^{(p)}_{\mathbf{k}}\rangle_{aLL} forms a band via linear superpositions of these orthonormal parton orbitals. Crucially, one can show that, in this new viewpoint, this band |ϕ𝐤(p)⟩a​L​L|\phi^{(p)}_{\mathbf{k}}\rangle_{aLL} indeed carries Chern number C=1C=1 (based on the parton-version of the resolution of identity Eq.(61), see Eq.(77) and discussions nearby).

The same change of viewpoint can be done for the electrons. Suppose we attempt to compute the Hdet many-body electron wavefunction in the discrete coherent-state basis on the Fine-Grid. Namely, given the full fusion tensor Tz​j​k..T_{zjk..} where z∈Fine-Gridz\in\text{Fine-Grid}, we want to compute the value:

⟨z1(e),z2(e),…,zNe(e)|Ψ(e)⟩=Hdet(Tsub),\displaystyle\langle z^{(e)}_{1},z_{2}^{(e)},...,z^{(e)}_{N_{e}}|\Psi^{(e)}\rangle=\text{Hdet}(T^{\text{sub}}), (63)

where zi(e)∈Fine-Gridz^{(e)}_{i}\in\text{Fine-Grid}, and the cubic tensor TsubT^{\text{sub}} is formed by stacking the ziz_{i} slices of TT. Because we only look for the value of the hyperdeterminant, it does not matter if one views {|z(e)⟩,z∈Fine-Grid}\{|z^{(e)}\rangle,z\in\text{Fine-Grid}\} as an orthonormal basis or not, as long as the fusion tensor TT is unchanged.

III.2.3 A Grassmann tensor-network picture

The main point from the previous discussion is that, for the purpose of computing the value of Hdet wavefunctions in the showcase examples, it is perfectly fine to think of the discrete-coherent state basis {|z(e)⟩,z∈Fine-Grid}\{|z^{(e)}\rangle,z\in\text{Fine-Grid}\} and the parton generalized coherent states {|z;𝐦(p)⟩,z∈Fine-Grid,∀𝐦}\{|z;\mathbf{m}^{(p)}\rangle,z\in\text{Fine-Grid},\forall\mathbf{m}\} as orthonormal in their respective Hilbert spaces.

In this new viewpoint, the Hdet wavefunctions in the showcase examples have a simple picture. It is much easier to work with orthonormal bases since we can use the standard second-quantized formulation. Introducing the electron operator bz†b_{z}^{\dagger} (cz†c_{z}^{\dagger}) for bosonic (fermionic) electron, and fermionic parton operator fz,𝐦(p)†f_{z,\mathbf{m}}^{(p)\dagger} for these orthonormal bases, the full fusion can be formulated as a single fusion operator 𝐅^=∑z𝐅^z\hat{\mathbf{F}}=\sum_{z}\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{z} :

e∼\displaystyle e\sim f(1)​f(2):\displaystyle f^{(1)}f^{(2)}:
𝐅^≡\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{F}}\equiv ∑z𝐅^z,𝐅^z≡∑αλα​bz†​fz;𝐦α(1)(1)​fz;𝐦α(2)(2);\displaystyle\sum_{z}\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{z},\;\;\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{z}\equiv\sum_{\alpha}\lambda_{\alpha}b_{z}^{\dagger}f_{z;\mathbf{m}^{(1)}_{\alpha}}^{(1)}f_{z;\mathbf{m}^{(2)}_{\alpha}}^{(2)};
e∼\displaystyle e\sim f(1)​f(2)​f(3):\displaystyle f^{(1)}f^{(2)}f^{(3)}:
𝐅^≡\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{F}}\equiv ∑z𝐅^z,𝐅^z≡∑αλα​cz†​fz;𝐦α(1)(1)​fz;𝐦α(2)(2)​fz;𝐦α(3)(3);\displaystyle\sum_{z}\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{z},\;\;\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{z}\equiv\sum_{\alpha}\lambda_{\alpha}c_{z}^{\dagger}f_{z;\mathbf{m}^{(1)}_{\alpha}}^{(1)}f_{z;\mathbf{m}^{(2)}_{\alpha}}^{(2)}f_{z;\mathbf{m}^{(3)}_{\alpha}}^{(3)}; (64)

where the summation over zz is for z∈Fine-Gridz\in\text{Fine-Grid}.

Note that, by comparing with the fusion operator in Eq. (14), we make two significant advances. First, 𝐅^\hat{\mathbf{F}} is written as a summation of local terms – each 𝐅^z\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{z} local-fusion operator is defined to be the term at position zz in Eq.(64). Second, in Eq.(14), despite the coherent-state bases not being physically orthonormal, after the change of viewpoint, we can still formulate 𝐅^\hat{\mathbf{F}} in second-quantized operators.

Up to an unimportant overall normalization factor, following Eq.(17), the Hdet wavefunction is obtained by applying 𝐅^Ne\hat{\mathbf{F}}^{N_{e}} to the tensor product of free parton states |Ψ(p)⟩|\Psi^{(p)}\rangle:

|Ψ(e)⟩=𝐅^Ne​|Ψ(1)⟩​|Ψ(2)⟩​…=𝐅^Ne​|ΨM​F⟩,\displaystyle|\Psi^{(e)}\rangle=\hat{\mathbf{F}}^{N_{e}}|\Psi^{(1)}\rangle|\Psi^{(2)}\rangle...=\hat{\mathbf{F}}^{N_{e}}|\Psi^{MF}\rangle, (65)

where we defined the full parton mean-field state |ΨM​F⟩≡|Ψ(1)⟩​|Ψ(2)⟩​…|\Psi^{MF}\rangle\equiv|\Psi^{(1)}\rangle|\Psi^{(2)}\rangle....

Here, the exponent NeN_{e} in 𝐅^Ne\hat{\mathbf{F}}^{N_{e}} makes sure that all partons are fused into electrons, resulting in a fully electronic state (note that each |Ψ(p)⟩|\Psi^{(p)}\rangle is a Slater determinant state with fixed NeN_{e} partons). On the other hand, it would be more elegant to revise our formulation so that NeN_{e} is not present in the fusion.

In fact, we can now take advantage of the new viewpoint, so that the result of the many-body fusion 𝐅^Ne\hat{\mathbf{F}}^{N_{e}} can be written as a product of (mutually commuting) local-fusion quantum gates {𝐂^z}\{\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{z}\} not involving NeN_{e}:

|Ψ(e)⟩=𝐅^Ne​|ΨM​F⟩=∏z∈Fine-Grid𝐂^z​|ΨM​F⟩.\displaystyle|\Psi^{(e)}\rangle=\hat{\mathbf{F}}^{N_{e}}|\Psi^{MF}\rangle=\prod_{z\in\text{Fine-Grid}}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{z}|\Psi^{MF}\rangle. (66)

Here, to avoid confusion with the local fusion operator 𝐅^z\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{z}, we will call operators 𝐂^z\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{z} the local-fusion gates.

The operator 𝐂^z\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{z} can be explicitly constructed. For this purpose, we consider the local Fock spaces at the Fine-Grid site-zz for the electrons ℱz(e)\mathcal{F}_{z}^{(e)} and partons ℱz(p)\mathcal{F}_{z}^{(p)}. Denoting |0z(e)⟩∈ℱz(e)|0_{z}^{(e)}\rangle\in\mathcal{F}_{z}^{(e)} and |0z(p)⟩∈ℱz(p)|0_{z}^{(p)}\rangle\in\mathcal{F}_{z}^{(p)} as their vacuum states, also denoting |0z(all ​p)⟩≡⊗p|0z(p)⟩∈ℱz(all ​p)≡⊗pℱz(p)|0_{z}^{(\text{all }p)}\rangle\equiv\otimes_{p}|0_{z}^{(p)}\rangle\in\mathcal{F}_{z}^{(\text{all }p)}\equiv\otimes_{p}\mathcal{F}_{z}^{(p)} as the tensor product for all parton species,

e∼f(1)⋅f(2):\displaystyle e\sim f^{(1)}\cdot f^{(2)}:
𝐂^z≡|0z(e)⟩​⟨0z(all ​p)|+∑n=1∞𝐅^znn!∙(|0z(e)⟩​⟨0z(all ​p)|),\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{z}\equiv|0_{z}^{(e)}\rangle\langle 0_{z}^{(\text{all }p)}|+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{z}^{n}}{n!}\bullet(|0_{z}^{(e)}\rangle\langle 0_{z}^{(\text{all }p)}|),
e∼f(1)⋅f(2)⋅f(3):\displaystyle e\sim f^{(1)}\cdot f^{(2)}\cdot f^{(3)}:
𝐂^z≡|0z(e)⟩​⟨0z(all ​p)|+𝐅^z∙(|0z(e)⟩​⟨0z(all ​p)|).\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{z}\equiv|0_{z}^{(e)}\rangle\langle 0_{z}^{(\text{all }p)}|+\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{z}\bullet(|0_{z}^{(e)}\rangle\langle 0_{z}^{(\text{all }p)}|). (67)

Here, we introduced an action "∙""\bullet" of 𝐅^zn\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{z}^{n} to the operator |0z(e)⟩​⟨0z(all ​p)||0_{z}^{(e)}\rangle\langle 0_{z}^{(\text{all }p)}|, which is defined by moving all the parton operators (maintaining the order) f(p)f^{(p)} to the right of |0z(e)⟩​⟨0z(all ​p)||0_{z}^{(e)}\rangle\langle 0_{z}^{(\text{all }p)}| (so that they act on ⟨0z(all ​p)|\langle 0_{z}^{(\text{all }p)}| from the right), and moving all the electron operators (bz†b_{z}^{\dagger} or cz†c_{z}^{\dagger}) to the left of |0z(e)⟩​⟨0z(all ​p)||0_{z}^{(e)}\rangle\langle 0_{z}^{(\text{all }p)}| (so they act on |0z(e)⟩|0_{z}^{(e)}\rangle from the left). For fermionic electrons, due to the Pauli exclusion principle, the power series truncates to n=1n=1.

For example:

e∼f(1)⋅f(2)⋅f(3):\displaystyle e\sim f^{(1)}\cdot f^{(2)}\cdot f^{(3)}:
𝐂^z=|0z(e)⟩​⟨0z(all ​p)|\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{z}=|0_{z}^{(e)}\rangle\langle 0_{z}^{(\text{all }p)}|
+∑αλα(cz†|0z(e)⟩)⋅(⟨0z(all ​p)|fz;𝐦α(1)(1)fz;𝐦α(2)(2)fz;𝐦α(3)(3)).\displaystyle+\sum_{\alpha}\lambda_{\alpha}(c_{z}^{\dagger}|0_{z}^{(e)}\rangle)\cdot(\langle 0_{z}^{(\text{all }p)}|f^{(1)}_{z;\mathbf{m}^{(1)}_{\alpha}}f^{(2)}_{z;\mathbf{m}^{(2)}_{\alpha}}f^{(3)}_{z;\mathbf{m}^{(3)}_{\alpha}}). (68)

Namely, 𝐂^z:ℱz(all ​p)↦Fz(e)\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{z}:\mathcal{F}^{(\text{all }p)}_{z}\mapsto F^{(e)}_{z} is a linear map between the two Fock spaces. With "∙""\bullet" notation, we generally have:

𝐂^z=exp⁡(𝐅^z)∙(|0z(e)⟩​⟨0z(all ​p)|)\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{z}=\exp(\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{z})\bullet(|0_{z}^{(e)}\rangle\langle 0_{z}^{(\text{all }p)}|) (69)

With the definition Eq.(67), it is straightforward to show that the property Eq.(66) is satisfied. Here, the product of two gates 𝐂^z​𝐂^z′:ℱz(all ​p)⊗ℱz′(all ​p)↦ℱz(e)⊗ℱz′(e)\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{z}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{z^{\prime}}:\mathcal{F}^{(\text{all }p)}_{z}\otimes\mathcal{F}^{(\text{all }p)}_{z^{\prime}}\mapsto\mathcal{F}^{(e)}_{z}\otimes\mathcal{F}^{(e)}_{z^{\prime}} should be understood as the tensor product. Explicitly, this map can be naturally obtained by moving all parton operators fz(p)f^{(p)}_{z} and fz′(p)f^{(p)}_{z^{\prime}} to the right (so that they act on the vacuum of partons from the right), and the electron operators to the left (so that they act on the vacuum of electrons from the left). It is important to note that when moving the fermion operators (either electron or parton) around, they satisfy anticommutation relations, and the fermion sign needs to be included.

Crucially, the local-fusion gate 𝐂^z\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{z}’s total fermion parity is even. Consequently, the order of multiplication in ∏z𝐂^z\prod_{z}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{z} is immaterial: 𝐂^z​𝐂^z′=𝐂^z′​𝐂^z\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{z}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{z^{\prime}}=\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{z^{\prime}}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{z}.

Such a local fusion structure is most conveniently illustrated using a Grassmann tensor-network language[46, 28], in which a Grassmann variable replaces a second-quantized fermionic operator. It is well-known that, when |Ψ(p)⟩|\Psi^{(p)}\rangle is topological (e.g., with nonzero Chern number), a Gaussian tensor-network representation of |Ψ(p)⟩|\Psi^{(p)}\rangle has an obstruction when the virtual-bond dimension is finite [32, 107] in the thermodynamic limit. However, as a conceptual language, it is fine to consider a finite-size system without specifying the virtual-bond dimension.

In this picture, each Slater-determinant |Ψ(p)⟩|\Psi^{(p)}\rangle is represented as a layer of Gaussian Grassmann tensor-network[77, 46, 32] on the Fine-Grid, with the local orbitals |z;𝐦(p)⟩|z;\mathbf{m}^{(p)}\rangle represented as the outgoing ”physical-legs” of the parton (i.e., Grassmann variables). The local fusion 𝐂^z\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{z} can be viewed as a non-Gaussian Grassmann tensor (i.e., a quantum gate). The 𝐂^z\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{z} gate has incoming parton’s physical-legs, and one outgoing electron’s physical-leg. The electron’s physical-leg will be a Grassmann (bosonic) variable if it is fermionic (bosonic). See Fig.4 for an illustration.

In order to compute a physical observable O^(e)\hat{O}^{(e)} of the electron, one needs to compute ⟨O^(e)⟩≡⟨Ψ(e)|O^(e)|Ψ(e)⟩⟨Ψ(e)|Ψ(e)⟩\langle\hat{O}^{(e)}\rangle\equiv\frac{\langle\Psi^{(e)}|\hat{O}^{(e)}|\Psi^{(e)}\rangle}{\langle\Psi^{(e)}|\Psi^{(e)}\rangle}. As a concrete example, one may consider density-density correlator O^(e)=n^ω(e)​n^ζ(e)\hat{O}^{(e)}=\hat{n}^{(e)}_{\omega}\hat{n}^{(e)}_{\zeta} (other observables can be easily generalized), where ω,ζ∈Fine-Grid\omega,\zeta\in\text{Fine-Grid}, and n^z(e)=bz†​bz\hat{n}^{(e)}_{z}=b^{\dagger}_{z}b_{z} (n^z(e)=cz†​cz\hat{n}^{(e)}_{z}=c^{\dagger}_{z}c_{z}) for the bosonic (fermionic) electron case. Ref.[129] points out that any four-fermion interaction energy of the electron can be computed based on ⟨n^ω(e)​n^ζ(e)⟩,∀ω,ζ∈Fine-Grid\langle\hat{n}^{(e)}_{\omega}\hat{n}^{(e)}_{\zeta}\rangle,\;\forall\omega,\zeta\in\text{Fine-Grid}.

In this Grassmann tensor-network picture,

⟨n^ω(e)​n^ζ(e)⟩=⟨ΨM​F|∏z𝐂^z†⋅n^ω(e)​n^ζ(e)⋅∏z𝐂^z|ΨM​F⟩⟨ΨM​F|∏z𝐂^z†⋅∏z𝐂^z|ΨM​F⟩.\displaystyle\langle\hat{n}^{(e)}_{\omega}\hat{n}^{(e)}_{\zeta}\rangle=\frac{\langle\Psi^{MF}|\prod_{z}\hat{\mathbf{C}}^{\dagger}_{z}\cdot\hat{n}^{(e)}_{\omega}\hat{n}^{(e)}_{\zeta}\cdot\prod_{z}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{z}|\Psi^{MF}\rangle}{\langle\Psi^{MF}|\prod_{z}\hat{\mathbf{C}}^{\dagger}_{z}\cdot\prod_{z}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{z}|\Psi^{MF}\rangle}. (70)

We define

𝐏^z≡\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{z}\equiv 𝐂^z†​𝐂^z,\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{C}}^{\dagger}_{z}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{z}, 𝐧^z≡\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{z}\equiv 𝐂^z†​n^z(e)​𝐂^z.\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{C}}^{\dagger}_{z}\hat{n}^{(e)}_{z}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{z}. (71)

These operators now directly act on the parton mean-field state, and have a simple geometric picture: the local gate 𝐏^z\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{z} is obtained by contracting the electron physical leg between the gates 𝐂^z†\hat{\mathbf{C}}^{\dagger}_{z} and 𝐂^z\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{z}, while the local gate 𝐧^z\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{z} is obtained by sandwiching n^z(e)\hat{n}^{(e)}_{z} between them. See Fig.4 for an illustration.

With these local gates, we have:

⟨n^ω(e)​n^ζ(e)⟩=⟨ΨM​F|𝐧^ω​𝐧^ζ​∏z≠ω,ζ𝐏^z|ΨM​F⟩⟨ΨM​F|∏z𝐏^z|ΨM​F⟩.\displaystyle\langle\hat{n}^{(e)}_{\omega}\hat{n}^{(e)}_{\zeta}\rangle=\frac{\langle\Psi^{MF}|\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{\omega}\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{\zeta}\prod_{z\neq\omega,\zeta}\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{z}|\Psi^{MF}\rangle}{\langle\Psi^{MF}|\prod_{z}\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{z}|\Psi^{MF}\rangle}. (72)

For a general electronic observable O^D(e)\hat{O}^{(e)}_{D}, where D⊂Fine-GridD\subset\text{Fine-Grid} is formed by some sites, one can similarly define the quantum gate

𝐎^D≡∏z∈D𝐂^z†⋅O^D(e)⋅∏z∈D𝐂^z,\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{O}}_{D}\equiv\prod_{z\in D}\hat{\mathbf{C}}^{\dagger}_{z}\cdot\hat{O}^{(e)}_{D}\cdot\prod_{z\in D}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{z}, (73)

and

⟨O^D(e)⟩=⟨ΨM​F|𝐎^D​∏z∉D𝐏^z|ΨM​F⟩⟨ΨM​F|∏z𝐏^z|ΨM​F⟩.\displaystyle\langle\hat{O}^{(e)}_{D}\rangle=\frac{\langle\Psi^{MF}|\hat{\mathbf{O}}_{D}\prod_{z\notin D}\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{z}|\Psi^{MF}\rangle}{\langle\Psi^{MF}|\prod_{z}\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{z}|\Psi^{MF}\rangle}. (74)

Eq.(74) captures the key consequence of the locality structure of Hdet wavefunctions. We will come back to it later because it implies systematic ways to numerically simulate Hdet wavefunctions.

III.2.4 Example: Jain’s ν=25\nu=\frac{2}{5} state

As a concrete example, let’s explicitly write down the parton operators fz,𝐦(p)(p)f^{(p)}_{z,\mathbf{m}^{(p)}} and the fusion operator 𝐅^z\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{z} for the fermionic Jain’s ν=25\nu=\frac{2}{5} state on the Fine-Grid, after the change of viewpoint. In this example, there are three species of partons: np=3n_{\rm p}=3, carrying electric charge q(1)=q(2)=25q^{(1)}=q^{(2)}=\frac{2}{5} (filling LLL), q(3)=15q^{(3)}=\frac{1}{5} (filling both LLL and 1st LL). Based on Eq.(55), parton species p=1,2p=1,2 each have two orbitals per site-zz on the Fine-Grid, corresponding to generalized coherent states |z(0)(p)⟩0​L​L|z^{(p)}_{(0)}\rangle_{0LL} and |z(1)(p)⟩0​L​L|z^{(p)}_{(1)}\rangle_{0LL}, denoted as 𝐦(p)=1,2\mathbf{m}^{(p)}=1,2 respectively. For parton species p=3p=3, we need three orbitals per site-zz, corresponding to |z(0)(3)⟩0​L​L|z^{(3)}_{(0)}\rangle_{0LL}, |z(0)(3)⟩1​L​L|z^{(3)}_{(0)}\rangle_{1LL},|z(1)(3)⟩1​L​L|z^{(3)}_{(1)}\rangle_{1LL}, denoted as 𝐦(3)=1,2,3\mathbf{m}^{(3)}=1,2,3 respectively. The fusion operator 𝐅^z\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{z}, according to Eq.(55), has the form in Eq.(64) with R=4R=4, and:

α=\displaystyle\alpha= 1:\displaystyle 1: λ1=\displaystyle\lambda_{1}= 1,\displaystyle 1, 𝐦1(1)=\displaystyle\mathbf{m}^{(1)}_{1}= 1,\displaystyle 1, 𝐦1(2)=\displaystyle\mathbf{m}^{(2)}_{1}= 1,\displaystyle 1, 𝐦1(3)=\displaystyle\mathbf{m}^{(3)}_{1}= 1,\displaystyle 1,
α=\displaystyle\alpha= 2:\displaystyle 2: λ2=\displaystyle\lambda_{2}= 25,\displaystyle\frac{\sqrt{2}}{5}, 𝐦2(1)=\displaystyle\mathbf{m}^{(1)}_{2}= 2,\displaystyle 2, 𝐦2(2)=\displaystyle\mathbf{m}^{(2)}_{2}= 1,\displaystyle 1, 𝐦2(3)=\displaystyle\mathbf{m}^{(3)}_{2}= 2,\displaystyle 2,
α=\displaystyle\alpha= 3:\displaystyle 3: λ3=\displaystyle\lambda_{3}= 25,\displaystyle\frac{\sqrt{2}}{5}, 𝐦3(1)=\displaystyle\mathbf{m}^{(1)}_{3}= 1,\displaystyle 1, 𝐦3(2)=\displaystyle\mathbf{m}^{(2)}_{3}= 2,\displaystyle 2, 𝐦3(3)=\displaystyle\mathbf{m}^{(3)}_{3}= 2,\displaystyle 2,
α=\displaystyle\alpha= 4:\displaystyle 4: λ4=\displaystyle\lambda_{4}= −45,\displaystyle-\frac{4}{5}, 𝐦4(1)=\displaystyle\mathbf{m}^{(1)}_{4}= 1,\displaystyle 1, 𝐦4(2)=\displaystyle\mathbf{m}^{(2)}_{4}= 1,\displaystyle 1, 𝐦4(3)=\displaystyle\mathbf{m}^{(3)}_{4}= 3.\displaystyle 3. (75)

Namely:

𝐅^z=\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{z}= cz†[fz,1(1)fz,1(2)fz,1(3)+25fz,2(1)fz,1(2)fz,2(3)\displaystyle c_{z}^{\dagger}\Big[f^{(1)}_{z,1}f^{(2)}_{z,1}f^{(3)}_{z,1}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{5}f^{(1)}_{z,2}f^{(2)}_{z,1}f^{(3)}_{z,2}
+25fz,1(1)fz,2(2)fz,2(3)−45fz,1(1)fz,1(2)fz,3(3)].\displaystyle+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{5}f^{(1)}_{z,1}f^{(2)}_{z,2}f^{(3)}_{z,2}-\frac{4}{5}f^{(1)}_{z,1}f^{(2)}_{z,1}f^{(3)}_{z,3}\Big]. (76)

The corresponding local fusion gate 𝐂^z\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{z} as Eq.(68) can be explicitly written down.

In order to compute physical quantities as in Eq.(74), we need to fully specify |ΨM​F⟩|\Psi^{MF}\rangle. Since it is a direct product of Slater determinants of partons, |ΨM​F⟩|\Psi^{MF}\rangle is fully specified by the single-body reduced density matrix (RDM): ⟨fz1,𝐦1(p)(p)†fz2,𝐦2(p)(p)⟩\langle f^{(p)\dagger}_{z_{1},\mathbf{m}^{(p)}_{1}}f^{(p)}_{z_{2},\mathbf{m}^{(p)}_{2}}\rangle. Below we explicitly write down these RDM elements.

According to the change of viewpoint Eq.(62), we should interpret the filled parton states as the linear superposition of the orthonormal local parton orbitals. Let’s denote the filled parton states to be |ϕk(p)⟩a​L​L|\phi^{(p)}_{k}\rangle_{aLL}. For the parton species p=1,2p=1,2, a=0a=0 and k=1,2,..,Nek=1,2,..,N_{e}. For the parton species p=3p=3, a=0,1a=0,1 and k=1,2,…,Ne2k=1,2,...,\frac{N_{e}}{2}. The only technical detail is that the |ϕk(p)⟩|\phi^{(p)}_{k}\rangle state given in Eq.(62) is not normalized after the change of viewpoint. To normalize it, we introduce the resolution of identity of the generalized coherent state before the change of viewpoint. It is easy to show that:

∑z∈Fine-Grid|z(m)(p)⟩​⟨z(n)(p)|a​L​L=δm​n​Ns(e)q(p)​𝟏a​L​L,\displaystyle\sum_{z\in{\text{Fine-Grid}}}|z_{(m)}^{(p)}\rangle\langle z_{(n)}^{(p)}|_{aLL}=\delta_{mn}\frac{N_{s}^{(e)}}{q^{(p)}}\mathbf{1}_{aLL}, (77)

where 𝟏a​L​L\mathbf{1}_{aLL} is the identity in parton-pp’s a​L​LaLL. This equation follows from the fact that the operator on the LHS commutes with all magnetic translations, so it must be proportional to the identity. The proportional coefficient can be found by taking the trace.

Using this resolution of identity, it is straightforward to show that if {|ϕk(p)⟩a​L​L}\{|\phi^{(p)}_{k}\rangle_{aLL}\} is an orthonormal basis before the change of viewpoint, it remains an orthogonal basis after the change of viewpoint, but with a norm:

∑m=0Ncoh,a​L​L(p)−1∑z∈Fine-Grid|⟨z(m)(p)|ϕ(p)⟩a​L​L|2=Ncoh,a​L​L(p)​Ns(e)q(p),\displaystyle\sum_{m=0}^{N^{(p)}_{{\rm coh},aLL}-1}\sum_{z\in\text{Fine-Grid}}|\langle z_{(m)}^{(p)}|\phi^{(p)}\rangle_{aLL}|^{2}=N^{(p)}_{{\rm coh},aLL}\frac{N_{s}^{(e)}}{q^{(p)}}, (78)

where Ncoh,a​L​L(p)N^{(p)}_{{\rm coh},aLL} is the number of generalized coherent state orbitals per site in the a​L​LaLL for parton-pp. In the present ν=25\nu=\frac{2}{5} example, Ncoh,0​L​L(1)=Ncoh,0​L​L(2)=2N^{(1)}_{{\rm coh},0LL}=N^{(2)}_{{\rm coh},0LL}=2, while Ncoh,0​L​L(3)=1,Ncoh,1​L​L(3)=2N^{(3)}_{{\rm coh},0LL}=1,N^{(3)}_{{\rm coh},1LL}=2.

With this normalization factor after the change of viewpoint, one can write f(p)†z,𝐦(p)f^{(p)\dagger}_{z,\mathbf{m}^{(p)}} operator as a linear superposition of the normalized filled state operator f(p)†k,a​L​Lf^{(p)\dagger}_{k,aLL}. Since we know ⟨fk,a​L​L(p)†fl,b​L​L(p)⟩=δk​lδa​b\langle f^{(p)\dagger}_{k,aLL}f^{(p)}_{l,bLL}\rangle=\delta_{kl}\delta_{ab}, the RDM ⟨fz1,𝐦1(p)(p)†fz2,𝐦2(p)(p)⟩\langle f^{(p)\dagger}_{z_{1},\mathbf{m}^{(p)}_{1}}f^{(p)}_{z_{2},\mathbf{m}^{(p)}_{2}}\rangle can be computed (recall 𝐦\mathbf{m} is a combination of generalized coherent state index-(m)(m) and the LL index-a​L​LaLL):

⟨fz1,(m1),a​L​L(p)†fz2,(m2),b​L​L(p)⟩\displaystyle\langle f^{(p)\dagger}_{z_{1},(m_{1}),aLL}f^{(p)}_{z_{2},(m_{2}),bLL}\rangle
=\displaystyle= q(p)Ncoh,a​L​L(p)​Ns(e)​δa​b​⟨(z2)(m2)(p)|(z1)(m1)(p)⟩a​L​L,\displaystyle\frac{q^{(p)}}{N^{(p)}_{{\rm coh},aLL}N_{s}^{(e)}}\delta_{ab}\left\langle(z_{2})^{(p)}_{(m_{2})}|(z_{1})^{(p)}_{(m_{1})}\right\rangle_{aLL}, (79)

where, on the RHS, the overlap between two generalized coherent states before the change of viewpoint is given in Eq.().

III.2.5 The definition of the locality-structure

The showcase examples motivate us to define the following general locality-structure of an Hdet wavefunction.

Definition: Consider a Hdet construction involving npn_{\text{p}} parton species on a certain Real-Space-Lattice. Each parton many-body state is a Slater-determinant |Ψ(p)⟩|\Psi^{(p)}\rangle (p=1,2,…,np.p=1,2,...,n_{\text{p}}.), corresponding to filling NeN_{e} single-particle states |ϕjp(p)⟩|\phi^{(p)}_{j_{p}}\rangle (jp=1,2,…,Nej_{p}=1,2,...,N_{e}). These single-particle states are linear superpositions of localized orthonormal basis {|𝐫;𝐦(p)⟩}\{|\mathbf{r};\mathbf{m}^{(p)}\rangle\}:

|ϕjp(p)⟩=∑𝐫,𝐦(p)⟨𝐫;𝐦(p)|ϕjp(p)⟩⋅|𝐫;𝐦(p)⟩.\displaystyle|\phi^{(p)}_{j_{p}}\rangle=\sum_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{m}^{(p)}}\langle\mathbf{r};\mathbf{m}^{(p)}|\phi^{(p)}_{j_{p}}\rangle\cdot|\mathbf{r};\mathbf{m}^{(p)}\rangle. (80)

In addition, we choose a localized single-particle basis for electrons {|𝐫;𝐦(e)⟩}\{|\mathbf{r};\mathbf{m}^{(e)}\rangle\}, indexed by ii, that could be overcomplete. Here, for either electron’s or parton’s orbital, 𝐫∈\mathbf{r}\in Real-Space-Lattice labels its position, and 𝐦\mathbf{m} labels other quantum numbers. We say that the fusion tensor TT admits a locality structure if there exist local parton states |𝛗α,i(p)⟩|\bm{\varphi}^{(p)}_{\alpha,i}\rangle such that:

Ti,j1,j2,…,jnp≡⟨𝐫i;𝐦i(e)​|∘|​∏p=1npϕjp(p)⟩\displaystyle T_{i,j_{1},j_{2},...,j_{n_{\text{p}}}}\equiv\langle\mathbf{r}_{i};\mathbf{m}_{i}^{(e)}|\mkern-1.0mu\mathord{\circ}\mkern-1.0mu|\prod_{p=1}^{n_{\text{p}}}\phi^{(p)}_{j_{p}}\rangle
=\displaystyle= ∑α=1Riλα,i​∏p=1np⟨𝝋α,i(p)|ϕjp(p)⟩,\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha=1}^{R_{i}}\lambda_{\alpha,i}\prod_{p=1}^{n_{\text{p}}}\langle\bm{\varphi}^{(p)}_{\alpha,i}|\phi^{(p)}_{j_{p}}\rangle, (81)

where |𝝋α,i(p)⟩|\bm{\varphi}^{(p)}_{\alpha,i}\rangle, up to an exponentially small tail, has nonzero overlap with the real-space basis only in the vicinity of the electron’s position 𝐫i\mathbf{r}_{i}:

|⟨𝐫;𝐦(p)|𝝋α,i(p)⟩|≲e−|𝐫−𝐫i|l when |𝐫−𝐫i|≫l,\displaystyle|\langle\mathbf{r};\mathbf{m}^{(p)}|\bm{\varphi}^{(p)}_{\alpha,i}\rangle|\lesssim e^{-\frac{|\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_{i}|}{l}}\text{ when }|\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_{i}|\gg l, (82)

where ll is a certain finite length-scale.

Practically, one may truncate the exponential tail so that |⟨𝐫;𝐦(p)|𝝋α,i(p)⟩≠0|\langle\mathbf{r};\mathbf{m}^{(p)}|\bm{\varphi}^{(p)}_{\alpha,i}\rangle\neq 0 only over a finite support |𝐫−𝐫i|<l~|\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_{i}|<\tilde{l} with some finite length l~\tilde{l}. When the number of fusion channels RiR_{i} is finite (which is always physically true for a finite-size sample), it is convenient to introduce ancilla parton orbitals at site-𝐫i\mathbf{r}_{i} by increasing the index 𝐦(p)\mathbf{m}^{(p)}, representing copies of the nearby parton orbitals. With these ancilla introduced, the fusion can be chosen to be on-site: |𝝋α,i(p)⟩=|𝐫i;𝐦α,i(p)⟩|\bm{\varphi}^{(p)}_{\alpha,i}\rangle=|\mathbf{r}_{i};\mathbf{m}_{\alpha,i}^{(p)}\rangle. Namely:

Ti,j1,j2,…,jnp≡⟨𝐫i;𝐦i(e)​|∘|​∏p=1npϕjp(p)⟩\displaystyle T_{i,j_{1},j_{2},...,j_{n_{\text{p}}}}\equiv\langle\mathbf{r}_{i};\mathbf{m}_{i}^{(e)}|\mkern-1.0mu\mathord{\circ}\mkern-1.0mu|\prod_{p=1}^{n_{\text{p}}}\phi^{(p)}_{j_{p}}\rangle
=\displaystyle= ∑α=1Riλα,i∏p=1np⟨𝐫i;𝐦α,i(p)|ϕjp(p)⟩,\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha=1}^{R_{i}}\lambda_{\alpha,i}\prod_{p=1}^{n_{\text{p}}}\langle\mathbf{r}_{i};\mathbf{m}_{\alpha,i}^{(p)}|\phi^{(p)}_{j_{p}}\rangle, (83)

This on-site fusion allows one to translate the above definition of the locality-structure into the formulation of a fused Gaussian Grassmann tensor-network as in Fig.4. The Hdet state |Ψ(e)⟩|\Psi^{(e)}\rangle can be obtained via |Ψ(e)⟩=𝐅^Ne​|ΨM​F⟩≡𝐅^Ne​∏p=1np|Ψ(p)⟩|\Psi^{(e)}\rangle=\hat{\mathbf{F}}^{N_{e}}|\Psi^{MF}\rangle\equiv\hat{\mathbf{F}}^{N_{e}}\prod_{p=1}^{n_{\text{p}}}|\Psi^{(p)}\rangle using the second-quantized fusion operator 𝐅^=∑i𝐅^i\hat{\mathbf{F}}=\sum_{i}\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{i}, where the on-site fusion operator

𝐅^i≡∑α=1Riλα,i⋅ci†⋅∏p=1npfi,𝐦α,i(p)(p).\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{i}\equiv\sum_{\alpha=1}^{R_{i}}\lambda_{\alpha,i}\cdot c^{\dagger}_{i}\cdot\prod_{p=1}^{n_{\text{p}}}f^{(p)}_{i,\mathbf{m}^{(p)}_{\alpha,i}}. (84)

Here we introduced the second-quantized operator ci†c^{\dagger}_{i} for electrons. (ci†c_{i}^{\dagger} can be either bosonic or fermionic depending on whether npn_{\text{p}} is even or odd. Again, even if the electronic orbitals {|𝐫i,𝐦i(e)⟩}\{|\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{m}_{i}^{(e)}\rangle\} may be overcomplete, one still can use the standard second-quantization formulation as if they are orthonormal, i.e., via the change of viewpoint.) The orthonormal second-quantized operators fi,𝐦i(p)(p)f^{(p)}_{i,\mathbf{m}_{i}^{(p)}}’s are located at site 𝐫i\mathbf{r}_{i}: 𝐦i(p)\mathbf{m}_{i}^{(p)} is defined to be the collection of all parton-pp orbital labels in the local Fock space assigned to electronic orbital-ii, and fi,𝐦α,i(p)(p)f^{(p)}_{i,\mathbf{m}^{(p)}_{\alpha,i}} is participating in the fusion channel α\alpha.

Finally, by introducing additional ancilla parton orbitals, one can always make sure that if two different electronic orbitals i,i′i,i^{\prime} are located on the same site: 𝐫i=𝐫i′\mathbf{r}_{i}=\mathbf{r}_{i^{\prime}} and 𝐦i(e)≠𝐦i′(e)\mathbf{m}_{i}^{(e)}\neq\mathbf{m}_{i^{\prime}}^{(e)}, then 𝐦i(p)∩𝐦i′(p)\mathbf{m}_{i}^{(p)}\cap\mathbf{m}_{i^{\prime}}^{(p)} is empty. Namely, parton Fock spaces associated with ii and i′i^{\prime} are distinct. This property allows the convenient mutually commuting fusion gate formalism:

|Ψ(e)⟩=𝐅^Ne​|ΨM​F⟩=∏i𝐂^i​|ΨM​F⟩,\displaystyle|\Psi^{(e)}\rangle=\hat{\mathbf{F}}^{N_{e}}|\Psi^{MF}\rangle=\prod_{i}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{i}|\Psi^{MF}\rangle, (85)

where:

𝐂^i≡|0i(e)⟩​⟨0i(all ​p)|+∑n=1∞𝐅^inn!∙(|0i(e)⟩​⟨0i(all ​p)|)\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{i}\equiv|0_{i}^{(e)}\rangle\langle 0_{i}^{(\text{all }p)}|+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{i}^{n}}{n!}\bullet(|0_{i}^{(e)}\rangle\langle 0_{i}^{(\text{all }p)}|)
=exp⁡(𝐅^i)∙(|0i(e)⟩​⟨0i(all ​p)|),\displaystyle\quad\;=\exp(\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{i})\bullet(|0_{i}^{(e)}\rangle\langle 0_{i}^{(\text{all }p)}|),

where |0i(all ​p)⟩|0_{i}^{(\text{all }p)}\rangle is the vacuum of all partons, whether they participate in this fusion gate or not. For fermionic electrons, the summation of nn truncates to n=1n=1. For bosonic electrons, the summation truncates to a finite nmaxn_{\rm max} determined by the fusion channels (since the partons are fermionic). After introducing gates 𝐏^i≡𝐂^i†​𝐂^i\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{i}\equiv\hat{\mathbf{C}}^{\dagger}_{i}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{i}, and observable 𝐎^D≡∏i∈D𝐂^i†⋅O^D(e)⋅∏i∈D𝐂^i\hat{\mathbf{O}}_{D}\equiv\prod_{i\in D}\hat{\mathbf{C}}^{\dagger}_{i}\cdot\hat{O}^{(e)}_{D}\cdot\prod_{i\in D}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{i}, Eq.(74) is directly generalized.

IV Two types of model systems

There are two common types of model systems giving rise to fractionalized states of matter: (A) A model defined with full real-space degrees of freedom (e.g., a tight-binding model with interactions), and (B) a model already projected into a topological band (e.g., a Chern band). As mentioned in Sec.III.2.1, the treatments of the Hdet wavefunctions in these two model types are different. For type-(A) models, one can construct the locality-structure of the fusion tensor based on the real-space orthonormal Wannier orbitals of electrons. For type-(B) models, one needs to work with overcomplete discrete coherent states of electrons. In this section, we will present physical examples of how to construct Hdet wavefunctions for both types of model systems.

IV.1 Type-(A) example: QSL

Traditionally, many quantum spin liquid (QSL) states are represented using the so-called Abrikosov-fermion formulation[2, 136]:

𝐒Abr.𝐫=12∑a​b𝖿(a)†𝐫𝝈a​b𝖿(b)𝐫,\displaystyle\mathbf{S}^{\text{Abr.}}_{\mathbf{r}}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{ab}\mathsf{f}^{(a)\dagger}_{\mathbf{r}}\bm{\sigma}_{ab}\mathsf{f}^{(b)}_{\mathbf{r}}, (87)

where 𝐫\mathbf{r} labels the real-space site, and a,b=↑,↓a,b=\uparrow,\downarrow label the spin. By introducing spin-12\frac{1}{2} fermion 𝖿𝐫(a)\mathsf{f}^{(a)}_{\mathbf{r}}, the local Hilbert space is enlarged to 44-dimensional: {|0⟩,𝖿(↑)†|0⟩,𝖿(↓)†|0⟩,𝖿(↑)†𝖿(↓)†|0⟩}\{|0\rangle,\mathsf{f}^{(\uparrow)\dagger}|0\rangle,\mathsf{f}^{(\downarrow)\dagger}|0\rangle,\mathsf{f}^{(\uparrow)\dagger}\mathsf{f}^{(\downarrow)\dagger}|0\rangle\}. The physical spin-12\frac{1}{2} physical Hilbert space is recovered after enforcing the one-𝖿\mathsf{f}-fermion-per-site constraint: ∑a𝖿(a)†𝐫𝖿(a)𝐫=1,∀𝐫\sum_{a}\mathsf{f}^{(a)\dagger}_{\mathbf{r}}\mathsf{f}^{(a)}_{\mathbf{r}}=1,\forall\mathbf{r}.

In order to construct a QSL wavefunction, one first writes down a free fermion mean-field state of 𝖿\mathsf{f}-fermions |ΨM​F⟩|\Psi^{MF}\rangle. If there is no pairing between 𝖿(↑)\mathsf{f}^{(\uparrow)} and 𝖿(↓)\mathsf{f}^{(\downarrow)}, |ΨM​F⟩|\Psi^{MF}\rangle would be a tensor product of two Slater determinants, one for each spin: |ΨM​F⟩=|Ψ(↑)⟩⊗|Ψ(↓)⟩|\Psi^{MF}\rangle=|\Psi^{(\uparrow)}\rangle\otimes|\Psi^{(\downarrow)}\rangle. This is the typical case of the so-called U⁡(1)U(1) QSL[136, 80, 104].

To make a connection with our formulation of the Hdet wavefunction, it is convenient to map the S=12S=\frac{1}{2} model into a hard-core boson model, via the identification:

|↑⟩=\displaystyle|\uparrow\rangle= |1⟩=b†​|0⟩,\displaystyle|1\rangle=b^{\dagger}|0\rangle, |↓⟩=\displaystyle|\downarrow\rangle= |0⟩\displaystyle|0\rangle (88)

We may call these hard-core bosons the bosonic electrons. At the same time, we perform a particle-hole transformation for 𝖿(↓)\mathsf{f}^{(\downarrow)} only: 𝖿(↑)≡f,𝖿(↓)≡h†\mathsf{f}^{(\uparrow)}\equiv f,\mathsf{f}^{(\downarrow)}\equiv h^{\dagger}. The mean-field state is still a product of two Slater determinants: |ΨM​F⟩=|Ψ(↑−f)⟩⊗|Ψ(↓−h)⟩|\Psi^{MF}\rangle=|\Psi^{(\uparrow-f)}\rangle\otimes|\Psi^{(\downarrow-h)}\rangle. In the language of the hard-core boson bb and f,hf,h partons, the projection into the physical local Hilbert space can be exactly represented using the local fusion operator 𝐅^𝐫\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{\mathbf{r}}:

𝐅^𝐫Abr.=b𝐫†​h𝐫​f𝐫.\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{F}}^{\text{Abr.}}_{\mathbf{r}}=b_{\mathbf{r}}^{\dagger}h_{\mathbf{r}}f_{\mathbf{r}}. (89)

The corresponding local fusion gate 𝐂^𝐫\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{\mathbf{r}} is:

𝐂^𝐫Abr.=|0𝐫(e)⟩​⟨0𝐫(all ​p)|+|1𝐫(e)⟩​⟨0𝐫(all ​p)|​h𝐫​f𝐫\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{C}}^{\text{Abr.}}_{\mathbf{r}}=|0_{\mathbf{r}}^{(e)}\rangle\langle 0_{\mathbf{r}}^{(\text{all }p)}|+|1_{\mathbf{r}}^{(e)}\rangle\langle 0_{\mathbf{r}}^{(\text{all }p)}|h_{\mathbf{r}}f_{\mathbf{r}}
=\displaystyle= |↓𝐫⟩⟨0𝐫(all ​p)|+|↑𝐫⟩⟨0𝐫(all ​p)|h𝐫f𝐫.\displaystyle|\downarrow_{\mathbf{r}}\rangle\langle 0_{\mathbf{r}}^{(\text{all }p)}|+|\uparrow_{\mathbf{r}}\rangle\langle 0_{\mathbf{r}}^{(\text{all }p)}|h_{\mathbf{r}}f_{\mathbf{r}}. (90)

Namely, the traditional Abrikosov-fermion construction of the U(1) QSL is nothing but a very special Hdet wavefunction with a locality structure: there is exactly one on-site fusion channel (R=1R=1). It is well-known that the spin wavefunction of the U⁡(1)U(1) QSL |Ψ(Abr.)⟩=∏𝐫𝐂^𝐫Abr.​|ΨM​F⟩|\Psi^{(\text{Abr.})}\rangle=\prod_{\mathbf{r}}\hat{\mathbf{C}}^{\text{Abr.}}_{\mathbf{r}}|\Psi^{MF}\rangle is a product of two determinants. In the past few decades, such Abrikosov-fermion QSL wavefunctions have been widely studied via variational Monte Carlo techniques[44, 91, 104, 65, 66, 61].

The key point raised by the present work is that fusion need not be limited to a single channel. Namely, the parton images of the physical spin states {|↑𝐫⟩,|↓𝐫⟩}\{|\uparrow_{\mathbf{r}}\rangle,|\downarrow_{\mathbf{r}}\rangle\} do not need to be simple product states. In the presence of only SzS_{z} spin rotation symmetry, it is straightforward to introduce multiple fusion channels in the previous hard-core picture. For example, one may introduce additional parton orbitals, labeled by 𝐦(a)\mathbf{m}^{(a)}, so that:

𝐂^𝐫=|↓𝐫⟩⟨0𝐫(all ​p)|+∑α=1Rλα|↑𝐫⟩⟨0𝐫(all ​p)|h𝐫,𝐦(↓)αf𝐫,𝐦(↑)α,\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{\mathbf{r}}=|\downarrow_{\mathbf{r}}\rangle\langle 0_{\mathbf{r}}^{(\text{all }p)}|+\sum_{\alpha=1}^{R}\lambda_{\alpha}|\uparrow_{\mathbf{r}}\rangle\langle 0_{\mathbf{r}}^{(\text{all }p)}|h_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{m}^{(\downarrow)}_{\alpha}}f_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{m}^{(\uparrow)}_{\alpha}}, (91)

leading to a hyperdeterminant of a rank-3 fusion tensor TT for the spin (i.e., hard-core boson) wavefunction.

In the above SzS_{z}-symmetric case, the parton image of |↑⟩|\uparrow\rangle spin is an entangled state. But the parton image of |↓⟩|\downarrow\rangle spin is a product state: the parton vacuum. However, in the presence of the full S​U​(2)SU(2) spin rotation symmetry, both parton images of |↑⟩|\uparrow\rangle and |↓⟩|\downarrow\rangle spins need to be entangled states for an Hdet structure. How to perform such a construction?

Interestingly, motivated by high-temperature superconductivity, Zhang and Sachdev[147] recently introduced an ancilla construction for correlated electronic states. In the special case of an undoped system, their construction exactly yields an Hdet QSL wavefunction respecting S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetry, whose fusion tensor has CPD-rank R=2R=2. Below we introduce their construction for the undoped case and reveal the connection with the Hdet structure.

In the Zhang-Sachdev (ZS) construction for a spin-1/21/2 system, for each spin on site-𝐫\mathbf{r}, three spin-12\frac{1}{2} fermionic parton orbitals are introduced: 𝖿𝐫,u(a),𝖿𝐫,v(a),𝖿𝐫,w(a)\mathsf{f}^{(a)}_{\mathbf{r},u},\mathsf{f}^{(a)}_{\mathbf{r},v},\mathsf{f}^{(a)}_{\mathbf{r},w}, where a=↑,↓a=\uparrow,\downarrow labels the spin, and u,v,wu,v,w labels the orbital.

The physical spin is represented as the spin-singlet formed by the u/vu/v fermions together with the spin-carrying ww-fermion. In terms of the fusion gate of 𝖿\mathsf{f}:

𝐂^𝐫ZS\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{\mathbf{r}}^{\text{ZS}} =|↓𝐫⟩⟨(↑𝐫,u↓𝐫,v−↓𝐫,u↑𝐫,v)↓𝐫,w|\displaystyle=|\downarrow_{\mathbf{r}}\rangle\langle\big(\uparrow_{\mathbf{r},u}\downarrow_{\mathbf{r},v}-\downarrow_{\mathbf{r},u}\uparrow_{\mathbf{r},v}\big)\downarrow_{\mathbf{r},w}|
+|↑𝐫⟩⟨(↑𝐫,u↓𝐫,v−↓𝐫,u↑𝐫,v)↑𝐫,w|\displaystyle+|\uparrow_{\mathbf{r}}\rangle\langle\big(\uparrow_{\mathbf{r},u}\downarrow_{\mathbf{r},v}-\downarrow_{\mathbf{r},u}\uparrow_{\mathbf{r},v}\big)\uparrow_{\mathbf{r},w}| (92)

Crucially, both parton images of |↑⟩|\uparrow\rangle and |↓⟩|\downarrow\rangle are entangled states in an S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetric fashion.

To translate the ZS construction to the Hdet construction, it is convenient to consider a mapping between a spin-12\frac{1}{2} system and a hard-core boson system different from Eq.(88). Instead of one hard-core boson orbital per site, introduce two hard-core boson orbitals per site b𝐫,𝐦(e)b_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{m}^{(e)}} labeled by 𝐦(e)=1,2\mathbf{m}^{(e)}=1,2:

|↑⟩=\displaystyle|\uparrow\rangle= |11,12⟩=b1†b2†|0⟩,\displaystyle|1_{1},1_{2}\rangle=b_{1}^{\dagger}b_{2}^{\dagger}|0\rangle, |↓⟩=\displaystyle|\downarrow\rangle= |11,02⟩=b1†|0⟩.\displaystyle|1_{1},0_{2}\rangle=b_{1}^{\dagger}|0\rangle. (93)

Both boson orbitals are considered as physical d.o.f., but the boson-11 orbital is always filled on every site.

Now consider a parton mean-field state |ΨM​F⟩|\Psi^{MF}\rangle involving S​U​(2)SU(2) symmetric mixing between the u/v/wu/v/w orbitals, with a total of 3​Ns​i​t​e3N_{site} filled single-particle parton states (half of which are spin-↑\uparrow). (In the simple limit when ww-fermion does not mix with u,vu,v-fermions, it is easy to see that Zhang-Sachdev construction goes back to the traditional Abrikosov fermion construction.) Next, similar to the construction before, we perform the particle-hole transformation for the spin-↓\downarrow partons only, for all three orbitals. The mean-field state is a product of two Slater determinants, one for ↑\uparrow-particles, one for ↓\downarrow-holes: |ΨM​F⟩=|Ψ(↑−f)⟩⊗|Ψ(↓−h)⟩|\Psi^{MF}\rangle=|\Psi^{(\uparrow-f)}\rangle\otimes|\Psi^{(\downarrow-h)}\rangle. Now the local fusion operator, in the b𝐫,𝐦(e)b_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{m}^{(e)}} formalism, can be written as:

𝐅^𝐫,1ZS=\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{F}}^{\rm ZS}_{\mathbf{r},1}= b𝐫,1†​(h𝐫,u​f𝐫,u−h𝐫,v​f𝐫,v),\displaystyle b_{\mathbf{r},1}^{\dagger}(h_{\mathbf{r},u}f_{\mathbf{r},u}-h_{\mathbf{r},v}f_{\mathbf{r},v}), 𝐅^𝐫,2ZS=\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{F}}^{\rm ZS}_{\mathbf{r},2}= b𝐫,2†​h𝐫,w​f𝐫,w,\displaystyle b_{\mathbf{r},2}^{\dagger}h_{\mathbf{r},w}f_{\mathbf{r},w}, (94)

whose corresponding 𝐂^𝐫,𝐦(e)ZS\hat{\mathbf{C}}^{\rm ZS}_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{m}^{(e)}} fusion gate are defined according to Eq.(III.2.5). The physical spin wavefunction is obtained via:

|ΨQ​S​LZS⟩≡∏𝐫,𝐦(e)=1,2𝐂^𝐫,𝐦(e)ZS​|Ψ(↑−f)⟩⊗|Ψ(↓−h)⟩.\displaystyle|\Psi^{\text{ZS}}_{QSL}\rangle\equiv\prod_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{m}^{(e)}=1,2}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{m}^{(e)}}^{\text{ZS}}|\Psi^{(\uparrow-f)}\rangle\otimes|\Psi^{(\downarrow-h)}\rangle. (95)

It is easy to see that |ΨQ​S​LZS⟩|\Psi^{\text{ZS}}_{QSL}\rangle is exactly an Hdet wavefunction of a rank-3 tensor Ti​j​kZST_{ijk}^{\text{ZS}} defined below, where i=1,2,…,2​Ns​i​t​e;j,k=1,2,…​3​Ns​i​t​e2i=1,2,...,2N_{site};\;j,k=1,2,...\frac{3N_{site}}{2}.

Introducing the filled single-particle parton states |ϕj(↑−f)⟩|\phi_{j}^{(\uparrow-f)}\rangle and |ϕk(↓−h)⟩|\phi_{k}^{(\downarrow-h)}\rangle, and an indexing of sites 𝐫l\mathbf{r}_{l} (l=1,2,…​Ns​i​t​el=1,2,...N_{site}), we define:

∙ If\displaystyle\bullet\text{ If } i=1,2,…,Ns​i​t​e, (first-half):\displaystyle i=1,2,...,N_{site},\text{ (first-half)}:
Ti​j​kZS\displaystyle T_{ijk}^{\text{ZS}} ≡⟨0|f𝐫i,u|ϕj(↑−f)⟩​⟨0|h𝐫i,u|ϕk(↓−h)⟩\displaystyle\equiv\langle 0|f_{\mathbf{r}_{i},u}|\phi_{j}^{(\uparrow-f)}\rangle\langle 0|h_{\mathbf{r}_{i},u}|\phi_{k}^{(\downarrow-h)}\rangle
−⟨0|f𝐫i,v|ϕj(↑−f)⟩​⟨0|h𝐫i,v|ϕk(↓−h)⟩.\displaystyle-\langle 0|f_{\mathbf{r}_{i},v}|\phi_{j}^{(\uparrow-f)}\rangle\langle 0|h_{\mathbf{r}_{i},v}|\phi_{k}^{(\downarrow-h)}\rangle.
∙ If\displaystyle\bullet\text{ If } i′≡(i−Ns​i​t​e)=1,2,…,Ns​i​t​e, (second-half):\displaystyle i^{\prime}\equiv(i-N_{site})=1,2,...,N_{site},\text{ (second-half)}:
Ti​j​kZS\displaystyle T_{ijk}^{\text{ZS}} ≡⟨0|f𝐫i′,w|ϕj(↑−f)⟩​⟨0|h𝐫i′,w|ϕk(↓−h)⟩.\displaystyle\equiv\langle 0|f_{\mathbf{r}_{i^{\prime}},w}|\phi_{j}^{(\uparrow-f)}\rangle\langle 0|h_{\mathbf{r}_{i^{\prime}},w}|\phi_{k}^{(\downarrow-h)}\rangle. (96)

For a given spin configuration |{s𝐫}⟩|\{s_{\mathbf{r}}\}\rangle (s𝐫=↑,↓s_{\mathbf{r}}=\uparrow,\downarrow), one builds a cubic sub-tensor Ti​j​ksubT_{ijk}^{\text{sub}} of TZST^{\text{ZS}} as follows. The first i=1,2,…,Ns​i​t​ei=1,2,...,N_{site} slices of Ti​j​ksubT_{ijk}^{\text{sub}} are fixed and are equal to the corresponding slices in the first-half of TZST^{\text{ZS}}. The last i′≡(i−Ns​i​t​e)=1,2,…,Ns​i​t​e2i^{\prime}\equiv(i-N_{site})=1,2,...,\frac{N_{site}}{2} slices of Ti​j​ksubT_{ijk}^{\text{sub}} are specified by the Ns​i​t​e2\frac{N_{site}}{2} spin-↑\uparrow positions in the spin configuration – one picks the corresponding slices in second-half of TZST^{\text{ZS}}. As illustrated in Fig.1(b), |ΨQ​S​LZS⟩|\Psi^{\text{ZS}}_{QSL}\rangle is defined via:

⟨{s𝐫}|ΨQ​S​LZS⟩=Hdet​(Tsub).\displaystyle\langle\{s_{\mathbf{r}}\}|\Psi^{\text{ZS}}_{QSL}\rangle=\text{Hdet}(T^{\text{sub}}). (97)

It is straightforward to further generalize the Zhang-Sachdev construction. One simple approach is introducing even more parton orbitals, leading to an Hdet structure with a larger CPD-rank. But even with the same number of parton orbitals (three spin-1/2 fermionic partons per site), because of the Clebsch-Gordon(CG) series 12⊗12⊗12=12⊕12⊕32\frac{1}{2}\otimes\frac{1}{2}\otimes\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2}\oplus\frac{1}{2}\oplus\frac{3}{2}, one can introduce yet another linearly independent S​U​(2)SU(2)-symmetric fusion channel, leading to a Hdet structure with CPD-rank R=3R=3. Denoting the fusion amplitudes in the two relevant CG channels as λ1,λ2\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}, one can show the generalized fusion operators:

𝐅^𝐫,1=\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{\mathbf{r},1}= b𝐫,1†​[λ1​(h𝐫,u​f𝐫,u−h𝐫,v​f𝐫,v)+λ2​(h𝐫,u​f𝐫,u−h𝐫,w​f𝐫,w)]\displaystyle b_{\mathbf{r},1}^{\dagger}\big[\lambda_{1}(h_{\mathbf{r},u}f_{\mathbf{r},u}-h_{\mathbf{r},v}f_{\mathbf{r},v})+\lambda_{2}(h_{\mathbf{r},u}f_{\mathbf{r},u}-h_{\mathbf{r},w}f_{\mathbf{r},w})\big]
=\displaystyle= b𝐫,1†​[(λ1+λ2)​h𝐫,u​f𝐫,u−λ1​h𝐫,v​f𝐫,v−λ2​h𝐫,w​f𝐫,w],\displaystyle b_{\mathbf{r},1}^{\dagger}\big[(\lambda_{1}+\lambda_{2})h_{\mathbf{r},u}f_{\mathbf{r},u}-\lambda_{1}h_{\mathbf{r},v}f_{\mathbf{r},v}-\lambda_{2}h_{\mathbf{r},w}f_{\mathbf{r},w}\big],
𝐅^𝐫,2=\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{\mathbf{r},2}= b𝐫,2†​[h𝐫,u​f𝐫,u+h𝐫,v​f𝐫,v+h𝐫,w​f𝐫,w].\displaystyle b_{\mathbf{r},2}^{\dagger}[h_{\mathbf{r},u}f_{\mathbf{r},u}+h_{\mathbf{r},v}f_{\mathbf{r},v}+h_{\mathbf{r},w}f_{\mathbf{r},w}]. (98)

The corresponding rank-3 fusion tensor TT and |ΨQSL⟩|\Psi_{\rm QSL}\rangle follow straightforwardly.

At the minimal level, these Hdet QSL constructions are expected to capture microscopic details of the spin wavefunctions beyond the traditional Abrikosov fermion method.

IV.2 Type-(B) example: FCI

Here, we consider a model Hamiltonian HCBH_{\text{CB}} on a torus, describing a partially filled Chern band with Chern number C=1C=1 together with interactions. HCBH_{\text{CB}} is fully constrained within the Chern band. It is well-known that such a Chern band can be mapped to the lowest Landau Level (LLL), preserving all crystalline symmetries[103, 71, 62]. Following this mapping, HCBH_{\text{CB}} can be exactly mapped to a model HLLLH_{\text{LLL}} inside the LLL, but with the lattice-potential/interaction breaking the Galilean invariance[103, 62]. The lattice translation and rotation symmetries are mapped into the discrete magnetic translation and rotation symmetries in the LLL[71, 62]. We only need to demonstrate how to construct the fusion tensor TT for the Hdet trial wavefunctions |Ψ(e)⟩|\Psi^{(e)}\rangle for HLLLH_{\text{LLL}}.

After choosing the (Ns(e))2(N^{(e)}_{s})^{2} discrete coherent states forming an overcomplete basis {|z(e)⟩}\{|z^{(e)}\rangle\}, z∈z\inFine-Grid, the construction of the fusion tensor TT is conceptually straightforward. Here, the main technical challenge in treating the overcomplete electronic basis is ensuring the correct linear dependence among the tensor slices Tz,…T_{z,...} with fixed zz. Namely, based on the definition of the fusion tensor Eq.(5), among the (Ns(e))2(N^{(e)}_{s})^{2} slices, only Ns(e)N^{(e)}_{s} are linearly independent. Thanks to the fusion amplitudes analytically computed in the showcase examples Eq.(33,52,53,60), this challenge is already resolved – these amplitudes automatically ensure the correct linear dependence.

Importantly, since the partons’ states are constructed from full real-space local orbitals after the change of viewpoint, as shown in Sec.V.3.8, we can write down the effective theories of Hdet states in the usual field-theory language, without resorting to the noncommutative field theories.

Given these fusion amplitudes, to construct the fusion tensor TT, we need only specify the filled parton single-particle states |ϕj(p)⟩|\phi^{(p)}_{j}\rangle. Comparing with FQH systems, the effect of the lattice-potential/interaction breaking the Galilean invariance in FCI systems is simply the hybridization between the parton Landau levels (as well as changing the shape/topology/Bloch-states of the Fermi sea in the case of CFL) (see Sec.V.3.8 for details).

As in all parton constructions, to obtain a symmetric electronic state, the parton states need to respect the symmetry in a projective fashion[136]. In general, one must perform a careful analysis of the projective symmetry group (PSG) for the filled parton states. Here, however, the situation is slightly simpler, since the PSG transformation is already encoded in single-particle states in each parton Landau level.

For example, consider a parton species-pp carrying electric charge q(p)=13q^{(p)}=\frac{1}{3}, as in the case of ν=13\nu=\frac{1}{3} FCI states. We may construct |ϕj(p)⟩|\phi^{(p)}_{j}\rangle using the Bloch basis.

First, we select a finite number of Landau levels for the parton, for instance, the LL index nL​L=0,1,2,…,nmaxn_{LL}=0,1,2,...,n_{\text{max}}. Next, if the original model HCBH_{\text{CB}} has lattice translation primitive vectors 𝐚1,𝐚2\mathbf{a}_{1},\mathbf{a}_{2}, then the corresponding magnetic translations T𝐚1(p),T𝐚2(p)T^{(p)}_{\mathbf{a}_{1}},T^{(p)}_{\mathbf{a}_{2}} for the parton do not commute, as dictated by the Girvin-MacDonald-Platzman (GMP) algebra:

T𝐚1(p)​T𝐚2(p)=ei​2​π3​T𝐚2(p)​T𝐚1(p)\displaystyle T^{(p)}_{\mathbf{a}_{1}}T^{(p)}_{\mathbf{a}_{2}}=e^{i\frac{2\pi}{3}}T^{(p)}_{\mathbf{a}_{2}}T^{(p)}_{\mathbf{a}_{1}} (99)

In order to construct the Bloch basis in a given parton LL with index nL​Ln_{LL}, one has to enlarge the unit cell by three times. One choice is to consider the pair of commuting magnetic translations: T𝐚1(p)​3,T𝐚2(p)T^{(p)3}_{\mathbf{a}_{1}},T^{(p)}_{\mathbf{a}_{2}}, and label their mutual eigenstate by the momentum 𝐤\mathbf{k}. As a result, we obtain the Bloch basis: {|ϕ𝐤(p)⟩n​L​L}\{|\phi^{(p)}_{\mathbf{k}}\rangle_{nLL}\}. (The details can be found in Ref.[62])

The filled parton states {|ϕ𝐤(p)⟩}\{|\phi^{(p)}_{\mathbf{k}}\rangle\} can then be represented as a linear superposition of the Bloch basis at each fixed 𝐤\mathbf{k}:

|ϕ𝐤(p)⟩=∑n=0nmaxAn,𝐤(p)⋅|ϕ𝐤(p)⟩n​L​L.\displaystyle|\phi^{(p)}_{\mathbf{k}}\rangle=\sum_{n=0}^{n_{\text{max}}}A^{(p)}_{n,\mathbf{k}}\cdot|\phi^{(p)}_{\mathbf{k}}\rangle_{nLL}. (100)

Given the superposition coefficients An,𝐤(p)A^{(p)}_{n,\mathbf{k}} for all parton species, the fusion tensor TT can be found by the multi-linear superposition of the fusion amplitudes in Eq.(33,52,53,60). Notice that these fusion amplitudes are computed in the infinite plane. Therefore, on a finite-size torus, the fusion amplitudes will have finite-size corrections, which are exponentially small when the system size ≫l\gg l (ll is the magnetic length, which is comparable with the lattice constant of HCBH_{\text{CB}}). For the system sizes that we studied in Sec.VI.3, we find numerically that these finite-size effects are negligible.

It is important to notice that An,𝐤(p)A^{(p)}_{n,\mathbf{k}} at different 𝐤\mathbf{k} points are still related by the magnetic translation T𝐚1(p)T^{(p)}_{\mathbf{a}_{1}}, sending |ϕ𝐤(p)⟩→|ϕ𝐤+𝐆23(p)⟩|\phi^{(p)}_{\mathbf{k}}\rangle\rightarrow|\phi^{(p)}_{\mathbf{k}+\frac{\mathbf{G}_{2}}{3}}\rangle; as well as the magnetic rotation RR, sending the triplet subspace (|ϕ𝐤(p)⟩,|ϕ𝐤+𝐆23(p)⟩,|ϕ𝐤+2​𝐆23(p)⟩)→(|ϕR​𝐤(p)⟩,|ϕR​𝐤+𝐆23(p)⟩,|ϕR​𝐤+2​𝐆23(p)⟩)(|\phi^{(p)}_{\mathbf{k}}\rangle,|\phi^{(p)}_{\mathbf{k}+\frac{\mathbf{G}_{2}}{3}}\rangle,|\phi^{(p)}_{\mathbf{k}+\frac{2\mathbf{G}_{2}}{3}}\rangle)\rightarrow(|\phi^{(p)}_{R\mathbf{k}}\rangle,|\phi^{(p)}_{R\mathbf{k}+\frac{\mathbf{G}_{2}}{3}}\rangle,|\phi^{(p)}_{R\mathbf{k}+\frac{2\mathbf{G}_{2}}{3}}\rangle). (𝐆2\mathbf{G}_{2} is the reciprocal vector conjugate to 𝐚2\mathbf{a}_{2}.) The details of the symmetry analysis are a bit technical, which we will present elsewhere due to the scope of this paper. But conceptually it is straightforward: the collection of symmetry-related |ϕ𝐤(p)⟩|\phi^{(p)}_{\mathbf{k}}\rangle (i.e., the projective 𝐤\mathbf{k}-star) must form an irreducible projective representation of the space group. (For interested readers, these projective irreps, particularly at the high symmetry 𝐤\mathbf{k} points, are already manifest in each parton LL. By changing the parton LL index nLLn_{\text{LL}}, all inequivalent projective irreps can be found.)

In Sec.VI.3, we will follow this prescription exactly to construct Hdet wavefunctions for FCI systems and numerically simulate them.

V Effective theories: Variational manifold path integral

In the context of fermionic-parton descriptions of fractionalized states of matter, the effective field theory involves fermionic fields coupled to gauge fields. To this end, there are two common ways to introduce the gauge fields into the formulation. The first way introduces gauge fields to implement the constraints to project the parton degrees of freedom back to physical degrees of freedom[15, 4, 63, 80, 134, 106, 113, 114, 136], which we call constraint gauge fields. The second way, on the other hand, involves writing the conserved parton currents as the curl of gauge fields 𝐣=∇×a\mathbf{j}=\nabla\times a, which we call hydrodynamic gauge fields[135, 18]. The second way leads to the K-matrix descriptions of general abelian topologically ordered states, which can be shown to be the dual theory of the constraint-gauge field description[134].

Both methods have advantages and disadvantages. The hydrodynamic approach directly captures the topological part of the effective field theory and allows a consistent construction of the edge effective theories. On the other hand, it is unclear how to treat partons filling bands with higher Chern numbers, especially when such bands lead to nonabelian topological orders. Importantly, the hydrodynamic approach cannot provide microscopic information of the system (e.g., parton band structure).

The constraint-gauge-field approach is more general and can capture parton bands with high Chern numbers. It also reveals microscopic information, such as parton band structures at the mean-field level, although it is unclear how to systematically improve beyond the mean-field (e.g., to obtain reliable energetics of the collective modes). Such a constraint-gauge-field approach usually starts with introducing a gauge group G​GGG (e.g., for Abrikosov-fermion construction, G​G=S​U​(2)GG=SU(2)[4, 3, 136]), whose generators are parton fermion bilinears. The projection (i.e., fusion in this paper) into the physical degrees of freedom is implemented by requiring the physical state to be a G​GGG gauge singlet. The problem is that, when the number of parton orbitals is large and multiple fusion channels are present, like in the Hdet case, the G​GGG singlet condition does not enforce the fusion gate.

To have a simple demonstration of this technical problem, consider a local fusion operator for a hard-core boson type-(A) model with two parton species:

𝐅^𝐫=\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{\mathbf{r}}= b𝐫†​P𝐫,\displaystyle b_{\mathbf{r}}^{\dagger}P_{\mathbf{r}}, P𝐫≡\displaystyle P_{\mathbf{r}}\equiv ∑α=1Rf𝐫,α(1)​f𝐫,α(2).\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha=1}^{R}f^{(1)}_{\mathbf{r},\alpha}f^{(2)}_{\mathbf{r},\alpha}. (101)

This fusion operator has a U⁡(R)U(R) gauge redundancy: f𝐫(1)†→f𝐫(1)†Uf_{\mathbf{r}}^{(1)\dagger}\rightarrow f_{\mathbf{r}}^{(1)\dagger}U, f𝐫(2)†→f𝐫(2)†UTf_{\mathbf{r}}^{(2)\dagger}\rightarrow f_{\mathbf{r}}^{(2)\dagger}U^{T} (f𝐫(p)†f_{\mathbf{r}}^{(p)\dagger} is the row vector formed by f𝐫,α(p)†f_{\mathbf{r},\alpha}^{(p)\dagger}), leaving the fusion operator invariant. However, the U⁡(R)U(R) singlet condition is not enough to enforce this fusion: for instance, the four-parton state (P𝐫†)2​|0all−p⟩(P_{\mathbf{r}}^{\dagger})^{2}|0^{\rm all-p}\rangle is also a U⁡(R)U(R) singlet, and nonzero for R>1R>1. One cannot specify the single ”parton-image state” of the hard-core boson: P𝐫†​|0all−p⟩P_{\mathbf{r}}^{\dagger}|0^{\rm all-p}\rangle solely by the U⁡(R)U(R) singlet condition, and the traditional way to construct effective theories cannot even apply.

In addition, it is known that the details of G​GGG are not relevant to the low-energy physics. As pointed out by a seminal work by Wen[136], the low-energy gauge fluctuations are controlled by the so-called invariant gauge group I​G​GIGG. For example, in the context of U⁡(1)U(1) QSL, I​G​G=U⁡(1)IGG=U(1). Physically, the parton state Higgs out the additional gauge modes in G​GGG, leaving only the I​G​GIGG at low-energy.

Here, we attempt to construct the effective theory avoiding the technical problem mentioned above. By introducing the concept of the variational manifold path integral, which is a path-integral version of the time-dependent variational principle, we show that the Hdet wavefunctions are associated with full microscopic effective field theory descriptions involving fermions coupled with fluctuating G​GGG lattice gauge fields. After the Higgs mechanism, the fluctuating I​G​GIGG lattice gauge fields remain at low energy. The physical outcome is two-fold. First, by writing down the effective field theories, one immediately knows the universal long-range properties associated with a Hdet ground state trial wavefunction, i.e., the nature of the quantum phase it belongs to. Second, given the efficient simulation methods for Hdet wavefunctions (e.g., see Sec.VI), in principle, one can obtain a microscopic effective field theory with reliable energetics, from which, for instance, one should be able to extract accurate dispersions of collective modes (e.g., magnetorotons in FCI.) to compare with results from other numerical methods (e.g., ED, QMC, DMRG).

We will first introduce the concept of the variational manifold path integral as an approximation technique, and demonstrate it in the well-known time-dependent Hartree-Fock treatment. Next, we apply this technique to construct the effective theories for Hdet wavefunctions.

V.1 Variational manifold path integral: General Setup

V.1.1 VMPI as the quantum version of the time-dependent variational principle

The variational manifold path integral (VMPI) introduced here is nothing but the path integral version of the well-known time-dependent variational principle(TDVP) [30, 36, 88, 76]. The basic idea of TDVP is to constrain the equation of motion of the quantum state in a variational manifold. Consider a manifold of normalized many-body variational wavefunctions |Φ⁡(𝝀)⟩|\Phi(\bm{\lambda})\rangle, smoothly parameterized by a real vector 𝝀=(λ1,λ2,…)\bm{\lambda}=(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},...), Dirac–Frenkel TDVP introduces a Lagrangian in the real-time formulation:

LTDVP=\displaystyle L_{\text{TDVP}}= ⟨Φ(𝝀(t))|i∂t−H|Φ(𝝀(t))⟩\displaystyle\langle\Phi(\bm{\lambda}(t))|\,i\partial_{t}-H\,|\Phi(\bm{\lambda}(t))\rangle
=\displaystyle= −∑aAa(𝝀)λ˙a−E(𝝀),\displaystyle-\sum_{a}A_{a}(\bm{\lambda})\,\dot{\lambda}_{a}-E(\bm{\lambda}), (102)

where HH is the many-body Hamiltonian, E⁡(𝝀)E(\bm{\lambda}) is the variational energy, and Aa​(𝝀)A_{a}(\bm{\lambda}) is the Berry connection:

Aa(𝝀)≡−i⟨Φ(𝝀)|∂a|Φ(𝝀)⟩.\displaystyle A_{a}(\bm{\lambda})\equiv-i\langle\Phi(\bm{\lambda})|\partial_{a}|\Phi(\bm{\lambda})\rangle. (103)

Crucially, the parameter 𝝀\bm{\lambda} is treated classically in TDVP, whose Euler-Lagrange equation of motion (EOM) is:

−∑bFa​b(𝝀)λ˙b=∂aE(𝝀),\displaystyle-\sum_{b}F_{ab}(\bm{\lambda})\,\dot{\lambda}_{b}=\partial_{a}E(\bm{\lambda}), (104)

where Fa​bF_{ab} is the Berry curvature:

Fa​b​(𝝀)≡∂aAb−∂bAa=2​Im​⟨∂aΦ|∂bΦ⟩.\displaystyle F_{ab}(\bm{\lambda})\equiv\partial_{a}A_{b}-\partial_{b}A_{a}=2\text{Im}\langle\partial_{a}\Phi|\partial_{b}\Phi\rangle. (105)

Although it cannot be rigorously justified in most practical situations, TDVP has been widely applied as an approximation method in quantum many-body systems[50, 76], with the time-dependent Hartree-Fock (TDHF) treatment as a specific example.

The standard practice of TDVP is to first identify the variational ground state |Φ⁡(𝝀¯)⟩|\Phi(\bar{\bm{\lambda}})\rangle via the static problem ∂aE⁡(𝝀¯)=0\partial_{a}E(\bar{\bm{\lambda}})=0. Then, for small perturbations 𝝀=𝝀¯+δ​𝝀\bm{\lambda}=\bar{\bm{\lambda}}+\delta\bm{\lambda}, the linearized EOM describes coupled harmonic oscillators. Introducing the Hessian matrix Va​b≡∂a∂bE⁡(𝝀¯)V_{ab}\equiv\partial_{a}\partial_{b}E(\bar{\bm{\lambda}}):

−∑bFa​b(𝝀¯)δλ˙b≈∑bVa​bδλb,\displaystyle-\sum_{b}F_{ab}(\bar{\bm{\lambda}})\,\delta\dot{\lambda}_{b}\approx\sum_{b}V_{ab}\,\delta\lambda_{b}, (106)

from which one can find collective modes (e.g., gapless Goldstone mode) dispersion[126, 111, 110]. Equivalently, Eq.(106) can be obtained from the Gaussian order Lagrangian LTDVPGL^{\rm G}_{\rm TDVP}:

LTDVP=\displaystyle L_{\rm TDVP}= LTDVPG+O(δ𝝀3), where:\displaystyle L^{\rm G}_{\rm TDVP}+O(\delta\bm{\lambda}^{3}),\;\;\text{ where:}
LTDVPG≡\displaystyle L^{\rm G}_{\rm TDVP}\equiv −12∑a​bFa​b(𝝀¯)δλaδλ˙b−12∑a​bVa​bδλaδλb.\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{ab}F_{ab}(\bar{\bm{\lambda}})\delta\lambda_{a}\delta\dot{\lambda}_{b}-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{ab}V_{ab}\delta\lambda_{a}\delta\lambda_{b}. (107)

For instance, consider the case that 𝝀\bm{\lambda} labels the spatial-dependent spin-density-wave order parameter; one can obtain the spin-wave dispersion from the EOM Eq.(106). However, due to the classical treatment of variational parameters, one cannot automatically obtain the quantum mechanics of the collective modes: e.g., magnons. In order to obtain magnons, one would have to quantize the spin-wave manually.

The natural improvement of the TDVP is to introduce quantum mechanics of the collective modes in the first place: instead of treating 𝝀\bm{\lambda} as classical variables, one treats it quantum mechanically via a path integral, which exactly leads to VMPI. This path integral treatment is not only elegant, but also necessary for sophisticated quantum many-body systems, which we will comment on shortly in Sec.V.3.

In order to define a path integral in the variational manifold, one needs to define an integration measure. A minimal requirement for a well-defined integration measure is reparameterization-invariance. Up to an unknown scalar factor f⁡(𝝀)f(\bm{\lambda}), this is fixed by the Fubini–Study quantum metric:

d​μ​(𝝀)≡f⁡(𝝀)​det[g⁡(𝝀)]​∏ad​λa,\displaystyle d\mu(\bm{\lambda})\equiv f(\bm{\lambda})\sqrt{\det\big[g(\bm{\lambda})\big]}\prod_{a}d\lambda_{a}, (108)

where the quantum metric

ga​b​(𝝀)≡Re​[⟨∂aΦ|∂bΦ⟩−⟨∂aΦ|Φ⟩​⟨Φ|∂bΦ⟩].\displaystyle g_{ab}(\bm{\lambda})\equiv\text{Re}[\langle\partial_{a}\Phi|\partial_{b}\Phi\rangle-\langle\partial_{a}\Phi|\Phi\rangle\langle\Phi|\partial_{b}\Phi\rangle]. (109)

With this integration measure, the TDVP action can be formulated as a path integral. We begin from the saddle-point state time-evolution amplitude

⟨Φ(𝝀¯)|𝒯exp[−i∫−T2T2dtH]|Φ(𝝀¯)⟩.\displaystyle\langle\Phi(\bar{\bm{\lambda}})|\,\mathcal{T}\exp\!\Big[-i\int_{-\frac{T}{2}}^{\frac{T}{2}}dt\,H\Big]|\Phi(\bar{\bm{\lambda}})\rangle. (110)

As in standard QFT analysis, eventually T→∞​(1−i​ϵ)T\rightarrow\infty(1-i\epsilon) when correlators are computed. Discretizing time into NN slices (labeled by ss) T=N⋅Δ​tT=N\cdot\Delta t, by inserting an operator for every time slice-ss:

Ω≡∫d​μ​(𝝀)​|Φ⁡(𝝀)⟩​⟨Φ⁡(𝝀)|,\displaystyle\Omega\equiv\int d\mu(\bm{\lambda})|\Phi(\bm{\lambda})\rangle\langle\Phi(\bm{\lambda})|, (111)

we define VMPI amplitude as an approximation for the amplitude above:

ZVMPI\displaystyle Z_{\text{VMPI}}
≡\displaystyle\equiv ∫∏s=1N−1d​μ​(𝝀s)​⟨Φ⁡(𝝀s+1)|e−i​Δ​t​H|Φ⁡(𝝀s)⟩,\displaystyle\int\prod_{s=1}^{N-1}d\mu(\bm{\lambda}_{s})\langle\Phi(\bm{\lambda}_{s+1})|e^{-i\Delta tH}|\Phi(\bm{\lambda}_{s})\rangle, (112)

where we identified 𝝀0=𝝀N=𝝀¯\bm{\lambda}_{0}=\bm{\lambda}_{N}=\bar{\bm{\lambda}}. In the continuum limit N→∞N\rightarrow\infty, we obtain the path integral of the TDVP action:

ZVMPI=∫𝒟⁡[𝝀⁡(t)]​exp⁡[i​∫d​t​LTDVP​(𝝀⁡(t))].\displaystyle Z_{\text{VMPI}}=\int\mathcal{D}[\bm{\lambda}(t)]\exp\Big[i\int dtL_{\text{TDVP}}(\bm{\lambda}(t))\Big]. (113)

In some situations, the unknown function f⁡(𝝀)f(\bm{\lambda}) can be further fixed by other requirements, such as requiring the operator Ω\Omega to contain a resolution of identity of a sub-Hilbert space, or the invariance under certain symmetries. Fortunately, for most situations in this paper, we do not need to fix f⁡(𝝀)f(\bm{\lambda}): We will primarily only consider the path integral up to Gaussian order fluctuations around its saddle point 𝝀⁡(t)=𝝀¯+δ​𝝀​(t)\bm{\lambda}(t)=\bar{\bm{\lambda}}+\delta\bm{\lambda}(t). At the Gaussian order, one may set f⁡(𝝀⁡(t))=f⁡(𝝀¯)f(\bm{\lambda}(t))=f(\bar{\bm{\lambda}}) to be the value at the saddle point, as shown below.

In typical interacting-field-theory analyses, the Gaussian order approximation can only be rigorously justified by additional expansion parameters, such as in the large-NN expansion or the semiclassical ℏ\hbar-expansion. For instance, in the ℏ\hbar-expansion, we have the scaling 𝝀¯∼O⁡(ℏ0)\bar{\bm{\lambda}}\sim O(\hbar^{0}) and δ​𝝀∼ℏ1/2\delta{\bm{\lambda}}\sim\hbar^{1/2}. It is easy to show that the effect of the deviation f⁡(𝝀¯+δ​𝝀​(t))−f⁡(𝝀¯)f(\bar{\bm{\lambda}}+\delta\bm{\lambda}(t))-f(\bar{\bm{\lambda}}) only contributes a subleading term, down by a factor of ℏ\hbar compared to the Gaussian order path integral taken with f⁡(𝝀¯)f(\bar{\bm{\lambda}}).

We would like to point out that we do not intend to justify the Gaussian-order approximation via rigorous expansion schemes in this paper; instead, we take a physics-motivated viewpoint: Gaussian-order fluctuations must be taken into account for quantum mechanics. So, at least one needs to identify the correct effective field theory for variational wavefunctions up to this order. In principle, one could generalize the VMPI analysis presented here beyond the Gaussian order, at which point the measure f⁡(𝛌)f(\bm{\lambda}) will become an important issue.

If the operator Ω\Omega contains a resolution of identity for the low-energy subspace of the quantum system of interest, then the VMPI treatment would be exact for the low-energy physics. However, in many interesting situations, including the situation in this paper, this may not be the case. As TDVP, in many situations, one may not be able to justify VMPI rigorously. Nevertheless, VMPI is a natural improvement of the TDVP, where quantum fluctuations of the variational parameters are considered.

V.1.2 Zero-point motion, Kähler condition, and VMPI Wavefunctions

VMPI alone is sufficient to define all time-ordered correlators of the variational parameters, such as ⟨𝒯⁡[δ​λa​(t)​δ​λb​(0)]⟩\langle\mathcal{T}[\delta\lambda_{a}(t)\delta\lambda_{b}(0)]\rangle. In this sense, it is already a full quantum field theory when 𝝀\bm{\lambda} describes spatially dependent fields. However, an important missing piece is how to translate δ​𝝀\delta\bm{\lambda} as quantum operators acting on physical wavefunctions in the original Hilbert space where the variational manifold {|Φ⁡(𝝀)⟩}\{|\Phi(\bm{\lambda})\rangle\} lives in. Without this Hilbert-space wavefunction translation, the correlators of δ​𝝀\delta\bm{\lambda} lose their microscopic meaning. It turns out that this translation becomes natural and canonical when an additional condition for the variational manifold is satisfied, the Kähler condition (defined below).

For example, the Gaussian order classical EOM Eq.(106) leads to classical eigenmodes as decoupled harmonic oscillators. In the VMPI treatment, we should expect these harmonic oscillators to be quantum mechanical with zero-point motion of δ​𝝀\delta\bm{\lambda}, where we assume the number of variational parameters N𝝀N_{\bm{\lambda}} to be even. One may view one half of δ​𝝀\delta\bm{\lambda} as qq’s, and the other half as pp’s. Namely, even the ground state of the VMPI treatment should not be viewed as a single state in the variational manifold |Φ⁡(𝝀¯)⟩|\Phi(\bar{\bm{\lambda}})\rangle. Instead, we expect VMPI to describe linear superpositions of variational wavefunctions:

|ΨVMPI⟩=∫d​μ​(𝝀)​|Φ⁡(𝝀)⟩​CΨ​(𝝀),\displaystyle|\Psi_{\rm VMPI}\rangle=\int d\mu(\bm{\lambda})|\Phi(\bm{\lambda})\rangle C_{\Psi}(\bm{\lambda}), (114)

where CΨ​(𝝀)C_{\Psi}(\bm{\lambda}) is superposition coefficient. This is the crucial conceptual improvement of VMPI over TDVP, in which one considers only a single |Φ⁡(𝝀)⟩|\Phi(\bm{\lambda})\rangle. Since the variational states {|Ψ⁡(𝝀)⟩}\{|\Psi(\bm{\lambda})\rangle\} are not orthogonal, CΨ​(𝝀)C_{\Psi}(\bm{\lambda}) is not unique for a given state. It is better to instead label |ΨVMPI⟩|\Psi_{\rm VMPI}\rangle by the VMPI wavefunction, defined as:

ΨVMPI​(𝝀)≡⟨Φ⁡(𝝀)|ΨVMPI⟩.\displaystyle\Psi_{\rm VMPI}(\bm{\lambda})\equiv\langle\Phi(\bm{\lambda})|\Psi_{\rm VMPI}\rangle. (115)

In defining VMPI, the key object is the operator Ω\Omega in Eq.(111), which we do not assume to contain an exact resolution of identity even for the low energy subspace of the Hamiltonian. The minimal requirement for a physically reasonable VMPI wavefunction |ΨVMPI⟩|\Psi_{\rm VMPI}\rangle, which describes the zero-point motion as well as possible quantum excitations for those harmonic oscillators, is to satisfy the condition:

Minimal Requirement: Ω|ΨVMPI⟩=|ΨVMPI⟩,\displaystyle\text{Minimal Requirement: }\Omega|\Psi_{\rm VMPI}\rangle=|\Psi_{\rm VMPI}\rangle, (116)

under a properly defined normalization factor in the integration measure d​μ​(𝝀)d\mu(\bm{\lambda}).

The time evolution of |ΨVMPI⟩|\Psi_{\rm VMPI}\rangle under VMPI is expected to lead to a Schrödinger-type equation for ΨVMPI​(𝝀,t)\Psi_{\rm VMPI}(\bm{\lambda},t). Intuitively, within Gaussian order approximation, we expect this quantum equation of motion to be identical to that obtained by canonically quantizing LTDVPGL_{\rm TDVP}^{G} in Eq.(107). It turns out that this intuition is not automatically satisfied.

At this point, we introduce the Kähler condition: the variational manifold near the saddle point |Φ⁡(𝛌)⟩|\Phi(\bm{\lambda})\rangle is Kähler if and only if there exists a local complex coordinate 𝛌⁡[𝐳¯,𝐳]\bm{\lambda}[\bar{\mathbf{z}},\mathbf{z}] with 𝐳=(z1,z2,…,zN𝛌2)\mathbf{z}=(z_{1},z_{2},...,z_{\frac{N_{\bm{\lambda}}}{2}}) and an unnormalized section |Φ~​(𝛌)⟩|\tilde{\Phi}(\bm{\lambda})\rangle, such that the |Φ~​(𝐳)⟩≡|Φ~​(𝛌⁡[𝐳¯,𝐳])⟩|\tilde{\Phi}(\mathbf{z})\rangle\equiv|\tilde{\Phi}(\bm{\lambda}[\bar{\mathbf{z}},\mathbf{z}])\rangle is holomorphic in 𝐳\mathbf{z} in the neighborhood of the saddle point.

Note that the variational wavefunction |Φ⁡(𝝀)⟩|\Phi(\bm{\lambda})\rangle is normalized. An unnormalized section |Φ~​(𝝀)⟩|\tilde{\Phi}(\bm{\lambda})\rangle means that |Φ~​(𝝀)⟩=c⁡(𝝀)​|Φ⁡(𝝀)⟩|\tilde{\Phi}(\bm{\lambda})\rangle=c(\bm{\lambda})|\Phi(\bm{\lambda})\rangle with some nonzero complex function c⁡(𝝀)c(\bm{\lambda}) near the saddle point. A many-body state |Φ~​(𝐳)⟩|\tilde{\Phi}(\mathbf{z})\rangle is holomorphic in 𝐳\mathbf{z} is defined as follows: In a fixed basis {|n⟩}\{|n\rangle\} spanning the full many-body Hilbert space (not the variational manifold), the complex overlap function ⟨n|Φ~​(𝐳)⟩\langle n|\tilde{\Phi}(\mathbf{z})\rangle is holomorphic in 𝐳\mathbf{z}(i.e., independent of 𝐳¯\bar{\mathbf{z}}), ∀n\forall n. WLOG, we will assume the saddle point is labeled by 𝐳=0\mathbf{z}=0: 𝝀⁡[𝟎,𝟎]=𝝀¯\bm{\lambda}[\bm{0},\bm{0}]=\bar{\bm{\lambda}}.

Under this condition, the Schrödinger-type equation for ΨVMPI​(𝝀,t)\Psi_{\rm VMPI}(\bm{\lambda},t) is elegant, and the previously mentioned intuition is nicely satisfied. Although it is a strong condition for variational manifold, as we will show, Hdet wavefunctions, the central topic of this paper, satisfy the Kähler condition.

Note that, as shown in later discussions, the convenient parameterization of Hdet wavefunctions contains gauge redundancies: pure gauge transformations of 𝝀\bm{\lambda} do not change the physical Hdet wavefunction. In this case, the dimension of the variational manifold is less than N𝝀N_{\bm{\lambda}}, and the map 𝐳→|Φ~​(𝐳)⟩\mathbf{z}\rightarrow|\tilde{\Phi}(\mathbf{z})\rangle is many-to-one. However, based on the Holomorphic-Constant-Rank Theorem[48], as long as this map has a constant Jacobian rank rr (i.e., the map is regular and the variational manifold is 2​r2r-dimensional), one can always perform a holomorphic change of variable 𝐳=𝐳⁡(𝝎)\mathbf{z}=\mathbf{z}(\bm{\omega}) such that in the new complex variable |Φ~​(𝝎)⟩≡|Φ~​(𝐳⁡(𝝎))⟩|\tilde{\Phi}(\bm{\omega})\rangle\equiv|\tilde{\Phi}(\mathbf{z}(\bm{\omega}))\rangle only depends on (ω1,ω2,..,ωr)(\omega_{1},\omega_{2},..,\omega_{r}). The map (ω1,ω2,..,ωr)→|Φ~(𝝎)⟩(\omega_{1},\omega_{2},..,\omega_{r})\rightarrow|\tilde{\Phi}(\bm{\omega})\rangle is then bijective. Consequently, WLOG, in this subsection, we will assume the dimension of the variational manifold is N𝛌N_{\bm{\lambda}} and the map 𝐳→|Φ~​(𝐳)⟩\mathbf{z}\rightarrow|\tilde{\Phi}(\mathbf{z})\rangle is locally bijective. Mathematically, 𝐳\mathbf{z} is a local coordinate chart of the variational manifold.

The Kähler condition gives the variational manifold an elegant local geometry. Let’s consider a generic overlap of two unnormalized variational wavefunctions near the saddle point 𝐳=𝟎\mathbf{z}=\mathbf{0}, labeled by ii and ff. Defining

ℳ⁡(𝐳¯f,𝐳i)≡log⁡[⟨Φ~​(𝐳f)|Φ~​(𝐳i)⟩],\displaystyle\mathcal{M}(\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{f},\mathbf{z}_{i})\equiv\log[\langle\tilde{\Phi}(\mathbf{z}_{f})|\tilde{\Phi}(\mathbf{z}_{i})\rangle], (117)

the holomorphic and Hermiticity condition of overlap dictates its most general Taylor expansion up to the quadratic order:

ℳ⁡(𝐳¯f,𝐳i)=\displaystyle\mathcal{M}(\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{f},\mathbf{z}_{i})= c+𝐚T​𝐳i+𝐚¯T​𝐳¯f\displaystyle c+\mathbf{a}^{T}\mathbf{z}_{i}+\bar{\mathbf{a}}^{T}\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{f}
+\displaystyle+ 12​[𝐳iT​P​𝐳i+𝐳¯fT​P¯​𝐳¯f]+𝐳iT​G​𝐳¯f+O⁡(𝐳3),\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\big[\mathbf{z}_{i}^{T}P\mathbf{z}_{i}+\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{f}^{T}\bar{P}\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{f}\big]+\mathbf{z}_{i}^{T}G\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{f}+O(\mathbf{z}^{3}), (118)

where we use matrix formulation: PT=P,G†=GP^{T}=P,G^{\dagger}=G, and 𝐳\mathbf{z} is a column vector.

Perform a holomorphic gauge transformation:

|Φ~​(𝐳)⟩→e−h⁡(𝐳)​|Φ~​(𝐳)⟩,\displaystyle|\tilde{\Phi}(\mathbf{z})\rangle\rightarrow e^{-h(\mathbf{z})}|\tilde{\Phi}(\mathbf{z})\rangle, (119)

after which:

ℳ⁡(𝐳¯f,𝐳i)→ℳ⁡(𝐳¯f,𝐳i)−h⁡(𝐳i)−h⁡(𝐳f)¯.\displaystyle\mathcal{M}(\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{f},\mathbf{z}_{i})\rightarrow\mathcal{M}(\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{f},\mathbf{z}_{i})-h(\mathbf{z}_{i})-\overline{h(\mathbf{z}_{f})}. (120)

If we choose h⁡(𝐳)=c2+𝐚T​𝐳+12​𝐳T​P​𝐳h(\mathbf{z})=\frac{c}{2}+\mathbf{a}^{T}\mathbf{z}+\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{z}^{T}P\mathbf{z}, the function ℳ\mathcal{M} only has the GG-term left, which is the gauge we will be working in for the discussion below:

ℳ⁡(𝐳¯f,𝐳i)=𝐳iT​G​𝐳¯f+O⁡(𝐳3)\displaystyle\mathcal{M}(\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{f},\mathbf{z}_{i})=\mathbf{z}_{i}^{T}G\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{f}+O(\mathbf{z}^{3}) (121)

When 𝐳i=𝐳f=𝐳\mathbf{z}_{i}=\mathbf{z}_{f}=\mathbf{z}, ℳ⁡(𝐳¯,𝐳)=𝐳T​G​𝐳¯+O⁡(𝐳3)\mathcal{M}(\bar{\mathbf{z}},\mathbf{z})=\mathbf{z}^{T}G\bar{\mathbf{z}}+O(\mathbf{z}^{3}) is the log of the positive wavefunction norm square of |Φ~​(𝐳)⟩|\tilde{\Phi}(\mathbf{z})\rangle, and GG encodes the real Fubini-Study quantum metric g⁡(𝝀¯)g(\bar{\bm{\lambda}}) (see Eq.(109)). To see this, consider the normalized state:

|Φ(𝐳)⟩≡e−ℳ(𝐳¯,𝐳)/2|Φ~(𝐳)⟩.\displaystyle|\Phi(\mathbf{z})\rangle\equiv e^{-\mathcal{M}(\bar{\mathbf{z}},\mathbf{z})/2}|\tilde{\Phi}(\mathbf{z})\rangle. (122)

We warn the readers that here, we should have written it as |Φ⁡(𝐳¯,𝐳)⟩|\Phi(\bar{\mathbf{z}},\mathbf{z})\rangle, since the normalization factor depends on 𝐳¯\bar{\mathbf{z}}. However, to simplify notation, we still use a single 𝐳\mathbf{z} to label |Φ⁡(𝐳)⟩|\Phi(\mathbf{z})\rangle, which is the only notation in this section violating holomorphic convention.

Introducing the real coordinates

zα≡12(qα+ipα),α=1,2,..,N𝝀2,\displaystyle z_{\alpha}\equiv\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(q_{\alpha}+ip_{\alpha}),\;\;\alpha=1,2,..,\frac{N_{\bm{\lambda}}}{2}, (123)

and the real and imaginary parts of GG:

G=S+i​T,ST=S,TT=−T,\displaystyle G=S+iT,\;\;S^{T}=S,\;\;T^{T}=-T, (124)

after grouping (q,p)(q,p) into the real variational parameter vector 𝝀⁡[𝐳¯,𝐳]=(𝒒,𝒑)\bm{\lambda}[\bar{\mathbf{z}},\mathbf{z}]=(\bm{q},\bm{p}) (with 𝝀¯=𝟎\bar{\bm{\lambda}}=\bm{0}), direct calculation shows that the matrix g⁡(𝝀¯)g(\bar{\bm{\lambda}}) is:

g⁡(𝝀¯)=12​(ST−TS)q​p.\displaystyle g(\bar{\bm{\lambda}})=\frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}S&T\\ -T&S\end{pmatrix}_{qp}. (125)

Since 𝐳\mathbf{z} is a local coordinate chart, g⁡(𝝀¯)g(\bar{\bm{\lambda}}) must be positive definite, so is GG. After a linear transformation of 𝐳\mathbf{z}, GG can be brought to identity. We arrive at the canonical coordinate:

ℳ⁡(𝐳¯f,𝐳i)=𝐳iT​𝐳¯f+O⁡(𝐳3).\displaystyle\mathcal{M}(\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{f},\mathbf{z}_{i})=\mathbf{z}_{i}^{T}\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{f}+O(\mathbf{z}^{3}). (126)

Based on Eq.(117,122), the overlap of normalized states in this coordinate is:

⟨Φ⁡(𝐳f)|Φ⁡(𝐳i)⟩=exp​[−𝐳fT​𝐳¯f+𝐳iT​𝐳¯i2+𝐳iT​𝐳¯f+O⁡(𝐳3)].\displaystyle\langle\Phi(\mathbf{z}_{f})|\Phi(\mathbf{z}_{i})\rangle=\text{exp}\Big[-\frac{\mathbf{z}^{T}_{f}\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{f}+\mathbf{z}^{T}_{i}\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{i}}{2}+\mathbf{z}^{T}_{i}\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{f}+O(\mathbf{z}^{3})\Big]. (127)

From this, the Berry curvature matrix F⁡(𝝀¯)F(\bar{\bm{\lambda}}) in the real (q,p)(q,p)-coordinate can be computed (see Eq.(105)):

g⁡(𝝀¯)=12​(𝟏𝟎𝟎𝟏)q​p,F⁡(𝝀¯)=(𝟎𝟏−1𝟎)q​p.\displaystyle g(\bar{\bm{\lambda}})=\frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{1}&\mathbf{0}\\ \mathbf{0}&\mathbf{1}\end{pmatrix}_{qp},\;\;F(\bar{\bm{\lambda}})=\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{0}&\mathbf{1}\\ \mathbf{-}1&\mathbf{0}\end{pmatrix}_{qp}. (128)

As a coordinate-independent statement, g,Fg,F satisfy

F​g−1​F=−4​g,\displaystyle Fg^{-1}F=-4g, (129)

a consequence of the Kähler condition.

The VMPI wavefunction in Eq.(115) can now be written using 𝐳,𝐳¯\mathbf{z},\bar{\mathbf{z}}:

ΨVMPI​(𝐳¯,𝐳)≡⟨Φ⁡(𝐳)|ΨVMPI⟩.\displaystyle\Psi_{\rm VMPI}(\bar{\mathbf{z}},\mathbf{z})\equiv\langle\Phi(\mathbf{z})|\Psi_{\rm VMPI}\rangle. (130)

We also consider another version of VMPI wavefunction, defined using the unnormalized variational state:

Ψ~​(𝐳¯)≡⟨Φ~​(𝐳)|ΨVMPI⟩,\displaystyle\tilde{\Psi}(\bar{\mathbf{z}})\equiv\langle\tilde{\Phi}(\mathbf{z})|\Psi_{\rm VMPI}\rangle, (131)

which is explicitly holomorphic in 𝐳¯\bar{\mathbf{z}}. Eq.(122) gives the relation between these two versions:

ΨVMPI​(𝐳¯,𝐳)=e−ℳ⁡(𝐳¯,𝐳)2​Ψ~​(𝐳¯).\displaystyle\Psi_{\rm VMPI}(\bar{\mathbf{z}},\mathbf{z})=e^{-\frac{\mathcal{M}(\bar{\mathbf{z}},\mathbf{z})}{2}}\tilde{\Psi}(\bar{\mathbf{z}}). (132)

We can now examine the minimal requirement Eq.(116). Writing Ω=∫d​μ​(𝐳i)​|Φ⁡(𝐳i)⟩​⟨Φ⁡(𝐳i)|\Omega=\int d\mu(\mathbf{z}_{i})|\Phi(\mathbf{z}_{i})\rangle\langle\Phi(\mathbf{z}_{i})|, this requirement is equivalent to:

Ψ~​(𝐳¯f)=∫d​μ​(𝐳i)​exp​[ℳ⁡(𝐳¯f,𝐳i)−ℳ⁡(𝐳¯i,𝐳i)]​Ψ~​(𝐳¯i).\displaystyle\tilde{\Psi}(\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{f})=\int d\mu(\mathbf{z}_{i})\text{exp}\big[\mathcal{M}(\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{f},\mathbf{z}_{i})-\mathcal{M}(\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{i},\mathbf{z}_{i})\big]\tilde{\Psi}(\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{i}). (133)

At the Gaussian order, it is safe to set the integral measure as:

d​μG​(𝐳)≡∏αd2​zαπ=∏αd​Re​[zα]​d​Im​[zα]π.\displaystyle d\mu^{\rm G}(\mathbf{z})\equiv\prod_{\alpha}\frac{d^{2}z_{\alpha}}{\pi}=\prod_{\alpha}\frac{d{\rm Re}[z_{\alpha}]d{\rm Im}[z_{\alpha}]}{\pi}. (134)

In addition, with Eq.(126), the minimal requirement at the Gaussian order becomes

Ψ~​(𝐳¯f)=∫d​μG​(𝐳i)​exp​[−𝐳iT​𝐳¯i+𝐳iT​𝐳¯f]​Ψ~​(𝐳¯i),\displaystyle\tilde{\Psi}(\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{f})=\int d\mu^{\rm G}(\mathbf{z}_{i})\text{exp}\big[-\mathbf{z}_{i}^{T}\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{i}+\mathbf{z}_{i}^{T}\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{f}\big]\tilde{\Psi}(\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{i}), (135)

which, by standard Bargmann calculus, is always satisfied. It means that, although Ω\Omega may not be a resolution of identity in the low-energy subspace of the original Hamiltonian, it is a resolution of identity for the VMPI wavefunctions, at the Gaussian order.

V.1.3 VMPI Schrödinger equation, the ground state and excited states

Representing the quadratic variational energy using the Hessian matrix VV:

δ​E​[𝐳¯,𝐳]≡\displaystyle\delta E[\bar{\mathbf{z}},\mathbf{z}]\equiv 12​𝝀​[𝐳¯,𝐳]T​V​𝝀​[𝐳¯,𝐳]\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\bm{\lambda}[\bar{\mathbf{z}},\mathbf{z}]^{T}V\bm{\lambda}[\bar{\mathbf{z}},\mathbf{z}]
≡\displaystyle\equiv 𝐳T​A​𝐳¯+12​[𝐳T​B​𝐳+𝐳¯T​B¯​𝐳¯],\displaystyle\mathbf{z}^{T}A\bar{\mathbf{z}}+\frac{1}{2}\Big[\mathbf{z}^{T}B\mathbf{z}+\bar{\mathbf{z}}^{T}\bar{B}\bar{\mathbf{z}}\Big], (136)

where we defined the 𝐳,𝐳¯\mathbf{z},\bar{\mathbf{z}}-basis N𝝀2×N𝝀2\frac{N_{\bm{\lambda}}}{2}\times\frac{N_{\bm{\lambda}}}{2} matrices A,BA,B, satisfying A†=A,BT=BA^{\dagger}=A,B^{T}=B. The Gaussian order TDVP Lagrangian (see Eq.(107)) in the 𝐳\mathbf{z} coordinate is:

LTDVPG\displaystyle L_{\rm TDVP}^{\rm G} =i2​(𝐳˙T​𝐳¯−𝐳T​𝐳¯˙)−δ​E​[𝐳¯,𝐳]\displaystyle=\frac{i}{2}\left(\dot{\mathbf{z}}^{T}\bar{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{z}^{T}\dot{\bar{\mathbf{z}}}\right)-\delta E[\bar{\mathbf{z}},\mathbf{z}]
=i2​(𝐳˙T​𝐳¯−𝐳T​𝐳¯˙)−𝐳T​A​𝐳¯−12​[𝐳T​B​𝐳+𝐳¯T​B¯​𝐳¯].\displaystyle=\frac{i}{2}\left(\dot{\mathbf{z}}^{T}\bar{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{z}^{T}\dot{\bar{\mathbf{z}}}\right)-\mathbf{z}^{T}A\bar{\mathbf{z}}-\frac{1}{2}\left[\mathbf{z}^{T}B\mathbf{z}+\bar{\mathbf{z}}^{T}\bar{B}\bar{\mathbf{z}}\right]. (137)

Under VMPI time-evolution, we can now write down the Schrödinger-type equation for Ψ~​(𝐳¯,t)\tilde{\Psi}(\bar{\mathbf{z}},t). The short-time evolution over a single VMPI step (see Eq.(112)) leads to the linear-Δ​t\Delta t change of VMPI wavefunction:

ΨVMPI​(𝐳f,𝐳¯f,t+Δ​t)\displaystyle\Psi_{\rm VMPI}(\mathbf{z}_{f},\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{f},t+\Delta t)
=\displaystyle= ∫d​μ​(𝐳i)​⟨Φ⁡(𝐳f)|e−i​Δ​t​H|Φ⁡(𝐳i)⟩​ΨVMPI​(𝐳i,𝐳¯i,t)\displaystyle\int d\mu(\mathbf{z}_{i})\langle\Phi(\mathbf{z}_{f})|e^{-i\Delta tH}|\Phi(\mathbf{z}_{i})\rangle\Psi_{\rm VMPI}(\mathbf{z}_{i},\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{i},t)
≐\displaystyle\doteq ∫d​μ​(𝐳i)​⟨Φ⁡(𝐳f)|Φ⁡(𝐳i)⟩​(1−i​Δ​t​ℋVMPI​(𝐳¯f,𝐳i))\displaystyle\int d\mu(\mathbf{z}_{i})\langle\Phi(\mathbf{z}_{f})|\Phi(\mathbf{z}_{i})\rangle\big(1-i\Delta t\mathcal{H}_{\rm VMPI}(\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{f},\mathbf{z}_{i})\big)
⋅ΨVMPI​(𝐳i,𝐳¯i,t),\displaystyle\cdot\Psi_{\rm VMPI}(\mathbf{z}_{i},\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{i},t), (138)

where the Hamiltonian matrix element ℋVMPI​(𝐳¯f,𝐳i)\mathcal{H}_{\rm VMPI}(\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{f},\mathbf{z}_{i}) is defined as:

ℋVMPI​(𝐳¯f,𝐳i)≡⟨Φ~​(𝐳f)|H|Φ~​(𝐳i)⟩⟨Φ~​(𝐳f)|Φ~​(𝐳i)⟩.\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\rm VMPI}(\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{f},\mathbf{z}_{i})\equiv\frac{\langle\tilde{\Phi}(\mathbf{z}_{f})|H|\tilde{\Phi}(\mathbf{z}_{i})\rangle}{\langle\tilde{\Phi}(\mathbf{z}_{f})|\tilde{\Phi}(\mathbf{z}_{i})\rangle}. (139)
