Note that we use the unnormalized variational states in ℋVMPI\mathcal{H}_{\rm VMPI} for the holomorphic property, which, together with the Hermiticity property, lead to the most general quadratic expansion of ℋVMPI\mathcal{H}_{\rm VMPI}:

ℋVMPI​(𝐳¯f,𝐳i)=\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\rm VMPI}(\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{f},\mathbf{z}_{i})= E⁡(𝝀¯)+𝒓T​𝐳i+𝒓¯T​𝐳¯f+𝐳iT​C​𝐳¯f\displaystyle E(\bar{\bm{\lambda}})+\bm{r}^{T}\mathbf{z}_{i}+\bar{\bm{r}}^{T}\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{f}+\mathbf{z}_{i}^{T}C\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{f}
+\displaystyle+ 12​[𝐳iT​D​𝐳i+𝐳¯fT​D¯​𝐳¯f]+O⁡(𝐳3),\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\Big[\mathbf{z}_{i}^{T}D\mathbf{z}_{i}+\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{f}^{T}\bar{D}\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{f}\Big]+O(\mathbf{z}^{3}), (140)

The saddle-point condition dictates no linear term is present and 𝒓=0\bm{r}=0. The matching condition with δ​E​[𝐳¯,𝐳]\delta E[\bar{\mathbf{z}},\mathbf{z}] when 𝐳i=𝐳f=𝐳\mathbf{z}_{i}=\mathbf{z}_{f}=\mathbf{z} dictates C=AC=A and D=BD=B. Namely, ℋVMPI≡ℋVMPIG+O⁡(𝐳3)\mathcal{H}_{\rm VMPI}\equiv\mathcal{H}_{\rm VMPI}^{\rm G}+O(\mathbf{z}^{3}), and the Gaussian order

ℋVMPIG​(𝐳¯f,𝐳i)=\displaystyle\mathcal{H}^{\rm G}_{\rm VMPI}(\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{f},\mathbf{z}_{i})= E⁡(𝝀¯)+𝐳iT​A​𝐳¯f\displaystyle E(\bar{\bm{\lambda}})+\mathbf{z}_{i}^{T}A\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{f}
+\displaystyle+ 12​[𝐳iT​B​𝐳i+𝐳¯fT​B¯​𝐳¯f].\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\Big[\mathbf{z}_{i}^{T}B\mathbf{z}_{i}+\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{f}^{T}\bar{B}\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{f}\Big]. (141)

This is the point where the Kähler condition plays a crucial role: without the holomorphic property provided by the Kähler condition, even at the Gaussian order, the form of the matrix element ℋVMPIG​(𝐳¯f,𝐳i)\mathcal{H}^{\rm G}_{\rm VMPI}(\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{f},\mathbf{z}_{i}) cannot be fixed by the diagonal element δ​E​[𝐳,𝐳¯]\delta E[\mathbf{z},\bar{\mathbf{z}}]. Note that the TDVP Lagrangian only depends on the diagonal elements. Therefore, without the Kähler condition, the VMPI quantization and canonical quantization of LTDVPGL^{\rm G}_{\rm TDVP} are generally different.

Utilizing Gaussian order d​μG​(𝐳)d\mu^{\rm G}(\mathbf{z}), Eq.(127) and the Bargmann calculus, one can replace 𝐳i\mathbf{z}_{i} in ℋVMPI\mathcal{H}_{\rm VMPI} by the partial derivative column vector ∂𝐳¯f\partial_{\bar{\mathbf{z}}_{f}} after performing the integral in Eq.(138). We arrive at the Gaussian-order VMPI Schrödinger equation for VMPI wavefunction Ψ~\tilde{\Psi}:

i​∂tΨ~​(𝐳¯,t)=HVMPIG​Ψ~​(𝐳¯,t),\displaystyle i\partial_{t}\tilde{\Psi}(\bar{\mathbf{z}},t)=H^{\rm G}_{\rm VMPI}\tilde{\Psi}(\bar{\mathbf{z}},t), (142)

with the VMPI Hamiltonian defined as

HVMPIG=E(𝝀¯)+𝐳¯TAT∂𝐳¯+12[∂𝐳¯TB∂𝐳¯+𝐳¯TB¯𝐳¯],\displaystyle H^{\rm G}_{\rm VMPI}=E(\bar{\bm{\lambda}})+\bar{\mathbf{z}}^{T}A^{T}\partial_{\bar{\mathbf{z}}}+\frac{1}{2}\Big[\partial_{\bar{\mathbf{z}}}^{T}B\partial_{\bar{\mathbf{z}}}+\bar{\mathbf{z}}^{T}\bar{B}\bar{\mathbf{z}}\Big], (143)

where, according to Bargmann calculus, ∂𝐳¯\partial_{\bar{\mathbf{z}}} in AA-term stands to the right of 𝐳¯\bar{\mathbf{z}}.

HVMPIGH^{\rm G}_{\rm VMPI} is exactly equivalent to the canonically quantized LTDVPGL^{\rm G}_{\rm TDVP} in Eq.(137). In the (q,p)(q,p)-coordinate introduced in Eq.(123) , the Berry’s phase term in LTDVPGL^{\rm G}_{\rm TDVP} becomes:

LTDVPBerry=12​∑α(pα​q˙α−p˙α​qα)≐∑αpα​q˙α.\displaystyle L^{\rm Berry}_{\rm TDVP}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\alpha}(p_{\alpha}\dot{q}_{\alpha}-\dot{p}_{\alpha}q_{\alpha})\doteq\sum_{\alpha}p_{\alpha}\dot{q}_{\alpha}. (144)

where ≐\doteq means up to a total time-derivative. Canonical quantization replaces (q,p)(q,p) by operators, satisfying:

[q^α,p^β]=i​δα​β,[q^α,q^β]=0,[p^α,p^β]=0.\displaystyle[\hat{q}_{\alpha},\hat{p}_{\beta}]=i\delta_{\alpha\beta},\;\;[\hat{q}_{\alpha},\hat{q}_{\beta}]=0,\;\;[\hat{p}_{\alpha},\hat{p}_{\beta}]=0. (145)

After introducing canonical boson operators:

b^α≡12​(q^α+i​p^α),[b^α,b^β†]=δα​β,[b^α,b^β]=0,\displaystyle\hat{b}_{\alpha}\equiv\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(\hat{q}_{\alpha}+i\hat{p}_{\alpha}),\;\;[\hat{b}_{\alpha},\hat{b}^{\dagger}_{\beta}]=\delta_{\alpha\beta},\;\;[\hat{b}_{\alpha},\hat{b}_{\beta}]=0, (146)

we obtain the normal-ordered canonical quantization Hamiltonian:

Hcan.G=E⁡(𝝀¯)+𝒃^†T​AT​𝒃^+12​[𝒃^T​B​𝒃^+𝒃^†T​B¯​𝒃^†].\displaystyle H^{\rm G}_{\rm can.}=E(\bar{\bm{\lambda}})+\hat{\bm{b}}^{\dagger T}A^{T}\hat{\bm{b}}+\frac{1}{2}\Big[\hat{\bm{b}}^{T}B\hat{\bm{b}}+\hat{\bm{b}}^{\dagger T}\bar{B}\hat{\bm{b}}^{\dagger}\Big]. (147)

If we use the normalized overcomplete coherent state basis {|𝐳⟩}\{|\mathbf{z}\rangle\} satisfying b^α​|𝐳⟩=zα​|𝐳⟩\hat{b}_{\alpha}|\mathbf{z}\rangle=z_{\alpha}|\mathbf{z}\rangle, a normalized quantum state |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle in this canonical quantization Hilbert space can be written as a phase-space wavefunction ψ⁡(𝐳,𝐳¯)≡⟨𝐳|ψ⟩\psi(\mathbf{z},\bar{\mathbf{z}})\equiv\langle\mathbf{z}|\psi\rangle. ψ⁡(𝐳,𝐳¯)\psi(\mathbf{z},\bar{\mathbf{z}}) can be shown to have the form ψ⁡(𝐳,𝐳¯)=e−𝐳T​𝐳¯2​ψ~​(𝐳¯)\psi(\mathbf{z},\bar{\mathbf{z}})=e^{-\frac{\mathbf{z}^{T}\bar{\mathbf{z}}}{2}}\tilde{\psi}(\bar{\mathbf{z}}), where ψ~​(𝐳¯)\tilde{\psi}(\bar{\mathbf{z}}) is holomorphic in 𝐳¯\bar{\mathbf{z}}. It is well known that when acting on ψ~​(𝐳¯)\tilde{\psi}(\bar{\mathbf{z}}), the boson operators can be identified as:

b^α↔∂∂z¯α,b^α†↔z¯α.\displaystyle\hat{b}_{\alpha}\leftrightarrow\frac{\partial}{\partial\bar{z}_{\alpha}},\;\;\hat{b}^{\dagger}_{\alpha}\leftrightarrow\bar{z}_{\alpha}. (148)

Therefore, the VMPI Hamiltonian HVMPIGH^{\rm G}_{\rm VMPI} in Eq.(143) and Hcan.GH^{\rm G}_{\rm can.} in Eq.(147) are equivalent.

Under the Kähler condition, we now know that the Gaussian-order VMPI has full microscopic meaning. The ground state and excited states of the quadratic Hamiltonian Hcan.GH^{\rm G}_{\rm can.} are easily obtained by Bogoliubov transformation – leading to the eigen boson modes. Equivalently, the ground state and excited states for the VMPI wavefunction – the linear superpositions of the original variational wavefunction |Φ⁡(𝝀)⟩|\Phi(\bm{\lambda})\rangle, are also fully solved. The VMPI correlators of variational parameters such as ⟨𝒯⁡[δ​λa​(t)​δ​λb​(0)]⟩\langle\mathcal{T}[\delta\lambda_{a}(t)\delta\lambda_{b}(0)]\rangle can now be microscopically translated as the correlators of concrete quantum operators acting on VMPI wavefunctions using the dictionary Eq.(146) and Eq.(148).

Practically, the Bogoliubov transformation boils down to finding positive-frequency ων\omega_{\nu} eigen boson operators:

γ^ν†=𝐱νT​𝒃^†−𝐲νT​𝒃^,γ^ν=𝐱ν†​𝒃^−𝐲ν†​𝒃^†,\displaystyle\hat{\gamma}^{\dagger}_{\nu}=\mathbf{x}^{T}_{\nu}\hat{\bm{b}}^{\dagger}-\mathbf{y}^{T}_{\nu}\hat{\bm{b}},\;\;\;\;\hat{\gamma}_{\nu}=\mathbf{x}^{\dagger}_{\nu}\hat{\bm{b}}-\mathbf{y}^{\dagger}_{\nu}\hat{\bm{b}}^{\dagger}, (149)

where (column) eigenvector (𝐱ν,𝐲ν)(\mathbf{x}_{\nu},\mathbf{y}_{\nu}) satisfies:

(ATB¯−B−A)​(𝐱ν𝐲ν)=ων​(𝐱ν𝐲ν),\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}A^{T}&\bar{B}\\ -B&-A\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{x}_{\nu}\\ \mathbf{y}_{\nu}\end{pmatrix}=\omega_{\nu}\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{x}_{\nu}\\ \mathbf{y}_{\nu}\end{pmatrix},
𝐱ν†​𝐱μ−𝐲ν†​𝐲μ=δν​μ,𝐱νT​𝐲μ−𝐲νT​𝐱μ=0.\displaystyle\mathbf{x}_{\nu}^{\dagger}\mathbf{x}_{\mu}-\mathbf{y}_{\nu}^{\dagger}\mathbf{y}_{\mu}=\delta_{\nu\mu},\;\;\mathbf{x}_{\nu}^{T}\mathbf{y}_{\mu}-\mathbf{y}_{\nu}^{T}\mathbf{x}_{\mu}=0. (150)

Collecting these column eigenvectors into matrices:

𝐗≡(𝐱1,𝐱2​…),𝐘≡(𝐲1,𝐲2​…),\displaystyle\mathbf{X}\equiv(\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{2}...),\;\;\;\mathbf{Y}\equiv(\mathbf{y}_{1},\mathbf{y}_{2}...), (151)

the eigen boson operator vector is:

𝜸^=𝐗†​𝒃^−𝐘†​𝒃^†,𝜸^†=𝐗T​𝒃^†−𝐘T​𝒃^.\displaystyle\hat{\bm{\gamma}}=\mathbf{X}^{\dagger}\hat{\bm{b}}-\mathbf{Y}^{\dagger}\hat{\bm{b}}^{\dagger},\;\;\;\hat{\bm{\gamma}}^{\dagger}=\mathbf{X}^{T}\hat{\bm{b}}^{\dagger}-\mathbf{Y}^{T}\hat{\bm{b}}. (152)

The boson Hamiltonian is diagonalized: Hcan.G=E⁡(𝝀¯)+EVMPIzero−point+∑νων​γ^ν†​γ^νH^{\rm G}_{\rm can.}=E(\bar{\bm{\lambda}})+E_{\rm VMPI}^{\rm zero-point}+\sum_{\nu}\omega_{\nu}\hat{\gamma}^{\dagger}_{\nu}\hat{\gamma}_{\nu} with VMPI zero-point energy:

EVMPIzero−point≡12​(∑νων−Tr​A).\displaystyle E_{\rm VMPI}^{\rm zero-point}\equiv\frac{1}{2}\Big(\sum_{\nu}\omega_{\nu}-{\rm Tr}A\Big). (153)

In particular, the VMPI ground state wavefunction is

Ψ~VMPI,GS​(𝐳¯)=1|det𝐗|​exp⁡[12​𝐳¯T​𝐒​𝐳¯],\displaystyle\tilde{\Psi}_{\rm VMPI,GS}(\bar{\mathbf{z}})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{|\det\mathbf{X}|}}\exp\Big[\frac{1}{2}\bar{\mathbf{z}}^{T}\mathbf{S}\bar{\mathbf{z}}\Big],
where ​𝐒≡(𝐗†)−1​𝐘†.\displaystyle\text{where }\mathbf{S}\equiv(\mathbf{X}^{\dagger})^{-1}\mathbf{Y}^{\dagger}. (154)

The one-boson excited state VMPI wavefunction is:

Ψ~VMPI,ν​(𝐳¯)=γ^ν†​Ψ~VMPI,GS​(𝐳¯)\displaystyle\tilde{\Psi}_{\rm VMPI,\nu}(\bar{\mathbf{z}})=\hat{\gamma}_{\nu}^{\dagger}\tilde{\Psi}_{\rm VMPI,GS}(\bar{\mathbf{z}})
=\displaystyle= [𝐱νT𝐳¯−𝐲νT∂𝐳¯]⋅Ψ~VMPI,GS(𝐳¯)\displaystyle[\mathbf{x}_{\nu}^{T}\bar{\mathbf{z}}-\mathbf{y}_{\nu}^{T}\partial_{\bar{\mathbf{z}}}]\cdot\tilde{\Psi}_{\rm VMPI,GS}(\bar{\mathbf{z}})
=\displaystyle= [(𝐱νT−𝐲νT​𝐒)​𝐳¯]⋅Ψ~VMPI,GS​(𝐳¯),\displaystyle[(\mathbf{x}_{\nu}^{T}-\mathbf{y}_{\nu}^{T}\mathbf{S})\bar{\mathbf{z}}]\cdot\tilde{\Psi}_{\rm VMPI,GS}(\bar{\mathbf{z}}), (155)

where we used ∂𝐳¯Ψ~VMPI,GS​(𝐳¯)=𝐒​𝐳¯⋅Ψ~VMPI,GS​(𝐳¯)\partial_{\bar{\mathbf{z}}}\tilde{\Psi}_{\rm VMPI,GS}(\bar{\mathbf{z}})=\mathbf{S}\bar{\mathbf{z}}\cdot\tilde{\Psi}_{\rm VMPI,GS}(\bar{\mathbf{z}}).

In principle, the VMPI quantization (i.e., VMPI wavefunctions and the VMPI Schrödinger equation) may be generalized beyond the Gaussian order, where the integral measure d​μ​(𝐳)d\mu(\mathbf{z}) needs to be solved to satisfy the minimal requirement Eq.(133).

V.2 Application of VMPI in Time-dependent Hartree-Fock

V.2.1 Thouless parameterization, saddle point analysis

Next, we demonstrate the application of VMPI as an improvement of TDHF, where the variational manifold is formed by Slater determinants (pairing is not considered) – the simplest Hdet wavefunctions for rank-2 fusion tensors, and we will see that VMPI leads to a microscopic effective field theory. In this simple situation, obviously, one may obtain the effective theory following the traditional route: applying the Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation to decouple the electron interactions, then performing a saddle-point analysis. However, as we will see shortly in the application to Hdet wavefunctions, VMPI is a much more general construction.

Many results in the current Slater-determinant VMPI application are equivalent to those from the well-known Random-Phase-Approximation (RPA) treatment. Nevertheless, the general framework and notation established in this subsection will prove to be very useful when we move on to the Hdet application.

A Slater determinant is fully specified by the 1-body reduced density matrix (RDM, i.e., the correlation matrix) ρi​j≡⟨cj†​ci⟩\rho_{ij}\equiv\langle c_{j}^{\dagger}c_{i}\rangle, satisfying ρ2=ρ\rho^{2}=\rho, where i=1,2​…​dim​ℋ(e)i=1,2...\text{dim}\mathcal{H}^{(e)} labels the real-space orbital basis of electrons (ii may be interpreted as {𝐫i,𝐦i}\{\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{m}_{i}\} where 𝐦\mathbf{m} labels the additional quantum numbers, e.g. spin.). Therefore, one may use ρ\rho as the variational parameter: |Φ⁡(ρ)⟩|\Phi(\rho)\rangle. For a many-body Hamiltonian HH, the variational energy function E⁡(ρ)≡⟨Φ⁡(ρ)|H|Φ⁡(ρ)⟩E(\rho)\equiv\langle\Phi(\rho)|H|\Phi(\rho)\rangle can be used to define the effective hopping amplitudes tt:

ti​j​(ρ)≡∂E⁡(ρ)∂ρj​i\displaystyle t_{ij}(\rho)\equiv\frac{\partial E(\rho)}{\partial\rho_{ji}} (156)

Here, since ρi​j=ρj​i∗\rho_{ij}=\rho_{ji}^{*} are not independent, the derivative should be interpreted as ∂∂ρj​i≡12​(∂∂Re​ρj​i−i​∂∂Im​ρj​i)\frac{\partial}{\partial\rho_{ji}}\equiv\frac{1}{2}(\frac{\partial}{\partial\text{Re}\rho_{ji}}-i\frac{\partial}{\partial\text{Im}\rho_{ji}}) in terms of real derivatives. Consequently, tt is Hermitian. Note that, although the physical ρ\rho is constrained by ρ2=ρ\rho^{2}=\rho, E⁡(ρ)E(\rho) is a well-defined symbolic expression via Wick’s theorem and consequently all the derivatives are well-defined.

One may further define an effective free-fermion Hamiltonian h^​(ρ)\hat{h}(\rho):

h^​(ρ)≡∑i​jti​j​(ρ)​ci†​cj.\displaystyle\hat{h}(\rho)\equiv\sum_{ij}t_{ij}(\rho)c_{i}^{\dagger}c_{j}\;. (157)

For the static Hartree-Fock, one needs to find the variational ground state, labeled by ρ¯\bar{\rho}. The linear-order variation of E⁡(ρ)E(\rho) must vanish, which is equivalent to [t⁡(ρ¯),ρ¯]=0[t(\bar{\rho}),\bar{\rho}]=0, and can be achieved by the self-consistent condition: the ground state of h^​(ρ¯)\hat{h}(\bar{\rho}) is also labeled by ρ¯\bar{\rho}.

We further define the Hessian 𝒦\mathcal{K} of E⁡(ρ)E(\rho) at ρ¯\bar{\rho}:

𝒦i​j,k​l≡\displaystyle\mathcal{K}_{ij,kl}\equiv ∂2E⁡(ρ¯)∂ρj​i​∂ρl​k,\displaystyle\frac{\partial^{2}E(\bar{\rho})}{\partial\rho_{ji}\partial\rho_{lk}}, [𝒦^​X]i​j≡\displaystyle[\hat{\mathcal{K}}X]_{ij}\equiv ∑k​l𝒦i​j,k​l​Xl​k.\displaystyle\sum_{kl}\mathcal{K}_{ij,kl}X_{lk}. (158)

Consider the real linear space MhM_{\rm h} formed by Hermitian matrices with the same size as ρi​j\rho_{ij}, it is natural to define a real inner product:

\llangle​X,Y​\rrangle≡∑i​jXi​j​Yj​i,\displaystyle\llangle X,Y\rrangle\equiv\sum_{ij}X_{ij}Y_{ji}, (159)

and the superoperator 𝒦^\hat{\mathcal{K}} introduced above should be viewed as an operator acting in MhM_{\rm h}. Since 𝒦i​j,k​l=𝒦k​l,i​j\mathcal{K}_{ij,kl}=\mathcal{K}_{kl,ij} and 𝒦i​j,k​l=𝒦j​i,l​k∗\mathcal{K}_{ij,kl}=\mathcal{K}^{*}_{ji,lk}, 𝒦^\hat{\mathcal{K}} is symmetric: \llangle​X,𝒦^​Y​\rrangle=\llangle​𝒦^​X,Y​\rrangle\llangle X,\hat{\mathcal{K}}Y\rrangle=\llangle\hat{\mathcal{K}}X,Y\rrangle.

For a deformation δ​ρ\delta\rho around ρ¯\bar{\rho}, up to quadratic order:

E⁡(ρ¯+δ​ρ)=\displaystyle E(\bar{\rho}+\delta\rho)= E⁡(ρ¯)+\llangle​t​(ρ¯),δ​ρ​\rrangle+12​\llangle​δ​ρ,𝒦^​δ​ρ​\rrangle+O⁡(δ​ρ3).\displaystyle E(\bar{\rho})+\llangle t(\bar{\rho}),\delta\rho\rrangle+\frac{1}{2}\llangle\delta\rho,\hat{\mathcal{K}}\delta\rho\rrangle+O(\delta\rho^{3}). (160)

At this point, we introduce the Thouless parameterization of δ​ρ\delta\rho near ρ¯\bar{\rho}: ρ=ρ¯+δ​ρ\rho=\bar{\rho}+\delta\rho[126]. Consider a general small unitary transformation |Φ⁡(ρ¯+δ​ρ)⟩=ei​Ξ^​(κ)​|Φ⁡(ρ¯)⟩|\Phi(\bar{\rho}+\delta\rho)\rangle=e^{i\hat{\Xi}(\kappa)}|\Phi(\bar{\rho})\rangle, with small Hermitian operator Ξ^​(κ)≡∑𝐩𝐡(−i)​κ𝐩𝐡​c𝐩†​c𝐡+h.c.\hat{\Xi}(\kappa)\equiv\sum_{\mathbf{ph}}(-i)\kappa_{\mathbf{ph}}c_{\mathbf{p}}^{\dagger}c_{\mathbf{h}}+h.c. where 𝐩,𝐡\mathbf{p},\mathbf{h} label the empty and filled single-particle eigen-basis of ρ¯\bar{\rho} (and t⁡(ρ¯)t(\bar{\rho})), respectively. In this basis, ρ¯\bar{\rho} is diagonal: ρ¯𝐡𝐡′=δ𝐡𝐡′\bar{\rho}_{\mathbf{hh^{\prime}}}=\delta_{\mathbf{hh^{\prime}}}, and other matrix elements vanish. Up to the quadratic order of κ\kappa, the induced δ​ρ\delta\rho can be found:

δ​ρ𝐩𝐡=\displaystyle\delta\rho_{\mathbf{ph}}= κ𝐩𝐡,\displaystyle\kappa_{\mathbf{ph}}, δ​ρ𝐡𝐩=\displaystyle\delta\rho_{\mathbf{hp}}= κ𝐩𝐡∗,\displaystyle\kappa_{\mathbf{ph}}^{*},
δ​ρ𝐡𝐡′=\displaystyle\delta\rho_{\mathbf{hh^{\prime}}}= −∑𝐩κ𝐩𝐡∗κ𝐩𝐡′,\displaystyle-\sum_{\mathbf{p}}\kappa_{\mathbf{ph}}^{*}\kappa_{\mathbf{ph^{\prime}}}, δ​ρ𝐩𝐩′=\displaystyle\delta\rho_{\mathbf{pp^{\prime}}}= ∑𝐡κ𝐩𝐡​κ𝐩′​𝐡∗.\displaystyle\sum_{\mathbf{h}}\kappa_{\mathbf{ph}}\kappa_{\mathbf{p^{\prime}h}}^{*}. (161)

Precisely, we also introduce the matrix form of Ξ^​(κ)\hat{\Xi}(\kappa):

Ξ​(κ)𝐩𝐡≡\displaystyle\Xi(\kappa)_{\mathbf{ph}}\equiv −i​κ𝐩𝐡,\displaystyle-i\kappa_{\mathbf{ph}}, Ξ​(κ)𝐡𝐩≡\displaystyle\Xi(\kappa)_{\mathbf{hp}}\equiv i​κ𝐩𝐡∗.\displaystyle i\kappa^{*}_{\mathbf{ph}}. (162)

The RDM for the rotated state ei​Ξ^​(κ)​|Φ⁡(ρ¯)⟩e^{i\hat{\Xi}(\kappa)}|\Phi(\bar{\rho})\rangle is then:

ei​Ξ​(κ)∘ρ¯≡ei​Ξ​(κ)​ρ¯​e−i​Ξ​(κ)=ρ¯+δ​ρ.\displaystyle e^{i\Xi(\kappa)}\circ\bar{\rho}\equiv e^{i\Xi(\kappa)}\bar{\rho}e^{-i\Xi(\kappa)}=\bar{\rho}+\delta\rho. (163)

Eq.(161) is simply the consequence of the identity:

δ​ρ=i⁡[Ξ⁡(κ),ρ¯]−12​[Ξ⁡(κ),[Ξ⁡(κ),ρ¯]]+O⁡(κ3).\displaystyle\delta\rho=i[\Xi(\kappa),\bar{\rho}]-\frac{1}{2}[\Xi(\kappa),[\Xi(\kappa),\bar{\rho}]]+O(\kappa^{3}). (164)

At this point, we mention that, in a closely related parameterization of the current variational manifold formed by Slater determinants, it is obvious that the Kähler condition is satisfied. Consider an unnormalized state:

|Φ~​(κ~)⟩≡exp⁡[∑𝐩𝐡κ~𝐩𝐡​c𝐩†​c𝐡]​|Φ⁡(ρ¯)⟩.\displaystyle|\tilde{\Phi}(\tilde{\kappa})\rangle\equiv\exp\big[\sum_{\mathbf{ph}}\tilde{\kappa}_{\mathbf{ph}}c_{\mathbf{p}}^{\dagger}c_{\mathbf{h}}\big]|\Phi(\bar{\rho})\rangle. (165)

Comparing with |Φ⁡(κ~)⟩|\Phi(\tilde{\kappa})\rangle, the only difference is that the Hermitian conjugate term in Ξ^​(κ~)\hat{\Xi}(\tilde{\kappa}): −∑𝐩𝐡κ~∗𝐩𝐡c𝐡†c𝐩-\sum_{\mathbf{ph}}\tilde{\kappa}^{*}_{\mathbf{ph}}c_{\mathbf{h}}^{\dagger}c_{\mathbf{p}} (which annihilates |Φ⁡(ρ¯)⟩|\Phi(\bar{\rho})\rangle) is absent. The advantage here is that |Φ~​(κ~)⟩|\tilde{\Phi}(\tilde{\kappa})\rangle is clearly holomorphic in κ~\tilde{\kappa}, and it is easy to show that |Φ~​(κ~)⟩|\tilde{\Phi}(\tilde{\kappa})\rangle is a Slater determinant:

|Φ~​(κ~)⟩=∏𝐡(c𝐡†+∑𝐩κ~𝐩𝐡​c𝐩†)​|0⟩.\displaystyle|\tilde{\Phi}(\tilde{\kappa})\rangle=\prod_{\mathbf{h}}(c^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{h}}+\sum_{\mathbf{p}}\tilde{\kappa}_{\mathbf{ph}}c_{\mathbf{p}}^{\dagger})|0\rangle. (166)

By construction, this is a Kähler coordinate for the variational manifold.

If one normalizes |Φ~​(κ~)⟩|\tilde{\Phi}(\tilde{\kappa})\rangle, one can compare the κ\kappa and κ~\tilde{\kappa} coordinates for the same Slater determinant, leading to

κ~𝐩𝐡=κ𝐩𝐡+O⁡(κ3).\displaystyle\tilde{\kappa}_{\mathbf{ph}}=\kappa_{\mathbf{ph}}+O(\kappa^{3}). (167)

Therefore, for the present Gaussian order analysis, it does not matter if one uses κ\kappa or κ~\tilde{\kappa}.

Using κ\kappa as 𝝀\bm{\lambda} to parameterize the small fluctuations, plugging into the TDVP Lagrangian Eq.(102), one obtains up to the Gaussian order:

LTDVP=\displaystyle L_{\text{TDVP}}= i2​(𝜿˙T​𝜿¯−𝜿T​𝜿¯˙)−𝜿T​𝐀​𝜿¯\displaystyle\frac{i}{2}\left(\dot{\bm{\kappa}}^{T}\bar{\bm{\kappa}}-\bm{\kappa}^{T}\dot{\bar{\bm{\kappa}}}\right)-\bm{\kappa}^{T}\mathbf{A}\bar{\bm{\kappa}}
−12​[𝜿T​𝐁​𝜿+𝜿¯T​𝐁¯​𝜿¯]+O⁡(𝜿3),\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}\Big[\bm{\kappa}^{T}\mathbf{B}\bm{\kappa}+\bar{\bm{\kappa}}^{T}\bar{\mathbf{B}}\bar{\bm{\kappa}}\Big]+O(\bm{\kappa}^{3}), (168)

where 𝜿\bm{\kappa} is the column vector obtained by reshaping the matrix κ𝐩𝐡\kappa_{\mathbf{ph}} using the composite index 𝐩𝐡\mathbf{ph}. Using the composite index, 𝐀,𝐁\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B} matrices are defined as:

𝐀𝐩𝐡,𝐩′​𝐡′≡\displaystyle\mathbf{A}_{\mathbf{ph},\mathbf{p^{\prime}h^{\prime}}}\equiv (ϵ𝐩−ϵ𝐡)​δ𝐩𝐩′​δ𝐡𝐡′+𝒦𝐡𝐩,𝐩′​𝐡′,\displaystyle(\epsilon_{\mathbf{p}}-\epsilon_{\mathbf{h}})\delta_{\mathbf{pp^{\prime}}}\delta_{\mathbf{hh^{\prime}}}+\mathcal{K}_{\mathbf{hp},\mathbf{p^{\prime}h^{\prime}}},
𝐁𝐩𝐡,𝐩′​𝐡′≡\displaystyle\mathbf{B}_{\mathbf{ph},\mathbf{p^{\prime}h^{\prime}}}\equiv 𝒦𝐡𝐩,𝐡′​𝐩′,\displaystyle\mathcal{K}_{\mathbf{hp},\mathbf{h^{\prime}p^{\prime}}}, (169)

satisfying 𝐀†=𝐀\mathbf{A}^{\dagger}=\mathbf{A}, 𝐁T=𝐁\mathbf{B}^{T}=\mathbf{B}.

The first term in Eq.(168) is the Berry’s phase: ⟨Φ(κ(t))|i∂t|Φ(κ(t))⟩\langle\Phi(\kappa(t))|i\partial_{t}|\Phi(\kappa(t))\rangle which coincides with that of canonical bosons. Namely, the coordinate 𝛋\bm{\kappa} is already canonical and can be literally identified as 𝐳\mathbf{z} in our general VMPI quantization discussion, and all results from Eq.(127) to Eq.(155) can be immediately applied.

To further improve the notation, we define the tangent subspace of Hermitian matrices at the saddle point:

Tρ¯≡{X=X†,ρ¯​X​ρ¯=0,(1−ρ¯)​X​(1−ρ¯)=0}⊂Mh,\displaystyle T_{\bar{\rho}}\equiv\{X=X^{\dagger},\bar{\rho}X\bar{\rho}=0,(1-\bar{\rho})X(1-\bar{\rho})=0\}\subset M_{\rm h}, (170)

i.e., those Hermitian matrices with only nonzero 𝐩𝐡\mathbf{ph} and 𝐡𝐩\mathbf{hp} blocks. The Thouless parameterization κ\kappa is an explicit coordinate for Tρ¯T_{\bar{\rho}}: κ𝐡𝐩=κ𝐩𝐡∗\kappa_{\mathbf{hp}}=\kappa^{*}_{\mathbf{ph}}.

Next, the bare kinetic energy (ϵ𝐩−ϵ𝐡)(\epsilon_{\mathbf{p}}-\epsilon_{\mathbf{h}})-term and the Berry’s phase term can be captured by defining superoperators 𝒢^\hat{\mathcal{G}} and ℱ^\hat{\mathcal{F}} acting in Tρ¯T_{\bar{\rho}}: ∀X∈Tρ¯\forall X\in T_{\bar{\rho}},

(𝒢^​X)𝐩𝐡≡\displaystyle(\hat{\mathcal{G}}X)_{\mathbf{ph}}\equiv (ϵ𝐩−ϵ𝐡)​X𝐩𝐡,\displaystyle(\epsilon_{\mathbf{p}}-\epsilon_{\mathbf{h}})X_{\mathbf{ph}}, (𝒢^​X)𝐡𝐩≡\displaystyle(\hat{\mathcal{G}}X)_{\mathbf{hp}}\equiv (ϵ𝐩−ϵ𝐡)​X𝐡𝐩,\displaystyle(\epsilon_{\mathbf{p}}-\epsilon_{\mathbf{h}})X_{\mathbf{hp}},
(ℱ^​X)𝐩𝐡≡\displaystyle(\hat{\mathcal{F}}X)_{\mathbf{ph}}\equiv −i​X𝐩𝐡,\displaystyle-iX_{\mathbf{ph}}, (ℱ^​X)𝐡𝐩≡\displaystyle(\hat{\mathcal{F}}X)_{\mathbf{hp}}\equiv i​X𝐡𝐩.\displaystyle iX_{\mathbf{hp}}. (171)

𝒢^\hat{\mathcal{G}} is symmetric and positive definite (\llangle​X,𝒢^​Y​\rrangle=\llangle​𝒢^​X,Y​\rrangle\llangle X,\hat{\mathcal{G}}Y\rrangle=\llangle\hat{\mathcal{G}}X,Y\rrangle, \llangle​X,𝒢^​X​\rrangle>0\llangle X,\hat{\mathcal{G}}X\rrangle>0), while ℱ^\hat{\mathcal{F}} is antisymmetric (\llangle​X,ℱ^​Y​\rrangle=−\llangle​ℱ^​X,Y​\rrangle\llangle X,\hat{\mathcal{F}}Y\rrangle=-\llangle\hat{\mathcal{F}}X,Y\rrangle).

Physically, the superoperator ℱ^\hat{\mathcal{F}} is nothing but the Berry’s curvature in the tangent space: consider two small κ1,κ2∈Tρ¯\kappa_{1},\kappa_{2}\in T_{\bar{\rho}}, then

\llangle​κ1,ℱ^​κ2​\rrangle\displaystyle\llangle\kappa_{1},\hat{\mathcal{F}}\kappa_{2}\rrangle
=\displaystyle= 2⋅Im​[⟨Φ⁡(ei​Ξ​(κ1)∘ρ¯)|Φ⁡(ei​Ξ​(κ2)∘ρ¯)⟩]κ1​κ2​-part+O⁡(κ3)\displaystyle 2\cdot\rm{Im}\big[\langle\Phi(e^{i\Xi(\kappa_{1})}\circ\bar{\rho})|\Phi(e^{i\Xi(\kappa_{2})}\circ\bar{\rho})\rangle\big]_{\kappa_{1}\kappa_{2}\text{-part}}+O(\kappa^{3})
=\displaystyle= 2⋅Im​[⟨ei​Ξ^​(κ1)​Φ​(ρ¯)|ei​Ξ^​(κ2)​Φ​(ρ¯)⟩]κ1​κ2​-part+O⁡(κ3)\displaystyle 2\cdot\rm{Im}\big[\langle e^{i\hat{\Xi}(\kappa_{1})}\Phi(\bar{\rho})|e^{i\hat{\Xi}(\kappa_{2})}\Phi(\bar{\rho})\rangle\big]_{\kappa_{1}\kappa_{2}\text{-part}}+O(\kappa^{3})
=\displaystyle= −i⁡⟨Φ⁡(ρ¯)|[Ξ^​(κ1),Ξ^​(κ2)]|Φ⁡(ρ¯)⟩+O⁡(κ3).\displaystyle-i\langle\Phi(\bar{\rho})|[\hat{\Xi}(\kappa_{1}),\hat{\Xi}(\kappa_{2})]|\Phi(\bar{\rho})\rangle+O(\kappa^{3}). (172)

As we will see later, when we study Hdet wavefunctions, the corresponding ℱ^\hat{\mathcal{F}} superoperator can still be defined via the first equal sign, although it cannot generally be exactly computed, and the latter lines no longer hold.

The TDVP Lagrangian can now be compactly written as:

LTDVP=−12​\llangle​κ,ℱ^​κ˙​\rrangle−12​\llangle​κ,(𝒢^+𝒦^)​κ​\rrangle+O⁡(κ3)\displaystyle L_{\rm{TDVP}}=-\frac{1}{2}\llangle\kappa,\hat{\mathcal{F}}\dot{\kappa}\rrangle-\frac{1}{2}\llangle\kappa,(\hat{\mathcal{G}}+\hat{\mathcal{K}})\kappa\rrangle+O(\kappa^{3}) (173)

Comparing with the notation in Eq.(107) in the general setup section, FF should be identified with ℱ^\hat{\mathcal{F}}, VV should be identified with 𝒢^+𝒦^\hat{\mathcal{G}}+\hat{\mathcal{K}}.

One may add a source term involving J⁡(t)∈Tρ¯J(t)\in T_{\bar{\rho}} in the Lagrangian to facilitate the computation of correlation functions:

LJ−κ≡\llangle​J,κ​\rrangle=∑𝐩𝐡[J𝐩𝐡∗​(t)​κ𝐩𝐡​(t)+J𝐩𝐡​(t)​κ𝐩𝐡∗​(t)]\displaystyle L_{J-\kappa}\equiv\llangle J,\kappa\rrangle=\sum_{\mathbf{ph}}\Big[J^{*}_{\mathbf{ph}}(t)\,\kappa_{\mathbf{ph}}(t)+J_{\mathbf{ph}}(t)\,\kappa^{*}_{\mathbf{ph}}(t)\Big] (174)

Up to the Gaussian order of κ\kappa, the unknown function f⁡(κ)f(\kappa) in the integration measure does not matter since it only gives higher-order terms. We have the generating functional in VMPI formulation:

Zκ​[J]≡∫𝒟⁡[κ∗​(t),κ⁡(t)]​exp⁡[i​∫d​t​(LTDVP+LJ−κ)].\displaystyle Z_{\kappa}[J]\equiv\int\mathcal{D}[\kappa^{*}(t),\kappa(t)]\exp\!\Big[i\int dt\,(L_{\text{TDVP}}+L_{J-\kappa})\Big]. (175)

The time-ordered κ\kappa correlator can be computed as:

⟨𝒯​κ𝐩𝐡​(t)​κ𝐩′​𝐡′​(t′)⟩=δ2​[−i​ln⁡Zκ​[J]]δ​J𝐩𝐡∗​(t)​δ​J𝐩′​𝐡′∗​(t′)|J=0.\displaystyle\langle\mathcal{T}\kappa_{\mathbf{ph}}(t)\kappa_{\mathbf{p^{\prime}h^{\prime}}}(t^{\prime})\rangle=\left.\frac{\delta^{2}[-i\ln Z_{\kappa}[J]]}{\delta J^{*}_{\mathbf{ph}}(t)\delta J^{*}_{\mathbf{p^{\prime}h^{\prime}}}(t^{\prime})}\right|_{J=0}. (176)

The poles of this κ\kappa-correlator lead to bosonic collective modes.

V.2.2 Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the effective theory of TDHF

But our goal is not the κ\kappa-theory, since it is fully bosonic – the fermions (electrons here) were bosonized as κ\kappa. Next, we will refermionize the κ\kappa-theory, and show that it is equivalent to a fermion theory coupling with Hubbard-Stratonovich (HS) fields, up to the Gaussian order.

For this purpose, it is convenient to first perform the standard HS transformation for the residual interaction 𝒦\mathcal{K}-term in Eq.(160) before inserting the Thouless parameterization. Let the subspace

VHS≡Im​(𝒦^)⊂Mh\displaystyle V_{\rm HS}\equiv\text{Im}(\hat{\mathcal{K}})\subset M_{\rm h} (177)

be the image of the superoperator in Eq.(158). Precisely speaking, VHSV_{\rm HS} is spanned by eigenmatrices of 𝒦^\hat{\mathcal{K}} with nonzero eigenvalues (note that, since 𝒦^\hat{\mathcal{K}} is symmetric in the real linear space MhM_{\rm h}, its eigenvalues are all real.). Introducing the projector superoperator 𝒫^HS\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{\rm HS} to the subspace VHSV_{\rm HS}, we define 𝒦^HS−1≡𝒫^HS​𝒦^−1​𝒫^HS\hat{\mathcal{K}}_{\rm HS}^{-1}\equiv\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{\rm HS}\hat{\mathcal{K}}^{-1}\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{\rm HS}. The HS transformation is:

e−i2​\llangle​δ​ρ,𝒦^​δ​ρ​\rrangle=e−i2∑i​jδρi​j[𝒦^δρ]j​i\displaystyle e^{-\frac{i}{2}\llangle\delta\rho,\hat{\mathcal{K}}\delta\rho\rrangle}=e^{-\frac{i}{2}\sum_{ij}\delta\rho_{ij}[\hat{\mathcal{K}}\delta\rho]_{ji}}
=\displaystyle= 𝒩∫D[χ]exp[−i∑i​jχi​jδρj​i+i2∑i​jχi​j[(𝒦^HS−1χ)]j​i]\displaystyle\mathcal{N}\int D[\chi]\exp\!\Big[-i\sum_{ij}\chi_{ij}\delta\rho_{ji}+\frac{i}{2}\sum_{ij}\chi_{ij}\big[(\hat{\mathcal{K}}^{-1}_{\rm HS}\chi)\big]_{ji}\Big]
=\displaystyle= 𝒩​∫D⁡[χ]​exp⁡[−i​\llangle​χ,δ​ρ​\rrangle+i2​\llangle​χ,𝒦^HS−1​χ​\rrangle],\displaystyle\mathcal{N}\int D[\chi]\exp\!\Big[-i\llangle\chi,\delta\rho\rrangle+\frac{i}{2}\llangle\chi,\hat{\mathcal{K}}^{-1}_{\rm HS}\chi\rrangle\Big], (178)

where 𝒩\mathcal{N} is an unimportant normalization constant, and D⁡[χ]D[\chi] is the integration over Hermitian matrices χ∈VHS\chi\in V_{\rm HS}.

We now can rewrite the VMPI as a field theory involving both fluctuating κ\kappa and χ\chi:

Zκ​[J]=∫𝒟⁡[κ∗​(t),κ⁡(t),χ⁡(t)]​exp⁡[i​∫d​t​(Lκ,χ+LJ−κ)],\displaystyle Z_{\kappa}[J]=\int\mathcal{D}[\kappa^{*}(t),\kappa(t),\chi(t)]\exp\!\Big[i\int dt\,(L_{\kappa,\chi}+L_{J-\kappa})\Big], (179)

where

Lκ,χ=\displaystyle L_{\kappa,\chi}= −12​\llangle​κ,ℱ^​κ˙​\rrangle−12​\llangle​κ,𝒢^​κ​\rrangle\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}\llangle\kappa,\hat{\mathcal{F}}\dot{\kappa}\rrangle-\frac{1}{2}\llangle\kappa,\hat{\mathcal{G}}\kappa\rrangle
−\llangle​χ,κ​\rrangle+12​\llangle​χ,𝒦^HS−1​χ​\rrangle+O⁡((χ,κ)3)\displaystyle-\llangle\chi,\kappa\rrangle+\frac{1}{2}\llangle\chi,\hat{\mathcal{K}}^{-1}_{\rm HS}\chi\rrangle+O((\chi,\kappa)^{3}) (180)

The κ−χ\kappa-\chi theory above is still fully bosonic. Now we show that the κ−χ\kappa-\chi theory is equivalent to an effective fermion-χ\chi theory up to the Gaussian order. Introducing complex Grassmann variables ψi​(t)\psi_{i}(t), we define the effective Lagrangian

Leff≡\displaystyle L_{\text{eff}}\equiv ∑i​j[ψ¯i​(i​∂tδi​j−ti​j​(ρ¯))​ψj−χi​j​(ψ¯i​ψj−ρ¯j​i)]\displaystyle\sum_{ij}\Big[\bar{\psi}_{i}(i\partial_{t}\delta_{ij}-t_{ij}(\bar{\rho}))\psi_{j}-\chi_{ij}(\bar{\psi}_{i}\psi_{j}-\bar{\rho}_{ji})\Big]
+12​\llangle​χ,𝒦^HS−1​χ​\rrangle,\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2}\llangle\chi,\hat{\mathcal{K}}^{-1}_{\rm HS}\chi\rrangle, (181)

and the corresponding source term and generating functional:

Lψ−J=\displaystyle L_{\psi-J}= ∑𝐩𝐡[J𝐩𝐡∗​(t)​ψ¯𝐡​(t)​ψ𝐩​(t)+J𝐩𝐡​(t)​ψ¯𝐩​(t)​ψ𝐡​(t)]\displaystyle\sum_{\mathbf{ph}}[J^{*}_{\mathbf{ph}}(t)\bar{\psi}_{\mathbf{h}}(t)\psi_{\mathbf{p}}(t)+J_{\mathbf{ph}}(t)\bar{\psi}_{\mathbf{p}}(t)\psi_{\mathbf{h}}(t)]
Zeff​[J]=\displaystyle Z_{\text{eff}}[J]= ∫𝒟⁡[ψ¯​(t),ψ⁡(t),χ⁡(t)]​exp⁡[i​∫d​t​(Leff+Lψ−J)].\displaystyle\int\mathcal{D}[\bar{\psi}(t),\psi(t),\chi(t)]\exp\!\Big[i\int dt\,(L_{\text{eff}}+L_{\psi-J})\Big]. (182)

The point is that, up to Gaussian order, the two generating functionals are identical Zeff​[J]=Zκ​[J]Z_{\rm eff}[J]=Z_{\kappa}[J]. In addition, after integrating out κ\kappa in κ−χ\kappa-\chi theory, the resulting χ\chi-only action is identical to that obtained by integrating out fermions in the effective theory (up to Gaussian order). For example, the correlator ⟨𝒯⁡[ρi​j​(t)​ρk​l​(t′)]⟩VMPI\langle\mathcal{T}[\rho_{ij}(t)\rho_{kl}(t^{\prime})]\rangle_{\text{VMPI}} using the path integral Eq.(175) will be identical (up to Gaussian order) to the correlator ⟨𝒯⁡[ψ¯j​(t)​ψi​(t)​ψ¯l​(t′)​ψk​(t′)]⟩eff\langle\mathcal{T}[\bar{\psi}_{j}(t)\psi_{i}(t)\bar{\psi}_{l}(t^{\prime})\psi_{k}(t^{\prime})]\rangle_{\text{eff}} using the path integral Eq.(182). And the collective modes in the original κ\kappa-theory are reproduced in the effective theory. Namely, we have refermionized the VMPI action.

Finally, we explain the identification between the fermionic theory LeffL_{\text{eff}} in Eq.(181) and the bosonic theory Lκ,χL_{\kappa,\chi} in Eq.(180) in an intuitive fashion, since we will use similar technique for the effective theories of Hdet wavefunctions soon. The only difference between them lies in the choice of formulation in the path integral. Consider a fixed χ⁡(t)\chi(t) path. The fermion part of the path integral of LeffL_{\text{eff}} can be obtained by the single-body (time-dependent) kernel:

h^χ​(t)≡∑i​j[ti​j​(ρ¯)+χi​j​(t)]​ci†​cj.\displaystyle\hat{h}_{\chi}(t)\equiv\sum_{ij}[t_{ij}(\bar{\rho})+\chi_{ij}(t)]c_{i}^{\dagger}c_{j}. (183)

If one inserts the resolution of identity of usual fermion coherent states into the time slices, LeffL_{\text{eff}} is obtained in terms of Grassmann variables ψ¯,ψ\bar{\psi},\psi. On the other hand, it can be shown that all Slater determinants labeled by ρi​j\rho_{ij} also form a resolution of identity for the NN-electron Hilbert space:

𝟏N=∫d​μ​(ρ)​|Φ⁡(ρ)⟩​⟨Φ⁡(ρ)|,\displaystyle\mathbf{1}_{N}=\int d\mu(\rho)|\Phi(\rho)\rangle\langle\Phi(\rho)|, (184)

where the measure μ⁡(ρ)\mu(\rho) (up to an unimportant overall constant) is exactly the Fubini–Study quantum metric in Eq.(108) with f⁡(ρ)=1f(\rho)=1. Precisely speaking, the integration here is over the complex Grassmannian manifold Gr​(N,M)≡U⁡(M)U⁡(N)×U⁡(M−N)\text{Gr}(N,M)\equiv\frac{U(M)}{U(N)\times U(M-N)} where MM is the dimension of the single-particle Hilbert space ℋ(e)\mathcal{H}^{(e)}. The Thouless parameterization is a local coordinate for this manifold. It would be more convenient if Gr​(N,M)\text{Gr}(N,M) has a global coordinate, but unfortunately, it does not. If one inserts Eq.(184) into the time slices of the path integral of Eq.(183), then Lκ,χL_{\kappa,\chi} is obtained.

The resolution of identity Eq.(184), although being an elegant mathematical fact, is not crucial to establish the equivalence of the two theories at the Gaussian order. As noted earlier, the details of the factor f⁡(ρ)f(\rho) in the integration measure do not affect the path integral at Gaussian order.

Here, we are dealing with a particularly simple case of Slater determinants: the Berry’s phase term in Lκ,χL_{\kappa,\chi} (the first term) Eq.(180) can be computed exactly, which is just a different formulation of the fermion Berry’s phase: ∑iψ¯i(i∂t)ψi\sum_{i}\bar{\psi}_{i}(i\partial_{t})\psi_{i}. We will see that the situation for Hdet wavefunctions is more complicated.

V.2.3 Continuous Symmetry, Ward Identity and Goldstone zero modes

TDHF is known to be a conserving approximation, leading to gapless Goldstone modes when a continuous symmetry is spontaneously broken. Here we show the algebraic structure behind this statement. Soon, in our discussion of the effective theories of the Hdet wavefunctions, the similar algebraic structure will be present.

Consider a U​(1)QU(1)_{Q} symmetry of the Hamiltonian HH, generated by Q^\hat{Q}

Q^=∑i​jQi​j​ci†​cj,\displaystyle\hat{Q}=\sum_{ij}Q_{ij}c_{i}^{\dagger}c_{j}, (185)

in both the operator and matrix formulation:

D^​(θ)≡\displaystyle\hat{D}(\theta)\equiv ei​θ​Q^,\displaystyle e^{i\theta\hat{Q}}, D⁡(θ)≡\displaystyle D(\theta)\equiv ei​θ​Q.\displaystyle e^{i\theta Q}. (186)

Performing the unitary rotation for the state |Φ⁡(ρQ​(θ))⟩≡D^​(θ)​|Φ⁡(ρ)⟩|\Phi(\rho_{Q}(\theta))\rangle\equiv\hat{D}(\theta)|\Phi(\rho)\rangle, one finds the ρi​j\rho_{ij} matrix transforms as

ρ↦ρQ​(θ)=D⁡(θ)​ρ​D†​(θ),\displaystyle\rho\mapsto\rho_{Q}(\theta)=D(\theta)\rho D^{\dagger}(\theta), (187)

Since the variational energy is symmetry invariant E⁡(ρQ​(θ))=E⁡(ρ)E\big(\rho_{Q}(\theta)\big)=E(\rho), Eq.(156) leads to the covariance of t⁡(ρ)t(\rho)

t⁡(ρQ​(θ))=D⁡(θ)​t​(ρ)​D†​(θ).\displaystyle t\big(\rho_{Q}(\theta)\big)=D(\theta)\,t(\rho)\,D^{\dagger}(\theta). (188)

This is the origin of the Ward identity in the TDHF analysis.

Suppose ρ¯\bar{\rho} is a saddle point spontaneously breaking the U​(1)QU(1)_{Q}-symmetry:

ρ¯Q​(θ)≡D⁡(θ)​ρ¯​D†​(θ)≠ρ¯,\displaystyle\bar{\rho}_{Q}(\theta)\equiv D(\theta)\bar{\rho}D^{\dagger}(\theta)\neq\bar{\rho}, (189)

then ρ¯Q​(θ)\bar{\rho}_{Q}(\theta) is also a saddle point:

[t⁡(ρ¯Q​(θ)),ρ¯Q​(θ)]=0.\displaystyle[t(\bar{\rho}_{Q}(\theta)),\bar{\rho}_{Q}(\theta)]=0. (190)

For a small θ\theta, the symmetry-induced linear-order change ρ¯Q​(θ)−ρ¯\bar{\rho}_{Q}(\theta)-\bar{\rho} is:

(δ​ρQ)i​j≡θ⋅d​ρ¯Q​(θ)i​jd​θ|θ=0=i​θ​[Q,ρ¯]i​j.\displaystyle(\delta\rho_{Q})_{ij}\equiv\theta\cdot\left.\frac{d\bar{\rho}_{Q}(\theta)_{ij}}{d\theta}\right|_{\theta=0}=i\theta[Q,\bar{\rho}]_{ij}. (191)

Similarly, we define the symmetry-induced linear-order variation of the effective hopping:

(χQ)i​j≡θ⋅d​t​(ρ¯Q​(θ))i​jd​θ|θ=0=i​θ​[Q,t⁡(ρ¯)]i​j.\displaystyle(\chi_{Q})_{ij}\equiv\theta\cdot\left.\frac{d\,t(\bar{\rho}_{Q}(\theta))_{ij}}{d\theta}\right|_{\theta=0}=i\theta[Q,t(\bar{\rho})]_{ij}. (192)

Both δ​ρQ,χQ\delta\rho_{Q},\chi_{Q} matrices are Hermitian.

Since t⁡(ρ)t(\rho) is the first derivative of E⁡(ρ)E(\rho), the variation of tt, i.e., χQ\chi_{Q} is related to the second derivative of E⁡(ρ)E(\rho) – the Hessian 𝒦\mathcal{K}. Precisely:

i​θ​[Q,t⁡(ρ¯)]i​j=(χQ)i​j=∑k​l𝒦i​j,k​l​(δ​ρQ)l​k=[𝒦^​δ​ρQ]i​j.\displaystyle i\theta[Q,t(\bar{\rho})]_{ij}=(\chi_{Q})_{ij}=\sum_{kl}\mathcal{K}_{ij,kl}(\delta\rho_{Q})_{lk}=[\hat{\mathcal{K}}\,\delta\rho_{Q}]_{ij}. (193)

Eq.(193) can be identified as the Ward identity in the real-space basis. If the generator QQ were not a symmetry, although [𝒦^​δ​ρQ]i​j[\hat{\mathcal{K}}\,\delta\rho_{Q}]_{ij} is still the linear-order change of the effective hopping for the rotated state D^​(θ)​|Φ​(ρ)⟩\hat{D}(\theta)|\Phi(\rho)\rangle, it would not be directly related to i​θ​[Q,t⁡(ρ¯)]i​ji\theta[Q,t(\bar{\rho})]_{ij}.

In the particle–hole (𝐩𝐡\mathbf{ph}) basis which diagonalizes both ρ¯\bar{\rho} and t⁡(ρ¯)t(\bar{\rho}), together with the Thouless parameterization, Eq.(191,192) lead to:

κQ,𝐩𝐡≡(δ​ρQ)𝐩𝐡=i​θ​Q𝐩𝐡,(χQ)𝐩𝐡=−(ϵ𝐩−ϵ𝐡)​κQ,𝐩𝐡.\displaystyle\kappa_{Q,\mathbf{ph}}\equiv(\delta\rho_{Q})_{\mathbf{ph}}=i\theta Q_{\mathbf{ph}},\;(\chi_{Q})_{\mathbf{ph}}=-(\epsilon_{\mathbf{p}}-\epsilon_{\mathbf{h}})\kappa_{Q,\mathbf{ph}}. (194)

Note that, κQ\kappa_{Q} only has off-diagonal 𝐩𝐡,𝐡𝐩\mathbf{ph},\mathbf{hp} components, while χQ\chi_{Q} generally also has 𝐩𝐩′,𝐡𝐡′\mathbf{pp^{\prime}},\mathbf{hh^{\prime}} components. In other words, we know δ​ρQ=κQ∈Tρ¯\delta\rho_{Q}=\kappa_{Q}\in T_{\bar{\rho}} and χQ∈VHS\chi_{Q}\in V_{\rm HS} (from Eq.(193)), but χQ\chi_{Q} may not be in Tρ¯T_{\bar{\rho}}. The relation κQ,𝐩𝐡=i​θ​Q𝐩𝐡\kappa_{Q,\mathbf{ph}}=i\theta Q_{\mathbf{ph}} leads to a useful identity for later discussion:

ei​θ​Q^​|Φ⁡(ρ¯)⟩=ei​θ​∑𝐡Q𝐡𝐡⋅ei​Ξ^​(κQ)​|Φ⁡(ρ¯)⟩+O⁡(θ2).\displaystyle e^{i\theta\hat{Q}}|\Phi(\bar{\rho})\rangle=e^{i\theta\sum_{\mathbf{h}}Q_{\mathbf{h}\mathbf{h}}}\cdot e^{i\hat{\Xi}(\kappa_{Q})}|\Phi(\bar{\rho})\rangle+O(\theta^{2}). (195)

Namely ei​θ​Q^​|Φ⁡(ρ¯)⟩e^{i\theta\hat{Q}}|\Phi(\bar{\rho})\rangle and ei​Ξ^​(κQ)​|Φ⁡(ρ¯)⟩e^{i\hat{\Xi}(\kappa_{Q})}|\Phi(\bar{\rho})\rangle only differ by a gauge choice at θ\theta-linear order.

We now introduce the projection superoperator 𝒫^T\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{T} to the Tρ¯T_{\bar{\rho}} subspace, and similar to 𝒦^HS−1≡𝒫^HS​𝒦^−1​𝒫^HS\hat{\mathcal{K}}^{-1}_{\rm HS}\equiv\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{\rm HS}\hat{\mathcal{K}}^{-1}\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{\rm HS}, we define 𝒢^T−1≡𝒫^T​𝒢^−1​𝒫^T\hat{\mathcal{G}}^{-1}_{T}\equiv\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{T}\hat{\mathcal{G}}^{-1}\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{T}. The above relations can then be compactly written as:

𝒫^T​χQ=\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{T}\chi_{Q}= −𝒢^​κQ,\displaystyle-\hat{\mathcal{G}}\kappa_{Q}, χQ=\displaystyle\chi_{Q}= 𝒦^​κQ,\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{K}}\kappa_{Q},
−𝒢^T−1​χQ=\displaystyle-\hat{\mathcal{G}}_{T}^{-1}\chi_{Q}= κQ,\displaystyle\kappa_{Q}, 𝒦^HS−1​χQ=\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{K}}_{\rm HS}^{-1}\chi_{Q}= 𝒫^HS​κQ,\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{\rm HS}\kappa_{Q}, (196)

leading to the Ward identity in the κ\kappa-language:

(𝒢^+𝒫^T​𝒦^)​κQ=\displaystyle(\hat{\mathcal{G}}+\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{T}\hat{\mathcal{K}})\kappa_{Q}= 0,\displaystyle 0, \llangle​κQ,(𝒢^+𝒦^)​κQ​\rrangle=\displaystyle\llangle\kappa_{Q},(\hat{\mathcal{G}}+\hat{\mathcal{K}})\kappa_{Q}\rrangle= 0,\displaystyle 0, (197)

and the corresponding one in the χ\chi-language:

(𝒫^HS​𝒢^T−1+𝒦^HS−1)​χQ=\displaystyle(\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{\rm HS}\hat{\mathcal{G}}^{-1}_{T}+\hat{\mathcal{K}}_{\rm HS}^{-1})\chi_{Q}= 0,\displaystyle 0, \llangle​χQ,(𝒢^T−1+𝒦^HS−1)​χQ​\rrangle=\displaystyle\llangle\chi_{Q},(\hat{\mathcal{G}}^{-1}_{T}+\hat{\mathcal{K}}_{\rm HS}^{-1})\chi_{Q}\rrangle= 0.\displaystyle 0. (198)

The superoperator 𝒢^T−1\hat{\mathcal{G}}^{-1}_{T} acting on Tρ¯T_{\bar{\rho}}:

(𝒢^T−1​X)𝐩𝐡≡\displaystyle(\hat{\mathcal{G}}^{-1}_{T}X)_{\mathbf{ph}}\equiv 1ϵ𝐩−ϵ𝐡​X𝐩𝐡,\displaystyle\frac{1}{\epsilon_{\mathbf{p}}-\epsilon_{\mathbf{h}}}X_{\mathbf{ph}}, (𝒢^T−1​X)𝐡𝐩≡\displaystyle(\hat{\mathcal{G}}^{-1}_{T}X)_{\mathbf{hp}}\equiv 1ϵ𝐩−ϵ𝐡​X𝐡𝐩,\displaystyle\frac{1}{\epsilon_{\mathbf{p}}-\epsilon_{\mathbf{h}}}X_{\mathbf{hp}}, (199)

has a familiar form of the first-order perturbation theory and a simple physical interpretation. Consider a single-body Hamiltonian h^χ≡∑i​j[ti​j​(ρ¯)+χi​j]​ci†​cj\hat{h}_{\chi}\equiv\sum_{ij}[t_{ij}(\bar{\rho})+\chi_{ij}]c_{i}^{\dagger}c_{j} and its ground state RDM ρ⁡(χ)\rho(\chi). We know ρ⁡(χ=0)=ρ¯\rho(\chi=0)=\bar{\rho}. 𝒢^T−1\hat{\mathcal{G}}^{-1}_{T} is exactly describing the linear-order change: ρ⁡(χ)−ρ¯≡δ​ρ​(χ)=−𝒢^T−1​χ+O⁡(χ2)\rho(\chi)-\bar{\rho}\equiv\delta\rho(\chi)=-\hat{\mathcal{G}}^{-1}_{T}\chi+O(\chi^{2}). Since δ​ρ=κ\delta\rho=\kappa to the linear order, κ=−𝒢^T−1​χ\kappa=-\hat{\mathcal{G}}^{-1}_{T}\chi is a static relation between the Thouless parameter of ρ⁡(χ)\rho(\chi) and χ\chi.

To see how the Ward identity leads to Goldstone zero modes, we first work out the linearized EOM from the κ\kappa-theory LTDVPL_{\rm TDVP} in Eq.(173). In frequency space κ⁡(t)=∫d​ω2​π​κ​(ω)​e−i​ω​t\kappa(t)=\int\frac{d\omega}{2\pi}\kappa(\omega)e^{-i\omega t}, the κ\kappa-EOM is

[−i​ω​ℱ^+𝒢^+𝒫^T​𝒦^]​κ​(ω)=0.\displaystyle\Big[-i\omega\hat{\mathcal{F}}+\hat{\mathcal{G}}+\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{T}\hat{\mathcal{K}}\Big]\kappa(\omega)=0. (200)

Therefore Eq.(197) dictates κQ\kappa_{Q} being ω=0\omega=0 mode.

To find the χ\chi-EOM, we first integrate out κ\kappa in Lκ,χL_{\kappa,\chi} in Eq.(180), giving rise to the χ\chi-action in the frequency space (up to Gaussian order):

Sχ=12​∫d​ω2​π​χ​(−ω)​[𝒫^HS​(−i​ω​ℱ^+𝒢^)T−1+𝒦^HS−1]​χ​(ω),\displaystyle S_{\chi}=\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{d\omega}{2\pi}\chi(-\omega)\Big[\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{\rm HS}(-i\omega\hat{\mathcal{F}}+\hat{\mathcal{G}})_{T}^{-1}+\hat{\mathcal{K}}_{\rm HS}^{-1}\Big]\chi(\omega), (201)

where, similar to 𝒢^T−1\hat{\mathcal{G}}_{T}^{-1}, the superoperator inverse (𝒪^)T−1(\hat{\mathcal{O}})^{-1}_{T} for 𝒪^\hat{\mathcal{O}} acting within Tρ¯T_{\bar{\rho}} should be interpreted as 𝒫^T​𝒪^−1​𝒫^T\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{T}\hat{\mathcal{O}}^{-1}\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{T}. The linearized χ\chi-EOM in terms of eigen equation is then:

[𝒫^HS​(−i​ω​ℱ^+𝒢^)T−1+𝒦^HS−1]​χ​(ω)=0,\displaystyle\Big[\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{\rm HS}(-i\omega\hat{\mathcal{F}}+\hat{\mathcal{G}})_{T}^{-1}+\hat{\mathcal{K}}_{\rm HS}^{-1}\Big]\chi(\omega)=0, (202)

and Eq.(198) dictates χQ\chi_{Q} being ω=0\omega=0 mode.

For the purpose of collective modes, whether one wants to work with κ\kappa or χ\chi languages is a personal preference – they are dual degrees of freedom capturing the same physics. χ\chi describes the Weiss-field fluctuations while κ\kappa describes the corresponding density-matrix fluctuations. For example, one can check that every χ\chi-eigenmode satisfying Eq.(202) can be mapped to a κ\kappa-eigenmode satisfying Eq.(200) with the same frequency via:

χ→κ:κ⁡(ω)=−(−i​ω​ℱ^+𝒢^)T−1​χ​(ω).\displaystyle\chi\rightarrow\kappa:\kappa(\omega)=-(-i\omega\hat{\mathcal{F}}+\hat{\mathcal{G}})^{-1}_{T}\chi(\omega). (203)

For the purpose of later Hdet discussions, we are particularly interested in the effective theory in the form of LeffL_{\rm eff} in Eq.(181), and will now focus on the χ\chi-language. Eq.(203) is convenient since the zero-point motion and quantum excitation of the χ\chi-eigenmode have a concrete meaning in the VMPI wavefunction ΨVMPI​(κ)\Psi_{\rm VMPI}(\kappa), which is written in the κ\kappa-language.

In our subsequent discussion of effective theories of Hdet wavefunctions, we will investigate the emergent gauge dynamics and demonstrate the U⁡(1)U(1) gauge fluctuations as a concrete example. Although the continuous symmetry and the gauge redundancy are fundamentally different physically, the gauge dynamics (e.g., the Maxwell equation, the Chern-Simons(CS)-term) emerge due to the Ward identity for the gauge redundancy, quite similar to how the Goldstone mode dynamics emerge due to the Ward identity for spontaneous symmetry breaking. The lessons learned here will prove very helpful.

V.2.4 Type-I and Type-II Goldstone dispersions

In the later Hdet discussion, we will encounter two kinds of U⁡(1)U(1) gauge dynamics in the long-wavelength limit: the gapless photon phases governed by the Maxwell term, and the topological phases governed by the CS term. The crucial difference between them is that the Maxwell term contains second time derivatives, while the CS term contains first time derivatives.

Interestingly, in parallel, even in the current TDHF demonstration, there are also two kinds of long-wavelength Goldstone mode dispersions: ω∼|𝐪|\omega\sim|\mathbf{q}| (Type-I) as in an antiferromagnet, and ω∼𝐪2\omega\sim\mathbf{q}^{2} (Type-II) as in a ferromagnet. As we will see, the physical origin for these two Goldstone-mode types is quite similar to the physical origin for Maxwell and CS gauge dynamics: the effective Lagrangian for type-I Goldstone modes only contains second time derivatives, while for type-II Goldstone modes it contains first time derivatives. Again, the lessons we learn here will prove useful when we microscopically compute the Maxwell and CS terms in the Hdet gauge dynamics.

Note that we are now focusing on the χ\chi-language to describe Goldstone modes. When χ\chi was first introduced via the HS transformation, it did not have dynamics (i.e., time derivatives). The χ\chi-dynamics is generated upon integrating out κ\kappa as in Eq.(201). We will first present a general analysis of translationally invariant systems, which is fully microscopic and can be used to compute the full collective-mode dispersions. We then focus on long-wavelength behavior to understand the origin of type-I vs. type-II Goldstone dispersions.

Quite generally, we assume that the effective hopping ti​j​(ρ¯)t_{ij}(\bar{\rho}) is short-ranged. Introducing a double index: i=(𝐑,𝛂)i=(\mathbf{R},\bm{\upalpha}), where 𝐑\mathbf{R} labels the (possibly enlarged) unit cell position, while 𝛂\bm{\upalpha} labels orbitals within the unit cell, we have

t​(ρ¯)(𝐑,𝛂),(𝐑+𝜹,𝛃)=t𝛂​𝛃;𝜹.\displaystyle t(\bar{\rho})_{(\mathbf{R},\bm{\upalpha}),(\mathbf{R}+\bm{\delta},\bm{\upbeta})}=t_{\bm{\upalpha}\bm{\upbeta};\bm{\delta}}. (204)

It is convenient to perform the lattice Fourier transformation to transform all Hermitian matrices in MhM_{\rm h} to the momentum space. Recall that MhM_{\rm h} is a real linear space. For the purpose of the Fourier transformation, we complexify MhM_{\rm h} into MhℂM_{\rm h}^{\mathbb{C}}. We define a 𝐪\mathbf{q}-space vector for MhℂM_{\rm h}^{\mathbb{C}}: X𝛂​𝛃;𝜹​(𝐪)X_{\bm{\upalpha}\bm{\upbeta};\bm{\delta}}(\mathbf{q}) based on its tensor value:

X(𝐑,𝛂),(𝐑+𝜹,𝛃)=1Nuc​∑𝐪ei​𝐪⋅𝐑​X𝛂​𝛃;𝜹​(𝐪),\displaystyle X_{(\mathbf{R},\bm{\upalpha}),(\mathbf{R}+\bm{\delta},\bm{\upbeta})}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{\rm uc}}}\sum_{\mathbf{q}}e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{R}}X_{\bm{\upalpha}\bm{\upbeta};\bm{\delta}}(\mathbf{q}), (205)

where NucN_{\rm uc} is the number of unit-cells and 𝐪∈\mathbf{q}\in Brillouin Zone (BZ). For each fixed 𝐪∈BZ\mathbf{q}\in\rm BZ, we denote the complex linear space spanned by all X𝛂​𝛃;𝜹​(𝐪)X_{\bm{\upalpha}\bm{\upbeta};\bm{\delta}}(\mathbf{q}) as Mh​(𝐪)M_{\rm h}(\mathbf{q}). Thus:

Mhℂ=⨁𝐪Mh​(𝐪).\displaystyle M_{\rm h}^{\mathbb{C}}=\bigoplus_{\mathbf{q}}M_{\rm h}(\mathbf{q}). (206)

In this formalism, t⁡(ρ¯)=t𝛂​𝛃;𝜹​(𝟎)∈Mh​(𝟎)t(\bar{\rho})=t_{\bm{\upalpha}\bm{\upbeta};\bm{\delta}}(\mathbf{0})\in M_{\rm h}(\mathbf{0}).

The original inner product \llangle​X,Y​\rrangle=∑i​jXi​j​Yj​i\llangle X,Y\rrangle=\sum_{ij}X_{ij}Y_{ji} on MhM_{\rm h} in Eq.(159) can be extended as a bilinear form to MhℂM_{\rm h}^{\mathbb{C}} maintaining its form. One finds that:

\llangle​X,Y​\rrangle=∑𝐪\llangle​X​(−𝐪),Y⁡(𝐪)​\rrangle,\displaystyle\llangle X,Y\rrangle=\sum_{\mathbf{q}}\llangle X(-\mathbf{q}),Y(\mathbf{q})\rrangle, (207)

where the 𝐪\mathbf{q}-space bilinear form is

\llangle​X​(−𝐪),Y⁡(𝐪)​\rrangle≡∑𝛂​𝛃;𝜹ei​𝐪⋅𝜹​X𝛂​𝛃;𝜹​(−𝐪)​Y𝛃​𝛂;−𝜹​(𝐪).\displaystyle\llangle X(-\mathbf{q}),Y(\mathbf{q})\rrangle\equiv\sum_{\bm{\upalpha}\bm{\upbeta};\bm{\delta}}e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\bm{\delta}}X_{\bm{\upalpha}\bm{\upbeta};\bm{\delta}}(-\mathbf{q})Y_{\bm{\upbeta}\bm{\upalpha};-\bm{\delta}}(\mathbf{q}). (208)

By momentum conservation, this bilinear form can be nonzero only for such a −𝐪,𝐪-\mathbf{q},\mathbf{q} pair.

In addition, ∀X⁡(𝐪)∈Mh​(𝐪)\forall X(\mathbf{q})\in M_{\rm h}(\mathbf{q}), one can show its Hermitian conjugate X​(𝐪)†∈Mh​(−𝐪)X(\mathbf{q})^{\dagger}\in M_{\rm h}(-\mathbf{q}) is:

[X(𝐪)†]𝛂​𝛃;𝜹(−𝐪)=e−i𝐪⋅𝜹X𝛃​𝛂;−𝜹∗(𝐪)\displaystyle[X(\mathbf{q})^{\dagger}]_{\bm{\upalpha}\bm{\upbeta};\bm{\delta}}(-\mathbf{q})=e^{-i\mathbf{q}\cdot\bm{\delta}}X^{*}_{\bm{\upbeta}\bm{\upalpha};-\bm{\delta}}(\mathbf{q}) (209)

The original real linear space MhM_{\rm h} is formed by those X∈MhℂX\in M_{\rm h}^{\mathbb{C}} satisfying X⁡(−𝐪)=X​(𝐪)†X(-\mathbf{q})=X(\mathbf{q})^{\dagger}.

Finally, the Hermitian conjugate operation allows one to define an inner product within Mh​(𝐪)M_{\rm h}(\mathbf{q}) for a fixed 𝐪\mathbf{q}:

⟨X⁡(𝐪),Y⁡(𝐪)⟩𝐪≡\llangle​X​(𝐪)†,Y⁡(𝐪)​\rrangle=∑𝛂​𝛃;𝜹X𝛂​𝛃;𝜹∗​(𝐪)​Y𝛂​𝛃;𝜹​(𝐪).\displaystyle\langle X(\mathbf{q}),Y(\mathbf{q})\rangle_{\mathbf{q}}\equiv\llangle X(\mathbf{q})^{\dagger},Y(\mathbf{q})\rrangle=\sum_{\bm{\upalpha}\bm{\upbeta};\bm{\delta}}X^{*}_{\bm{\upalpha}\bm{\upbeta};\bm{\delta}}(\mathbf{q})Y_{\bm{\upalpha}\bm{\upbeta};\bm{\delta}}(\mathbf{q}). (210)

With these understandings for the 𝐪\mathbf{q}-space algebraic structure, we now consider the important subspaces Tρ¯,VHS⊂MhT_{\bar{\rho}},V_{\rm HS}\subset M_{\rm h}. After complexification we have Tρ¯ℂ,VHSℂ⊂MhℂT^{\mathbb{C}}_{\bar{\rho}},V^{\mathbb{C}}_{\rm HS}\subset M_{\rm h}^{\mathbb{C}}, which can be further decomposed into fixed-𝐪\mathbf{q} subspaces:

Tρ¯ℂ=\displaystyle T^{\mathbb{C}}_{\bar{\rho}}= ⨁𝐪Tρ¯​(𝐪),\displaystyle\bigoplus_{\mathbf{q}}T_{\bar{\rho}}(\mathbf{q}), Tρ¯​(𝐪)≡\displaystyle T_{\bar{\rho}}(\mathbf{q})\equiv Tρ¯ℂ∩Mh​(𝐪),\displaystyle T^{\mathbb{C}}_{\bar{\rho}}\cap M_{\rm h}(\mathbf{q}),
VHSℂ=\displaystyle V^{\mathbb{C}}_{\rm HS}= ⨁𝐪VHS​(𝐪),\displaystyle\bigoplus_{\mathbf{q}}V_{\rm HS}(\mathbf{q}), VHS​(𝐪)≡\displaystyle V_{\rm HS}(\mathbf{q})\equiv VHSℂ∩Mh​(𝐪).\displaystyle V^{\mathbb{C}}_{\rm HS}\cap M_{\rm h}(\mathbf{q}). (211)

The general χ\chi-field in action Eq.(201), in momentum space, becomes χ​(𝐪)∈VHS​(𝐪)\chi(\mathbf{q})\in V_{\rm HS}(\mathbf{q}). Due to translation symmetry, all superoperators defined previously act within fixed-𝐪\mathbf{q} subspaces. For instance:

(−i​ω​ℱ^+𝒢^)T−1​(𝐪):\displaystyle(-i\omega\hat{\mathcal{F}}+\hat{\mathcal{G}})^{-1}_{T}(\mathbf{q}): Tρ¯​(𝐪)→Tρ¯​(𝐪),\displaystyle\;\;T_{\bar{\rho}}(\mathbf{q})\rightarrow T_{\bar{\rho}}(\mathbf{q}),
𝒫^HS​(𝐪),𝒦^HS−1​(𝐪):\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{\rm HS}(\mathbf{q}),\hat{\mathcal{K}}_{\rm HS}^{-1}(\mathbf{q}): VHS​(𝐪)→VHS​(𝐪).\displaystyle\;\;V_{\rm HS}(\mathbf{q})\rightarrow V_{\rm HS}(\mathbf{q}). (212)

In fact, it is easy to show that, w.r.t. the inner product defined in Eq.(210), the superoperators 𝒦^​(𝐪),𝒦^HS−1​(𝐪),𝒢^​(𝐪),𝒢^T−1​(𝐪),𝒫^T​(𝐪),𝒫^HS​(𝐪)\hat{\mathcal{K}}(\mathbf{q}),\hat{\mathcal{K}}_{\rm HS}^{-1}(\mathbf{q}),\hat{\mathcal{G}}(\mathbf{q}),\hat{\mathcal{G}}^{-1}_{T}(\mathbf{q}),\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{T}(\mathbf{q}),\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{\rm HS}(\mathbf{q}) are all Hermitian in respective subspaces that they act on, while ℱ^​(𝐪)\hat{\mathcal{F}}(\mathbf{q}) is anti-Hermitian.

One may solve the linearized EOM in 𝐪\mathbf{q}-space to find general collective mode dispersions:

𝒟^​(𝐪,ω)​χ​(𝐪,ω)=0,where\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{q},\omega)\chi(\mathbf{q},\omega)=0,\;\;\text{where }
𝒟^​(𝐪,ω)≡\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{q},\omega)\equiv 𝒫^HS​(𝐪)​(−i​ω​ℱ^+𝒢^)T−1​(𝐪)+𝒦^HS−1​(𝐪),\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{\rm HS}(\mathbf{q})(-i\omega\hat{\mathcal{F}}+\hat{\mathcal{G}})_{T}^{-1}(\mathbf{q})+\hat{\mathcal{K}}_{\rm HS}^{-1}(\mathbf{q}), (213)

and 𝒟^​(𝐪,ω):VHS​(𝐪)→VHS​(𝐪)\hat{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{q},\omega):V_{\rm HS}(\mathbf{q})\rightarrow V_{\rm HS}(\mathbf{q}) is Hermitian.

Next, we will prepare for the long-wavelength analysis of the Goldstone modes. At this point, we need to make further assumptions for the real-space form of superoperator 𝒦^\hat{\mathcal{K}}. Quite generally, we assume that the Hessian 𝒦\mathcal{K} in Eq.(158) admits a translation invariant form:

𝒦(𝐑,𝛂),(𝐑+𝜹,𝛃),(𝐑′,𝛄),(𝐑′+𝜹′,𝛌)\displaystyle\mathcal{K}_{(\mathbf{R},\bm{\upalpha}),(\mathbf{R}+\bm{\delta},\bm{\upbeta}),(\mathbf{R}^{\prime},\bm{\upgamma}),(\mathbf{R}^{\prime}+\bm{\delta}^{\prime},\bm{\uplambda})}
=\displaystyle= ∑A,B=1Nww𝛂​𝛃;𝜹A​MA​B​(𝐑−𝐑′)​w𝛄​𝛌;𝜹′B,\displaystyle\sum_{A,B=1}^{N_{w}}w^{A}_{\bm{\upalpha}\bm{\upbeta};\bm{\delta}}M_{AB}(\mathbf{R}-\mathbf{R}^{\prime})w^{B}_{\bm{\upgamma}\bm{\uplambda};\bm{\delta}^{\prime}}, (214)

where {w𝛂​𝛃;𝜹A}\{w^{A}_{\bm{\upalpha}\bm{\upbeta};\bm{\delta}}\} (A=1,2,..NwA=1,2,..N_{w}) labels a linearly-independent set of fixed Hermitian bond tensors satisfying wA𝛂​𝛃;𝜹=wA∗𝛃​𝛂;−𝜹w^{A}_{\bm{\upalpha}\bm{\upbeta};\bm{\delta}}=w^{A*}_{\bm{\upbeta}\bm{\upalpha};-\bm{\delta}}. In addition, we assume that MA​B​(𝚫)M_{AB}(\bm{\Delta}) is not too long-ranged so that its Fourier transform is a continuous function near 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0. It is well-known that, for sufficiently long-ranged interactions, the would-be Goldstone-mode dispersion can become gapped near 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0. Note that, the exact Goldstone zero-mode analysis in the previous section is still valid even in that case, however, due to the singularity of the momentum space kernel near 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0, those zero modes cannot be lifted into dispersive modes. If the underlying interaction is truly short-ranged, then MA​B​(𝚫)M_{AB}(\bm{\Delta}) will have a finite support of 𝚫\bm{\Delta} and its Fourier transform is a smooth function; in addition, the number of bond tensors NwN_{w} participating in 𝒦\mathcal{K} will be finite, constrained by a finite support of 𝜹\bm{\delta}.

The Fourier transform of the Hermitian bond tensors leads to NwN_{w} vectors {w𝛂​𝛃;𝜹A​(𝐪)}∈Mh​(𝐪)\{w^{A}_{\bm{\upalpha}\bm{\upbeta};\bm{\delta}}(\mathbf{q})\}\in M_{\rm h}(\mathbf{q}) for every 𝐪\mathbf{q}, whose tensor values w𝛂​𝛃;𝜹Aw^{A}_{\bm{\upalpha}\bm{\upbeta};\bm{\delta}} are independent of 𝐪\mathbf{q}. The crucial consequence of the real-space form of 𝒦\mathcal{K} in Eq.(214) is that, after acting on an arbitrary 𝐪\mathbf{q}-space basis vector X𝛂​𝛃;𝜹​(𝐪)X_{\bm{\upalpha}\bm{\upbeta};\bm{\delta}}(\mathbf{q}) as in Eq.(205), it is obvious that 𝒦^​X𝛂​𝛃;𝜹​(𝐪)\hat{\mathcal{K}}X_{\bm{\upalpha}\bm{\upbeta};\bm{\delta}}(\mathbf{q}) must be in the NwN_{w}-dimensional linear subspace Vw​(𝐪)V_{w}(\mathbf{q}) spanned by {w𝛂​𝛃;𝜹A​(𝐪)}\{w^{A}_{\bm{\upalpha}\bm{\upbeta};\bm{\delta}}(\mathbf{q})\}. Since 𝒦^​(𝐪)\hat{\mathcal{K}}(\mathbf{q}) is Hermitian w.r.t. inner product Eq.(210), one may view 𝒦^​(𝐪)\hat{\mathcal{K}}(\mathbf{q}) as an operator 𝒦^​(𝐪):Vw​(𝐪)→Vw​(𝐪)\hat{\mathcal{K}}(\mathbf{q}):V_{w}(\mathbf{q})\rightarrow V_{w}(\mathbf{q}).

We define:

KA​B​(𝐪)≡⟨wA​(𝐪),𝒦^​(𝐪)​wB​(𝐪)⟩𝐪,\displaystyle K_{AB}(\mathbf{q})\equiv\langle w^{A}(\mathbf{q}),\hat{\mathcal{K}}(\mathbf{q})w^{B}(\mathbf{q})\rangle_{\mathbf{q}}, (215)

which is automatically a Hermitian matrix of A,BA,B. Finally, we assume that the matrix KA​B​(𝐪)K_{AB}(\mathbf{q}) is full-rank (at least for small 𝐪\mathbf{q}’s). This allows us to immediately identify VHS​(𝐪)≡Im⁡(𝒦^​(𝐪))=Vw​(𝐪)V_{\rm HS}(\mathbf{q})\equiv{\rm Im}(\hat{\mathcal{K}}(\mathbf{q}))=V_{w}(\mathbf{q}), and Nw=dim⁡[VHS​(𝐪)]N_{w}=\rm{dim}[V_{\rm HS}(\mathbf{q})].

Now, we consider the general situation where there may be more than one U⁡(1)U(1) symmetries are spontaneously broken. Denoting the number of linearly independent broken symmetry generators as nGn_{\rm G}, we label these generators by QaQ_{a} (a=1,2..nGa=1,2..n_{\rm G}). Because both QaQ_{a} and t⁡(ρ¯)t(\bar{\rho}) are translational invariant, their commutator as in Eq.(192) – the Goldstone zero mode χQa\chi_{Q_{a}} must be translational invariant and in VHS​(𝟎)V_{\rm HS}(\mathbf{0}). We denote these vectors as u𝛂​𝛃;𝜹a​(𝟎)u^{a}_{\bm{\upalpha}\bm{\upbeta};\bm{\delta}}(\mathbf{0}):

χQa=i​θa​[Qa,t⁡(ρ¯)]≡θa⋅𝗎𝛂​𝛃;𝜹a​(𝟎)∈VHS​(𝟎).\displaystyle\chi_{Q_{a}}=i\theta_{a}[Q_{a},t(\bar{\rho})]\equiv\theta_{a}\cdot\mathsf{u}^{a}_{\bm{\upalpha}\bm{\upbeta};\bm{\delta}}(\mathbf{0})\in V_{\rm HS}(\mathbf{0}). (216)

Consequently, the Hermitian bond tensors {𝗎𝛂​𝛃;𝜹a}\{\mathsf{u}^{a}_{\bm{\upalpha}\bm{\upbeta};\bm{\delta}}\} (a=1,2,..,nG)(a=1,2,..,n_{\rm G}) are inside the real linear space spanned by {w𝛂​𝛃;𝜹A}\{w^{A}_{\bm{\upalpha}\bm{\upbeta};\bm{\delta}}\} (A=1,2,..,NwA=1,2,..,N_{w}). WLOG, we can choose the tensors {w𝛂​𝛃;𝜹A}\{w^{A}_{\bm{\upalpha}\bm{\upbeta};\bm{\delta}}\} (A=1,2,..,NwA=1,2,..,N_{w}) so that w𝛂​𝛃;𝜹a=𝗎𝛂​𝛃;𝜹aw^{a}_{\bm{\upalpha}\bm{\upbeta};\bm{\delta}}=\mathsf{u}^{a}_{\bm{\upalpha}\bm{\upbeta};\bm{\delta}} (a=1,2,…,nGa=1,2,...,n_{\rm G}).

We denote the subspace spanned by {w𝛂​𝛃;𝜹A​(𝐪)}\{w^{A}_{\bm{\upalpha}\bm{\upbeta};\bm{\delta}}(\mathbf{q})\} (A=1,2,..,nGA=1,2,..,n_{\rm G}) as VG​(𝐪)V_{\rm G}(\mathbf{q}) (the Goldstone subspace), and the subspace spanned by {w𝛂​𝛃;𝜹A​(𝐪)}\{w^{A}_{\bm{\upalpha}\bm{\upbeta};\bm{\delta}}(\mathbf{q})\} (A=nG+1,..,NwA=n_{\rm G}+1,..,N_{w}) as V⟂​(𝐪)V_{\perp}(\mathbf{q}). Consequently, VHS​(𝐪)=VG​(𝐪)⊕V⟂​(𝐪)V_{\rm HS}(\mathbf{q})=V_{\rm G}(\mathbf{q})\oplus V_{\perp}(\mathbf{q}).

We can write down the χ\chi-action in Eq.(201) in the momentum-frequency space:

Sχ=∫d​ω4​π​∑𝐪\llangle​χ​(−𝐪,−ω),𝒟^​(𝐪,ω)​χ​(𝐪,ω)​\rrangle,\displaystyle S_{\chi}=\int\frac{d\omega}{4\pi}\sum_{\mathbf{q}}\llangle\chi(-\mathbf{q},-\omega),\hat{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{q},\omega)\chi(\mathbf{q},\omega)\rrangle, (217)

where we used the bilinear form defined in Eq.(208).

Expanding the general χ\chi-field using the {wA​(𝐪)}\{w^{A}(\mathbf{q})\} basis:

χ⁡(𝐪,ω)\displaystyle\chi(\mathbf{q},\omega) =∑A=1nGϕA​(𝐪,ω)​wA​(𝐪)\displaystyle=\sum_{A=1}^{n_{\rm G}}\phi_{A}(\mathbf{q},\omega)w^{A}(\mathbf{q})
+∑B=1Nw−nGηB(𝐪,ω)wB+nG(𝐪),\displaystyle+\sum_{B=1}^{N_{w}-n_{\rm G}}\eta_{B}(\mathbf{q},\omega)w^{B+n_{\rm G}}(\mathbf{q}), (218)

we have, in concrete matrix form:

Sχ=\displaystyle S_{\chi}= ∫d​ω4​π​∑𝐪(ϕ⁡(−𝐪,−ω),η⁡(−𝐪,−ω))\displaystyle\int\frac{d\omega}{4\pi}\sum_{\mathbf{q}}\big(\phi(-\mathbf{q},-\omega),\eta(-\mathbf{q},-\omega)\big)
⋅(DGG​(𝐪,ω)DG⟂​(𝐪,ω)D⟂G​(𝐪,ω)D⟂⁣⟂​(𝐪,ω))Nw×Nw⋅(ϕ⁡(𝐪,ω)η⁡(𝐪,ω)),\displaystyle\cdot\begin{pmatrix}D_{\rm{GG}}(\mathbf{q},\omega)&D_{\rm{G}\perp}(\mathbf{q},\omega)\\ D_{\perp\rm{G}}(\mathbf{q},\omega)&D_{\perp\perp}(\mathbf{q},\omega)\end{pmatrix}_{N_{w}\times N_{w}}\cdot\begin{pmatrix}\phi(\mathbf{q},\omega)\\ \eta(\mathbf{q},\omega)\end{pmatrix}, (219)

where G,⟂\rm G,\perp label components in VG,V⟂V_{\rm G},V_{\perp}, and

DA​B​(𝐪,ω)\displaystyle D_{AB}(\mathbf{q},\omega) ≡\llangle​wA​(−𝐪),𝒟^​(𝐪,ω)​wB​(𝐪)​\rrangle\displaystyle\equiv\llangle w^{A}(-\mathbf{q}),\hat{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{q},\omega)w^{B}(\mathbf{q})\rrangle
=⟨wA​(𝐪),𝒟^​(𝐪,ω)​wB​(𝐪)⟩𝐪.\displaystyle=\langle w^{A}(\mathbf{q}),\hat{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{q},\omega)w^{B}(\mathbf{q})\rangle_{\mathbf{q}}. (220)

The last equality follows from the hermiticity of the tensors {wA}\{w^{A}\}. For simplicity, we further assume that the fermion 𝐩𝐡\mathbf{ph} spectrum is fully gapped, since the general coupling between Goldstone bosons with gapless fermion matter requires sophisticated analysis[130]. Under this assumption, DA​BD_{AB} is a regular function of (𝐪,ω)(\mathbf{q},\omega): e.g. it cannot have |𝐪||\mathbf{q}|-linear dependence. Moreover, χ\chi being a Hermitian matrix and 𝒟^\hat{\mathcal{D}} being a Hermitian superoperator dictates that:

ϕA​(−𝐪,−ω)=\displaystyle\phi_{A}(-\mathbf{q},-\omega)= ϕA∗​(𝐪,ω),ηA​(−𝐪,−ω)=ηA∗​(𝐪,ω),\displaystyle\phi_{A}^{*}(\mathbf{q},\omega),\;\;\eta_{A}(-\mathbf{q},-\omega)=\eta_{A}^{*}(\mathbf{q},\omega),
DA​B​(−𝐪,−ω)=\displaystyle D_{AB}(-\mathbf{q},-\omega)= DA​B∗​(𝐪,ω)=DB​A​(𝐪,ω)\displaystyle D^{*}_{AB}(\mathbf{q},\omega)=D_{BA}(\mathbf{q},\omega) (221)

Namely the full DA​B​(𝐪,ω)D_{AB}(\mathbf{q},\omega) matrix is Hermitian, together with the EOM:

(DGG​(𝐪,ω)DG⟂​(𝐪,ω)D⟂G​(𝐪,ω)D⟂⁣⟂​(𝐪,ω))⋅(ϕ⁡(𝐪,ω)η⁡(𝐪,ω))=0.\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}D_{\rm{GG}}(\mathbf{q},\omega)&D_{\rm{G}\perp}(\mathbf{q},\omega)\\ D_{\perp\rm{G}}(\mathbf{q},\omega)&D_{\perp\perp}(\mathbf{q},\omega)\end{pmatrix}\cdot\begin{pmatrix}\phi(\mathbf{q},\omega)\\ \eta(\mathbf{q},\omega)\end{pmatrix}=0. (222)

Now we are ready to perform the long-wavelength analysis. The Ward identity Eq.(198) can be written as:

𝒟^​(𝟎,0)​wA​(𝟎)=\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{D}}(\mathbf{0},0)w^{A}(\mathbf{0})= 0,\displaystyle 0, A=\displaystyle A= 1,2,..,nG.\displaystyle 1,2,..,n_{\rm G}. (223)

Since the DA​BD_{AB} matrix is Hermitian, we know that:

DGG​(𝟎,0)=\displaystyle D_{\rm{GG}}(\mathbf{0},0)= 0,\displaystyle 0, DG⟂​(𝟎,0)=\displaystyle D_{\rm{G}\perp}(\mathbf{0},0)= 0,\displaystyle 0, D⟂G​(𝟎,0)=\displaystyle D_{\perp\rm{G}}(\mathbf{0},0)= 0.\displaystyle 0. (224)

Quite generally, we assume that the orthogonal block is nonsingular (i.e. gapped) and denote it as Δ≡D⟂⁣⟂​(𝟎,0)\Delta\equiv D_{\perp\perp}(\mathbf{0},0).

For a small 𝐪\mathbf{q}, the solution of EOM leads to:

η⁡(𝐪,ω)\displaystyle\eta(\mathbf{q},\omega) =−D⟂⁣⟂​(𝐪,ω)−1​D⟂G​(𝐪,ω)​ϕ​(𝐪,ω)\displaystyle=-D_{\perp\perp}(\mathbf{q},\omega)^{-1}D_{\perp\rm G}(\mathbf{q},\omega)\phi(\mathbf{q},\omega)
∼O⁡(|𝐪|,ω)​ϕ​(𝐪,ω),\displaystyle\sim O(|\mathbf{q}|,\omega)\phi(\mathbf{q},\omega), (225)

since Δ−1\Delta^{-1} is finite. Physically, it means that, to the leading order of the gradient expansion, the small-𝐪\mathbf{q} Goldstone mode only contains ϕ\phi components, and can be generated by a spatial-dependent (with the wavevector 𝐪\mathbf{q}) symmetry rotation.

Upon integrating out the gapped η\eta-modes, we arrive at the effective action in the Goldstone subspace VG​(𝐪)V_{\rm G}(\mathbf{q}):

SG=∫d​ω4​π​∑𝐪ϕ⁡(−𝐪,−ω)​Π​(𝐪,ω)​ϕ​(𝐪,ω),\displaystyle S_{\rm G}=\int\frac{d\omega}{4\pi}\sum_{\mathbf{q}}\phi(-\mathbf{q},-\omega)\Pi(\mathbf{q},\omega)\phi(\mathbf{q},\omega), (226)

where the reduced kernel is given by the Schur complement:

Π⁡(𝐪,ω)≡DGG​(𝐪,ω)−DG⟂​(𝐪,ω)​D⟂⁣⟂−1​(𝐪,ω)​D⟂G​(𝐪,ω)\displaystyle\Pi(\mathbf{q},\omega)\equiv D_{\rm{GG}}(\mathbf{q},\omega)-D_{\rm G\perp}(\mathbf{q},\omega)D^{-1}_{\perp\perp}(\mathbf{q},\omega)D_{\perp\rm G}(\mathbf{q},\omega) (227)

is also a regular function. Following Eq.(224), the reduced Ward identity is:

Π⁡(𝟎,0)=0.\displaystyle\Pi(\mathbf{0},0)=0. (228)

One may parameterize its small-(𝐪,ω)(\mathbf{q},\omega) expansion using constants 𝖡a​b,𝖢a​b,𝖦a​bI​J\mathsf{B}_{ab},\mathsf{C}_{ab},\mathsf{G}^{IJ}_{ab} (a,b=1,..,nGa,b=1,..,n_{\rm G}.):

Πa​b​(𝐪,ω)=\displaystyle\Pi_{ab}(\mathbf{q},\omega)= i​ω⋅𝖡a​b+ω2⋅𝖢a​b+∑u,v𝐪u​𝐪v⋅𝖦a​bu​v\displaystyle i\omega\cdot\mathsf{B}_{ab}+\omega^{2}\cdot\mathsf{C}_{ab}+\sum_{u,v}\mathbf{q}_{u}\mathbf{q}_{v}\cdot\mathsf{G}^{uv}_{ab}
+O⁡((|𝐪|,ω)3),\displaystyle+O((|\mathbf{q}|,\omega)^{3}), (229)

where the 𝐪\mathbf{q}-linear term is forbidden by the stability of variational energy minimum reached by ρ¯\bar{\rho}, while |𝐪||\mathbf{q}|-linear term is forbidden by regularity. (If the state |Φ⁡(ρ¯)⟩|\Phi(\bar{\rho})\rangle carries background flows, e.g., supercurrent in a Bose-Hubbard model, a Doppler term ∼ω⋅𝐪\sim\omega\cdot\mathbf{q} may be present. Here we assume it is not such a state.) From Eq.(221), we know that 𝖡\mathsf{B} is real antisymmetric, 𝖢\mathsf{C} and 𝖦\mathsf{G} are real symmetric (w.r.t. a,ba,b). Generically 𝖢,𝖦≠0\mathsf{C},\mathsf{G}\neq 0.

Type-I (type-II) Goldstone modes correspond to those a,ba,b components with 𝖡a​b=0\mathsf{B}_{ab}=0 (𝖡a​b≠0\mathsf{B}_{ab}\neq 0), leading to dispersion ω∼|𝐪|\omega\sim|\mathbf{q}| (ω∼|𝐪|2\omega\sim|\mathbf{q}|^{2}). The key point is that, as dictated by Eq.(227), 𝖡\mathsf{B} is completely determined by DGG​(𝐪=0,ω)D_{\rm{GG}}(\mathbf{q}=0,\omega): due to Eq.(224), DG⟂,D⟂GD_{\rm G\perp},D_{\perp\rm G} both at most host ω\omega-linear term, and consequently the correction DG⟂​(𝟎,ω)​D⟂⁣⟂−1​(𝟎,ω)​D⟂G​(𝟎,ω)∼O⁡(ω2)D_{\rm G\perp}(\mathbf{0},\omega)D^{-1}_{\perp\perp}(\mathbf{0},\omega)D_{\perp\rm G}(\mathbf{0},\omega)\sim O(\omega^{2}). Based on the definition of the χ\chi-kernel 𝒟^\hat{\mathcal{D}} in Eq.(213), because

(−i​ω​ℱ^+𝒢^)T−1=𝒢^T−1+i​ω​𝒢^T−1​ℱ^​𝒢^T−1+O⁡(ω2),\displaystyle(-i\omega\hat{\mathcal{F}}+\hat{\mathcal{G}})^{-1}_{T}=\hat{\mathcal{G}}^{-1}_{T}+i\omega\hat{\mathcal{G}}^{-1}_{T}\hat{\mathcal{F}}\hat{\mathcal{G}}^{-1}_{T}+O(\omega^{2}), (230)

using Eq.(216): wa​(𝟎)=1θa​χQaw^{a}(\mathbf{0})=\frac{1}{\theta_{a}}\chi_{Q_{a}}, one finds:

𝖡a​b=\displaystyle\mathsf{B}_{ab}= 1θa​θb⋅\llangle​χQa,𝒢^T−1​ℱ^​𝒢^T−1​χQb​\rrangle=1θa​θb⋅\llangle​κQa,ℱ^​κQb​\rrangle\displaystyle\frac{1}{\theta_{a}\theta_{b}}\cdot\llangle\chi_{Q_{a}},\hat{\mathcal{G}}^{-1}_{T}\hat{\mathcal{F}}\hat{\mathcal{G}}^{-1}_{T}\chi_{Q_{b}}\rrangle=\frac{1}{\theta_{a}\theta_{b}}\cdot\llangle\kappa_{Q_{a}},\hat{\mathcal{F}}\kappa_{Q_{b}}\rrangle

where we used the hermiticity of 𝒢^T−1\hat{\mathcal{G}}^{-1}_{T} and Eq.(196).

𝖡a​b\mathsf{B}_{ab} is real and antisymmetric, directly related to the many-body Berry’s curvature as in Eq.(105): using Eq.(172,195), and the gauge invariance of Berry’s curvature,

𝖡a​b=\displaystyle\mathsf{B}_{ab}= 2θa​θb⋅Im​[⟨ei​Ξ^​(κQa)​Φ​(ρ¯)|ei​Ξ^​(κQb)​Φ​(ρ¯)⟩]\displaystyle\frac{2}{\theta_{a}\theta_{b}}\cdot\text{Im}\big[\langle e^{i\hat{\Xi}(\kappa_{Q_{a}})}\Phi(\bar{\rho})|e^{i\hat{\Xi}(\kappa_{Q_{b}})}\Phi(\bar{\rho})\rangle\big]
=\displaystyle= 2θa​θb⋅Im​[⟨ei​θa​Q^a​Φ​(ρ¯)|ei​θb​Q^b​Φ​(ρ¯)⟩]θa​θb−part\displaystyle\frac{2}{\theta_{a}\theta_{b}}\cdot\text{Im}\big[\langle e^{i\theta_{a}\hat{Q}_{a}}\Phi(\bar{\rho})|e^{i\theta_{b}\hat{Q}_{b}}\Phi(\bar{\rho})\rangle\big]_{\theta_{a}\theta_{b}-\text{part}}
=\displaystyle= (−i)​⟨Φ⁡(ρ¯)|[Q^a,Q^b]|Φ⁡(ρ¯)⟩\displaystyle(-i)\langle\Phi(\bar{\rho})|[\hat{Q}_{a},\hat{Q}_{b}]|\Phi(\bar{\rho})\rangle
=\displaystyle= (−i)​Tr​(ρ¯​[Qa,Qb]).\displaystyle(-i)\text{Tr}(\bar{\rho}[Q_{a},Q_{b}]). (232)

For example, in a ferromagnetic state with moment along the zz-direction with Q^a=S^x\hat{Q}_{a}=\hat{S}_{x}, Q^b=S^y\hat{Q}_{b}=\hat{S}_{y}, the total spins along x,yx,y-directions, one finds 𝖡a​b∝⟨S^z⟩≠0\mathsf{B}_{ab}\propto\langle\hat{S}_{z}\rangle\neq 0. However, for an antiferromagnetic state, 𝖡a​b=0\mathsf{B}_{ab}=0.

V.2.5 Zero-point motion of Goldstone modes in VMPI wavefunctions

The advantage of VMPI over TDVP is the built-in quantum fluctuation of variational parameters. In the context of Goldstone mode fluctuations, their zero-point motion could qualitatively change the long-range behavior. For instance, consider a 1+1D single-band t−Jt-J model at half-filling. For simplicity of presentation, let’s assume JJ-term is easy-plane and ferromagnetic. When |J|≫t|J|\gg t, the static variational ground state |Φ⁡(ρ¯)⟩|\Phi(\bar{\rho})\rangle will be ferromagnetic with a fully gapped electronic bandstructure. If we choose the ferromagnetic moment in |Φ⁡(ρ¯)⟩|\Phi(\bar{\rho})\rangle along 𝐒x\mathbf{S}_{x}-direction, the Goldstone mode will be described by the fluctuation of the moment in 𝐒y\mathbf{S}_{y}-direction. Namely, in terms of the effective theory LeffL_{\rm eff} in Eq.(181), the gapped fermions are polarized along 𝐒x\mathbf{S}_{x}-direction, but their 𝐒y\mathbf{S}_{y}-direction moment is coupled with the fluctuating bosonic field (χQ\chi_{Q}-field) down to the lowest energy.

Standard Gaussian-order field theory calculation for LeffL_{\rm eff} shows a power-law at long distances for the equal-time correlator ⟨𝐒+​(𝐑)​𝐒−​(𝟎)⟩∼|𝐑|−η\langle\mathbf{S}^{+}(\mathbf{R})\mathbf{S}^{-}(\mathbf{0})\rangle\sim|\mathbf{R}|^{-\eta}, due to the zero-point motion of the Goldstone mode with dispersion ω∝|𝐪|\omega\propto|\mathbf{q}| – the well-known Kosterlitz-Thouless physics.

The point is that this physics is built into the VMPI treatment, both in terms of a microscopic field theory and microscopic wavefunctions. Precisely, as a linear-superposition of Slater determinants, the VMPI ground state |Ψ⟩VMPI,GS|\Psi\rangle_{\rm VMPI,GS} (see Eq.(154 and replacing 𝐳→𝜿\mathbf{z}\rightarrow\bm{\kappa}) already includes the zero-point motion of the Goldstone modes: if one measures the spin-spin correlation function in |Ψ⟩VMPI,GS|\Psi\rangle_{\rm VMPI,GS} (not |Φ⁡(ρ¯)⟩|\Phi(\bar{\rho})\rangle), the power-law order will be reproduced.

V.3 Application of VMPI in Hdet wavefunctions

In this subsection, applying the technique of VMPI, we study the effective theories of Hdet wavefunctions mainly focusing on type-(A) models, while commenting on type-(B) models in subsection V.3.8. For simplicity of presentation, here we again focus on the situation where there is only one electron’s orbital per real-space site, labeled by 𝐫\mathbf{r}. Each parton-pp’s mean-field state is labeled by its RDM ρ(p)\rho^{(p)}. These mean-field states are fused into an Hdet wavefunction via the local fusion operators 𝐅^𝐫\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{\mathbf{r}} as in Eq.(84) (or, equivalently, the local fusion gates 𝐂^𝐫\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{\mathbf{r}} as in Eq.III.2.5):

𝐅^𝐫≡∑α=1Rλα⋅c𝐫†⋅∏p=1npf𝐫,𝐦α(p)(p),\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{\mathbf{r}}\equiv\sum_{\alpha=1}^{R}\lambda_{\alpha}\cdot c^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{r}}\cdot\prod_{p=1}^{n_{\text{p}}}f^{(p)}_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{m}^{(p)}_{\alpha}}, (233)

where, for simplicity, we assume that λα\lambda_{\alpha} is independent of 𝐫\mathbf{r}.

Throughout this subsection, we assume that these fusion operators are fixed. Namely, all the CPD values λα\lambda_{\alpha} in Eq.(84) are not treated as variational parameters. This is motivated by the observations for both type-(A) and type-(B) models. For type-(A) models, the electronic local states are orthonormal. By introducing enough parton ancilla orbitals, one can always make different fusion channels not share parton orbitals. It is then possible to absorb λα\lambda_{\alpha} into one parton’s mean-field state without modifying the Hdet many-body wavefunction, after which all λα\lambda_{\alpha} can be set to unity. For type-(B) models, the overcompleteness of the Fine-Grid coherent states fixes the fusion amplitudes λα\lambda_{\alpha} in the FQH and FCI examples (see Eq.(33,52,53,60).

In our presentation, we often focus on the case of two parton species np=2n_{\text{p}}=2, i.e., rank-3 Hdet wavefunctions. The generalization to higher rank Hdet wavefunctions is straightforward.

An np=2n_{\rm p}=2 Hdet wavefunction |Φ⁡(ρ)⟩|\Phi(\rho)\rangle is then parameterized by two parton RDMs:

ρ≡{ρ(1),ρ(2)}.\displaystyle\rho\equiv\{\rho^{(1)},\rho^{(2)}\}. (234)

We will consider translational-invariant systems, possibly with an enlarged unit cell (e.g., due to magnetic translation). Consistent with the TDHF demonstration in the previous section, for each parton species-pp, we denote the parton orbital by:

i=(𝐫,𝐦)=(𝐑,𝛂),\displaystyle i=(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{m})=({\mathbf{R}},\bm{\upalpha}), (235)

where 𝐑\mathbf{R} labels the unit cell, and 𝛂\bm{\upalpha} collects all parton orbitals within the unit cell (i.e., different real-space sites 𝐫\mathbf{r} in one unit cell and the orbital label 𝐦\mathbf{m}). The real-space position of the orbital is denoted as 𝐫i\mathbf{r}_{i} or 𝐫⁡(𝐑,𝛂){\mathbf{r}}(\mathbf{R},\bm{\upalpha}), and the local orbital index is denoted as 𝐦i\mathbf{m}_{i}. The parton RDM is then:

ρi​j(p)≡⟨fj(p)†fi(p)⟩.\displaystyle\rho^{(p)}_{ij}\equiv\langle f^{(p)\dagger}_{j}f^{(p)}_{i}\rangle. (236)

We warn the reader that, in general, the range of the index-ii may depend on the parton species-pp, because in general, different parton species may have different numbers of orbitals per site. So technically, index-ii should be interpreted as i(p)i^{(p)}. However, to save notation, we neglect the superscript (p), which should not cause confusion.

Defining the parton-pp’ normalized mean-field state |Ψ(p)​(ρ(p))⟩|\Psi^{(p)}(\rho^{(p)})\rangle to be the Slater-determinant specified by ρ(p)\rho^{(p)}, the full parton mean-field state is

|ΨM​F​(ρ)⟩≡|Ψ(1)​(ρ(1))⟩⊗|Ψ(2)​(ρ(2))⟩,\displaystyle|\Psi^{MF}(\rho)\rangle\equiv|\Psi^{(1)}(\rho^{(1)})\rangle\otimes|\Psi^{(2)}(\rho^{(2)})\rangle, (237)

and via fusion:

|Ψ(e)​{ΨM​F}⟩≡\displaystyle|\Psi^{(e)}\{\Psi^{MF}\}\rangle\equiv 𝐂^|ΨM​F⟩, where: 𝐂^≡∏𝐫𝐂^𝐫,\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{C}}|\Psi^{MF}\rangle,\text{ where: }\hat{\mathbf{C}}\equiv\prod_{\mathbf{r}}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{\mathbf{r}},
|Φ​{ΨM​F}⟩≡\displaystyle|\Phi\{\Psi^{MF}\}\rangle\equiv |Ψ(e)​{ΨM​F}⟩⟨Ψ(e)​{ΨM​F}|Ψ(e)​{ΨM​F}⟩.\displaystyle\frac{|\Psi^{(e)}\{\Psi^{MF}\}\rangle}{\sqrt{\langle\Psi^{(e)}\{\Psi^{MF}\}|\Psi^{(e)}\{\Psi^{MF}\}\rangle}}. (238)

Throughout this paper, Φ\Phi denotes the normalized electronic state. |Φ​{ΨM​F}⟩|\Phi\{\Psi^{MF}\}\rangle should be viewed as the map from the parton’s mean-field state ΨM​F\Psi^{MF} to the electronic normalized state Φ\Phi. As a shorthand notation:

|Φ⁡(ρ)⟩≡|Φ⁡{ΨM​F​(ρ)}⟩.\displaystyle|\Phi(\rho)\rangle\equiv|\Phi\{\Psi^{MF}(\rho)\}\rangle. (239)

Crucially, the mean-field states {|ΨM​F​(ρ)⟩}\{|\Psi^{MF}(\rho)\rangle\}, as direct products of Slater determinants, form a manifold satisfying the Kähler condition – the parton’s Thouless parameterization, as mentioned near Eq.(165), is an explicit construction for its Kähler coordinate. Since the fusion operator is fixed, even after fusion, the Hdet states {|Φ⁡(ρ)⟩}\{|\Phi(\rho)\rangle\} still form a Kähler manifold.

V.3.1 Gauge covariant VMPI and the temporal gauge field a0a_{0}

Formally, one can immediately repeat the VMPI analysis using Hdet state |Φ⁡(ρ)⟩|\Phi(\rho)\rangle, similar to the former TDHF demonstration. However, there are two challenges: (1) Due to the NP-hardness of Hdet calculation, generally, both the Berry’s phase term ⟨Φ(ρ)|i∂t|Φ(ρ)⟩\langle\Phi(\rho)|i\partial_{t}|\Phi(\rho)\rangle and E⁡(ρ)E(\rho) cannot be computed exactly. (2) The gauge redundancy in the {ρ(1),ρ(2)}\{\rho^{(1)},\rho^{(2)}\} parameterization must be treated, leading to fluctuating gauge fields.

The challenge-(1) is a technical one, yet extremely important. Fortunately, as we will see in Sec.VI, Berry’s phase and E⁡(ρ)E(\rho) can still be approximately computed, order by order. In this subsection, to avoid confusion, we adapt the following notation: a subscript ”approx” means the quantity is computed in a certain approximate scheme for Hdet states; a subscript ”exact” means the quantity is computed using exact Hdet states; the absence of these subscripts means the quantity can be either the approximate one or the exact one.

Challenge-(2) captures the crucial physics and needs a thorough discussion. It also impacts our approximate scheme for Hdet calculations in Sec.VI.

As in all parton constructions, the parton parameterization for the physical wavefunction is redundant. In the present case, many different {ρ(1),ρ(2)}\{\rho^{(1)},\rho^{(2)}\} may label the same physical Hdet wavefunction – the key ingredient of gauge theories. This gauge redundancy is described by the gauge group G​GGG, defined as follows. Let the number of parton orbitals on a given site be norb(p)n^{(p)}_{\rm orb} (labeled by 𝐦(p)\mathbf{m}^{(p)}), the unitary rotation among these parton orbitals forms the U⁡(norb(p))U(n^{(p)}_{\rm orb}) group. Within the Hdet construction, G​GGG is defined to be the maximal subgroup of ∏pU⁡(norb(p))\prod_{p}U(n^{(p)}_{\rm orb}) leaving the fusion gate 𝐂^𝐫\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{\mathbf{r}} invariant:

GG≡{g∈∏pU(norb(p))|𝐂^𝐫U^𝐫(g)=\displaystyle GG\equiv\{g\in\prod_{p}U(n^{(p)}_{\rm orb})|\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{\mathbf{r}}\hat{U}_{\mathbf{r}}(g)= 𝐂^𝐫}.\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{\mathbf{r}}\}. (240)

Here U^𝐫​(g)\hat{U}_{\mathbf{r}}(g) is the second-quantized operator acting on the parton Fock space on site-𝐫\mathbf{r}. For example, in the Hdet construction Eq.(101), G​G=U⁡(R)GG=U(R).

Let NGN_{G} be the dimension of G​GGG, and denote its generators as Hermitian matrices TAT^{A}, A=0,…,NG−1A=0,...,N_{G}-1. TAT^{A} should be viewed as the direct sum of matrices in each parton’s local orbital space: Let TA,(p)T^{A,(p)} be the corresponding norb(p)×norb(p)n^{(p)}_{\rm orb}\times n^{(p)}_{\rm orb} matrix for parton-pp with elements T𝐦,𝐦′A,(p)T^{A,(p)}_{\mathbf{m},\mathbf{m}^{\prime}}, then TA=⊕TA,(p)T^{A}=\oplus T^{A,(p)}. {TA}\{T^{A}\} form the Lie algebra g​ggg of G​GGG, whose structure constant is defined as:

[TA,TB]=\displaystyle[T^{A},T^{B}]= i​fCA​B​TC.\displaystyle if^{AB}_{C}T^{C}. (241)

The site-dependent G​GGG gauge transformation is labeled by θ≡{θA​(𝐫)}\theta\equiv\{\theta^{A}(\mathbf{r})\}. We define matrices on the full parton real-space basis, as well as second-quantized operators:

[T𝐫A,(p)]i​j≡δ𝐫,𝐫i​δ𝐫,𝐫j​T𝐦i,𝐦jA,(p),\displaystyle[T_{\mathbf{r}}^{A,(p)}]_{ij}\equiv\delta_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}_{i}}\delta_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}_{j}}T_{\mathbf{m}_{i},\mathbf{m}_{j}}^{A,(p)},
T𝐫A≡⊕pT𝐫A,(p),T^𝐫A≡∑p,i​j[T𝐫A,(p)]i​jfi(p)†fj(p).\displaystyle T_{\mathbf{r}}^{A}\equiv\oplus_{p}T_{\mathbf{r}}^{A,(p)},\;\;\hat{T}^{A}_{\mathbf{r}}\equiv\sum_{p,ij}[T_{\mathbf{r}}^{A,(p)}]_{ij}f_{i}^{(p)\dagger}f_{j}^{(p)}. (242)

With this notation, the onsite gauge transformation in Eq.(240) is parameterized as U^𝐫​(g)=exp⁡[i​∑Aθ𝐫A​T^𝐫A]\hat{U}_{\mathbf{r}}(g)=\exp\Big[i\sum_{A}\theta_{\mathbf{r}}^{A}\hat{T}^{A}_{\mathbf{r}}\Big]. The site-dependent gauge transformation θ\theta has both a matrix form and a second-quantized operator form:

Λ(p)[θ]≡∑𝐫,AθA(𝐫)T𝐫A,(p),Λ[θ]≡⊕pΛ(p)[θ],Θ[θ]≡ei​Λ​[θ]\displaystyle\Lambda^{(p)}[\theta]\equiv\sum_{\mathbf{r},A}\theta^{A}(\mathbf{r})T^{A,(p)}_{\mathbf{r}},\;\Lambda[\theta]\equiv\oplus_{p}\Lambda^{(p)}[\theta],\;\Theta[\theta]\equiv e^{i\Lambda[\theta]}
Λ^[θ]≡∑p,i​jΛi​j(p)[θ]fi(p)†fj(p),Θ^[θ]≡ei​Λ^​[θ].\displaystyle\hat{\Lambda}[\theta]\equiv\sum_{p,ij}\Lambda^{(p)}_{ij}[\theta]f_{i}^{(p)\dagger}f_{j}^{(p)},\;\hat{\Theta}[\theta]\equiv e^{i\hat{\Lambda}[\theta]}. (243)

The map Λ:{θA​(𝐫)}→Mh\Lambda:\{\theta^{A}(\mathbf{r})\}\rightarrow M_{\rm h} is injective, so θ\theta and Λ⁡[θ]\Lambda[\theta] may be viewed as equivalent objects.

The gauge transformation on ρ\rho is denoted as:

ρ(p)→ρ~(p)=Θ(p)[θ]ρ(p)Θ(p)†[θ]≡G(θ)∘ρ.\displaystyle\rho^{(p)}\rightarrow\tilde{\rho}^{(p)}=\Theta^{(p)}[\theta]\rho^{(p)}\Theta^{(p)\dagger}[\theta]\equiv G(\theta)\circ\rho. (244)

For the np=2n_{\rm p}=2 case, one always has a U​(1)I⊂G​GU(1)_{I}\subset GG, and it is convenient to denote its generator as A=0A=0:

TA=0,(p)≡q(p)​𝟏,\displaystyle T^{A=0,(p)}\equiv\text{q}^{(p)}\mathbf{1},\;\; where gauge charge:
q(1)=1,q(2)=−1.\displaystyle\text{q}^{(1)}=1,\text{q}^{(2)}=-1. (245)

The special property for this U​(1)IU(1)_{I} subgroup is that: the spatial independent ei​θ​T0e^{i\theta T^{0}} always leaves ρ\rho invariant as in Eq.(244), since Θ(p)\Theta^{(p)} is an overall phase factor.

In an exact treatment of Hdet wavefunction, we have:

|Φ⁡(G⁡(θ)∘ρ)⟩exact=ei​ϕ​(θ,ρ)​|Φ⁡(ρ)⟩exact.\displaystyle|\Phi(G(\theta)\circ\rho)\rangle_{\rm exact}=e^{i\phi(\theta,\rho)}|\Phi(\rho)\rangle_{\rm exact}. (246)

Here, there is generally a nonzero phase ϕ⁡(θ,ρ)\phi(\theta,\rho). Its origin can be traced back to Eq.(237), where we choose a map from ρ\rho to the parton mean-field state |ΨM​F​(ρ)⟩|\Psi^{MF}(\rho)\rangle. However, this map is not unique: for example, it is perfectly fine to redefine |ΨM​F​(ρ)⟩→ei​χ​(ρ)​|ΨM​F​(ρ)⟩|\Psi^{MF}(\rho)\rangle\rightarrow e^{i\chi(\rho)}|\Psi^{MF}(\rho)\rangle, and consequently the exact physical state transforms as |Φ⁡(ρ)⟩exact→ei​χ​(ρ)​|Φ⁡(ρ)⟩exact|\Phi(\rho)\rangle_{\rm exact}\rightarrow e^{i\chi(\rho)}|\Phi(\rho)\rangle_{\rm exact}, and ϕ⁡(θ,ρ)\phi(\theta,\rho) transforms as:

ϕ⁡(θ,ρ)→ϕ⁡(θ,ρ)+χ⁡(G⁡(θ)∘ρ)−χ⁡(ρ).\displaystyle\phi(\theta,\rho)\rightarrow\phi(\theta,\rho)+\chi(G(\theta)\circ\rho)-\chi(\rho). (247)

For the purpose of explicit computation of the VMPI action shortly, it is convenient to introduce a related state:

|Φ⁡(G⁡(θ),ρ)⟩≡\displaystyle|\Phi(G(\theta);\rho)\rangle\equiv |Φ⁡{ei​Λ^​[θ]​ΨM​F​(ρ)}⟩.\displaystyle|\Phi\big\{e^{i\hat{\Lambda}[\theta]}\Psi^{MF}(\rho)\big\}\rangle. (248)

Clearly, the parton gauge transformation operator ei​Λ^​[θ]e^{i\hat{\Lambda}[\theta]} transforms the parton RDM as Eq.(244). Therefore, |ΨM​F​(G⁡(θ)∘ρ)⟩|\Psi^{MF}(G(\theta)\circ\rho)\rangle and ei​Λ^​[θ]​|ΨM​F​(ρ)⟩e^{i\hat{\Lambda}[\theta]}|\Psi^{MF}(\rho)\rangle can only differ by an overall phase factor. In addition, due to the definition of G​GGG, we have: ∏𝐫𝐂^𝐫​ei​Λ^​[θ]=∏𝐫𝐂^𝐫\prod_{\mathbf{r}}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{\mathbf{r}}e^{i\hat{\Lambda}[\theta]}=\prod_{\mathbf{r}}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{\mathbf{r}}, and consequently:

|Φ⁡(G⁡(θ),ρ)⟩exact=|Φ⁡(ρ)⟩exact,\displaystyle|\Phi(G(\theta);\rho)\rangle_{\rm exact}=|\Phi(\rho)\rangle_{\rm exact}, (249)

which is similar to Eq.(246), but without the phase factor ei​ϕ​(θ,ρ)e^{i\phi(\theta,\rho)}, dictating:

|ΨM​F​(G⁡(θ)∘ρ)⟩=ei​ϕ​(θ,ρ)​ei​Λ^​[θ]​|ΨM​F​(ρ)⟩.\displaystyle|\Psi^{MF}(G(\theta)\circ\rho)\rangle=e^{i\phi(\theta,\rho)}e^{i\hat{\Lambda}[\theta]}|\Psi^{MF}(\rho)\rangle. (250)

Gauge invariance will play a crucial role in our discussion. In the exact treatment, gauge invariance is already captured by Eqs. (246) and (249). However, because exactly simulating Hdet states is NP-hard, practical approximation schemes are necessary for large system sizes. For the purpose of VMPI, two types of quantities are needed: (1) The static properties like

E⁡(ρ)≡⟨Φ⁡(ρ)|H|Φ⁡(ρ)⟩,\displaystyle E(\rho)\equiv\langle\Phi(\rho)|H|\Phi(\rho)\rangle, (251)

and (2) the dynamical properties like the Berry’s phase from the overlap ⟨Φ⁡(ρ+δ​ρ)|Φ⁡(ρ)⟩\langle\Phi(\rho+\delta\rho)|\Phi(\rho)\rangle. An approximation scheme must satisfy some fundamental conditions for the approximate VMPI to be physically reasonable, which we define below.

We define an approximation scheme for computing the electronic observables in Hdet states to be statically conserving iff, ∀\forall electronic observable O(e)O^{(e)}, parton mean-field state |ΨM​F⟩|\Psi^{MF}\rangle, phase factor ei​αe^{i\alpha}, and gauge transformation of θ\theta, it satisfies:
