⟨Φ⁡{ei​α​ei​Λ^​[θ]​ΨM​F}|O(e)|Φ⁡{ei​α​ei​Λ^​[θ]​ΨM​F}⟩approx\displaystyle\langle\Phi\{e^{i\alpha}e^{i\hat{\Lambda}[\theta]}\Psi^{MF}\}|O^{(e)}|\Phi\{e^{i\alpha}e^{i\hat{\Lambda}[\theta]}\Psi^{MF}\}\rangle_{\rm approx}
=\displaystyle= ⟨Φ⁡{ΨM​F}|O(e)|Φ⁡{ΨM​F}⟩approx.\displaystyle\langle\Phi\{\Psi^{MF}\}|O^{(e)}|\Phi\{\Psi^{MF}\}\rangle_{\rm approx}. (252)

We also define an approximation scheme for computing overlaps of electronic Hdet states to be dynamically conserving iff, ∀\forall parton mean-field state |ΨiM​F⟩,|ΨfM​F⟩|\Psi^{MF}_{i}\rangle,|\Psi^{MF}_{f}\rangle, phase factors ei​αi,ei​αfe^{i\alpha_{i}},e^{i\alpha_{f}} and gauge transformation of θ\theta, it satisfies a gauge-invariance condition:

⟨Φ⁡{ei​αf​ei​Λ^​[θ]​ΨfM​F}|Φ⁡{ei​αi​ei​Λ^​[θ]​ΨiM​F}⟩approx\displaystyle\langle\Phi\{e^{i\alpha_{f}}e^{i\hat{\Lambda}[\theta]}\Psi^{MF}_{f}\}|\Phi\{e^{i\alpha_{i}}e^{i\hat{\Lambda}[\theta]}\Psi_{i}^{MF}\}\rangle_{\rm approx}
=\displaystyle= ei⁡(αi−αf)​⟨Φ⁡{ΨfM​F}|Φ⁡{ΨiM​F}⟩approx,\displaystyle e^{i(\alpha_{i}-\alpha_{f})}\langle\Phi\{\Psi_{f}^{MF}\}|\Phi\{\Psi_{i}^{MF}\}\rangle_{\rm approx}, (253)

as well as the elementary Hermiticity property:

⟨Φ⁡{ΨfM​F}|Φ⁡{ΨiM​F}⟩approx=⟨Φ⁡{ΨiM​F}|Φ⁡{ΨfM​F}⟩approx∗\displaystyle\langle\Phi\{\Psi^{MF}_{f}\}|\Phi\{\Psi_{i}^{MF}\}\rangle_{\rm approx}=\langle\Phi\{\Psi^{MF}_{i}\}|\Phi\{\Psi_{f}^{MF}\}\rangle^{*}_{\rm approx} (254)

In this paper, we ONLY consider approximation schemes that are both statically-conserving and dynamically-conserving. For example, the projective-expansion(PE) introduced in Sec.VI satisfies both conditions at any order.

The static-conserving condition is very natural, leading to the gauge invariance of the energy function: E⁡(ρ)=E⁡(G⁡(θ)∘ρ)E(\rho)=E(G(\theta)\circ\rho). On the other hand, compared to Eq.(249), the dynamical-conserving condition Eq.(253) is a much weaker requirement, in which the gauge transformation appears in both the ket and the bra – it is a double-sided gauge-invariance condition. In an exact treatment, we would have a single-sided gauge-invariance: ⟨Φ⁡(ρf)|Φ⁡(G⁡(θ),ρi)⟩exact=⟨Φ⁡(ρf)|Φ⁡(ρi)⟩exact\langle\Phi(\rho_{f})|\Phi(G(\theta);\rho_{i})\rangle_{\rm exact}=\langle\Phi(\rho_{f})|\Phi(\rho_{i})\rangle_{\rm exact} – a consequence of the exact implementation of Gauss’s law. It is unrealistic to expect the approximate overlap to also be single-sided gauge invariant, which would have required the approximate Hdet state to have Gauss’ law completely implemented.

More generally, there may be even larger gauge redundancies not captured by ∏pU⁡(norb(p))\prod_{p}U(n_{\rm orb}^{(p)}) when constructing states beyond the present Hdet formulation. For instance, consider the special case that the parton orbitals for different fusion channels are distinct, i.e., f𝐫,𝐦α(p)≠f𝐫,𝐦β(p)f^{(p)}_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{m}_{\alpha}}\neq f^{(p)}_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{m}_{\beta}} if α≠β\alpha\neq\beta. In this case, the orbital label 𝐦\mathbf{m} is not necessary and one may write f𝐫,α(p)≡f𝐫,𝐦α(p)f^{(p)}_{\mathbf{r},\alpha}\equiv f^{(p)}_{\mathbf{r},\mathbf{m}_{\alpha}}. The fusion operator Eq.(233) becomes 𝐅^𝐫≡∑α=1Rλα⋅c𝐫†⋅∏p=1npf𝐫,α(p)\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{\mathbf{r}}\equiv\sum_{\alpha=1}^{R}\lambda_{\alpha}\cdot c^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{r}}\cdot\prod_{p=1}^{n_{\text{p}}}f^{(p)}_{\mathbf{r},\alpha}. If one allows different parton species to hybridize yet using this 𝐅^𝐫\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{\mathbf{r}} to construct the physical wavefunction, one would have at least S​U​(np)SU(n_{\text{p}}) gauge redundancy, where the W∈S​U​(np)W\in SU(n_{\text{p}}) gauge transformation is f𝐫,α(p)→∑p′W​(𝐫)p​p′​f𝐫,α(p′)f^{(p)}_{\mathbf{r},\alpha}\rightarrow\sum_{p^{\prime}}W(\mathbf{r})_{pp^{\prime}}f^{(p^{\prime})}_{\mathbf{r},\alpha}. Obviously, the fusion operator 𝐅^𝐫\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{\mathbf{r}} in this special case is an S​U​(np)SU(n_{\text{p}}) singlet. The previous U​(1)I⊂G​GU(1)_{I}\subset GG redundancy is nothing but the diagonal subgroup of S​U​(np=2)SU(n_{\text{p}}=2). Therefore, if we use ρ(all ​p)\rho^{(\text{all }p)} to denote the single RDM of the hybridized parton mean-field state, then different ρ(all ​p)\rho^{(\text{all }p)}’s related by S​U​(np)SU(n_{\text{p}}) gauge transformations are labeling the identical physical wavefunction. Here, the hybridization of parton species leads to the hyperpfaffian-type mathematical structure[14, 86] for the physical wavefunction after fusion, beyond the current Hdet discussion, and we leave its detailed investigation as a future project. For the moment, we simply call such physical states constructed from species-hybridized mean-field states ρ(all ​p)\rho^{(\text{all }p)} via local fusion 𝐅^𝐫\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{\mathbf{r}} Hpfaffian states. Generally, as long as the fusion operator 𝐅^𝐫\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{\mathbf{r}} (or equivalently the fusion gate 𝐂^𝐫\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{\mathbf{r}}) is S​U​(np)SU(n_{\text{p}}) invariant, the corresponding Hpfaffian construction has the S​U​(np)SU(n_{\text{p}}) gauge redundancy.

No matter what the gauge group of the fusion is, the gauge group for the low-energy fluctuations, however, is really determined by the saddle point ρ¯\bar{\rho}. This low-energy gauge group is denoted as I​G​GIGG by Wen and is the remaining gauge group not Higgs-ed out by ρ¯\bar{\rho}. Precisely speaking, this I​G​GIGG group is identified as the gauge transformations that even leave the parton mean-field state invariant. In the present Hdet construction, for np=2n_{\rm p}=2, we already know U​(1)I⊂I​G​GU(1)_{I}\subset IGG. In this subsection, we will assume that I​G​G=U​(1)IIGG=U(1)_{I}. (Conceptually, the I​G​G=U​(1)np−1IGG=U(1)^{n_{\text{p}}-1}-gauge VMPI presented here can be straightforwardly generalized to the situations I​G​G=S​U​(np)IGG=SU(n_{\text{p}}) in a Hpfaffian construction.)

The space-time-dependent G​GGG gauge transformations, from the VMPI viewpoint, lead to fluctuations δ​ρpg\delta\rho_{\text{pg}} from ρ¯\bar{\rho} that do not cost any energy– the pure gauge modes. At long wavelengths, the I​G​GIGG part of the pure gauge modes will qualitatively affect the low-energy physics. One must consistently track these gauge modes in VMPI.

To keep track of such gauge modes, for every time slice-ss (s=1,…,N−1.s=1,...,N-1.) in the VMPI (see Eq.(112)), we explicitly insert the pure gauge redundancies in the integral measure:

∫d​μ​(ρs)≡∫d​μ​(ρi​j;s(1),ρi​j;s(2))→\displaystyle\int d\mu(\rho_{s})\equiv\int d\mu(\rho_{ij;s}^{(1)},\rho_{ij;s}^{(2)})\rightarrow
∫∏𝐫d​ηs​(𝐫)​∫d​μ​(G⁡(ηs)∘ρs),\displaystyle\int\prod_{\mathbf{r}}d\eta_{s}(\mathbf{r})\int d\mu(G(\eta_{s})\circ\rho_{s}), (255)

where d​ηs​(𝐫)d\eta_{s}(\mathbf{r}) is the G​GGG invariant Haar measure, and modify the projector:

|Φ⁡(ρs)⟩​⟨Φ⁡(ρs)|→|Φ⁡(G⁡(ηs)∘ρs)⟩​⟨Φ⁡(G⁡(ηs)∘ρs)|.\displaystyle|\Phi(\rho_{s})\rangle\langle\Phi(\rho_{s})|\rightarrow|\Phi(G(\eta_{s})\circ\rho_{s})\rangle\langle\Phi(G(\eta_{s})\circ\rho_{s})|. (256)

We require that the measure is gauge invariant:

d​μ​(G⁡(η)∘ρ)=d​μ​(ρ).\displaystyle d\mu(G(\eta)\circ\rho)=d\mu(\rho). (257)

We now define the time-component of the G​GGG gauge field on the time-links.

Θ−1​[ηs]​Θ​[ηs+1]=exp⁡[i​Δ​t​Λ​[a0;sfull]+O⁡(Δ​t2)],\displaystyle\Theta^{-1}[\eta_{s}]\Theta[\eta_{s+1}]=\exp\Big[i\Delta t\Lambda[a^{\text{full}}_{0;s}]+O(\Delta t^{2})\Big], (258)

where, to save notation later, we introduced the superscript ”full{}^{\text{full}}” since we will soon perform the saddle-point analysis a0full=a¯0+a0a^{\text{full}}_{0}=\bar{a}_{0}+a_{0}. In the continuum-tt limit:

Λ[a0full(t)]≡−iΘ−1[η(t)]∂tΘ[η(t)]=∑𝐫,Aa0full,A(𝐫,t)T𝐫A,\displaystyle\Lambda[a^{\text{full}}_{0}(t)]\equiv-i\Theta^{-1}[\eta(t)]\partial_{t}\Theta[\eta(t)]=\sum_{\mathbf{r},A}a_{0}^{\text{full},A}(\mathbf{r},t)T^{A}_{\mathbf{r}}, (259)

where a0full,A​(𝐫,t)a_{0}^{\text{full},A}(\mathbf{r},t) are real fields since Λ⁡[a0full​(t)]\Lambda[a^{\text{full}}_{0}(t)] is Hermitian.

The path integral ∫𝒟⁡[η]\int\mathcal{D}[\eta] can be replaced by ∫𝒟⁡[a0full]\int\mathcal{D}[a^{\text{full}}_{0}] after setting boundary condition η⁡(𝐫,−T2)=0\eta(\mathbf{r},-\frac{T}{2})=0. We have

ZVMPI=∫𝒟⁡[ρ⁡(t),a0full​(t)]​ei​∫d​t​LTDVP,\displaystyle Z_{\text{VMPI}}=\int\mathcal{D}[\rho(t),a^{\text{full}}_{0}(t)]e^{i\int dtL_{\text{TDVP}}}, (260)

with

LTDVP=\displaystyle L_{\text{TDVP}}= ⟨Φ(ρ(t),a0full(t))|i∂t−H|Φ(ρ(t),a0full(t))⟩\displaystyle\langle\Phi(\rho(t),a^{\text{full}}_{0}(t))|i\partial_{t}-H|\Phi(\rho(t),a^{\text{full}}_{0}(t))\rangle
=\displaystyle= LBerry−E⁡(ρ⁡(t)),\displaystyle L_{\text{Berry}}-E(\rho(t)), (261)

where the gauge-covariant state is defined by

|Φ⁡(ρ⁡(t),a0full​(t))⟩≡|Φ⁡[G⁡(η⁡(t))∘ρ⁡(t)]⟩,\displaystyle|\Phi(\rho(t),a^{\text{full}}_{0}(t))\rangle\equiv|\Phi\Big[G\big(\eta(t)\big)\circ\rho(t)\Big]\rangle, (262)

where η⁡(t)\eta(t) and a0full​(t)a^{\text{full}}_{0}(t) are related via Eq.(259), and the Berry’s phase term is:

LBerry≡⟨Φ(ρ(t),a0full(t))|i∂t|Φ(ρ(t),a0full(t))⟩.\displaystyle L_{\text{Berry}}\equiv\langle\Phi(\rho(t),a^{\text{full}}_{0}(t))|i\partial_{t}|\Phi(\rho(t),a^{\text{full}}_{0}(t))\rangle. (263)

Under a space-time dependent gauge transformation θ⁡(t)\theta(t) satisfying the boundary condition θ⁡(𝐫,−T2)=0\theta(\mathbf{r},-\frac{T}{2})=0, we have:

Θ⁡[η⁡(t)]→\displaystyle\Theta[\eta(t)]\rightarrow Θ⁡[η⁡(t)]​Θ−1​[θ⁡(t)],\displaystyle\Theta[\eta(t)]\Theta^{-1}[\theta(t)], ρ⁡(t)→\displaystyle\rho(t)\rightarrow G⁡(θ⁡(t))∘ρ⁡(t),\displaystyle G(\theta(t))\circ\rho(t), (264)

and the states on the RHS of Eq.(256) are explicitly gauge invariant: |Φ⁡([G⁡(ηs)∘G−1​(θs)]∘G⁡(θs)∘ρs)⟩=|Φ⁡(G⁡(ηs)∘ρs)⟩|\Phi([G(\eta_{s})\circ G^{-1}(\theta_{s})]\circ G(\theta_{s})\circ\rho_{s})\rangle=|\Phi(G(\eta_{s})\circ\rho_{s})\rangle. Consequently, LBerryL_{\rm Berry} is gauge invariant by construction. Since E⁡(ρ⁡(t))E(\rho(t)) is already gauge invariant due to the static-conserving condition, LTDVPL_{\rm TDVP} is gauge invariant. In the continuum-time limit, we have the gauge transformation labeled by {θ⁡(𝐫,t)}\{\theta(\mathbf{r},t)\}:

Λ⁡[a0full]\displaystyle\Lambda[a^{\text{full}}_{0}] →Θ⁡[θ]​Λ​[a0full]​Θ−1​[θ]+i⁡(∂tΘ⁡[θ])​Θ−1​[θ],\displaystyle\rightarrow\Theta[\theta]\Lambda[a^{\text{full}}_{0}]\Theta^{-1}[\theta]+i(\partial_{t}\Theta[\theta])\Theta^{-1}[\theta],
ρ⁡(t)\displaystyle\rho(t) →G⁡(θ⁡(t))∘ρ⁡(t).\displaystyle\rightarrow G(\theta(t))\circ\rho(t). (265)

If one would like to explicitly write down the transformation of each real field a0full,Aa_{0}^{\text{full},A}, we can define the adjoint-representation matrix RAB​[θ]R^{B}_{A}[\theta]:

Θ⁡[θ]​T𝐫A​Θ−1​[θ]≡∑BRAB​[θ⁡(𝐫)]​T𝐫B,\displaystyle\Theta[\theta]T^{A}_{\mathbf{r}}\Theta^{-1}[\theta]\equiv\sum_{B}R^{B}_{A}[\theta(\mathbf{r})]T_{\mathbf{r}}^{B}, (266)

and expand:

i⁡(∂tΘ⁡[θ])​Θ−1​[θ]=∑𝐫,BζB​(θ⁡(𝐫,t),θ˙​(𝐫,t))​T𝐫B.\displaystyle i(\partial_{t}\Theta[\theta])\Theta^{-1}[\theta]=\sum_{\mathbf{r},B}\zeta^{B}(\theta(\mathbf{r},t),\dot{\theta}(\mathbf{r},t))T_{\mathbf{r}}^{B}. (267)

Then

a0full,B​(𝐫,t)→\displaystyle a_{0}^{\text{full},B}(\mathbf{r},t)\rightarrow ∑ARAB​[θ⁡(𝐫,t)]​a0full,A​(𝐫,t)\displaystyle\sum_{A}R_{A}^{B}[\theta(\mathbf{r},t)]a_{0}^{\text{full},A}(\mathbf{r},t)
+ζB​(θ⁡(𝐫,t),θ˙​(𝐫,t)).\displaystyle+\zeta^{B}(\theta(\mathbf{r},t),\dot{\theta}(\mathbf{r},t)). (268)

For an infinitesimal gauge transformation θ≪1\theta\ll 1:

Θ⁡[θ]=1+i​Λ​[θ]+O⁡(θ2),\displaystyle\Theta[\theta]=1+i\Lambda[\theta]+O(\theta^{2}), (269)

Eq.(265) gives:

Λ⁡[a0full]→Λ⁡[a0full]−∂tΛ⁡[θ]+i⁡[Λ⁡[θ],Λ⁡[a0full]]+O⁡(θ2).\displaystyle\Lambda[a_{0}^{\text{full}}]\rightarrow\Lambda[a_{0}^{\text{full}}]-\partial_{t}\Lambda[\theta]+i[\Lambda[\theta],\Lambda[a_{0}^{\text{full}}]]+O(\theta^{2}). (270)

Using Eq.(241), the individual components transform as:

a0full,C​(𝐫,t)\displaystyle a_{0}^{\text{full},C}(\mathbf{r},t) →a0full,C​(𝐫,t)−∂tθC​(𝐫,t)\displaystyle\rightarrow a_{0}^{\text{full},C}(\mathbf{r},t)-\partial_{t}\theta^{C}(\mathbf{r},t)
−∑A​BfCA​BθA(𝐫,t)a0full,B(𝐫,t)+O(θ2).\displaystyle-\sum_{AB}f^{AB}_{C}\theta^{A}(\mathbf{r},t)a_{0}^{\text{full},B}(\mathbf{r},t)+O(\theta^{2}). (271)

Although the projector on the RHS of Eq.(256) is conceptually elegant for demonstrating the gauge invariance of LBerryL_{\rm Berry}, it is not convenient for its practical computation due to the unspecified phase ϕ⁡(θ,ρ)\phi(\theta,\rho). To practically compute LBerryL_{\rm Berry}, we replace the projector as:

|Φ⁡(G⁡(ηs)∘ρs)⟩​⟨Φ⁡(G⁡(ηs)∘ρs)|\displaystyle|\Phi(G(\eta_{s})\circ\rho_{s})\rangle\langle\Phi(G(\eta_{s})\circ\rho_{s})|
→\displaystyle\rightarrow |Φ⁡(G⁡(ηs),ρs)⟩​⟨Φ⁡(G⁡(ηs),ρs)|,\displaystyle|\Phi(G(\eta_{s});\rho_{s})\rangle\langle\Phi(G(\eta_{s});\rho_{s})|, (272)

where the state introduced in Eq.(248) is used. Based on the dynamical-conserving condition Eq.(253), SBerry≡∫d​t​LBerryS_{\rm Berry}\equiv\int dtL_{\rm Berry} remains unchanged under the replacement.

Precisely, because |ΨM​F​(G⁡(ηs)∘ρs)⟩|\Psi^{MF}(G(\eta_{s})\circ\rho_{s})\rangle and ei​Λ^​[ηs]​|ΨM​F​(ρs)⟩e^{i\hat{\Lambda}[\eta_{s}]}|\Psi^{MF}(\rho_{s})\rangle only differ by an overall phase factor ei​αse^{i\alpha_{s}}, setting θ=0\theta=0 in Eq.(253):

⟨Φ⁡(G⁡(ηs+1),ρs+1)|Φ⁡(G⁡(ηs),ρs)⟩\displaystyle\langle\Phi(G(\eta_{s+1});\rho_{s+1})|\Phi(G(\eta_{s});\rho_{s})\rangle
=\displaystyle= ei⁡(αs+1−αs)​⟨Φ⁡(G⁡(ηs+1)∘ρs+1)|Φ⁡(G⁡(ηs)∘ρs)⟩.\displaystyle e^{i(\alpha_{s+1}-\alpha_{s})}\langle\Phi(G(\eta_{s+1})\circ\rho_{s+1})|\Phi(G(\eta_{s})\circ\rho_{s})\rangle. (273)

Taking the continuum-tt limit, LBerryL_{\rm Berry} before and after the replacement Eq.(272) only differ by a total derivative d​αd​t\frac{d\alpha}{dt}, which does not change physics. However, after the replacement, LBerryL_{\rm Berry} is gauge-invariant up to a total derivative (see below).

From now on, we will only use the projector after the replacement Eq.(272) to define and compute LBerryL_{\rm Berry}. Instead of introducing new notations, we redefine:

|Φ⁡(ρ⁡(t),a0full​(t))⟩≡|Φ⁡[G⁡(η⁡(t));ρ⁡(t)]⟩,\displaystyle|\Phi(\rho(t),a^{\text{full}}_{0}(t))\rangle\equiv|\Phi\big[G(\eta(t));\rho(t)\big]\rangle, (274)

which replaces Eq.(262), so that Eq.(260,261,263) can be reused. Defining:

Q𝐫A​(ρ)≡i​dd​s​⟨Φ⁡{ei​s​T^𝐫A​ΨM​F​(ρ)}|Φ⁡{ΨM​F​(ρ)}⟩|s=0,\displaystyle Q^{A}_{\mathbf{r}}(\rho)\equiv i\left.\frac{d}{ds}\left\langle\Phi\Big\{e^{is\hat{T}^{A}_{\mathbf{r}}}\Psi^{MF}(\rho)\Big\}|\Phi\{\Psi^{MF}(\rho)\}\right\rangle\right|_{s=0}, (275)

LBerryL_{\text{Berry}} can be separated into two terms using the dynamical-conserving condition Eq.(253):

LBerry=\displaystyle L_{\text{Berry}}= ⟨Φ(ρ(t))|i∂t|Φ(ρ(t))⟩−∑𝐫,Aa0full,A(𝐫,t)Q𝐫A(ρ(t)).\displaystyle\langle\Phi(\rho(t))|i\partial_{t}|\Phi(\rho(t))\rangle-\sum_{\mathbf{r},A}a^{\text{full},A}_{0}(\mathbf{r},t)Q_{\mathbf{r}}^{A}(\rho(t)). (276)

To appreciate the physical meaning of the a0fulla^{\text{full}}_{0}-term, it is instructive to consider the mean-field approximation, where we use the parton mean-field states to compute overlaps (which is equivalent to the zeroth-order PE in Sec.VI, denoted by the subscript ”[0]”):

Q𝐫A​(ρ)|[0]=⟨ΨM​F​(ρ)|T^𝐫A|ΨM​F​(ρ)⟩.\displaystyle\left.Q^{A}_{\mathbf{r}}(\rho)\right|_{[0]}=\langle\Psi^{MF}(\rho)|\hat{T}^{A}_{\mathbf{r}}|\Psi^{MF}(\rho)\rangle. (277)

This is just the gauge charge density on the mean-field level. Since there is only one term of a0fulla^{\text{full}}_{0} in LTDVPL_{\rm TDVP}, the a0fulla^{\text{full}}_{0} saddle-condition is:

δ​LBerryδ​a0full|a¯0,ρ¯=0⇒Q𝐫A​(ρ¯)=0,∀𝐫,A,\displaystyle\left.\frac{\delta L_{\rm Berry}}{\delta a^{\text{full}}_{0}}\right|_{\bar{a}_{0},\bar{\rho}}=0\Rightarrow Q^{A}_{\mathbf{r}}(\bar{\rho})=0,\forall\mathbf{r},A, (278)

which is the static Gauss’s law constraint.

Generally, under a gauge transformation {θ⁡(𝐫,t)}\{\theta(\mathbf{r},t)\}, a0full​(t),ρ⁡(t)a^{\text{full}}_{0}(t),\rho(t) transform as Eq.(265). Based on Eq.(250,253), LBerryL_{\text{Berry}} transforms as:

LBerry→LBerry−dd​t​ϕ​(θ,ρ),\displaystyle L_{\text{Berry}}\rightarrow L_{\text{Berry}}-\frac{d}{dt}\phi(\theta,\rho), (279)

i.e., LBerryL_{\text{Berry}} is gauge invariant up to a total derivative.

Notice that throughout the discussion from Eq.(255) to Eq.(276), no ”exact” or ”approx” subscript is present, indicating these generally hold for both exact and approximate treatments of Hdet states. Careful readers may have already noted that, for an exact treatment, a0fulla^{\text{full}}_{0} actually does not enter the Lagrangian! Indeed, if we substitute Eq.(249) in Eq.(275), a0fulla^{\text{full}}_{0}-contribution vanishes. It is actually unnecessary to introduce a0fulla^{\text{full}}_{0} in the exact treatment since the path integrals ∫𝒟​[ρ⁡(t),a0full​(t)]exact\int\mathcal{D}[\rho(t),a^{\text{full}}_{0}(t)]_{\rm exact} and ∫𝒟​[ρ⁡(t)]exact\int\mathcal{D}[\rho(t)]_{\rm exact} only differ by an overall constant.

In fact, there is no surprise here. In a gauge theory, the physical meaning of a0fulla^{\text{full}}_{0} is to implement Gauss’s law. Without a0fulla^{\text{full}}_{0} the approximate action will not be gauge invariant, and the sole purpose of introducing a0fulla^{\text{full}}_{0} is to restore the gauge invariance. After integrating out a0fulla^{\text{full}}_{0}, the states that participate in the path integral are all gauge-invariant. But in the exact treatment, Gauss’s law is already implemented by the exact fusion 𝐂^\hat{\mathbf{C}}, which is qualitatively equivalent to the situation where a0fulla^{\text{full}}_{0} is already integrated out in an approximate treatment. We will return to this point shortly when we perform the saddle point analysis for Hdet VMPI. As a preview, it is helpful to note now that integrating out a0fulla^{\text{full}}_{0} does not affect any physical gauge dynamics.

For example, we will show that the saddle-point analysis for Hdet VMPI leads to a general quadratic action for (2+1)-D U​(1)IU(1)_{I} gauge dynamics:

Sgauge=∫d​ω4​π​∑𝐪,μ,ν𝐚μ​(−𝐪,−ω)​Πμ​ν​(𝐪,ω)​𝐚ν​(𝐪,ω),\displaystyle S^{\rm gauge}=\int\frac{d\omega}{4\pi}\sum_{\mathbf{q},\mu,\nu}\mathbf{a}_{\mu}(-\mathbf{q},-\omega)\Pi_{\mu\nu}(\mathbf{q},\omega)\mathbf{a}_{\nu}(\mathbf{q},\omega), (280)

where μ,ν=0,1,2\mu,\nu=0,1,2, 𝐚0≡a0full,A=0−a¯0A=0\mathbf{a}_{0}\equiv a_{0}^{{\text{full}},A=0}-\bar{a}_{0}^{A=0}, and SgaugeS_{\rm gauge} is obtained after integrating out the matter fields characterized by ρ⁡(t)\rho(t). Under a gauge transformation labeled by {θA=0​(𝐫,t)}\{\theta^{A=0}(\mathbf{r},t)\}, 𝐚0→𝐚0−∂tθA=0\mathbf{a}_{0}\rightarrow\mathbf{a}_{0}-\partial_{t}\theta^{A=0}, and 𝐚u→𝐚u−∂uθA=0\mathbf{a}_{u}\rightarrow\mathbf{a}_{u}-\partial_{u}\theta^{A=0}, where we introduce u,v=1,2u,v=1,2 to label the spatial components of the U​(1)IU(1)_{I} gauge fields. In (𝐪,ω)(\mathbf{q},\omega)-space:

𝐚μ​(𝐪,ω)→𝐚μ​(𝐪,ω)−i​qμ​θA=0​(𝐪,ω),\displaystyle\mathbf{a}_{\mu}(\mathbf{q},\omega)\rightarrow\mathbf{a}_{\mu}(\mathbf{q},\omega)-iq_{\mu}\theta^{A=0}(\mathbf{q},\omega), (281)

where qμ≡(−ω,𝐪)q_{\mu}\equiv(-\omega,\mathbf{q}). The gauge invariance of SgaugeS_{\rm gauge} leads to the well-known gauge Ward identity:

∑μqμ​Πμ​ν​(𝐪,ω)=∑νΠμ​ν​(𝐪,ω)​qν=0.\displaystyle\sum_{\mu}q_{\mu}\Pi_{\mu\nu}(\mathbf{q},\omega)=\sum_{\nu}\Pi_{\mu\nu}(\mathbf{q},\omega)q_{\nu}=0. (282)

The gauge Ward identity constrains the form of Π\Pi. Let’s assume the matter fields that we integrated out are all gapped. In an approximate Hdet treatment, such as the projective-expansion that we will introduce in Sec.VI, the gauge kernel Π\Pi will consequently be a regular function of (𝐪,ω)(\mathbf{q},\omega). To the linear-order (quadratic-order) of (𝐪,ω)(\mathbf{q},\omega), the allowed Chern-Simons term (Maxwell term) is given by ΠCS\Pi^{\rm CS} (ΠMax\Pi^{\rm Max}):

Πμ​νCS=\displaystyle\Pi^{\rm CS}_{\mu\nu}= −i​k2​π​ϵμ​ν​λ​qλ,\displaystyle\frac{-ik}{2\pi}\epsilon_{\mu\nu\lambda}q_{\lambda},
Π00Max=\displaystyle\Pi^{\rm Max}_{00}= ∑u​vχEu​v​𝐪u​𝐪v,Π0​uMax=Πu​0Max=ω​∑vχEu​v​𝐪v,\displaystyle\sum_{uv}\chi_{E}^{uv}\mathbf{q}_{u}\mathbf{q}_{v},\;\;\;\Pi^{\rm Max}_{0u}=\Pi^{\rm Max}_{u0}=\omega\sum_{v}\chi_{E}^{uv}\mathbf{q}_{v},
Πu​vMax=\displaystyle\Pi^{\rm Max}_{uv}= ω2​χEu​v−χB​(𝐪2​δu​v−𝐪u​𝐪v).\displaystyle\omega^{2}\chi_{E}^{uv}-\chi_{B}(\mathbf{q}^{2}\delta_{uv}-\mathbf{q}_{u}\mathbf{q}_{v}). (283)

Below, for simplicity of presentation, we will assume the isotropic form of χEu​v=χE⋅δu​v\chi_{E}^{uv}=\chi_{E}\cdot\delta_{uv}. In real space, we recover the familiar gauge actions under the Einstein convention:

SCS=\displaystyle S^{\rm CS}= k4​π​∫d​𝐫​𝑑t​ϵμ​ν​λ​𝐚μ​∂ν𝐚λ,\displaystyle\frac{k}{4\pi}\int d\mathbf{r}dt\epsilon_{\mu\nu\lambda}\mathbf{a}_{\mu}\partial_{\nu}\mathbf{a}_{\lambda},
SMax=\displaystyle S^{\rm Max}= 12​∫d​𝐫​𝑑t​[χE​(∂t𝐚u−∂u𝐚0)2−χB​(ϵu​v​∂u𝐚v)2].\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\int d\mathbf{r}dt\Big[\chi_{E}(\partial_{t}\mathbf{a}_{u}-\partial_{u}\mathbf{a}_{0})^{2}-\chi_{B}(\epsilon_{uv}\partial_{u}\mathbf{a}_{v})^{2}\Big]. (284)

Note that the gauge actions Eq.(283,284) have explicit 𝐚0\mathbf{a}_{0}-dependence. Therefore, they should really come from an approximate Hdet treatment, and should be interpreted as ΠapproxCS,ΠapproxMax\Pi^{\rm CS}_{\rm approx},\Pi^{\rm Max}_{\rm approx} and SapproxCS,SapproxMaxS^{\rm CS}_{\rm approx},S^{\rm Max}_{\rm approx}.

In an exact Hdet treatment, however, there should be no 𝐚0\mathbf{a}_{0}-dependence as previously mentioned, qualitatively corresponding to integrating out 𝐚0\mathbf{a}_{0} in SgaugeS^{\rm gauge} in Eq.(280). We then obtain the spatial-component-only reduced gauge action:

Sreducedgauge=∫d​ω4​π​∑𝐪,u,v𝐚u​(−𝐪,−ω)​𝖲u​v​(𝐪,ω)​𝐚v​(𝐪,ω),\displaystyle S^{\rm gauge}_{\rm reduced}=\int\frac{d\omega}{4\pi}\sum_{\mathbf{q},u,v}\mathbf{a}_{u}(-\mathbf{q},-\omega)\mathsf{S}_{uv}(\mathbf{q},\omega)\mathbf{a}_{v}(\mathbf{q},\omega), (285)

where u,v=1,2u,v=1,2 and

𝖲u​v​(𝐪≠0,ω)≡Πu​v​(𝐪,ω)−Πu​0​(𝐪,ω)​Π00−1​(𝐪,ω)​Π0​v​(𝐪,ω).\displaystyle\mathsf{S}_{uv}(\mathbf{q}\neq 0,\omega)\equiv\Pi_{uv}(\mathbf{q},\omega)-\Pi_{u0}(\mathbf{q},\omega)\Pi_{00}^{-1}(\mathbf{q},\omega)\Pi_{0v}(\mathbf{q},\omega). (286)

It is easy to show that the usual gauge Ward identity Eq.(282) leads to the reduced gauge Ward identity:

∑u𝐪u​𝖲u​v​(𝐪,ω)=∑v𝖲u​v​(𝐪,ω)​𝐪v=0,\displaystyle\sum_{u}\mathbf{q}_{u}\mathsf{S}_{uv}(\mathbf{q},\omega)=\sum_{v}\mathsf{S}_{uv}(\mathbf{q},\omega)\mathbf{q}_{v}=0, (287)

which means that the longitudinal spatial component of 𝐚u∝𝐪u\mathbf{a}_{u}\propto\mathbf{q}_{u} does not enter the action. In fact, this longitudinal spatial component is a gauge redundancy, and only the transverse component 𝐚u⟂𝐪u\mathbf{a}_{u}\perp\mathbf{q}_{u} is physical.

For instance, for the pure Maxwell-kernel ΠMax\Pi^{\rm Max}, we obtain the reduced kernel

𝖲u​vMax​(𝐪≠0,ω)=(χE​ω2−χB​|𝐪|2)​(δu​v−𝐪u​𝐪v𝐪2),\displaystyle\mathsf{S}_{uv}^{\rm Max}(\mathbf{q}\neq 0,\omega)=(\chi_{E}\omega^{2}-\chi_{B}|\mathbf{q}|^{2})\Big(\delta_{uv}-\frac{\mathbf{q}_{u}\mathbf{q}_{v}}{\mathbf{q}^{2}}\Big), (288)

leading to a linearly dispersive, transverse photon mode. On the other hand, if one starts with SCS+Max=SCS+SMaxS^{\rm CS+Max}=S^{\rm CS}+S^{\rm Max}, integrating out 𝐚0\mathbf{a}_{0} leads to a reduced kernel

𝖲u​vCS+Max​(𝐪≠0,ω)=\displaystyle\mathsf{S}_{uv}^{\rm CS+Max}(\mathbf{q}\neq 0,\omega)= (χE​ω2−χB​|𝐪|2−1χE​(k2​π)2)\displaystyle\Big(\chi_{E}\omega^{2}-\chi_{B}|\mathbf{q}|^{2}-\frac{1}{\chi_{E}}\big(\frac{k}{2\pi}\big)^{2}\Big)
⋅(δu​v−𝐪u​𝐪v𝐪2),\displaystyle\cdot\Big(\delta_{uv}-\frac{\mathbf{q}_{u}\mathbf{q}_{v}}{\mathbf{q}^{2}}\Big), (289)

describing a massive transverse photon mode.

The 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0 gauge kernel must be treated separately: Π00CS+Max​(𝟎,ω)=0\Pi^{\rm CS+Max}_{00}(\mathbf{0},\omega)=0 vanishes and one should directly work with Π\Pi without the Schur complement Eq.(286). In fact, 𝐚0​(𝐪=0,ω)\mathbf{a}_{0}(\mathbf{q}=0,\omega) is not present in SCS+MaxS^{\rm CS+Max} due to gauge invariance. For spatial gauge field 𝐚u\mathbf{a}_{u}, the 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0 modes correspond to 𝐫\mathbf{r}-independent flat connections, i.e., fluxes φx,φy\varphi_{x},\varphi_{y} through the torus holes:

𝐚x​(𝐫,t)=\displaystyle\mathbf{a}_{x}(\mathbf{r},t)= φx​(t)Lx,\displaystyle\frac{\varphi_{x}(t)}{L_{x}}, 𝐚y​(𝐫,t)=\displaystyle\mathbf{a}_{y}(\mathbf{r},t)= φy​(t)Ly.\displaystyle\frac{\varphi_{y}(t)}{L_{y}}. (290)

One finds:

𝖲u​vCS+Max​(𝐪=0,ω)=Πu​vCS+Max​(𝐪=0,ω)\displaystyle\mathsf{S}_{uv}^{\rm CS+Max}(\mathbf{q}=0,\omega)=\Pi_{uv}^{\rm CS+Max}(\mathbf{q}=0,\omega)
=\displaystyle= i​ω​k2​π​ϵu​v+χE​ω2​δu​v,\displaystyle i\omega\frac{k}{2\pi}\epsilon_{uv}+\chi_{E}\omega^{2}\delta_{uv}, (291)

and the corresponding Lagrangian:

L⁡(𝐪=0,t)=k4​π​(φy​φ˙x−φx​φ˙y)+χE2​(LyLx​φ˙x2+LxLy​φ˙y2).\displaystyle L(\mathbf{q}=0,t)=\frac{k}{4\pi}(\varphi_{y}\dot{\varphi}_{x}-\varphi_{x}\dot{\varphi}_{y})+\frac{\chi_{E}}{2}(\frac{L_{y}}{L_{x}}\dot{\varphi}^{2}_{x}+\frac{L_{x}}{L_{y}}\dot{\varphi}^{2}_{y}). (292)

When k≠0k\neq 0, we obtain |k||k|-fold ground state degeneracy on a torus from the VMPI of L⁡(𝐪=0)L(\mathbf{q}=0)[132, 131]. The pure CS limit 𝖲CS\mathsf{S}^{\rm CS} corresponds to χE=χB=0\chi_{E}=\chi_{B}=0, leading to an infinite mass gap and only the ground state sector, i.e., a topological quantum field theory. Here, we see the convenience of VMPI: because of the path integral, the theory is intrinsically quantum-mechanical.

In summary, in an exact Hdet treatment, we expect to obtain the reduced gauge action SreducedgaugeS^{\rm gauge}_{\rm reduced} in Eq.(285) and reduced, 𝐚u\mathbf{a}_{u}-only kernels consistent with 𝖲Max\mathsf{S}^{\rm Max} in Eq.(288) or 𝖲CS+Max\mathsf{S}^{\rm CS+Max} in Eq.(289,291), which do not miss any physics compared with the Π\Pi-kernels in Eq.(283) with 𝐚0\mathbf{a}_{0}-dependence.

V.3.2 Saddle point analysis and gauge Ward identity in the κ\kappa-language

At this point, we introduce saddle-point analysis for general calculation schemes, either approximate or exact. Denoting a0full=a¯0+a0a_{0}^{\rm full}=\bar{a}_{0}+a_{0}, one can always find the saddle point of LTDVPL_{\text{TDVP}} in the static-saddle gauge, where a¯0\bar{a}_{0} and ρ¯\bar{\rho} are time-independent. Here, ρ¯\bar{\rho} also needs to satisfy the saddle equation of a0a_{0} variation: δ​Lδ​a0|a¯0,ρ¯=0\left.\frac{\delta L}{\delta a_{0}}\right|_{\bar{a}_{0},\bar{\rho}}=0: Eq.(278). We will consider fluctuations around this saddle point {a¯0,ρ¯}\{\bar{a}_{0},\bar{\rho}\}. Due to the gauge invariance, the {θ⁡(𝐫,t)}\{\theta(\mathbf{r},t)\} gauge transformed one describes the same physical saddle point: ρ¯→ρ¯θ​(t)≡G⁡(θ⁡(t))∘ρ¯\bar{\rho}\rightarrow\bar{\rho}_{\theta}(t)\equiv G(\theta(t))\circ\bar{\rho}, and a¯0​(𝐫)→a¯0,θ​(𝐫,t)\bar{a}_{0}(\mathbf{r})\rightarrow\bar{a}_{0,\theta}(\mathbf{r},t) which is obtained via Eq.(268). These fluctuations are precisely the nonphysical pure gauge modes that should be singled out. Below, we will always work in the static-saddle gauge: a0full​(𝐫,t)=a¯0​(𝐫)+a0​(𝐫,t)a_{0}^{\rm full}(\mathbf{r},t)=\bar{a}_{0}(\mathbf{r})+a_{0}(\mathbf{r},t).

The a¯0\bar{a}_{0}-saddle equation is already given in Eq.(278). Next, we present the ρ¯\bar{\rho}-saddle equation. Defining a static energy including the a¯0\bar{a}_{0} contribution:

Est​(ρ,a¯0)≡E⁡(ρ)+∑𝐫,Aa¯0A​(𝐫)​Q𝐫A​(ρ),\displaystyle E_{\rm st}(\rho;\bar{a}_{0})\equiv E(\rho)+\sum_{\mathbf{r},A}\bar{a}_{0}^{A}(\mathbf{r})Q^{A}_{\mathbf{r}}(\rho), (293)

the effective hopping and Hessian for each parton species p=1,2p=1,2 can be defined:

ti​j(p)​(ρ,a¯0)≡\displaystyle t^{(p)}_{ij}(\rho;\bar{a}_{0})\equiv ∂Est∂ρj​i(p),\displaystyle\frac{\partial E_{\rm st}}{\partial\rho^{(p)}_{ji}}, 𝒦i​j,k​l(p​q)≡\displaystyle\mathcal{K}^{(pq)}_{ij,kl}\equiv ∂2Est∂ρj​i(p)​∂ρl​k(q)|ρ¯,a¯0.\displaystyle\left.\frac{\partial^{2}E_{\rm st}}{\partial\rho^{(p)}_{ji}\,\partial\rho^{(q)}_{lk}}\right|_{\bar{\rho},\bar{a}_{0}}. (294)

Up to quadratic order:

Est​(ρ¯+δ​ρ,a¯0)=Est​(ρ¯,a¯0)+∑p,i​jti​j(p)​(ρ¯,a¯0)​δ​ρj​i(p)\displaystyle E_{\rm st}(\bar{\rho}+\delta\rho;\bar{a}_{0})=E_{\rm st}(\bar{\rho};\bar{a}_{0})+\sum_{p,ij}t^{(p)}_{ij}(\bar{\rho};\bar{a}_{0})\,\delta\rho^{(p)}_{ji}
+12∑p,q∑i​j,k​l𝒦i​j,k​l(p​q)δρj​i(p)δρl​k(q)+O(δρ3).\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{p,q}\sum_{ij,kl}\mathcal{K}^{(pq)}_{ij,kl}\,\delta\rho^{(p)}_{ji}\delta\rho^{(q)}_{lk}+O(\delta\rho^{3}). (295)

Importantly, δ​ρ(1)\delta\rho^{(1)} and δ​ρ(2)\delta\rho^{(2)} are coupled via the inter-species Hessian components 𝒦(12)\mathcal{K}^{(12)} and 𝒦(21)\mathcal{K}^{(21)}. We also define the effective parton single-body Hamiltonian:

h^(ρ;a¯0)≡∑p∑i​jti​j(p)(ρ;a¯0)fi(p)†fj(p).\displaystyle\hat{h}(\rho;\bar{a}_{0})\equiv\sum_{p}\sum_{ij}t^{(p)}_{ij}(\rho;\bar{a}_{0})f^{(p)\dagger}_{i}f^{(p)}_{j}\;. (296)

The ρ¯\bar{\rho} saddle condition is the vanishing condition for the linear δ​ρ\delta\rho-term in Eq.(295) for all tangent δ​ρ\delta\rho, which is equivalent to the self-consistency condition: [t⁡(ρ¯,a¯0),ρ¯]=0[t(\bar{\rho};\bar{a}_{0}),\bar{\rho}]=0, or the ground state RDM of h^​(ρ¯,a¯0)\hat{h}(\bar{\rho};\bar{a}_{0}) is also ρ¯\bar{\rho}.

Now it is a good moment to introduce the vector space of Hermitian matrices relevant for Hdet wavefunctions and the associated inner product. We first define the real linear space Mh(p)M^{(p)}_{\rm h} for each parton species-pp formed by Hermitian matrices of the same size as ρi​j(p)\rho^{(p)}_{ij}. Their direct sum defines the full real linear space MhM_{\rm h}:

Mh≡Mh(1)⊕Mh(2).\displaystyle M_{\rm h}\equiv M^{(1)}_{\rm h}\oplus M^{(2)}_{\rm h}. (297)

An element X∈MhX\in M_{\rm h} can be represented as X={X(1),X(2)}X=\{X^{(1)},X^{(2)}\}, where X(p)∈Mh(p)X^{(p)}\in M^{(p)}_{\rm h}. We define the inner product in MhM_{\rm h}:

\llangle​X,Y​\rrangle≡∑p=12∑i​jXi​j(p)​Yj​i(p).\displaystyle\llangle X,Y\rrangle\equiv\sum_{p=1}^{2}\sum_{ij}X^{(p)}_{ij}Y^{(p)}_{ji}. (298)

We also define the superoperator 𝒦^\hat{\mathcal{K}} acting on MhM_{\rm h}:

[𝒦^​X]i​j(p)≡∑q=12∑k​l𝒦i​j,k​l(p​q)​Xl​k(q).\displaystyle[\hat{\mathcal{K}}X]^{(p)}_{ij}\equiv\sum_{q=1}^{2}\sum_{kl}\mathcal{K}^{(pq)}_{ij,kl}X^{(q)}_{lk}. (299)

Eq.(295) can be compactly written as:

Est​(ρ,a¯0)=\displaystyle E_{\rm st}(\rho;\bar{a}_{0})= Est​(ρ¯,a¯0)+\llangle​t​(ρ¯,a¯0),δ​ρ​\rrangle\displaystyle E_{\rm st}(\bar{\rho};\bar{a}_{0})+\llangle t(\bar{\rho};\bar{a}_{0}),\delta\rho\rrangle
+12​\llangle​δ​ρ,𝒦^​δ​ρ​\rrangle+O⁡(δ​ρ3).\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2}\llangle\delta\rho,\hat{\mathcal{K}}\delta\rho\rrangle+O(\delta\rho^{3}). (300)

One can further show that 𝒦^\hat{\mathcal{K}} is symmetric: ∀X,Y∈Mh\forall X,Y\in M_{\rm h},

\llangle​X,𝒦^​Y​\rrangle=\llangle​𝒦^​X,Y​\rrangle,\displaystyle\llangle X,\hat{\mathcal{K}}Y\rrangle=\llangle\hat{\mathcal{K}}X,Y\rrangle, (301)

which follows from identities 𝒦i​j,k​l(p​q)=𝒦k​l,i​j(q​p)\mathcal{K}^{(pq)}_{ij,kl}=\mathcal{K}^{(qp)}_{kl,ij} and 𝒦(p​q)i​j,k​l=𝒦(pq)∗j​i,l​k\mathcal{K}^{(pq)}_{ij,kl}=\mathcal{K}^{(pq)*}_{ji,lk}.

We now examine the gauge transformation of EstE_{\rm st}. Under a time-independent gauge transformation {θ⁡(𝐫)}\{\theta(\mathbf{r})\}: ρ→G⁡(θ)∘ρ\rho\rightarrow G(\theta)\circ\rho, and static-conserving condition leads to E⁡(ρ)=E⁡(G⁡(θ)∘ρ)E(\rho)=E(G(\theta)\circ\rho). For the second term, from Eq.(268), we know

a¯0B​(𝐫)→a¯0,θB​(𝐫)≡∑ARAB​(θ⁡(𝐫))​a¯0A​(𝐫),,\displaystyle\bar{a}_{0}^{B}(\mathbf{r})\rightarrow\bar{a}^{B}_{0,\theta}(\mathbf{r})\equiv\sum_{A}R_{A}^{B}(\theta(\mathbf{r}))\bar{a}_{0}^{A}(\mathbf{r}),, (302)

which is equivalent to Λ⁡[a¯0]→Θ⁡[θ]​Λ​[a¯0]​Θ†​[θ]\Lambda[\bar{a}_{0}]\rightarrow\Theta[\theta]\Lambda[\bar{a}_{0}]\Theta^{\dagger}[\theta]. One can show from the definition Eq.(275) and the dynamical-conserving condition:

Q𝐫B​(G⁡(θ)∘ρ)=[R−1]BA​(θ⁡(𝐫))​Q𝐫A​(ρ).\displaystyle Q_{\mathbf{r}}^{B}(G(\theta)\circ\rho)=[R^{-1}]^{A}_{B}(\theta(\mathbf{r}))Q^{A}_{\mathbf{r}}(\rho). (303)

Therefore, EstE_{\rm st} is gauge invariant:

Est​(ρ,a¯0)=Est​(G⁡(θ)∘ρ,a¯0,θ),\displaystyle E_{\rm st}(\rho;\bar{a}_{0})=E_{\rm st}(G(\theta)\circ\rho;\bar{a}_{0,\theta}), (304)

and Eq.(294) gives to the gauge covariance of the effective hopping,

t(p)(G(θ)∘ρ;a¯0,θ)=Θ(p)t(p)(ρ;a¯0)Θ(p)†,\displaystyle t^{(p)}\big(G(\theta)\circ\rho;\bar{a}_{0,\theta}\big)=\Theta^{(p)}\,t^{(p)}(\rho;\bar{a}_{0})\,\Theta^{(p)\dagger}, (305)

which in turn leads to the gauge Ward identity.

Next, we introduce the tangent space Tρ¯⊂MhT_{\bar{\rho}}\subset M_{\rm h} and the relevant superoperators, in parallel to the discussion near Eq.(161-171). Introducing the Thouless parameterization for each parton species:

Ξ^(p)(κ(p))≡∑𝐩𝐡[−iκ𝐩𝐡(p)f𝐩(p)†f𝐡(p)+h.c.],\displaystyle\hat{\Xi}^{(p)}(\kappa^{(p)})\equiv\sum_{\mathbf{ph}}\Big[-i\,\kappa^{(p)}_{\mathbf{ph}}f^{(p)\dagger}_{\mathbf{p}}f^{(p)}_{\mathbf{h}}+h.c.\Big], (306)

which transforms the parton mean-field state as ei​Ξ^(p)​(κ(p))​|Ψ(p)​(ρ¯(p))⟩=|Ψ(p)​(ei​Ξ^(p)​(κ(p))∘ρ¯(p))⟩e^{i\hat{\Xi}^{(p)}(\kappa^{(p)})}|\Psi^{(p)}(\bar{\rho}^{(p)})\rangle=|\Psi^{(p)}(e^{i\hat{\Xi}^{(p)}(\kappa^{(p)})}\circ\bar{\rho}^{(p)})\rangle.

Defining the tangent space Tρ¯(p)⊂Mh(p)T^{(p)}_{\bar{\rho}}\subset M^{(p)}_{\rm h}:

Tρ¯(p)≡\displaystyle T^{(p)}_{\bar{\rho}}\equiv {X(p)|ρ¯(p)X(p)ρ¯(p)=0,\displaystyle\{X^{(p)}|\;\bar{\rho}^{(p)}X^{(p)}\bar{\rho}^{(p)}=0,
(1−ρ¯(p))X(p)(1−ρ¯(p))=0}⊂Mh(p),\displaystyle(1-\bar{\rho}^{(p)})X^{(p)}(1-\bar{\rho}^{(p)})=0\}\subset M^{(p)}_{\rm h}, (307)

κ(p)\kappa^{(p)} is an explicit coordinate for Tρ¯(p)T^{(p)}_{\bar{\rho}}. We define the full tangent space:

Tρ¯≡Tρ¯(1)⊕Tρ¯(2)⊂Mh,\displaystyle T_{\bar{\rho}}\equiv T_{\bar{\rho}}^{(1)}\oplus T_{\bar{\rho}}^{(2)}\subset M_{\rm h}, (308)

and an element κ∈Tρ¯\kappa\in T_{\bar{\rho}} can be written as:

κ={κ(1),κ(2)}.\displaystyle\kappa=\{\kappa^{(1)},\kappa^{(2)}\}. (309)

We also define 𝒫^T\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{T} to be the projector into Tρ¯T_{\bar{\rho}}.

One may parameterize the Hdet state near the saddle point by κ\kappa as:

|Φ⁡(κ)⟩≡|Φ⁡(ρ⁡(κ))⟩≡|Φ⁡(ei​Ξ​(κ)∘ρ¯)⟩,\displaystyle|\Phi(\kappa)\rangle\equiv|\Phi(\rho(\kappa))\rangle\equiv|\Phi(e^{i\Xi(\kappa)}\circ\bar{\rho})\rangle, (310)

where

(ei​Ξ​(κ)∘ρ¯)(p)≡ei​Ξ(p)​(κ(p))∘ρ¯(p)\displaystyle\Big(e^{i\Xi(\kappa)}\circ\bar{\rho}\Big)^{(p)}\equiv e^{i\Xi^{(p)}(\kappa^{(p)})}\circ\bar{\rho}^{(p)}
=\displaystyle= ei​Ξ(p)​(κ(p))​ρ¯(p)​e−i​Ξ(p)​(κ(p)).\displaystyle e^{i\Xi^{(p)}(\kappa^{(p)})}\bar{\rho}^{(p)}e^{-i\Xi^{(p)}(\kappa^{(p)})}. (311)

Using the parton version of Eq.(161), one can write the Gaussian order of Est​(ρ⁡(κ),a¯0)−Est​(ρ¯,a¯0)≡δ​Est​(κ)E_{\rm st}(\rho(\kappa);\bar{a}_{0})-E_{\rm st}(\bar{\rho};\bar{a}_{0})\equiv\delta E_{\rm st}(\kappa) as

δ​Est​(κ)=12​\llangle​κ,(𝒢^+𝒦^)​κ​\rrangle+O⁡(κ3),\displaystyle\delta E_{\rm st}(\kappa)=\frac{1}{2}\llangle\kappa,(\hat{\mathcal{G}}+\hat{\mathcal{K}})\kappa\rrangle+O(\kappa^{3}), (312)

where the symmetric superoperator 𝒢^\hat{\mathcal{G}} acting in Tρ¯T_{\bar{\rho}} is defined as: ∀X∈Tρ¯\forall X\in T_{\bar{\rho}},

(𝒢^​X)𝐩𝐡(p)≡\displaystyle(\hat{\mathcal{G}}X)^{(p)}_{\mathbf{ph}}\equiv (ϵ𝐩(p)−ϵ𝐡(p))​X𝐩𝐡(p),\displaystyle(\epsilon^{(p)}_{\mathbf{p}}-\epsilon^{(p)}_{\mathbf{h}})X^{(p)}_{\mathbf{ph}}, (𝒢^​X)𝐡𝐩(p)≡\displaystyle(\hat{\mathcal{G}}X)^{(p)}_{\mathbf{hp}}\equiv (ϵ𝐩(p)−ϵ𝐡(p))​X𝐡𝐩(p).\displaystyle(\epsilon^{(p)}_{\mathbf{p}}-\epsilon^{(p)}_{\mathbf{h}})X^{(p)}_{\mathbf{hp}}.

Now, we consider a small gauge transformation θ≪1\theta\ll 1 and the θ\theta linear-order change of the effective hopping ti​j(p)t^{(p)}_{ij}:

(χθ(p))i​j≡dd​s​ti​j(p)​(G⁡(s​θ)∘ρ¯,a¯0,s​θ)|s=0,\displaystyle\big(\chi_{\theta}^{(p)}\big)_{ij}\equiv\left.\frac{d}{ds}\,t^{(p)}_{ij}\big(G(s\theta)\circ\bar{\rho};\bar{a}_{0,s\theta}\big)\right|_{s=0}, (314)

using Eq.(305), one finds

(χθ(p))i​j\displaystyle\big(\chi_{\theta}^{(p)}\big)_{ij} =i​[Λ(p)​[θ],t(p)​(ρ¯,a¯0)]i​j\displaystyle=i\big[\Lambda^{(p)}[\theta],t^{(p)}(\bar{\rho};\bar{a}_{0})\big]_{ij} (315)

On the other hand, because tt is the first-order derivative of EstE_{\rm st}, χθ\chi_{\theta} can be computed via the second-order derivative of EstE_{\rm st} involving the Hessian 𝒦\mathcal{K}, similar to how we obtain Eq.(193) in the TDHF demo. From Eq.(244), the θ\theta linear-order change G⁡(θ)∘ρ¯G(\theta)\circ\bar{\rho} is:

(κθ(p))i​j\displaystyle\big(\kappa_{\theta}^{(p)}\big)_{ij} ≡dd​s​[G⁡(s​θ)∘ρ¯](p)|s=0=i​[Λ(p)​[θ],ρ¯(p)]i​j.\displaystyle\equiv\left.\frac{d}{ds}\Big[G(s\theta)\circ\bar{\rho}\Big]^{(p)}\right|_{s=0}=i\big[\Lambda^{(p)}[\theta],\bar{\rho}^{(p)}\big]_{ij}. (316)

κθ∈Tρ¯\kappa_{\theta}\in T_{\bar{\rho}}. But due to the second term of EstE_{\rm st}, the Hessian 𝒦\mathcal{K} is not enough:

(χθ(p))i​j=\displaystyle\big(\chi_{\theta}^{(p)}\big)_{ij}= dd​s​∂∂ρj​i(p)​Est​(G⁡(s​θ)∘ρ¯,a¯0,s​θ)|s=0\displaystyle\left.\frac{d}{ds}\,\frac{\partial}{\partial\rho^{(p)}_{ji}}E_{\rm st}\big(G(s\theta)\circ\bar{\rho};\bar{a}_{0,s\theta}\big)\right|_{s=0}
=\displaystyle= [𝒦^​κθ]i​j(p)+∑𝐫,A(δθ​a¯0)A​(𝐫)​∂Q𝐫A​(ρ)∂ρj​i(p)|ρ¯,\displaystyle[\hat{\mathcal{K}}\kappa_{\theta}]^{(p)}_{ij}+\sum_{\mathbf{r},A}(\delta_{\theta}\bar{a}_{0})^{A}(\mathbf{r})\left.\frac{\partial Q^{A}_{\mathbf{r}}(\rho)}{\partial\rho^{(p)}_{ji}}\right|_{\bar{\rho}}, (317)

where δθ​a¯0\delta_{\theta}\bar{a}_{0} is the θ\theta linear-order of a¯0,θ\bar{a}_{0,\theta} in Eq.(302):

δθa¯0C(𝐫)≡−∑A,BfCA​BθA(𝐫)a¯0B(𝐫),\displaystyle\delta_{\theta}\bar{a}_{0}^{C}(\mathbf{r})\equiv-\sum_{A,B}f^{AB}_{C}\theta^{A}(\mathbf{r})\bar{a}^{B}_{0}(\mathbf{r}), (318)

or equivalently:

Λ⁡[δθ​a¯0]=i⁡[Λ⁡[θ],Λ⁡[a¯0]].\displaystyle\Lambda[\delta_{\theta}\bar{a}_{0}]=i[\Lambda[\theta],\Lambda[\bar{a}_{0}]]. (319)

Define a superoperator: ℬ^:Λ⁡[ξ]→Mh\hat{\mathcal{B}}:\Lambda[\xi]\rightarrow M_{\rm h} in terms of components:

[ℬ^​Λ​[ξ]]i​j(p)≡∑𝐫,AξA​(𝐫)​∂Q𝐫A​(ρ)∂ρj​i(p)|ρ¯,\displaystyle\big[\hat{\mathcal{B}}\Lambda[\xi]\big]^{(p)}_{ij}\equiv\sum_{\mathbf{r},A}\xi^{A}(\mathbf{r})\left.\frac{\partial Q^{A}_{\mathbf{r}}(\rho)}{\partial\rho_{ji}^{(p)}}\right|_{\bar{\rho}}, (320)

and consequently:

∑𝐫,AξA​(𝐫)​Q𝐫A​(ρ⁡(κ))=\llangle​ℬ^​Λ​[ξ],κ​\rrangle+O⁡(κ2).\displaystyle\sum_{\mathbf{r},A}\xi^{A}(\mathbf{r})Q^{A}_{\mathbf{r}}(\rho(\kappa))=\llangle\hat{\mathcal{B}}\Lambda[\xi],\kappa\rrangle+O(\kappa^{2}). (321)

One arrives at

χθ=𝒦^​κθ+ℬ^​Λ​[δθ​a¯0].\displaystyle\chi_{\theta}=\hat{\mathcal{K}}\,\kappa_{\theta}+\hat{\mathcal{B}}\Lambda[\delta_{\theta}\bar{a}_{0}]. (322)

This is the static gauge Ward identity in the real-space basis. In addition, t⁡(ρ¯,a¯0)=t⁡(ρ¯)+ℬ^​Λ​[a¯0]t(\bar{\rho};\bar{a}_{0})=t(\bar{\rho})+\hat{\mathcal{B}}\Lambda[\bar{a}_{0}], where t⁡(ρ¯)t(\bar{\rho}) is the derivative of E⁡(ρ)E(\rho) alone.

As a concrete example, if one uses the mean-field approximation to compute overlaps (see Eq.(277)), one has:

ℬ^[0]​Λ​[a0]=Λ⁡[a0],\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{B}}_{[0]}\Lambda[a_{0}]=\Lambda[a_{0}], (323)

i.e., the mean-field ℬ^[0]\hat{\mathcal{B}}_{[0]} is equivalent to identity.

Next, we move on to write down the Berry’s phase term LBerryL_{\rm Berry} in Eq.(276) in terms of κ\kappa and a0a_{0}. Let’s start with the first term in Eq.(276): ⟨Φ(κ)|i∂t|Φ(κ)⟩\langle\Phi(\kappa)|i\partial_{t}|\Phi(\kappa)\rangle, and define the Berry curvature superoperator ℱ^:Tρ¯→Tρ¯\hat{\mathcal{F}}:T_{\bar{\rho}}\rightarrow T_{\bar{\rho}}:

\llangle​κ1,ℱ^​κ2​\rrangle≡\displaystyle\llangle\kappa_{1},\hat{\mathcal{F}}\kappa_{2}\rrangle\equiv 2⋅Im⁡[⟨Φ⁡(κ1)|Φ⁡(κ2)⟩]|κ1​κ2−part,\displaystyle 2\cdot\left.\rm{Im}\big[\langle\Phi(\kappa_{1})|\Phi(\kappa_{2})\rangle\big]\right|_{\kappa_{1}\kappa_{2}-\text{part}}, (324)

which is antisymmetric following the Hermiticity property in Eq.(253): \llangle​X,ℱ^​Y​\rrangle=−\llangle​ℱ^​X,Y​\rrangle\llangle X,\hat{\mathcal{F}}Y\rrangle=-\llangle\hat{\mathcal{F}}X,Y\rrangle. Up to a total derivative, this term is determined by ℱ^\hat{\mathcal{F}} up to the Gaussian order:

⟨Φ(κ)|i∂t|Φ(κ)⟩=−12\llangleκ,ℱ^κ˙\rrangle+total deriv.+O(κ3)\displaystyle\langle\Phi(\kappa)|i\partial_{t}|\Phi(\kappa)\rangle=-\frac{1}{2}\llangle\kappa,\hat{\mathcal{F}}\dot{\kappa}\rrangle+\text{total deriv.}+O(\kappa^{3}) (325)

As an important general property, ∀\forall gauge transformations θ,η\theta,\eta, we have:

\llangle​κη,ℱ^​κθ​\rrangle=∑𝐫,A,B,CηA​(𝐫)​θB​(𝐫)​fCA​B​Q𝐫C​(ρ¯)=0,\displaystyle\llangle\kappa_{\eta},\hat{\mathcal{F}}\kappa_{\theta}\rrangle=\sum_{\mathbf{r},A,B,C}\eta^{A}(\mathbf{r})\theta^{B}(\mathbf{r})f^{AB}_{C}Q_{\mathbf{r}}^{C}(\bar{\rho})=0, (326)

where we use the saddle condition Eq.(278). This is a direct consequence of dynamically-conserving condition Eq.(253):

\llangle​κη,ℱ^​κθ​\rrangle=2​I​m​d2d​s​d​t​⟨Φ⁡(G⁡(s​η),ρ¯)|Φ⁡(G⁡(t​θ),ρ¯)⟩|s=t=0\displaystyle\llangle\kappa_{\eta},\hat{\mathcal{F}}\kappa_{\theta}\rrangle=2{\rm Im}\frac{d^{2}}{dsdt}\left.\langle\Phi(G(s\eta);\bar{\rho})|\Phi(G(t\theta);\bar{\rho})\rangle\right|_{s=t=0}
=\displaystyle= 2​I​m​d2d​s​d​t​⟨Φ⁡(ρ¯)|Φ⁡{e−i​s​Λ^​[η]​ei​t​Λ^​[θ]​ΨM​F​(ρ¯)}⟩|s=t=0,\displaystyle 2{\rm Im}\frac{d^{2}}{dsdt}\left.\langle\Phi(\bar{\rho})|\Phi\{e^{-is\hat{\Lambda}[\eta]}e^{it\hat{\Lambda}[\theta]}\Psi^{MF}(\bar{\rho})\}\rangle\right|_{s=t=0}, (327)

Using e−i​s​Λ^​[η]​ei​t​Λ^​[θ]=e−i​s​Λ^​[η]+i​t​Λ^​[θ]+s​t2​[Λ^​[η],Λ^​[θ]]+O⁡((s,t)3)e^{-is\hat{\Lambda}[\eta]}e^{it\hat{\Lambda}[\theta]}=e^{-is\hat{\Lambda}[\eta]+it\hat{\Lambda}[\theta]+\frac{st}{2}[\hat{\Lambda}[\eta],\hat{\Lambda}[\theta]]}+O((s,t)^{3}) and the Lie algebra Eq.(241), Eq.(326) is established. Here, note that we replaced |Φ⁡(G⁡(θ)∘ρ¯)⟩|\Phi(G(\theta)\circ\bar{\rho})\rangle by |Φ⁡(G⁡(θ),ρ¯)⟩|\Phi(G(\theta);\bar{\rho})\rangle in this calculation, but only the former one is what we used to define κθ\kappa_{\theta} in Eq.(316). However, ei​Λ^​[θ]​|ΨM​F​(ρ¯)⟩e^{i\hat{\Lambda}[\theta]}|\Psi^{MF}(\bar{\rho})\rangle and |ΨM​F​(G⁡(θ)∘ρ¯)⟩|\Psi^{MF}(G(\theta)\circ\bar{\rho})\rangle differ only by a phase factor (see Eq.(250)), based on the dynamical-conserving condition Eq.(253), this replacement can change the Berry connection but cannot change the Berry curvature.

For an exact Hdet calculation, we have an even stronger identity: ∀\forall gauge transformation θ\theta:

ℱ^exact​κθ=0,\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{F}}_{\rm exact}\kappa_{\theta}=0, (328)

since the gauge transformation does not change the exact Hdet wavefunction |Φ⁡(G⁡(θ),ρ¯)⟩exact=|Φ⁡(ρ¯)⟩exact|\Phi(G(\theta);\bar{\rho})\rangle_{\rm exact}=|\Phi(\bar{\rho})\rangle_{\rm exact}.

Next, we move on to the second term in Eq.(276). The a¯0\bar{a}_{0}-part of this term is already included in EstE_{\rm st}. For the remaining a0a_{0}-part, Eq.(278,320) allows us to write it up to the Gaussian order:

−∑𝐫,Aa0A(𝐫,t)Q𝐫A(ρ(t))=−\llangleℬ^Λ[a0],κ\rrangle+O((a0,κ)3),\displaystyle-\sum_{\mathbf{r},A}a^{A}_{0}(\mathbf{r},t)Q_{\mathbf{r}}^{A}(\rho(t))=-\llangle\hat{\mathcal{B}}\Lambda[a_{0}],\kappa\rrangle+O((a_{0},\kappa)^{3}), (329)

Generally, one can show that 𝒫^T​ℬ^​Λ​[a0]\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{T}\hat{\mathcal{B}}\Lambda[a_{0}] is fully determined by ℱ^\hat{\mathcal{F}} via the following identity:

𝒫^T​ℬ^​Λ​[a0]=\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{T}\hat{\mathcal{B}}\Lambda[a_{0}]= ℱ^​κa0,\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{F}}\kappa_{a_{0}},
⇔\llangleκ,ℬ^Λ[a0]\rrangle=\displaystyle\Leftrightarrow\llangle\kappa,\hat{\mathcal{B}}\Lambda[a_{0}]\rrangle= \llangle​κ,ℱ^​κa0​\rrangle,∀κ∈Tρ¯.\displaystyle\llangle\kappa,\hat{\mathcal{F}}\kappa_{a_{0}}\rrangle,\forall\kappa\in T_{\bar{\rho}}. (330)

The simplest way to see this is to consider the parallel transport around a small loop involving four nearby electronic states |Φ​{ΨM​F}⟩|\Phi\{\Psi^{MF}\}\rangle, labeled by four parton mean-field states |ΨM​F⟩|\Psi^{MF}\rangle:

|ΨM​F​(ρ¯)⟩→|ΨM​F​(ρ⁡(κ))⟩→|ΨM​F​(G⁡(a0)∘ρ⁡(κ))⟩\displaystyle|\Psi^{MF}(\bar{\rho})\rangle\rightarrow|\Psi^{MF}(\rho(\kappa))\rangle\rightarrow|\Psi^{MF}(G(a_{0})\circ\rho(\kappa))\rangle
→|ΨM​F​(G⁡(a0)∘ρ¯)⟩→|ΨM​F​(ρ¯)⟩.\displaystyle\rightarrow|\Psi^{MF}(G(a_{0})\circ\bar{\rho})\rangle\rightarrow|\Psi^{MF}(\bar{\rho})\rangle. (331)

The electronic (not parton’s) Berry’s phase for this small loop, to the order of a0​κa_{0}\kappa, gives the RHS. But if one replaces |ΨM​F​(G⁡(a0)∘ρ)⟩|\Psi^{MF}(G(a_{0})\circ\rho)\rangle by ei​Λ^​[a0]​|ΨM​F​(ρ)⟩e^{i\hat{\Lambda}[a_{0}]}|\Psi^{MF}(\rho)\rangle, the electronic Berry’s phase gives the LHS. Due to the dynamical-conserving condition Eq.(253), Berry’s phase must be identical before and after the replacement.

Putting together, and neglecting total derivatives, we arrive at:

LTDVP=\displaystyle L_{\rm TDVP}= −\llangleℬ^Λ[a0],κ\rrangle−12\llangleκ,(ℱ^∂t+𝒢^+𝒦^)κ\rrangle\displaystyle-\llangle\hat{\mathcal{B}}\Lambda[a_{0}],\kappa\rrangle-\frac{1}{2}\llangle\kappa,(\hat{\mathcal{F}}\partial_{t}+\hat{\mathcal{G}}+\hat{\mathcal{K}})\kappa\rrangle
+O⁡((a0,κ)3)\displaystyle+O((a_{0},\kappa)^{3}) (332)

Under a space-time dependent gauge transformation θ⁡(𝐫,t)≪1\theta(\mathbf{r},t)\ll 1, from Eq.(271,316), we have:

a0→\displaystyle a_{0}\rightarrow a0−θ˙+δθ​a¯0,κ→κ+κθ,\displaystyle a_{0}-\dot{\theta}+\delta_{\theta}\bar{a}_{0},\;\;\;\kappa\rightarrow\kappa+\kappa_{\theta}, (333)

where the first transformation can be equivalently written as: Λ⁡[a0]→Λ⁡[a0−θ˙]+i⁡[Λ⁡[θ],Λ⁡[a¯0]]\Lambda[a_{0}]\rightarrow\Lambda[a_{0}-\dot{\theta}]+i[\Lambda[\theta],\Lambda[\bar{a}_{0}]].

To understand the gauge transformation of the static part of LTDVPL_{\rm TDVP}, it is easy to show that

𝒫^T​χθ=−𝒢^​κθ.\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{T}\chi_{\theta}=-\hat{\mathcal{G}}\kappa_{\theta}. (334)

For example, Eq.(316) leads to (κθ(p))𝐩𝐡=i​(Λ(p)​[θ])𝐩𝐡\big(\kappa^{(p)}_{\theta}\big)_{\mathbf{ph}}=i\big(\Lambda^{(p)}[\theta]\big)_{\mathbf{ph}}, and Eq.(315) leads to (χθ(p))𝐩𝐡=−(ϵ𝐩(p)−ϵ𝐡(p))​(κθ(p))𝐩𝐡\big(\chi_{\theta}^{(p)}\big)_{\mathbf{ph}}=-(\epsilon^{(p)}_{\mathbf{p}}-\epsilon^{(p)}_{\mathbf{h}})\big(\kappa^{(p)}_{\theta}\big)_{\mathbf{ph}}.

Therefore, together with Eq.(322):

(𝒢^+𝒫^T​𝒦^)​κθ+𝒫^T​ℬ^​Λ​[δθ​a¯0]=\displaystyle(\hat{\mathcal{G}}+\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{T}\hat{\mathcal{K}})\kappa_{\theta}+\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{T}\hat{\mathcal{B}}\Lambda[\delta_{\theta}\bar{a}_{0}]= 0,\displaystyle 0, (335)

which is the static gauge Ward identity in the κ\kappa-language. With this, one can show that LTDVPL_{\text{TDVP}} is gauge invariant up to a total time derivative:

LTDVP→\displaystyle L_{\text{TDVP}}\rightarrow LTDVP−12​∂∂t​\llangle​κθ,ℱ^​κ​\rrangle,\displaystyle L_{\text{TDVP}}-\frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\llangle\kappa_{\theta},\hat{\mathcal{F}}\kappa\rrangle, (336)

where Eq.(326,330) are also used.

The equation of motion(eom) of LTDVPL_{\rm TDVP} in Eq.(332) should give the excitation spectrum in this Gaussian theory. In the frequency space, this eigen-equation is:

[−i​ω​ℱ^+𝒢^+𝒫^T​𝒦^]​κ​(ω)+𝒫^T​ℬ^​Λ​[a0​(ω)]=0,\displaystyle[-i\omega\hat{\mathcal{F}}+\hat{\mathcal{G}}+\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{T}\hat{\mathcal{K}}]\kappa(\omega)+\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{T}\hat{\mathcal{B}}\Lambda[a_{0}(\omega)]=0, (337)

under the linearized Gauss’s law constraint on κ\kappa implemented by the a0a_{0}-eom: ∀δ​a0\forall\delta a_{0}:

\llangle​ℬ^​Λ​[δ​a0​(−ω)],κ⁡(ω)​\rrangle=0⇔\llangle​κ,ℱ^​κδ​a0​\rrangle=0\displaystyle\llangle\hat{\mathcal{B}}\Lambda[\delta a_{0}(-\omega)],\kappa(\omega)\rrangle=0\Leftrightarrow\llangle\kappa,\hat{\mathcal{F}}\kappa_{\delta a_{0}}\rrangle=0 (338)

This is the Hdet analog of the eom Eq.(200), but with a0a_{0} fluctuations. Note that this Gauss’s law constraint Eq.(338) is not an additional condition in an exact Hdet study, due to the identity Eq.(328). Again, Gauss’s law is already implemented in an exact Hdet study, corresponding to integrating out a0a_{0}. On the other hand, Eq.(338) plays an important role in an approximate Hdet study.

Again, one way to understand the concrete meaning of Eq.(338) is to consider a mean-field approximation, corresponding to the zeroth-order projective expansion in Sec.VI: ℬ^[0]\hat{\mathcal{B}}_{[0]} is equivalent to the identity. Since κ=δ​ρ\kappa=\delta\rho to the linear order, the fluctuation of κ⁡(t)\kappa(t) should maintain the local gauge charge neutrality ⟨ΨM​F​(κ⁡(t))|T^𝐫A|ΨM​F​(κ⁡(t))⟩=0\langle\Psi^{MF}(\kappa(t))|\hat{T}_{\mathbf{r}}^{A}|\Psi^{MF}(\kappa(t))\rangle=0 at any tt up to O⁡(κ2)O(\kappa^{2}) – this is the dynamical Gauss’s law constraint at the mean-field level.

Since we are dealing with a gauge theory, there are solutions [κ⁡(ω),a0​(ω)][\kappa(\omega),a_{0}(\omega)] of Eq.(337,338) corresponding to the redundancy in the formalism: the pure gauge modes. These pure gauge modes are nonphysical and should be removed to isolate the physical modes. This is exactly the point of the gauge Ward identity, which allows one to sharply identify them. In the frequency space, Eq.(333) leads to pure gauge modes:

pure gauge: κpg(ω)=κθ⁡(ω),a0pg(ω)=iωθ(ω)+δθ⁡(ω)a¯0,\displaystyle\text{pure gauge: }\kappa^{\rm pg}(\omega)=\kappa_{\theta(\omega)},\;\;a^{\rm pg}_{0}(\omega)=i\omega\theta(\omega)+\delta_{\theta(\omega)}\bar{a}_{0}, (339)

which automatically satisfy the gauge Ward identity (i.e., Eq.(337,338)):

[−i​ω​ℱ^+𝒢^+𝒫^T​𝒦^]​κθ⁡(ω)+𝒫^T​ℬ^​Λ​[i​ω​θ​(ω)+δθ⁡(ω)​a¯0]=\displaystyle[-i\omega\hat{\mathcal{F}}+\hat{\mathcal{G}}+\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{T}\hat{\mathcal{K}}]\kappa_{\theta(\omega)}+\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{T}\hat{\mathcal{B}}\Lambda[i\omega\theta(\omega)+\delta_{\theta(\omega)}\bar{a}_{0}]= 0,\displaystyle 0,
\llangle​κθ,ℱ^​κδ​a0​\rrangle=\displaystyle\llangle\kappa_{\theta},\hat{\mathcal{F}}\kappa_{\delta a_{0}}\rrangle= 0,\displaystyle 0, (340)

where we used Eq.(326,330,335)

V.3.3 HS transformation and spatial I​G​GIGG gauge fields

As in our TDHF demo, the next step is to perform the HS transformation to decouple the Hessian 𝒦^\hat{\mathcal{K}}. We define the subspace VHS=Im​[𝒦^]⊂MhV_{\rm HS}=\text{Im}[\hat{\mathcal{K}}]\subset M_{\rm h} that the χ\chi-field lives in, the projector superoperator onto VHSV_{\rm HS}: 𝒫^HS\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{\rm HS}, as well as the inverse of 𝒦^\hat{\mathcal{K}} restricted to VHSV_{\rm HS}: 𝒦^HS−1≡𝒫^HS​𝒦^−1​𝒫^HS\hat{\mathcal{K}}_{\rm HS}^{-1}\equiv\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{\rm HS}\hat{\mathcal{K}}^{-1}\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{\rm HS} and the inverse of 𝒢^\hat{\mathcal{G}} restricted to Tρ¯T_{\bar{\rho}}: 𝒢^T−1≡𝒫^T​𝒢^−1​𝒫^T\hat{\mathcal{G}}_{T}^{-1}\equiv\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{T}\hat{\mathcal{G}}^{-1}\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{T}. From Eq.(315,322), we know χθ−ℬ^​Λ​[δθ​a¯0]\chi_{\theta}-\hat{\mathcal{B}}\Lambda[\delta_{\theta}\bar{a}_{0}] must be ∈VHS\in V_{\rm HS}. It is convenient to define:

𝜹θ​χ≡χθ−ℬ^​Λ​[δθ​a¯0],\displaystyle\bm{\delta}_{\theta}\chi\equiv\chi_{\theta}-\hat{\mathcal{B}}\Lambda[\delta_{\theta}\bar{a}_{0}], (341)

and we list the identities following Eq.(322,334):

𝒫^T​χθ=\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{T}\chi_{\theta}= −𝒢^​κθ,\displaystyle-\hat{\mathcal{G}}\kappa_{\theta}, 𝜹θ​χ=\displaystyle\bm{\delta}_{\theta}\chi= 𝒦^​κθ,\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{K}}\kappa_{\theta},
−𝒢^T−1​χθ=\displaystyle-\hat{\mathcal{G}}_{T}^{-1}\chi_{\theta}= κθ,\displaystyle\kappa_{\theta}, 𝒦^HS−1​𝜹θ​χ=\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{K}}_{\rm HS}^{-1}\bm{\delta}_{\theta}\chi= 𝒫^HS​κθ.\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{\rm HS}\kappa_{\theta}. (342)

These lead to the static Ward identity in the κ\kappa-language Eq.(335), and the corresponding one in the χ\chi-language:

(𝒫^HS​𝒢^T−1+𝒦^HS−1)​𝜹θ​χ+𝒫^HS​𝒢^T−1​ℬ^​Λ​[δθ​a¯0]\displaystyle(\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{\rm HS}\hat{\mathcal{G}}^{-1}_{T}+\hat{\mathcal{K}}_{\rm HS}^{-1})\bm{\delta}_{\theta}\chi+\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{\rm HS}\hat{\mathcal{G}}^{-1}_{T}\hat{\mathcal{B}}\Lambda[\delta_{\theta}\bar{a}_{0}]
=\displaystyle= 𝒫^HS​𝒢^T−1​χθ+𝒦^HS−1​𝜹θ​χ=0.\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{\rm HS}\hat{\mathcal{G}}^{-1}_{T}\chi_{\theta}+\hat{\mathcal{K}}_{\rm HS}^{-1}\bm{\delta}_{\theta}\chi=0. (343)

It is worth mentioning that, generally, only 𝜹θ​χ∈VHS\bm{\delta}_{\theta}\chi\in V_{\rm HS}, while χθ\chi_{\theta} may be outside. For the special gauge transformation θA=0​(𝐫,t)\theta^{A=0}(\mathbf{r},t), since U​(1)IU(1)_{I} is in the center of the G​GGG, we have δθ0​a¯0=0\delta_{\theta^{0}}\bar{a}_{0}=0, and consequently 𝜹θ0​χ=χθ0∈VHS\bm{\delta}_{\theta^{0}}\chi=\chi_{\theta^{0}}\in V_{\rm HS}.

The (κ,χ,a0)(\kappa,\chi,a_{0})-theory obtained after HS transformation can be written as:

V.3.4 Effective theory of Hdet wavefunction

Now it is clear that the gauge invariant theory Lκ,χ,a0L_{\kappa,\chi,a_{0}} in Eq.() can be viewed as the matter field κ\kappa coupled with fluctuating G​GGG gauge fields: a0a_{0} is the temporal component, while the hopping on bond t⁡(ρ¯,a¯0)+χt(\bar{\rho};\bar{a}_{0})+\chi encodes the spatial components. κ\kappa also couples with other, non-gauge bosonic fields described by the other parts of χ\chi. The only difference from the familiar effective theories is that the matter field is bosonic – the Thouless parameter κ\kappa for the underlying fermionic mean-field state. Here we refermionize the theory to obtain an effective theory of fermionic matter fields coupled to a dynamical G​GGG gauge field.

First of all, let’s write the full action of Lκ,χ,a0L_{\kappa,\chi,a_{0}} in the (𝐪,ω)(\mathbf{q},\omega) space:

Sκ,χ,a0=∑𝐪∫d​ω2​π[−\llangleχ~(−𝐪,−ω),κ(𝐪,ω)\rrangle\displaystyle S_{\kappa,\chi,a_{0}}=\sum_{\mathbf{q}}\int\frac{d\omega}{2\pi}\Big[-\llangle\tilde{\chi}(-\mathbf{q},-\omega),\kappa(\mathbf{q},\omega)\rrangle
−12​\llangle​κ​(−𝐪,−ω),(−i​ω​ℱ^+𝒢^)​(𝐪)​κ​(𝐪,ω)​\rrangle\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}\llangle\kappa(-\mathbf{q},-\omega),(-i\omega\hat{\mathcal{F}}+\hat{\mathcal{G}})(\mathbf{q})\kappa(\mathbf{q},\omega)\rrangle
+12\llangleχ(−𝐪,−ω),𝒦^HS−1χ(𝐪,ω)\rrangle]+O((κ,χ,a0)3),\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2}\llangle\chi(-\mathbf{q},-\omega),\hat{\mathcal{K}}^{-1}_{\rm HS}\chi(\mathbf{q},\omega)\rrangle\Big]+O((\kappa,\chi,a_{0})^{3}), (362)

where we combined a0a_{0} and χ\chi into a field χ~\tilde{\chi}:

χ~≡χ+ℬ^​Λ​[a0].\displaystyle\tilde{\chi}\equiv\chi+\hat{\mathcal{B}}\Lambda[a_{0}]. (363)

Similar to the TDHF demo in Eq.(181), we now write down a Gaussian-order candidate effective theory of fermions (ψ¯,ψ\bar{\psi},\psi), χ\chi and a0a_{0}:

Leff,[0]≡∑p=12∑i​j[Λ(p)​[a0]i​j+χi​j(p)]​ρ¯j​i(p)+12​\llangle​χ,𝒦^HS−1​χ​\rrangle\displaystyle L_{\rm eff,[0]}\equiv\sum_{p=1}^{2}\sum_{ij}\Big[\Lambda^{(p)}[a_{0}]_{ij}+\chi^{(p)}_{ij}\Big]\bar{\rho}^{(p)}_{ji}+\frac{1}{2}\llangle\chi,\hat{\mathcal{K}}_{\rm HS}^{-1}\chi\rrangle
+∑p,i​jψ¯i(p)[i∂tδi​j−Λ(p)[a0]i​j−ti​j(p)(ρ¯;a¯0)−χi​j(p)]ψj(p).\displaystyle+\sum_{p,ij}\bar{\psi}_{i}^{(p)}\Big[i\partial_{t}\delta_{ij}-\Lambda^{(p)}[a_{0}]_{ij}-t^{(p)}_{ij}(\bar{\rho};\bar{a}_{0})-\chi^{(p)}_{ij}\Big]\psi^{(p)}_{j}. (364)

Here, we define the gauge transformation labeled by θ⁡(𝐫,t)\theta(\mathbf{r},t) as:

ρ¯(p)→\displaystyle\bar{\rho}^{(p)}\rightarrow Θ(p)ρ¯(p)Θ(p)†,\displaystyle\Theta^{(p)}\bar{\rho}^{(p)}\Theta^{(p)\dagger},
Λ(p)​[a¯0]→\displaystyle\Lambda^{(p)}[\bar{a}_{0}]\rightarrow Θ(p)Λ(p)[a¯0]Θ(p)†,\displaystyle\Theta^{(p)}\Lambda^{(p)}[\bar{a}_{0}]\Theta^{(p)\dagger},
t(p)​(ρ¯,a¯0)+χ→\displaystyle t^{(p)}(\bar{\rho};\bar{a}_{0})+\chi\rightarrow Θ(p)(t(p)(ρ¯;a¯0)+χ)Θ(p)†,\displaystyle\Theta^{(p)}(t^{(p)}(\bar{\rho};\bar{a}_{0})+\chi)\Theta^{(p)\dagger},
Λ(p)​[a0]→\displaystyle\Lambda^{(p)}[a_{0}]\rightarrow Θ(p)Λ(p)[a0]Θ(p)†+i(∂tΘ(p))Θ(p)†,\displaystyle\Theta^{(p)}\Lambda^{(p)}[a_{0}]\Theta^{(p)\dagger}+i(\partial_{t}\Theta^{(p)})\Theta^{(p)\dagger},
ψ(p)→\displaystyle\psi^{(p)}\rightarrow Θ(p)ψ(p),ψ¯(p)→ψ¯(p)Θ(p)†,\displaystyle\Theta^{(p)}\psi^{(p)},\;\;\bar{\psi}^{(p)}\rightarrow\bar{\psi}^{(p)}\Theta^{(p)\dagger}, (365)

where Θ\Theta is a shorthand notation for Θ⁡[θ]\Theta[\theta] in Eq.(243). ψ\psi minimally couples with G​GGG gauge field and Leff0​t​hL^{\rm{0th}}_{\rm eff} is gauge invariant (up to a total derivative from the ρ¯\bar{\rho} background term).

Again, the reason for the subscript ”[0]” in Leff,[0]L_{\rm eff,[0]} is that, the 0th-order projective-expansion introduced in Sec.VI is a version of time-dependent mean-field approximation, in which one still uses the Slater-determinant mean-field state |ΨM​F​(ρ)⟩|\Psi^{MF}(\rho)\rangle in Eq.(237) to compute wavefunction overlaps, and consequently the Berry’s operator is known ℱ^=ℱ^[0]\hat{\mathcal{F}}=\hat{\mathcal{F}}_{[0]} – the canonical boson Berry’s phase as in the TDHF demo (see Eq.(171)) and ℬ^[0]=𝟏\hat{\mathcal{B}}_{[0]}=\mathbf{1}. If one uses the 0th-order projective-expansion to approximately compute the action Sκ,χ,a0S_{\kappa,\chi,a_{0}}, after using Thouless parameterization of Leff,[0]L_{\rm eff,[0]}, it is obvious that Sκ,χ,a0S_{\kappa,\chi,a_{0}} is exactly reproduced by Leff,[0]L_{\rm eff,[0]} up to the Gaussian order.

However, as long as one goes beyond the 0th-order projective-expansion to compute Sκ,χ,a0S_{\kappa,\chi,a_{0}}, Leff,[0]L_{\rm eff,[0]} is no longer an exact refermionized theory at the Gaussian order. Nevertheless, one may always introduce counterterms into LeffL_{\rm eff} so that it still reproduces Sκ,χ,a0S_{\kappa,\chi,a_{0}} at the Gaussian order, in the sense that after integrating out the matter fields (i.e., κ\kappa and ψ¯,ψ\bar{\psi},\psi), the same Gaussian order theory of (χ,a0)(\chi,a_{0}) is obtained. For example, the dispersion of collective modes will be exactly reproduced. Precisely,

Seff≡Seff,[0]+Sct​[χ,a0],\displaystyle S_{\rm eff}\equiv S_{\rm eff,[0]}+S_{\rm ct}[\chi,a_{0}], (366)

where the counterterm SctS_{\rm ct} describes additional couplings between χ,a0\chi,a_{0}-fields:

Sct[χ,a0]=∑𝐪∫d​ω4​π[\llangleχ~(−𝐪,−ω),(−iωℱ^+𝒢^)T−1χ~(𝐪,ω)\rrangle\displaystyle S_{\rm ct}[\chi,a_{0}]=\sum_{\mathbf{q}}\int\frac{d\omega}{4\pi}\Big[\llangle\tilde{\chi}(-\mathbf{q},-\omega),(-i\omega\hat{\mathcal{F}}+\hat{\mathcal{G}})_{T}^{-1}\tilde{\chi}(\mathbf{q},\omega)\rrangle
−\llangleχ~[0](−𝐪,−ω),(−iωℱ^[0]+𝒢^)T−1χ~[0](𝐪,ω)\rrangle].\displaystyle-\llangle\tilde{\chi}_{[0]}(-\mathbf{q},-\omega),(-i\omega\hat{\mathcal{F}}_{[0]}+\hat{\mathcal{G}})_{T}^{-1}\tilde{\chi}_{[0]}(\mathbf{q},\omega)\rrangle\Big]. (367)

Here χ~[0]≡χ+ℬ^[0]​Λ​[a0]\tilde{\chi}_{[0]}\equiv\chi+\hat{\mathcal{B}}_{[0]}\Lambda[a_{0}].

SeffS_{\rm eff} is gauge invariant up to the Gaussian order (and up to a total derivative). At the 0th-order projective-expansion approximation, SctS_{\rm ct} vanishes. Beyond the 0th-order projective-expansion(PE), the crucial question is whether the low-energy physics is modified qualitatively or not by SctS_{\rm ct}, e.g., whether there are additional topological CS terms contributed by SctS_{\rm ct}. One can argue that the answer will be negative, at least in the framework of projective expansion. As we will see in Sec.VI.2.3, as a local expansion, PE is not expected to modify global properties, such as the topological terms. Although we suspect the answer is generally negative even in an exact treatment of Hdet states with the locality structure, we do not have a sharp statement to make.

In summary, the microscopic Gaussian theory Lκ,χ,a0L_{\kappa,\chi,a_{0}} can be refermionized as LeffL_{\rm eff}, in which Grassmann variables minimally couple with G​GGG gauge fields. The saddle point of LeffL_{\rm eff}, still labeled by ρ¯,a¯0\bar{\rho},\bar{a}_{0}, Higgses G​GGG down to I​G​GIGG. Next, we demonstrate how to extract microscopic gauge dynamics via VMPI.

V.3.5 Gauge Ward identity in the χ\chi-language and long-wavelength gauge kernel

In this section, we will start with the action Sκ,χ,a0S_{\kappa,\chi,a_{0}} in Eq.(362). Integrating out the matter field κ\kappa and other bosonic fields in χ\chi, our goal is to obtain an effective action SI​G​GS^{IGG} for the acoustic U​(1)IU(1)_{I} gauge field 𝐚μ\mathbf{a}_{\mu} only. We assume that the matter field is fully gapped, and the practice outlined below provides a route to compute the microscopic dispersion of the gauge photon, as well as possible CS terms.

On the other hand, when the matter field is gapless, as in the situation of a composite Fermi liquid, the low-energy effective theory should not be of 𝐚μ\mathbf{a}_{\mu} only. Instead, one should only integrate out the high-energy matter fields. Assuming all other bosonic fields are massive, the low-energy effective theory is qualitatively described by gapless fermions coupled with the dynamical acoustic gauge field 𝐚μ\mathbf{a}_{\mu}. The discussion below will then be useful to compute the topological terms (i.e., CS-term in the present example) in the gauge dynamics, which come from integrating out high-energy matter fields only.

After integrating out the matter field κ\kappa in Sκ,χ,a0S_{\kappa,\chi,a_{0}}, one obtains the action Sχ,a0S_{\chi,a_{0}}:

+\llangleχ(−𝐪,−ω),𝒦^HS−1χ(𝐪,ω)\rrangle]+O((χ,a0)3).\displaystyle+\llangle\chi(-\mathbf{q},-\omega),\hat{\mathcal{K}}_{\rm HS}^{-1}\chi(\mathbf{q},\omega)\rrangle\Big]+O((\chi,a_{0})^{3}). (368)
