SI​G​G=∑𝐪∫d​ω4​π​∑μ,ν=0,x,y𝐚μ​(−𝐪,−ω)​Πμ​ν​(𝐪,ω)​𝐚ν​(𝐪,ω),\displaystyle S^{IGG}=\sum_{\mathbf{q}}\int\frac{d\omega}{4\pi}\sum_{\mu,\nu=0,x,y}\mathbf{a}_{\mu}(-\mathbf{q},-\omega)\Pi_{\mu\nu}(\mathbf{q},\omega)\mathbf{a}_{\nu}(\mathbf{q},\omega), (399)

where

Π≡D𝐚𝐚−D𝐚​η​Dη​η−1​Dη​𝐚.\displaystyle\Pi\equiv D_{\mathbf{a}\mathbf{a}}-D_{\mathbf{a}\eta}D_{\eta\eta}^{-1}D_{\eta\mathbf{a}}. (400)

The second row of Eq.(398) gives

𝒱0,η=−Dη​η−1​Dη​𝐚​𝒱0,𝐚,\displaystyle\mathcal{V}_{0,\eta}=-D_{\eta\eta}^{-1}D_{\eta\mathbf{a}}\mathcal{V}_{0,\mathbf{a}}, (401)

and substitution into the first row yields the exact reduced Ward identity

Π⁡(𝐪,ω)​𝒱0,𝐚​(𝐪,ω)=𝟎.\displaystyle\Pi(\mathbf{q},\omega)\mathcal{V}_{0,\mathbf{a}}(\mathbf{q},\omega)=\mathbf{0}. (402)

By Hermiticity, 𝒱0,𝐚†​Π=0\mathcal{V}_{0,\mathbf{a}}^{\dagger}\Pi=0 as well. Defining qμ≡(−ω,𝐪x,𝐪y)q_{\mu}\equiv(-\omega,\mathbf{q}_{x},\mathbf{q}_{y}) and keeping the leading gradient order, Eq.(402) becomes the familiar continuum Ward identity

∑νΠμ​ν​(𝐪,ω)​qν=0,∑μqμ​Πμ​ν​(𝐪,ω)=0.\displaystyle\sum_{\nu}\Pi_{\mu\nu}(\mathbf{q},\omega)q_{\nu}=0,\qquad\sum_{\mu}q_{\mu}\Pi_{\mu\nu}(\mathbf{q},\omega)=0. (403)

When the integrated-out κ\kappa matter field and η\eta fields are all gapped, regularity constrains the leading long-wavelength kernel to the Chern–Simons plus Maxwell form in Eq.(283). In an approximate Hdet treatment this gives the 3×33\times 3 kernel Πμ​ν\Pi_{\mu\nu} containing 𝐚0\mathbf{a}_{0}. In an exact Hdet treatment, where Gauss’s law is already implemented and 𝐚0\mathbf{a}_{0} is absent, one obtains the spatial reduced kernel 𝖲u​v\mathsf{S}_{uv} in Eq.(289).

The limitation of the quadratic gauge action SI​G​GS^{IGG} is that the underlying compactness of the U⁡(1)U(1)-gauge field is missed, which can be traced back to the Gaussian order approximation in VMPI. But this is only a technical challenge. One could recover the compactness of the U⁡(1)U(1)-gauge field by resorting to the original VMPI without expanding locally around a fixed ρ¯\bar{\rho}. We will soon see such an example in Sec.V.3.6. For instance, a single topological U⁡(1)U(1)-gauge monopole event is not included in the Gaussian theory. In a compact U⁡(1)U(1) pure gauge theory without a CS term, it is well-known that the symmetry-allowed monopole events could lead to confinement of the gauge field[100]. One can still use the original VMPI to compute the quantum numbers carried by monopoles, i.e., whether they are symmetry-allowed.

It is well-known that if the monopole carries a nonzero U​(1)QU(1)_{Q}-symmetry charge (e.g., bosonic electron number), the single monopole event is forbidden in the presence of the U​(1)QU(1)_{Q} symmetry: The photon phase is nothing but the dual description of the superfluid phase spontaneously breaking U​(1)QU(1)_{Q} symmetry (denoted as U​(1)QU(1)_{Q}-SF phase), and the gapless photon is the U​(1)QU(1)_{Q} Goldstone mode written in the gauge-field formulation[98, 29, 34].

V.3.6 Flat connections on a torus and Chern-Simons level

The CS-term features the first time derivative. Parallel to the discussion for Type-I/Type-II Goldstone modes in our TDHF demo Eq.(230–232), here we show that the CS-level kk can be directly computed using the spatial gauge fields 𝐚u​(𝐪=0,t)\mathbf{a}_{u}(\mathbf{q}=0,t)– the flat connections. This point is particularly important for an exact Hdet calculation, in which case one cannot read kk out from 𝖲⁡(𝐪≠0,ω)\mathsf{S}(\mathbf{q}\neq 0,\omega) as in Eq.(289).

Define:

Πu​v​(𝟎,ω)=i​ω​𝖡u​v+O⁡(ω2)\displaystyle\Pi_{uv}(\mathbf{0},\omega)=i\omega\mathsf{B}_{uv}+O(\omega^{2}) (404)

The goal is to compute the 𝖡u​v\mathsf{B}_{uv}. First, we show that i​ω​𝖡u​vi\omega\mathsf{B}_{uv} is just the ω\omega-linear term in the full kernel D𝐚u​𝐚vD_{\mathbf{a}_{u}\mathbf{a}_{v}} in Eq.(390). This is because in the Schur complement Eq.(400), the acoustic gauge Ward identity Eq.(398) at ω=0\omega=0 but arbitrary small 𝐪\mathbf{q} dictates that D𝐚u​η​(𝟎,0)=Dη​𝐚u​(𝟎,0)=0D_{\mathbf{a}_{u}\eta}(\mathbf{0},0)=D_{\eta\mathbf{a}_{u}}(\mathbf{0},0)=0. The second term in Eq.(400) at most scales as ω2\omega^{2}.

Consequently, we should compute 𝖡u​v\mathsf{B}_{uv} directly from D𝐚u​𝐚vD_{\mathbf{a}_{u}\mathbf{a}_{v}}. Based on Eq.(391), the small ω\omega-expansion (−i​ω​ℱ^+𝒢^)T−1=𝒢^T−1+i​ω​𝒢^T−1​ℱ^​𝒢^T−1+O⁡(ω2)(-i\omega\hat{\mathcal{F}}+\hat{\mathcal{G}})_{T}^{-1}=\hat{\mathcal{G}}_{T}^{-1}+i\omega\hat{\mathcal{G}}_{T}^{-1}\hat{\mathcal{F}}\hat{\mathcal{G}}_{T}^{-1}+O(\omega^{2}) leads to:

𝖡u​v=1θu​θv​\llangle​κu​(𝟎),ℱ^​κv​(𝟎)​\rrangle,\displaystyle\mathsf{B}_{uv}=\frac{1}{\theta_{u}\theta_{v}}\llangle\kappa_{u}(\mathbf{0}),\hat{\mathcal{F}}\kappa_{v}(\mathbf{0})\rrangle, (405)

where we introduced small parameters θu≪1\theta_{u}\ll 1 and defined:

κu(𝐪=𝟎)≡−𝒢^T−1⋅[θu𝗐u(𝐪=𝟎)].\displaystyle\kappa_{u}(\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{0})\equiv-\hat{\mathcal{G}}_{T}^{-1}\cdot[\theta_{u}\mathsf{w}^{u}(\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{0})]. (406)

Following the discussion below Eq.(199) and the definition of the ℱ^\hat{\mathcal{F}} superoperator Eq.(324), we arrive at:

𝖡u​v=2θu​θv​Im​[⟨Φ⁡(κu)|Φ⁡(κv)⟩]|θu​θv−part.\displaystyle\mathsf{B}_{uv}=\frac{2}{\theta_{u}\theta_{v}}\left.{\rm Im}\big[\langle\Phi(\kappa_{u})|\Phi(\kappa_{v})\rangle\big]\right|_{\theta_{u}\theta_{v}-{\rm part}}. (407)

If we parameterize 𝐚u​(𝐪=0,t)\mathbf{a}_{u}(\mathbf{q}=0,t) as the flux variable φu\varphi_{u} as Eq.(290), 𝖡x​y\mathsf{B}_{xy} is nothing but the Berry curvature of Hdet wavefunctions |Φ⁡(φx,φy)⟩|\Phi(\varphi_{x},\varphi_{y})\rangle that is obtained by adding flat connections on top of ρ¯\bar{\rho}.

Note that due to the Gaussian order expansion, the prescription above is for the local Berry’s curvature 𝖡u​v\mathsf{B}_{uv} at a certain ρ¯\bar{\rho}. To recover the compactness of the gauge flux, one simply computes 𝖡u​v​(φx,φy)\mathsf{B}_{uv}(\varphi_{x},\varphi_{y}) for a sequence of ρ¯​(φx,φy)\bar{\rho}(\varphi_{x},\varphi_{y}) by varying φx,φy\varphi_{x},\varphi_{y}, and there is no fundamental principle forbidding the φx,φy\varphi_{x},\varphi_{y}-dependence in 𝖡u​v\mathsf{B}_{uv}:

𝖡x​y​(φx,φy)=2​I​m​[⟨∂φxΦ⁡(φx,φy)|∂φyΦ⁡(φx,φy)⟩]\displaystyle\mathsf{B}_{xy}(\varphi_{x},\varphi_{y})=2{\rm Im}[\langle\partial_{\varphi_{x}}\Phi(\varphi_{x},\varphi_{y})|\partial_{\varphi_{y}}\Phi(\varphi_{x},\varphi_{y})\rangle] (408)

In general, the Berry’s phase part of the Lagrangian for φx,φy\varphi_{x},\varphi_{y} is:

LBerry​(φx,φy)=𝖠x​(φx,φy)​φ˙x+𝖠y​(φx,φy)​φ˙y,\displaystyle L_{\rm Berry}(\varphi_{x},\varphi_{y})=\mathsf{A}_{x}(\varphi_{x},\varphi_{y})\dot{\varphi}_{x}+\mathsf{A}_{y}(\varphi_{x},\varphi_{y})\dot{\varphi}_{y},
where ​∂φx𝖠y−∂φy𝖠x=𝖡x​y​(φx,φy).\displaystyle\text{where }\partial_{\varphi_{x}}\mathsf{A}_{y}-\partial_{\varphi_{y}}\mathsf{A}_{x}=\mathsf{B}_{xy}(\varphi_{x},\varphi_{y}). (409)

The large gauge transformation leads to compactness φu+2​π≃φu\varphi_{u}+2\pi\simeq\varphi_{u}. When the matter fields are all gapped, φu\varphi_{u} flux insertion does not cause many-body level crossing, and φu+2​π\varphi_{u}+2\pi and φu\varphi_{u} label the same physical Hdet state. Consequently, the CS-level is quantized to an integer kk:

∫02​πd​φx​∫02​πd​φy​𝖡x​y​(φx,φy)=2​π​k.\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2\pi}d\varphi_{x}\int_{0}^{2\pi}d\varphi_{y}\;\mathsf{B}_{xy}(\varphi_{x},\varphi_{y})=2\pi k. (410)

It is worth noting that the ground state degeneracy |k||k| (k≠0)(k\neq 0) is not modified when 𝖡x​y​(φx,φy)\mathsf{B}_{xy}(\varphi_{x},\varphi_{y}) is nonuniform, as long as 𝖡x​y​(φx,φy)\mathsf{B}_{xy}(\varphi_{x},\varphi_{y}) is sign-definite, possibly up to isolated zeros. Mathematically, this result can be shown via geometric quantization[16]. Physically, the simpler way to see the result is to perform a smooth change of variable for the φx,φy\varphi_{x},\varphi_{y} space: X⁡(φx,φy),Y⁡(φx,φy)X(\varphi_{x},\varphi_{y}),Y(\varphi_{x},\varphi_{y}), with identification X≃X+2​πX\simeq X+2\pi,Y≃Y+2​πY\simeq Y+2\pi such that in the new coordinate 𝖡x​y​(X,Y)=k2​π\mathsf{B}_{xy}(X,Y)=\frac{k}{2\pi} is uniform. Consequently, the Lagrangian is LBerry​(X,Y)=k2​π​Y​X˙L_{\rm Berry}(X,Y)=\frac{k}{2\pi}Y\dot{X}, and canonical quantization leads to [Y^,k2​π​X^]=i[\hat{Y},\frac{k}{2\pi}\hat{X}]=i. The 2​π2\pi-periodicity of Y^\hat{Y} dictates that k2​π​X^\frac{k}{2\pi}\hat{X} can only take integer eigenvalues. The 2​π2\pi-periodicity of X^\hat{X} means only |k||k| states are physically distinct.

Nevertheless, if one computes 𝖡x​y​(φx,φy)\mathsf{B}_{xy}(\varphi_{x},\varphi_{y}) using Eq.(408) by the mean-field wavefunction (i.e., at the 0th-order projective-expansion approximation), 𝖡x​y0​t​h​(φx,φy)\mathsf{B}^{\rm 0th}_{xy}(\varphi_{x},\varphi_{y}) will be uniform (i.e., φx,φy\varphi_{x},\varphi_{y}-independent), and the CS-level kk is simply the summation of the Chern numbers carried by each parton mean-field state. k=C(1)+C(2)k=C^{(1)}+C^{(2)}. It is very likely, although we cannot prove, that generally kk is not modified beyond the mean-field level even in an exact treatment.

We have numerically checked that, however, for the exact bosonic Laughlin ν=1/2\nu=1/2 wavefunction (an Hdet wavefunction with the number of fusion channels R=1R=1), 𝖡x​y​(φx,φy)\mathsf{B}_{xy}(\varphi_{x},\varphi_{y}) is non-uniform, does not change sign, and has isolated zeros, and the total integral remains quantized to k=2k=2 as in the mean-field calculation. The simplest way to see this is to consider Haldane-Rezayi’s construction for the Laughlin ν=1k\nu=\frac{1}{k} wavefunctions on a torus[51], where the dependence of the boundary-conditions (φx,φy)(\varphi_{x},\varphi_{y}) only appears in the center-of-mass (c.m) part of the wavefunction Fkc.m.​(Z,φx,φy)F_{k}^{\rm c.m.}(Z;\varphi_{x},\varphi_{y}) (Eq.12 in Ref[51]), where Z≡∑i=1NeziZ\equiv\sum_{i=1}^{N_{e}}z_{i}. Based on the parton construction, each parton is in a k=1k=1 IQH state. Therefore, the c.m. part of the electronic wavefunction can be obtained as Fk=2c.m.(e)​(Z,φx,φy)=Fk=1c.m.(1)​(Z,φx,φy)⋅Fk=1c.m.(2)​(Z,−φx,−φy)F_{k=2}^{\rm c.m.(e)}(Z;\varphi_{x},\varphi_{y})=F_{k=1}^{\rm c.m.(1)}(Z;\varphi_{x},\varphi_{y})\cdot F_{k=1}^{\rm c.m.(2)}(Z;-\varphi_{x},-\varphi_{y}), whose Berry’s curvature 𝖡x​y​(φx,φy)\mathsf{B}_{xy}(\varphi_{x},\varphi_{y}) can be easily computed independent of system-size, as shown in Fig.5.

To study the low-energy CS-term with gapless matter such as CFL, one should not integrate out all matter fields. Instead, only the high-energy gapped partons should be integrated out, and the gapless parton forming the Fermi surface should be kept. We leave a detailed Hdet analysis of gapless matter fields to a future project.

V.3.7 Zero-point motion of gauge fields in VMPI wavefunctions

In the previous subsection, we outlined how to use VMPI to compute the ground-state degeneracy in a topologically ordered Hdet state, using flat connections φx\varphi_{x} and φy\varphi_{y} of the gauge field. Although the computational scheme is well-anticipated, conceptually it clarifies why VMPI is fundamentally necessary for treating quantum many-body systems. If one treats variational wavefunctions classically, one would run into confusion: there are infinite possible φx,φy\varphi_{x},\varphi_{y}, each one labels a variational ground state. Does that mean there is an infinite number of ground states?

Here we present another example in which VMPI helps solve a known puzzle in QSL and FCI. From the effective field theory of traditional Abrikosov fermion QSL construction (see Sec.IV.1 for connection with the general Hdet construction), it is known that the quantum spin state described by a gapped fermion band structure featuring Chern number C(↑)=1C^{(\uparrow)}=1 for f(↑)f^{(\uparrow)}-parton and C(↓)=−1C^{(\downarrow)}=-1 for f(↓)f^{(\downarrow)}-parton actually describes a X​YXY-ordered state spontaneously breaking the 𝐒z\mathbf{S}_{z}-conservation. But previous Monte Carlo simulation shows that after exact projection, the physical spin wavefunction for such a parton bandstructure only gives a power-law correlation function ⟨Φ⁡(ρ¯)|𝐒𝐫+​𝐒0−|Φ⁡(ρ¯)⟩∼r−η\langle\Phi(\bar{\rho})|\mathbf{S}^{+}_{\mathbf{r}}\mathbf{S}_{0}^{-}|\Phi(\bar{\rho})\rangle\sim r^{-\eta}[105], contradicting a true long-range order.

In the Hdet language, as explained in detail in Sec.IV.1, we map the spin-1/2 system into a hard-core boson problem (i.e., 𝐒𝐫+→b𝐫†\mathbf{S}^{+}_{\mathbf{r}}\rightarrow b_{\mathbf{r}}^{\dagger}), and perform a particle-hole transformation for f(↓)f^{(\downarrow)}-parton only: f(↓)→h(↓)†f^{(\downarrow)}\rightarrow h^{(\downarrow)\dagger}. The local fusion rule is simple: b†𝐫=f(↑)†𝐫h(↓)†𝐫b^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{r}}=f^{(\uparrow)\dagger}_{\mathbf{r}}h^{(\downarrow)\dagger}_{\mathbf{r}} – only one fusion channel per site. The spin state is now constructed by fusing the gapped mean-field state with C(↑)=1C^{(\uparrow)}=1 for f(↑)f^{(\uparrow)} (carrying gauge charge +1+1) and C(↓)=−1C^{(\downarrow)}=-1 for h(↓)h^{(\downarrow)} (carrying gauge charge −1-1). The monopole operator inserts a 2​π2\pi gauge flux, and consequently creates both a f(↑)f^{(\uparrow)}-parton and h(↓)h^{(\downarrow)}-parton – a spin flip 𝐒+\mathbf{S}^{+} operator.

This already indicates that one should not expect to have a long-range spin correlation in a single Hdet spin wavefunction |Φ⁡(ρ¯)⟩|\Phi(\bar{\rho})\rangle: It is the monopole-antimonopole correlation function that is supposed to have true long-range order, which requires that the spin wavefunction can capture gauge-field fluctuations so that, at least, the magnetic flux in a local region can change by ±2​π\pm 2\pi. But for a single Hdet state |Φ⁡(ρ¯)⟩|\Phi(\bar{\rho})\rangle, there is no gauge field fluctuation (zero-point motion).

Again, a correct method should include the gauge photon’s zero-point motion, which is built into the VMPI treatment: both as a microscopic field theory and as microscopic wavefunctions. At the Gaussian order, although total magnetic flux through the torus sample cannot change, locally the flux can change ±2​π\pm 2\pi. If one measures the spin-spin correlation function in the VMPI ground state |Ψ⟩VMPI,GS|\Psi\rangle_{\rm VMPI,GS} (see Eq.(154)) – a linear superposition of Hdet states that may be challenging to simulate exactly, the true long-range order will be reproduced. Here, since the spatial gauge field 𝐚u\mathbf{a}_{u} is a part of χ\chi-field, Eq.(371) will be useful to translate its zero-point motion into the variational manifold labeled by κ\kappa.

V.3.8 Special considerations for type-(B) models: Fine-Grid as the UV completion

The VMPI and effective theories for Hdet wavefunctions that we have constructed so far use the full real-space variables ρi​j,χi​j\rho_{ij},\chi_{ij}, etc. A careful reader may have realized that this framework can be problematic for type-(B) models. To see the issue, let’s focus on a type-(B) model within the LLL–as mentioned previously, an FCI model within a partially filled Chern number ±1\pm 1 band can always be mapped to a model within the partially filled LLL (see Ref[62] for details). In such a type-(B) model, i,ji,j in ρi​j(p)\rho^{(p)}_{ij} label the parton local orbitals {|z(m)(p)⟩n​L​L}\{|z^{(p)}_{(m)}\rangle_{nLL}\} (i.e., generalized coherent states Eq.(41) but after the change of viewpoint).

If one allows ρi​j\rho_{ij} to fluctuate arbitrarily, as described by the Thouless parameterization Eq.(306), the electronic Hdet state |Φ⁡(ρ)⟩|\Phi(\rho)\rangle will not be a legitimate many-body state inside the LLL. Based on the derivation of the local fusion tensor Eq.(33,52,53,60), |Φ⁡(ρ)⟩|\Phi(\rho)\rangle is an Hdet state within the LLL only if each parton’s mean-field state before the change of viewpoint is a Slater determinant in the parton’s LL basis.

Concretely, if we denote the Bloch-basis for parton-pp’s n​L​LnLL as |ϕ𝐤(p)⟩n​L​L|\phi^{(p)}_{\mathbf{k}}\rangle_{nLL} as in Sec.IV.2, and the associated fermion operator as 𝖿n,𝐤(p)\mathsf{f}^{(p)}_{n,\mathbf{k}}, the parton RDM before the change of viewpoint is:

ρm,n;𝐪(p)(𝐤)≡⟨𝖿n,𝐤+𝐪(p)†𝖿m,𝐤(p)⟩.\displaystyle\rho^{(p)}_{m,n;\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{k})\equiv\langle\mathsf{f}^{(p)\dagger}_{n,\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q}}\mathsf{f}^{(p)}_{m,\mathbf{k}}\rangle. (411)

ρm,n;𝐪(p)​(𝐤)\rho^{(p)}_{m,n;\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{k}) fully determines the filled parton state before the change of viewpoint and ρi​j(p)\rho^{(p)}_{ij} after the change of viewpoint: ρm,n,𝐪(p)​(𝐤)\rho^{(p)}_{m,n,\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{k}) strongly constrains the form of ρi​j(p)\rho^{(p)}_{ij}.

For example, consider a Laughlin wavefunction where all partons only fill their lowest LL: ρm,n;𝐪(p)​(𝐤)=1\rho^{(p)}_{m,n;\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{k})=1 iff 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0 and m=n=0m=n=0, and otherwise ρm,n;𝐪(p)​(𝐤)=0\rho^{(p)}_{m,n;\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{k})=0. One can choose a single local orbital |z(0)(p)⟩0​L​L|z^{(p)}_{(0)}\rangle_{0LL} per parton species-pp on each z∈z\inFine-Grid to describe the Laughlin state. Although there are (Ns(e))2(N_{s}^{(e)})^{2} such orbitals per parton species, i.e., ρi​j(p)\rho^{(p)}_{ij} is a (Ns(e))2×(Ns(e))2(N_{s}^{(e)})^{2}\times(N_{s}^{(e)})^{2} matrix, ρi​j(p)\rho^{(p)}_{ij} is completely fixed.

Therefore, only the fluctuation described by ρm,n;𝐪(p)​(𝐤)\rho^{(p)}_{m,n;\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{k}) (not a completely general ρi​j\rho_{ij}) corresponds to fluctuations of electronic Hdet wavefunctions inside the LLL. The right way to view the Hdet wavefunctions described by a general ρi​j\rho_{ij} is that they are inside a UV-completed many-body Fock space – the Fine-Grid Fock space, larger than the original many-body Fock space inside the LLL.

Precisely speaking, given the type-(B) Hamiltonian HL​L​LH_{LLL} within the LLL, one should consider a UV-completed lattice model defined on the Fine-Grid (FG) after the change of viewpoint, where the electrons’ discrete-coherent-state basis is considered as orthonormal (whose second-quantized operator is czc_{z}):

HFG≡HL​L​LFG+Δ⋅N^⟂,\displaystyle H_{\rm FG}\equiv H^{\rm FG}_{LLL}+\Delta\cdot\hat{N}_{\perp}, (412)

where HL​L​LFGH^{\rm FG}_{LLL} acting on the Fine-Grid Fock space is a Hamiltonian in terms of cc-operators based on HL​L​LH_{LLL}, N^⟂\hat{N}_{\perp} is an operator measuring the electron number outside the LLL, both of which will be defined shortly. Δ>0\Delta>0 is an energy penalty. The point is that, in the Δ→∞\Delta\rightarrow\infty limit, HFGH_{\rm FG} is mathematically equivalent to HL​L​LH_{LLL} at finite energies. Consequently, in the VMPI and effective-theory treatment for type-(B) models, it is fine to allow general ρi​j\rho_{ij} fluctuations, but the Hamiltonian HH in the VMPI action Eq.(332) should be understood as HFGH_{\rm FG} (in the limit of Δ→∞\Delta\rightarrow\infty) instead of HL​L​LH_{LLL}. In this sense, all the previous discussions in the real-space basis, e.g., exact gauge Ward identities, directly apply to type-(B) models.

Energetically, Δ→∞\Delta\rightarrow\infty enforces the finite-energy fluctuations of ρi​j(p)\rho^{(p)}_{ij} to be constrained by ρm,n;𝐪(p)​(𝐤)\rho^{(p)}_{m,n;\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{k}). In the VMPI discussion of Type-(A) model where the Hdet manifold is parameterized by ρi​j(p)\rho^{(p)}_{ij}, the gauge redundancies must be carefully dealt with so that, for example, nonphysical pure gauge modes are isolated and removed. However, if one chooses to use ρm,n;𝐪(p)​(𝐤)\rho^{(p)}_{m,n;\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{k}) to parameterize the Hdet manifold for the Type-(B) model (with a finite number of parton LLs), it appears to us that one effectively fixes the gauge and the pure-gauge modes are not present in our preliminary simulations. Consequently, the a0fulla^{\rm full}_{0}-insertion in VMPI may not be even needed in this case.

For example, in the ρm,n;𝐪(p)​(𝐤)\rho^{(p)}_{m,n;\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{k}) parameterization, the single-body parton Hamiltonian at 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0 (i.e., respecting the commuting subgroup of the magnetic translation symmetry used to define the Bloch-basis 𝐤\mathbf{k}) of a type-(B) FCI model is:

𝗁^(p)(𝐤)≡∑n,m𝗍n​m(p)(𝐤)𝖿n,𝐤(p)†𝖿m,𝐤(p),𝗍n​m(p)(𝐤)≡∂E⁡(ρ)∂ρm,n;𝐪=0(p)​(𝐤).\displaystyle\hat{\mathsf{h}}^{(p)}(\mathbf{k})\equiv\sum_{n,m}\mathsf{t}^{(p)}_{nm}(\mathbf{k})\mathsf{f}^{(p)\dagger}_{n,\mathbf{k}}\mathsf{f}^{(p)}_{m,\mathbf{k}},\;\mathsf{t}^{(p)}_{nm}(\mathbf{k})\equiv\frac{\partial E(\rho)}{\partial\rho^{(p)}_{m,n;\mathbf{q}=0}(\mathbf{k})}. (413)

Here, 𝗁^(p)​(𝐤)\hat{\mathsf{h}}^{(p)}(\mathbf{k}) should be understood as 𝗁^(p)​(𝐤,ρ)\hat{\mathsf{h}}^{(p)}(\mathbf{k};\rho), since it is a Hamiltonian depending on ρm,n;𝟎(p′)​(𝐤)\rho^{(p^{\prime})}_{m,n;\mathbf{0}}(\mathbf{k}) for all parton species p′=1,…,npp^{\prime}=1,...,n_{\rm p}. Finding the saddle point ρ¯\bar{\rho} boils down to the self-consistency condition: ρm,n;𝐪(p)​(𝐤)\rho^{(p)}_{m,n;\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{k}) is nonzero only for 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0, and the ground state of 𝗁^(p)​(𝐤)\hat{\mathsf{h}}^{(p)}(\mathbf{k}) is also ρm,n;𝟎(p)​(𝐤)\rho^{(p)}_{m,n;\mathbf{0}}(\mathbf{k}). As advertised in Sec.IV.2, the FCI physics causes the hybridization between the parton LLs, mathematically described by ρm,n;𝟎(p)​(𝐤)\rho^{(p)}_{m,n;\mathbf{0}}(\mathbf{k}). In addition, the finite-energy collective modes at 𝐪\mathbf{q} should be computed using VMPI via the Thouless parameters κm,n;𝐪(p)​(𝐤)\kappa^{(p)}_{m,n;\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{k}) of ρm,n;𝐪(p)​(𝐤)\rho^{(p)}_{m,n;\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{k}) near the saddle.

Next, we sharply define N^⟂\hat{N}_{\perp} and HL​L​LFGH^{\rm FG}_{LLL} in Eq.(412). N^⟂\hat{N}_{\perp} is defined as

N^⟂≡\displaystyle\hat{N}_{\perp}\equiv ∑z,w∈FGcz†[δz​w−[pL​L​L]z​w]cw, where:\displaystyle\sum_{z,w\in{\rm FG}}c_{z}^{\dagger}\Big[\delta_{zw}-[p_{LLL}]_{zw}\Big]c_{w},\;\;\text{ where:}
[pL​L​L]z​w≡\displaystyle[p_{LLL}]_{zw}\equiv 1Ns(e)​⟨z(e)|w(e)⟩0​L​L,\displaystyle\frac{1}{N_{s}^{(e)}}\langle z^{(e)}|w^{(e)}\rangle_{0LL}, (414)

and ⟨z(e)|w(e)⟩0​L​L\langle z^{(e)}|w^{(e)}\rangle_{0LL} is the overlap between discrete-coherent states before the change of viewpoint in Eq.(51) (with m=0m=0). Equivalently, if {|ϕk(e)⟩}\{|\phi^{(e)}_{k}\rangle\} is an orthonormal LLL basis before the change of viewpoint (e.g., the Bloch basis), then the matrix:

[pL​L​L]z​w=1Ns(e)​∑k⟨z(e)|ϕk(e)⟩​⟨ϕk(e)|w(e)⟩.\displaystyle[p_{LLL}]_{zw}=\frac{1}{N_{s}^{(e)}}\sum_{k}\langle z^{(e)}|\phi^{(e)}_{k}\rangle\langle\phi^{(e)}_{k}|w^{(e)}\rangle. (415)

After the change of viewpoint, according to Eq.(62), one should interpret |ϕk(e)⟩|\phi^{(e)}_{k}\rangle as the linear superposition of an orthonormal basis {|z(e)⟩}\{|z^{(e)}\rangle\}:

|ϕk(e)⟩=∑z∈FG⟨z(e)|ϕk(e)⟩⋅|z(e)⟩,\displaystyle|\phi^{(e)}_{k}\rangle=\sum_{z\in{\rm FG}}\langle z^{(e)}|\phi^{(e)}_{k}\rangle\cdot|z^{(e)}\rangle, (416)

and the factor 1Ns(e)\frac{1}{N_{s}^{(e)}} in [pL​L​L]z​w[p_{LLL}]_{zw} is due to the fact that 1Ns(e)​|ϕk(e)⟩\frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{s}^{(e)}}}|\phi^{(e)}_{k}\rangle is the normalized state after the change of viewpoint (see Eq.(77)): ∑z,w∈FGcz†​[pL​L​L]z​w​cw\sum_{z,w\in{\rm FG}}c_{z}^{\dagger}[p_{LLL}]_{zw}c_{w} measures the electron number inside the LLL, defined as the subspace spanned by {1Ns(e)​|ϕk(e)⟩}\{\frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{s}^{(e)}}}|\phi^{(e)}_{k}\rangle\}.

Now we define HL​L​LFGH^{\rm FG}_{LLL} acting on the Fine-Grid Fock space. The physical requirement for HL​L​LFGH^{\rm FG}_{LLL} is that when restricted to the LLL Fock space, it is equivalent to the original HL​L​LH_{LLL}. Due to the overcompleteness of the discrete-coherent-state, HL​L​LFGH^{\rm FG}_{LLL} satisfying this requirement is not unique. However, in Ref[129], a canonical choice for HL​L​LFGH^{\rm FG}_{LLL} is provided, together with a prescription to compute HL​L​LFGH^{\rm FG}_{LLL} for an arbitrary finite-size sample.

When the torus size LL is much larger than the magnetic length: L≫l(e)L\gg l^{(e)}, the form of HL​L​LFGH^{\rm FG}_{LLL} is particularly simple. In this case[129], up to exponentially small finite-size corrections, the prescription is to replace the LLL-projected density operator 𝝆(e)​(𝐪)=𝝆¯(e)​(𝐪)​e−𝐪2​(l(e))24\bm{\rho}^{(e)}(\mathbf{q})=\bar{\bm{\rho}}^{(e)}(\mathbf{q})e^{-\frac{\mathbf{q}^{2}(l^{(e)})^{2}}{4}} by the Fine-Grid density operator:

𝝆(e)​(𝐪)→n^𝐪,FG(e)≡∑z∈FGei​𝐪⋅𝐫z​n^z(e),n^z(e)≡cz†​cz.\displaystyle\bm{\rho}^{(e)}(\mathbf{q})\rightarrow\hat{n}^{(e)}_{\mathbf{q},{\rm FG}}\equiv\sum_{z\in{\rm FG}}e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{z}}\hat{n}_{z}^{(e)},\;\;\hat{n}_{z}^{(e)}\equiv c_{z}^{\dagger}c_{z}. (417)

Here, e−𝐪2​(l(e))24e^{-\frac{\mathbf{q}^{2}(l^{(e)})^{2}}{4}} is the form factor from the LLL projection, and 𝝆¯(e)​(𝐪)\bar{\bm{\rho}}^{(e)}(\mathbf{q}) are the operators satisfying the magnetic translation algebra (i.e., GMP-algebra[41]).

For example, let’s consider a type-(B) FCI model inside the LLL involving a periodic potential breaking the Galilean invariance and a bare-Coulomb interaction:

HL​L​L\displaystyle H_{LLL} =λ⋅∑𝐐∈Qperiod𝝆(e)​(𝐐)\displaystyle=\lambda\cdot\sum_{\mathbf{Q}\in Q_{\rm period}}\bm{\rho}^{(e)}(\mathbf{Q})
+12​A∑𝐪≠0q∈BZFG2​π|𝐪|:𝝆(e)(𝐪)𝝆(e)(−𝐪):,\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2A}\sum^{q\in{\rm BZ_{FG}}}_{\mathbf{q}\neq 0}\frac{2\pi}{|\mathbf{q}|}:\bm{\rho}^{(e)}(\mathbf{q})\bm{\rho}^{(e)}(-\mathbf{q}):, (418)

where AA is the sample area, QperiodQ_{\rm period} is a finite set of 𝐐\mathbf{Q} reciprocal vectors of the periodic potential while λ\lambda is its strength, BZFG\rm BZ_{FG} is the Brillouin Zone of the Fine-Grid. According to the prescription Eq.(417), the corresponding Fine-Grid Hamiltonian is nothing but:

HL​L​LFG=λ⋅∑𝐐∈Qperiodn^𝐐,FG(e)+12​A​∑𝐪≠0𝐪∈BZFG2​π|𝐪|:n^𝐪,FG(e)​n^−𝐪,FG(e):.\displaystyle H^{\rm FG}_{LLL}=\lambda\cdot\sum_{\mathbf{Q}\in Q_{\rm period}}\hat{n}^{(e)}_{\mathbf{Q},{\rm FG}}+\frac{1}{2A}\sum^{\mathbf{q}\in{\rm BZ_{FG}}}_{\mathbf{q}\neq 0}\frac{2\pi}{|\mathbf{q}|}:\hat{n}^{(e)}_{\mathbf{q},{\rm FG}}\hat{n}^{(e)}_{-\mathbf{q},{\rm FG}}:. (419)

In Sec.VI.3.3, we will exactly follow this prescription to simulate FCI models.

VI Simulating Hdet wavefunctions: Projective expansion

VI.1 Projective Expansion: General setup

VI.1.1 PE as a bookkeeping device

In this section, continuing the discussion of Hdet wavefunctions admitting a locality structure in Sec.III.2.5, we introduce a general and practical framework to simulate these Hdet wavefunctions: the Projective-Expansion (PE). The Hdet wavefunction involves local fusion gates (or equivalently, projection) that drastically change the wavefunction from the mean-field state |ΨM​F⟩|\Psi^{MF}\rangle (a direct product of Slater determinants of partons) to the Hdet state |Φ(e)⟩|\Phi^{(e)}\rangle whose unnormalized version |Ψ(e)⟩|\Psi^{(e)}\rangle is given in Eq.(85). PE is a systematic way to approximately simulate the physical state |Φ(e)⟩|\Phi^{(e)}\rangle, improvable order by order via an expansion scheme. The first question that one may ask is: ”What is PE expanding about?”.

Indeed, the full projection ∏i𝐂^i\prod_{i}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{i} has no intrinsically small parameter to expand about. As we will see, PE can be viewed as a bookkeeping device, with a formal expansion parameter ϵ\epsilon. For example, in PE for the expectation value ⟨O^D(e)⟩\langle\hat{O}_{D}^{(e)}\rangle of a physical operator O^D(e)\hat{O}_{D}^{(e)} on an Hdet state (DD is the spatial region where the observable has nonzero support), we will define a prescription to introduce a real parameter ϵ\epsilon: ⟨O^D(e)⟩​(ϵ)\langle\hat{O}_{D}^{(e)}\rangle(\epsilon), such that when ϵ=0\epsilon=0, the mean-field result is obtained, while when ϵ=1\epsilon=1, the exactly projected Hdet result is obtained. The PE calculation boils down to computing the power series

⟨O^D(e)⟩​(ϵ)=⟨O^D(e)⟩(0)+ϵ⋅⟨O^D(e)⟩(1)+ϵ2⋅⟨O^D(e)⟩(2)+….\displaystyle\langle\hat{O}_{D}^{(e)}\rangle(\epsilon)=\langle\hat{O}_{D}^{(e)}\rangle_{(0)}+\epsilon\cdot\langle\hat{O}_{D}^{(e)}\rangle_{(1)}+\epsilon^{2}\cdot\langle\hat{O}_{D}^{(e)}\rangle_{(2)}+.... (420)

Throughout this paper, we use the subscript (m) to denote the ϵ\epsilon-expansion order mm.

In practice, the PE will be truncated at a finite order, since the calculation becomes increasingly complicated as the order increases. Precisely, the calculation complexity follows a power-law w.r.t. both the system-size and the fusion-channel number RR, whose exponents increase linearly as the PE order increases. At the end of the calculation, one sets ϵ=1\epsilon=1 at the truncation order, yielding an approximate observable:

⟨O^D(e)⟩[0]=\displaystyle\langle\hat{O}_{D}^{(e)}\rangle_{[0]}= ⟨O^D(e)⟩(0),\displaystyle\langle\hat{O}_{D}^{(e)}\rangle_{(0)},
⟨O^D(e)⟩[1]=\displaystyle\langle\hat{O}_{D}^{(e)}\rangle_{[1]}= ⟨O^D(e)⟩(0)+⟨O^D(e)⟩(1),\displaystyle\langle\hat{O}_{D}^{(e)}\rangle_{(0)}+\langle\hat{O}_{D}^{(e)}\rangle_{(1)},
⟨O^D(e)⟩[2]=\displaystyle\langle\hat{O}_{D}^{(e)}\rangle_{[2]}= ⟨O^D(e)⟩(0)+⟨O^D(e)⟩(1)+⟨O^D(e)⟩(2),…\displaystyle\langle\hat{O}_{D}^{(e)}\rangle_{(0)}+\langle\hat{O}_{D}^{(e)}\rangle_{(1)}+\langle\hat{O}_{D}^{(e)}\rangle_{(2)},... (421)

Throughout this section, we use the subscript [m] to denote the PE quantity after collecting terms up to order-mm.

The 0th-order PE produces mean-field-level results. If one takes the infinite-order limit, the exactly projected Hdet observable is recovered. As we will see, even in the first few orders, PE already provides satisfactory improvement beyond mean-field.

Conceptually, the PE is analogous to the ϵ\epsilon-expansion technique[141] in field theory, which is very useful in computing critical exponents. In the ϵ\epsilon-expansion for the 3D classical Ising critical point, there is also no intrinsically small parameter. The physical spatial dimension is 33, while the ϵ\epsilon-expansion considers a formal spatial dimension 4−ϵ4-\epsilon, obtains a power series of ϵ\epsilon, and sets ϵ=1\epsilon=1 at a truncated order. The closest analogous technique to PE in literature, to our knowledge, is the diagrammatic-expansion technique for Gutzwiller wavefunctions[38, 20], although it was developed for electronic d.o.f. in the absence of partons.

Following the VMPI formulation of the microscopic effective theories in Sec.V.3, one needs to be able to compute two kinds of quantities for normalized Hdet states |Φ⁡(ρ)⟩|\Phi(\rho)\rangle to construct the microscopic VMPI action:

  1. 1.

    the static observable ⟨Φ⁡(ρ)|O^D(e)|Φ⁡(ρ)⟩\langle\Phi(\rho)|\hat{O}^{(e)}_{D}|\Phi(\rho)\rangle (denoted as static-properties).

  2. 2.

    the Berry’s phase via the wavefunction overlap ⟨Φ⁡(ρ+δ​ρ)|Φ⁡(ρ)⟩\langle\Phi(\rho+\delta\rho)|\Phi(\rho)\rangle (denoted as dynamical-properties).

We will start with the general PE setup and the general diagrammatic technique for closed-form results. Then we apply PE in model systems for benchmarking tests. Before all this, we would like to emphasize that the PE approximation order can differ for static and dynamical properties. For example, even if one uses the second-order PE to compute the static properties, one could still choose zeroth-order PE to compute Berry’s phases: from VMPI, all we require is the approximation scheme to be statically and dynamically conserving; mixed orders of PE for the two properties are allowed choices.

VI.1.2 PE for static properties

Now we describe the general PE prescription for static properties of Hdet states. First, we add a tunable real parameter into the local fusion gate Eq.(III.2.5) for electronic orbital-ii:

𝐂^i​(ϵ)≡exp⁡(γ​(ϵ)12​𝐅^i)∙(|0i(e)⟩​⟨0i(all ​p)|)\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{i}(\epsilon)\equiv\exp(\gamma(\epsilon)^{\frac{1}{2}}\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{i})\bullet(|0_{i}^{(e)}\rangle\langle 0_{i}^{(\text{all }p)}|)
=∑n=0∞γ​(ϵ)n2​[𝐅^inn!∙|0i(e)⟩​⟨0i(all ​p)|]≡∑n=0∞γ​(ϵ)n2​𝐂^i,n,\displaystyle=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\gamma(\epsilon)^{\frac{n}{2}}\Big[\frac{\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{i}^{n}}{n!}\bullet|0_{i}^{(e)}\rangle\langle 0_{i}^{(\text{all }p)}|\Big]\equiv\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\gamma(\epsilon)^{\frac{n}{2}}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{i,n}, (422)

where, for later discussions, we defined 𝐂^i,n\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{i,n} based on electron number sectors. (Recall for fermionic electrons the summation of nn truncates to n=1n=1. For bosonic electrons the summation truncates at a finite nn determined by the fusion channels. And with the change of viewpoint discussed in Sec.III.2.2, electron local orbitals are treated as orthonormal, even if the underlying electron basis is overcomplete.)

Comparing with the original local fusion gate Eq.(III.2.5), we multiplied a factor γ​(ϵ)12\gamma(\epsilon)^{\frac{1}{2}} to the local fusion operator 𝐅^i\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{i}, where γ⁡(ϵ)\gamma(\epsilon) is a positive real function that will be defined later. Clearly, the exact Hdet state obtained by the full projection ∏i𝐂^i​(ϵ)\prod_{i}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{i}(\epsilon) only differs from that obtained by ∏i𝐂^i\prod_{i}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{i} by an overall factor γ​(ϵ)Ne2\gamma(\epsilon)^{\frac{N_{e}}{2}}, and consequently it is perfectly fine to use 𝐂^i​(ϵ)\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{i}(\epsilon) to construct the Hdet state |Φ⁡(ρ)⟩|\Phi(\rho)\rangle.

The goal of the calculation is:

⟨O^D(e)⟩≡⟨Φ⁡(ρ)|O^D(e)|Φ⁡(ρ)⟩\displaystyle\langle\hat{O}^{(e)}_{D}\rangle\equiv\langle\Phi(\rho)|\hat{O}^{(e)}_{D}|\Phi(\rho)\rangle
=\displaystyle= ⟨ΨM​F​(ρ)|𝐎^D​(ϵ)​∏i≠D𝐏^i​(ϵ)|ΨM​F​(ρ)⟩⟨ΨM​F​(ρ)|∏i𝐏^i​(ϵ)|ΨM​F​(ρ)⟩,\displaystyle\frac{\langle\Psi^{MF}(\rho)|\hat{\mathbf{O}}_{D}(\epsilon)\prod_{i\neq D}\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{i}(\epsilon)|\Psi^{MF}(\rho)\rangle}{\langle\Psi^{MF}(\rho)|\prod_{i}\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{i}(\epsilon)|\Psi^{MF}(\rho)\rangle}, (423)

where

𝐏^i​(ϵ)≡\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{i}(\epsilon)\equiv 𝐂^i​(ϵ)†​𝐂^i​(ϵ),\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{i}(\epsilon)^{\dagger}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{i}(\epsilon),
𝐎^D​(ϵ)≡\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{O}}_{D}(\epsilon)\equiv ∏i∈D𝐂^i​(ϵ)†⋅O^D(e)⋅∏i∈D𝐂^i​(ϵ).\displaystyle\prod_{i\in D}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{i}(\epsilon)^{\dagger}\cdot\hat{O}_{D}^{(e)}\cdot\prod_{i\in D}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{i}(\epsilon). (424)

At this point, although we formally introduced ϵ\epsilon-dependence in many operators, the goal ⟨O^D(e)⟩\langle\hat{O}^{(e)}_{D}\rangle is independent of ϵ\epsilon. Due to the contraction of the electronic d.o.f in 𝐂^i​(ϵ)†​𝐂^i​(ϵ)\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{i}(\epsilon)^{\dagger}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{i}(\epsilon), 𝐏^i​(ϵ)\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{i}(\epsilon) depends on ϵ\epsilon through γ⁡(ϵ)\gamma(\epsilon), not γ​(ϵ)12\gamma(\epsilon)^{\frac{1}{2}}. Similarly, 𝐎^D​(ϵ)\hat{\mathbf{O}}_{D}(\epsilon) also only depends on γ⁡(ϵ)\gamma(\epsilon) for any particle-number conserving operator O^D(e)\hat{O}^{(e)}_{D}.

Precisely, because different electron-number sectors are orthogonal, we have:

𝐂^i,n†​𝐂^i,m=𝐂^i,n†​𝐂^i,n​δm​n,\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{C}}^{\dagger}_{i,n}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{i,m}=\hat{\mathbf{C}}^{\dagger}_{i,n}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{i,n}\delta_{mn}, (425)

and consequently,

𝐏^i​(ϵ)=∑n=0∞γ​(ϵ)n​[𝐂^i,n†​𝐂^i,n]≡∑n=0∞γ​(ϵ)n​𝐏^i,n,\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{i}(\epsilon)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\gamma(\epsilon)^{n}\Big[\hat{\mathbf{C}}^{\dagger}_{i,n}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{i,n}\Big]\equiv\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\gamma(\epsilon)^{n}\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{i,n}, (426)

where the operator 𝐏^i,n≡𝐂^i,n†​𝐂^i,n\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{i,n}\equiv\hat{\mathbf{C}}^{\dagger}_{i,n}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{i,n} acts on the local parton sub-Fock space with exactly nn partons per species. Therefore, 𝐏^i,n​𝐏^i,m=0\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{i,n}\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{i,m}=0, if m≠n.m\neq n., leading to

[𝐏^i,n,𝐏^i,m]=0,∀n,m.\displaystyle[\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{i,n},\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{i,m}]=0,\;\;\forall n,m. (427)

We also introduce the ϵ\epsilon-expansion of 𝐎^D​(ϵ)\hat{\mathbf{O}}_{D}(\epsilon) operator:

𝐎^D​(ϵ)=∑m≥0ϵm​𝐎^D,(m)\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{O}}_{D}(\epsilon)=\sum_{m\geq 0}\epsilon^{m}\hat{\mathbf{O}}_{D,(m)} (428)

Next, we define an operator 𝐐^i​(ϵ)\hat{\mathbf{Q}}_{i}(\epsilon) acting on the local parton Fock space interpolating between the identity operator 𝟏^\hat{\mathbf{1}} and 𝐏^i​(ϵ)\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{i}(\epsilon):

𝐐^i​(ϵ)≡𝟏^+ϵ⋅(𝐏^i​(ϵ)−𝟏^).\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{Q}}_{i}(\epsilon)\equiv\hat{\mathbf{1}}+\epsilon\cdot\Big(\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{i}(\epsilon)-\hat{\mathbf{1}}\Big). (429)

We then replace 𝐏^i​(ϵ)\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{i}(\epsilon) in Eq.(423) by 𝐐^i​(ϵ)\hat{\mathbf{Q}}_{i}(\epsilon), and define:

⟨O^D(e)⟩​(ϵ)≡⟨ΨM​F​(ρ)|𝐎^D​(ϵ)​∏i∉D𝐐^i​(ϵ)|ΨM​F​(ρ)⟩⟨ΨM​F​(ρ)|∏i𝐐^i​(ϵ)|ΨM​F​(ρ)⟩,\displaystyle\langle\hat{O}^{(e)}_{D}\rangle(\epsilon)\equiv\frac{\langle\Psi^{MF}(\rho)|\hat{\mathbf{O}}_{D}(\epsilon)\prod_{i\notin D}\hat{\mathbf{Q}}_{i}(\epsilon)|\Psi^{MF}(\rho)\rangle}{\langle\Psi^{MF}(\rho)|\prod_{i}\hat{\mathbf{Q}}_{i}(\epsilon)|\Psi^{MF}(\rho)\rangle}, (430)

⟨O^D(e)⟩​(ϵ)\langle\hat{O}^{(e)}_{D}\rangle(\epsilon) will depend on ϵ\epsilon. Since 𝐐^i​(1)=𝐏^i​(1)\hat{\mathbf{Q}}_{i}(1)=\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{i}(1), we have:

⟨O^D(e)⟩​(ϵ=1)=⟨O^D(e)⟩\displaystyle\langle\hat{O}^{(e)}_{D}\rangle(\epsilon=1)=\langle\hat{O}^{(e)}_{D}\rangle (431)

If we know the function γ⁡(ϵ)\gamma(\epsilon), one can expand ⟨O^D(e)⟩​(ϵ)\langle\hat{O}^{(e)}_{D}\rangle(\epsilon) in Eq.(430) as a power series of ϵ\epsilon by expanding both the numerator and denominator, as advertised. The technical details of the expansion will be given shortly in Sec.VI.2.1. The condition to fix γ⁡(ϵ)\gamma(\epsilon) is the electron-number sum-rule:

∑i⟨n^i(e)⟩​(ϵ)=Ne,∀ϵ.\displaystyle\sum_{i}\langle\hat{n}_{i}^{(e)}\rangle(\epsilon)=N_{e},\;\;\;\forall\epsilon. (432)

Practically, one should consider the power series expansion of γ⁡(ϵ)\gamma(\epsilon):

γ⁡(ϵ)=γ(0)+ϵ⋅γ(1)+ϵ2⋅γ(2)+…,\displaystyle\gamma(\epsilon)=\gamma_{(0)}+\epsilon\cdot\gamma_{(1)}+\epsilon^{2}\cdot\gamma_{(2)}+..., (433)

where expansion coefficients γ(m)\gamma_{(m)}’s are determined by Eq.(432) order by order.

For instance, for the 0th order ⟨n^i(e)⟩(0)\langle\hat{n}_{i}^{(e)}\rangle_{(0)}, all 𝐐^i​(ϵ)\hat{\mathbf{Q}}_{i}(\epsilon) in Eq.(430) will be identity since ϵ=0\epsilon=0 should be taken. 𝐧^i​(ϵ=0)=𝐂^i†​(ϵ=0)​n^i(e)​𝐂^i​(ϵ=0)\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{i}(\epsilon=0)=\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{i}^{\dagger}(\epsilon=0)\hat{n}_{i}^{(e)}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{i}(\epsilon=0) will be proportional to γ(0)\gamma_{(0)} for fermionic electrons. ∑i⟨n^i(e)⟩(0)=Ne\sum_{i}\langle\hat{n}_{i}^{(e)}\rangle_{(0)}=N_{e} can fix γ(0)\gamma_{(0)}, which can be viewed as the mean-field fugacity for electrons. Due to Eq.(432), we have ∑i⟨n^i(e)⟩(m)=0\sum_{i}\langle\hat{n}_{i}^{(e)}\rangle_{(m)}=0 for m≥1m\geq 1, which will fix higher order γ(m)\gamma_{(m)}’s. Iteratively, PE for the expectation value of any electron operator O^D(e)\hat{O}^{(e)}_{D} is well-defined.

Crucially, one only needs to compute operator expectation values on the mean-field state in PE (see Eq.(430)), which can be done straightforwardly using Wick’s theorem. Naturally, PE is a statically-conserving approximation at any order (see Eq.(252) for definition).

VI.1.3 PE for dynamical properties: quantum geometric tensor

We now move on to computing the Hdet wavefunction overlaps using PE, for the purpose of VMPI. Consider two parton RDMs: ρf\rho_{f} and ρi\rho_{i}, both in the vicinity of the saddle point ρ¯\bar{\rho}. We define the unnormalized PE overlap:

𝒩f​i​(ϵ)≡⟨ΨM​F​(ρf)|∏i𝐐^i​(ϵ)|ΨM​F​(ρi)⟩.\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{fi}(\epsilon)\equiv\langle\Psi^{MF}(\rho_{f})|\prod_{i}\hat{\mathbf{Q}}_{i}(\epsilon)|\Psi^{MF}(\rho_{i})\rangle. (434)

Here the γ⁡(ϵ)\gamma(\epsilon) function in 𝐐^i​(ϵ)\hat{\mathbf{Q}}_{i}(\epsilon) can be determined by the particle-number sum rule Eq.(432) on the saddle point mean-field state |ΨM​F​(ρ¯)⟩|\Psi^{MF}(\bar{\rho})\rangle. In this prescription, γ⁡(ϵ)\gamma(\epsilon) is independent of ρi,ρf\rho_{i},\rho_{f}.

The normalized PE overlap is defined as:

𝒮f​i​(ϵ)≡𝒩f​i​(ϵ)𝒩f​f​(ϵ)⋅𝒩i​i​(ϵ).\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{fi}(\epsilon)\equiv\frac{\mathcal{N}_{fi}(\epsilon)}{\sqrt{\mathcal{N}_{ff}(\epsilon)\cdot\mathcal{N}_{ii}(\epsilon)}}. (435)

We have the exact limit: 𝒮f​i​(ϵ=1)=⟨Φ⁡(ρf)|Φ⁡(ρi)⟩\mathcal{S}_{fi}(\epsilon=1)=\langle\Phi(\rho_{f})|\Phi(\rho_{i})\rangle.

For the purpose of VMPI, the central quantity of interest is Berry’s curvature Fa​bF_{ab} defined in Eq.(105). For simplicity of presentation, we will instead compute the full quantum geometric tensor 𝒬a​b\mathcal{Q}_{ab}, defined as follows. Consider two real numbers a,ba,b that parameterize the two states ρf​(a)\rho_{f}(a) and ρi​(b)\rho_{i}(b),

𝒬a​b​(ϵ)≡\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}_{ab}(\epsilon)\equiv ∂a∂blog⁡𝒮f​i​(ϵ)|ρf=ρi=ρ¯\displaystyle\partial_{a}\partial_{b}\left.\log\mathcal{S}_{fi}(\epsilon)\right|_{\rho_{f}=\rho_{i}=\bar{\rho}}
=\displaystyle= ∂a∂blog⁡𝒩f​i​(ϵ)|ρf=ρi=ρ¯,\displaystyle\partial_{a}\partial_{b}\left.\log\mathcal{N}_{fi}(\epsilon)\right|_{\rho_{f}=\rho_{i}=\bar{\rho}}, (436)

where the second equality follows the fact that Nf​fN_{ff} (Ni​iN_{ii}) only depends on aa (bb). The exact quantum metric and Berry’s curvature introduced in Eq.(109,105) correspond to the real and imaginary parts of 𝒬a​b​(ϵ=1)\mathcal{Q}_{ab}(\epsilon=1):

𝒬a​b​(ϵ=1)=ga​b​(ρ¯)+i2​Fa​b​(ρ¯).\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}_{ab}(\epsilon=1)=g_{ab}(\bar{\rho})+\frac{i}{2}F_{ab}(\bar{\rho}). (437)

Based on the Thouless parameterization for the tangent space Tρ¯T_{\bar{\rho}}, we know that any small deformation of ρ\rho near ρ¯\bar{\rho} is equivalent to applying a fermion bilinear operator on the mean-field state:

∂a|ΨM​F​(ρf​(a))⟩|ρf=ρ¯≡\displaystyle\partial_{a}\left.|\Psi^{MF}(\rho_{f}(a))\rangle\right|_{\rho_{f}=\bar{\rho}}\equiv X^a​|ΨM​F​(ρ¯)⟩,\displaystyle\hat{X}_{a}|\Psi^{MF}(\bar{\rho})\rangle,
∂b|ΨM​F​(ρi​(b))⟩|ρi=ρ¯≡\displaystyle\partial_{b}\left.|\Psi^{MF}(\rho_{i}(b))\rangle\right|_{\rho_{i}=\bar{\rho}}\equiv X^b​|ΨM​F​(ρ¯)⟩,\displaystyle\hat{X}_{b}|\Psi^{MF}(\bar{\rho})\rangle, (438)

where X^a,X^b\hat{X}_{a},\hat{X}_{b} are fermion bilinears of partons. Using Eq.(436), one finds that:

𝒬a​b​(ϵ)=⟨ΨM​F​(ρ¯)|X^a†​ℚ^​(ϵ)​X^b|ΨM​F​(ρ¯)⟩⟨ΨM​F​(ρ¯)|ℚ^​(ϵ)|ΨM​F​(ρ¯)⟩\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}_{ab}(\epsilon)=\frac{\langle\Psi^{MF}(\bar{\rho})|\hat{X}_{a}^{\dagger}\hat{\mathbb{Q}}(\epsilon)\hat{X}_{b}|\Psi^{MF}(\bar{\rho})\rangle}{\langle\Psi^{MF}(\bar{\rho})|\hat{\mathbb{Q}}(\epsilon)|\Psi^{MF}(\bar{\rho})\rangle}
−⟨ΨM​F​(ρ¯)|X^a†​ℚ^​(ϵ)|ΨM​F​(ρ¯)⟩⟨ΨM​F​(ρ¯)|ℚ^​(ϵ)|ΨM​F​(ρ¯)⟩​⟨ΨM​F​(ρ¯)|ℚ^​(ϵ)​X^b|ΨM​F​(ρ¯)⟩⟨ΨM​F​(ρ¯)|ℚ^​(ϵ)|ΨM​F​(ρ¯)⟩,\displaystyle-\frac{\langle\Psi^{MF}(\bar{\rho})|\hat{X}_{a}^{\dagger}\hat{\mathbb{Q}}(\epsilon)|\Psi^{MF}(\bar{\rho})\rangle}{\langle\Psi^{MF}(\bar{\rho})|\hat{\mathbb{Q}}(\epsilon)|\Psi^{MF}(\bar{\rho})\rangle}\frac{\langle\Psi^{MF}(\bar{\rho})|\hat{\mathbb{Q}}(\epsilon)\hat{X}_{b}|\Psi^{MF}(\bar{\rho})\rangle}{\langle\Psi^{MF}(\bar{\rho})|\hat{\mathbb{Q}}(\epsilon)|\Psi^{MF}(\bar{\rho})\rangle}, (439)

where we defined a shorthand notation:

ℚ^​(ϵ)≡∏i𝐐^i​(ϵ).\displaystyle\hat{\mathbb{Q}}(\epsilon)\equiv\prod_{i}\hat{\mathbf{Q}}_{i}(\epsilon). (440)

Obviously, ℚ^​(ϵ=0)=𝟏^\hat{\mathbb{Q}}(\epsilon=0)=\hat{\mathbf{1}}, and the zeroth order 𝒬a​b​(ϵ=0)\mathcal{Q}_{ab}(\epsilon=0) reduces to the mean-field quantum geometric tensor. Iteratively, the finite-order PE for 𝒬a​b​(ϵ)\mathcal{Q}_{ab}(\epsilon) can be performed in the same fashion as the static observable ⟨O^D(e)⟩​(ϵ)\langle\hat{O}^{(e)}_{D}\rangle(\epsilon). The technical details will be presented shortly.

Naturally, PE is a dynamically-conserving approximation at any order (see Eq.(253) for definition).

VI.2 Technical details

VI.2.1 Ordered-cumulants and the linked-cluster theorem

We have formulated PE mathematically in Eq.(430) and Eq.(439), for static and dynamical properties, respectively. Together with the sum rule Eq.(432) that fixes γ⁡(ϵ)\gamma(\epsilon), PE is already well-defined. However, it is worth mentioning some useful technical details in practical calculations. It turns out that PE is organized via the linked-cluster theorem[78] as in many other contexts of quantum many-body theories, from which we can obtain the closed-form for an arbitrary order PE quantity.

To facilitate the discussion, we will start with introducing some notations and definitions. For any operator A^\hat{A} acting on the parton Hilbert space, define:

⟨A^⟩ρ≡⟨ΨM​F​(ρ)|A^|ΨM​F​(ρ)⟩,\displaystyle\langle\hat{A}\rangle_{\rho}\equiv\langle\Psi^{MF}(\rho)|\hat{A}|\Psi^{MF}(\rho)\rangle, (441)

where |ΨM​F​(ρ)⟩|\Psi^{MF}(\rho)\rangle is a normalized direct product of parton’s Slater determinants. The local PE operator 𝐐^i​(ϵ)\hat{\mathbf{Q}}_{i}(\epsilon) in Eq.(429) can be expanded as a power series:

𝐐^i​(ϵ)≡𝟏^+∑m≥1ϵm​𝒒^i,(m).\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{Q}}_{i}(\epsilon)\equiv\hat{\mathbf{1}}+\sum_{m\geq 1}\epsilon^{m}\hat{\bm{q}}_{i,(m)}. (442)

The detailed form of the operator 𝒒^i,(m)\hat{\bm{q}}_{i,(m)} will depend on the fusion gate 𝐂^i\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{i} and γ⁡(ϵ)\gamma(\epsilon), however, it is important to note that all 𝒒^i,(m)\hat{\bm{q}}_{i,(m)} commute with each other:

[𝒒^i,(m),𝒒^j,(n)]=0,∀i,j,m,n.\displaystyle[\hat{\bm{q}}_{i,(m)},\hat{\bm{q}}_{j,(n)}]=0,\;\;\forall i,j,m,n. (443)

If i≠ji\neq j, the operators are acting on different electronic orbitals and commute. If i=ji=j, the commuting relation follows from Eq.(427), since any 𝒒^i,(m)\hat{\bm{q}}_{i,(m)} will be a linear superposition of 𝟏^\hat{\mathbf{1}} and 𝐏^i,n\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{i,n}’s.

For later purposes, we also introduce the logarithm of 𝐐^i​(ϵ)\hat{\mathbf{Q}}_{i}(\epsilon):

log⁡𝐐^i​(ϵ)≡𝐋^i​(ϵ)≡∑m≥1ϵm​𝒍^i,(m).\displaystyle\log\hat{\mathbf{Q}}_{i}(\epsilon)\equiv\hat{\mathbf{L}}_{i}(\epsilon)\equiv\sum_{m\geq 1}\epsilon^{m}\hat{\bm{l}}_{i,(m)}. (444)

Obviously,

[𝒍^i,(m),𝒍^j,(n)]=0,∀i,j,m,n,\displaystyle[\hat{\bm{l}}_{i,(m)},\hat{\bm{l}}_{j,(n)}]=0,\;\;\forall i,j,m,n, (445)

since 𝒍^i,(m)\hat{\bm{l}}_{i,(m)} can be represented in terms of 𝒒^i,(n)\hat{\bm{q}}_{i,(n)}. For example:

𝒍^i,(1)=\displaystyle\hat{\bm{l}}_{i,(1)}= 𝒒^i,(1),\displaystyle\hat{\bm{q}}_{i,(1)}, 𝒍^i,(2)=\displaystyle\hat{\bm{l}}_{i,(2)}= 𝒒^i,(2)−12​𝒒^i,(1)2,\displaystyle\hat{\bm{q}}_{i,(2)}-\frac{1}{2}\hat{\bm{q}}_{i,(1)}^{2}, \displaystyle... (446)

Ordered-cumulants: For any order list of operators, A^1,A^2,…,A^n\hat{A}_{1},\hat{A}_{2},...,\hat{A}_{n}, we now define the ordered-cumulants as:

𝒞ρ​(A^1,…,A^n)≡∂s1…​∂snG{A^l}​({sl})|s1=…=sn=0,\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{A}_{1},...,\hat{A}_{n})\equiv\left.\partial_{s_{1}}...\partial_{s_{n}}G_{\{\hat{A}_{l}\}}(\{s_{l}\})\right|_{s_{1}=...=s_{n}=0}, (447)

where

G{A^l}​({sl})≡log⁡⟨es1​A^1​…​esn​A^n⟩ρ\displaystyle G_{\{\hat{A}_{l}\}}(\{s_{l}\})\equiv\log\left\langle e^{s_{1}\hat{A}_{1}}...e^{s_{n}\hat{A}_{n}}\right\rangle_{\rho} (448)

If we denote

⟨A^a1​A^a2​…​A^am⟩ρ≡Ma1​a2​…​am,\displaystyle\langle\hat{A}_{a_{1}}\hat{A}_{a_{2}}...\hat{A}_{a_{m}}\rangle_{\rho}\equiv M_{a_{1}a_{2}...a_{m}}, (449)

the first few ordered-cumulants are:

𝒞ρ​(A^1)=M1,\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{A}_{1})=M_{1},
𝒞ρ​(A^1,A^2)=M12−M1​M2,\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{A}_{1},\hat{A}_{2})=M_{12}-M_{1}M_{2},
𝒞ρ​(A^1,A^2,A^3)=M123−M1​M23−M12​M3\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{A}_{1},\hat{A}_{2},\hat{A}_{3})=M_{123}-M_{1}M_{23}-M_{12}M_{3}
−M13​M2+2​M1​M2​M3,\displaystyle\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;-M_{13}M_{2}+2M_{1}M_{2}M_{3},
𝒞ρ​(A^1,A^2,A^3,A^4)=M1234−M1​M234−M12​M34\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{A}_{1},\hat{A}_{2},\hat{A}_{3},\hat{A}_{4})=M_{1234}-M_{1}M_{234}-M_{12}M_{34}
−M13​M24−M14​M23−M123​M4−M124​M3−M134​M2\displaystyle-M_{13}M_{24}-M_{14}M_{23}-M_{123}M_{4}-M_{124}M_{3}-M_{134}M_{2}
+2​M1​M2​M34+2​M1​M3​M24+2​M1​M4​M23+2​M12​M3​M4\displaystyle+2M_{1}M_{2}M_{34}+2M_{1}M_{3}M_{24}+2M_{1}M_{4}M_{23}+2M_{12}M_{3}M_{4}
+2​M13​M2​M4+2​M14​M2​M3−6​M1​M2​M3​M4.\displaystyle+2M_{13}M_{2}M_{4}+2M_{14}M_{2}M_{3}-6M_{1}M_{2}M_{3}M_{4}. (450)

Namely, disconnected expectation-value terms are all removed, and only linked clusters survive.

The ordered-cumulant features some useful properties, which we list below.

(1) Cumulant is multilinear:

𝒞ρ(..,aA^+bB^,..)=a𝒞ρ(..,A^,..)+b𝒞ρ(..,B^,..).\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(..,a\hat{A}+b\hat{B},..)=a\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(..,\hat{A},..)+b\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(..,\hat{B},..). (451)

(2) Cumulant for commuting operators:

If ​[A^l,A^l+1]=0,\displaystyle\text{If }[\hat{A}_{l},\hat{A}_{l+1}]=0,
then 𝒞ρ(..,A^l,A^l+1,..)=𝒞ρ(..,A^l+1,A^l,..).\displaystyle\text{then }\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(..,\hat{A}_{l},\hat{A}_{l+1},..)=\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(..,\hat{A}_{l+1},\hat{A}_{l},..). (452)

(3) Cumulant for identity operator: If A^l=𝟏^\hat{A}_{l}=\hat{\mathbf{1}} for some ll, all higher order

𝒞ρ(..,𝟏^,..)=0\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(..,\hat{\mathbf{1}},..)=0 (453)

except for 𝒞ρ​(𝟏^)=1\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{\mathbf{1}})=1.

(4) Cumulant for uncorrelated operators: In our PE simulation of Hdet states, ρ\rho is a direct product of Slater determinants for each parton species. For example, for two-parton case, ρ=ρ(1)⊗ρ(2)\rho=\rho^{(1)}\otimes\rho^{(2)}. Consider a sequence of operators: {A^l}\{\hat{A}_{l}\} (l=1,..,nl=1,..,n), every A^l\hat{A}_{l} only acts on a single species parton-plp_{l}’s Hilbert space. It is easy to show that:

𝒞ρ​(A^1,…,A^n)=0, unless all pl are identical.\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{A}_{1},...,\hat{A}_{n})=0,\text{ unless all $p_{l}$ are identical.} (454)

(5) Product-cumulant identities:

𝒞ρ​(X^1,…,X^p,A^1⋅A^2,Y^1,…,Y^q)\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{X}_{1},...,\hat{X}_{p},\hat{A}_{1}\cdot\hat{A}_{2},\hat{Y}_{1},...,\hat{Y}_{q})
=\displaystyle= 𝒞ρ​(X^1,…,X^p,A^1,A^2,Y^1,…,Y^q)\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{X}_{1},...,\hat{X}_{p},\hat{A}_{1},\hat{A}_{2},\hat{Y}_{1},...,\hat{Y}_{q})
+\displaystyle+ ∑S⊆{1,…,p}∑T⊆{1,…,q}𝒞ρ​(𝐗^S,A^1,𝐘^T)⋅𝒞ρ​(𝐗^SC,A^2,𝐘^TC),\displaystyle\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,...,p\}}\sum_{T\subseteq\{1,...,q\}}\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{\mathbf{X}}_{S},\hat{A}_{1},\hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{T})\cdot\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{\mathbf{X}}_{S^{C}},\hat{A}_{2},\hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{T^{C}}), (455)

where 𝐗^S\hat{\mathbf{X}}_{S} means the subsequence of X^1,…,X^p\hat{X}_{1},...,\hat{X}_{p} selected by the subset SS[83]. Superscript-C means complement. For example:

𝒞ρ​(A^1⋅A^2,Y^)\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{A}_{1}\cdot\hat{A}_{2},\hat{Y})
=\displaystyle= 𝒞ρ​(A^1,A^2,Y^)+𝒞ρ​(A^1,Y^)​𝒞ρ​(A^2)+𝒞ρ​(A^1)​𝒞ρ​(A^2,Y^).\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{A}_{1},\hat{A}_{2},\hat{Y})+\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{A}_{1},\hat{Y})\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{A}_{2})+\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{A}_{1})\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{A}_{2},\hat{Y}). (456)

As applications of Eq.(455), for A^,B^\hat{A},\hat{B} satisfying A^​B^=A^\hat{A}\hat{B}=\hat{A}, we have identities:

𝒞ρ​(A^,B^)=\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{A},\hat{B})= (1−⟨B^⟩ρ)​⟨A^⟩ρ\displaystyle(1-\langle\hat{B}\rangle_{\rho})\langle\hat{A}\rangle_{\rho}
𝒞ρ​(A^,B^,X^)=\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{A},\hat{B},\hat{X})= (1−⟨B^⟩ρ)​𝒞ρ​(A^,X^)−⟨A^⟩ρ​𝒞ρ​(B^,X^)\displaystyle(1-\langle\hat{B}\rangle_{\rho})\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{A},\hat{X})-\langle\hat{A}\rangle_{\rho}\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{B},\hat{X})
𝒞ρ​(X^,A^,B^)=\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{X},\hat{A},\hat{B})= (1−⟨B^⟩ρ)​𝒞ρ​(X^,A^)−⟨A^⟩ρ​𝒞ρ​(X^,B^).\displaystyle(1-\langle\hat{B}\rangle_{\rho})\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{X},\hat{A})-\langle\hat{A}\rangle_{\rho}\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{X},\hat{B}). (457)

For the special case A^2=A^\hat{A}^{2}=\hat{A}:

𝒞ρ​(A^,A^,X^)=\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{A},\hat{A},\hat{X})= (1−2​⟨A^⟩ρ)​𝒞ρ​(A^,X^)\displaystyle(1-2\langle\hat{A}\rangle_{\rho})\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{A},\hat{X})
𝒞ρ​(X^,A^,A^)=\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{X},\hat{A},\hat{A})= (1−2​⟨A^⟩ρ)​𝒞ρ​(X^,A^).\displaystyle(1-2\langle\hat{A}\rangle_{\rho})\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{X},\hat{A}). (458)

(6) Cumulant-bound: Physically, if ρ\rho describes a gapped short-range state with correlation length ξ\xi, let A^1,A^2,…,A^n\hat{A}_{1},\hat{A}_{2},...,\hat{A}_{n} be bounded local operators with supports D1,…,DnD_{1},...,D_{n}, then the ordered-cumulant will decay exponentially for a bipartition of the operators that are far apart in the real-space[56, 5]:

|𝒞ρ​(A^1,…,A^n)|<Cn​∏l‖A^l‖​exp⁡[−dist⁡(DI,DIC)ξ],\displaystyle|\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{A}_{1},...,\hat{A}_{n})|<C_{n}\prod_{l}\|\hat{A}_{l}\|\exp\Big[-\frac{{\rm dist}(D_{I},D_{I^{C}})}{\xi}\Big], (459)

where, ‖A^‖≡sup‖ψ‖=1​‖A^​|ψ⟩‖\|\hat{A}\|\equiv{\rm sup}_{\|\psi\|=1}\|\hat{A}|\psi\rangle\| is the operator norm of A^\hat{A}, CnC_{n} is some constant independent of {A^l}\{\hat{A}_{l}\}. II and ICI^{C} denote a bipartition of operators: I∪IC={1,2,..,n}I\cup I^{C}=\{1,2,..,n\}, and

DI≡\displaystyle D_{I}\equiv ∪l∈IDl,\displaystyle\cup_{l\in I}D_{l}, DIC≡\displaystyle D_{I^{C}}\equiv ∪l∉IDl.\displaystyle\cup_{l\notin I}D_{l}. (460)

As an intuitive interpretation, the linked clusters have a real-space meaning: any given operator must be adjacent to some other operator to have a sizable cumulant.

(7) Cumulant factorization: This is a consequence of the combination of the cumulant-bound Eq.(459) and the product-cumulant identity Eq.(455). For a gapped short-range state, consider an operator A^=A^1⋅A^2\hat{A}=\hat{A}_{1}\cdot\hat{A}_{2}: if the supports of A^1\hat{A}_{1} and A^2\hat{A}_{2}: DA1D_{A_{1}} and DA2D_{A_{2}} are far apart:

dist⁡(DA1,DA2)=R≫ξ,\displaystyle{\rm dist}(D_{A_{1}},D_{A_{2}})=R\gg\xi, (461)

assuming X^i\hat{X}_{i} and Y^j\hat{Y}_{j} each has a support whose length-scale ≲ξ\lesssim\xi, then a fixed finite-order cumulant factorizes:

𝒞ρ​(X^1,…,X^p,A^1⋅A^2,Y^1,…,Y^q)\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{X}_{1},...,\hat{X}_{p},\hat{A}_{1}\cdot\hat{A}_{2},\hat{Y}_{1},...,\hat{Y}_{q})
=\displaystyle= ∑S⊆{1,…,p}∑T⊆{1,…,q}𝒞ρ​(𝐗^S,A^1,𝐘^T)\displaystyle\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,...,p\}}\sum_{T\subseteq\{1,...,q\}}\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{\mathbf{X}}_{S},\hat{A}_{1},\hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{T})
⋅𝒞ρ​(𝐗^SC,A^2,𝐘^TC)+O⁡(e−R(p+q+1)​ξ),\displaystyle\cdot\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{\mathbf{X}}_{S^{C}},\hat{A}_{2},\hat{\mathbf{Y}}_{T^{C}})+O(e^{-\frac{R}{(p+q+1)\xi}}), (462)

because 𝒞ρ​(X^1,…,X^p,A^1,A^2,Y^1,…,Y^q)=O⁡(e−R(p+q+1)​ξ)\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{X}_{1},...,\hat{X}_{p},\hat{A}_{1},\hat{A}_{2},\hat{Y}_{1},...,\hat{Y}_{q})=O(e^{-\frac{R}{(p+q+1)\xi}}) (the denominator in the exponent is from the minimal bipartition distance achieved by equally spaced X,YX,Y operators between A1,A2A_{1},A_{2}). For example:

𝒞ρ​(A^1⋅A^2,Y^)\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{A}_{1}\cdot\hat{A}_{2},\hat{Y})
=\displaystyle= 𝒞ρ​(A^1,Y^)​𝒞ρ​(A^2)+𝒞ρ​(A^1)​𝒞ρ​(A^2,Y^)+O⁡(e−R2​ξ).\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{A}_{1},\hat{Y})\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{A}_{2})+\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{A}_{1})\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{A}_{2},\hat{Y})+O(e^{-\frac{R}{2\xi}}). (463)

(8) Full Taylor expansion of G{A^l}​({sl})G_{\{\hat{A}_{l}\}}(\{s_{l}\}):Ordered-cumulants also encode the full Taylor expansion of G{A^i}​({si})G_{\{\hat{A}_{i}\}}(\{s_{i}\}) defined in Eq.(448):

G{A^l}​({sl})\displaystyle G_{\{\hat{A}_{l}\}}(\{s_{l}\})
=\displaystyle= ∑k1,k2,…≥0[∏l=1nslklkl!]⋅𝒞ρ​(A^1[k1],A^2[k2],…,A^n[kn]),\displaystyle\sum_{k_{1},k_{2},...\geq 0}\Big[\prod_{l=1}^{n}\frac{s_{l}^{k_{l}}}{k_{l}!}\Big]\cdot\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{A}_{1}^{[k_{1}]},\hat{A}_{2}^{[k_{2}]},...,\hat{A}_{n}^{[k_{n}]}),
≡\displaystyle\equiv ∑{kl≥0}[∏l=1nslklkl!]⋅𝒞ρ({A^l[kl]}l∈{1,..,n})\displaystyle\sum_{\{k_{l}\geq 0\}}\Big[\prod_{l=1}^{n}\frac{s_{l}^{k_{l}}}{k_{l}!}\Big]\cdot\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\{\hat{A}_{l}^{[k_{l}]}\}_{l\in\{1,..,n\}}) (464)

where the notation A^l[kl]\hat{A}_{l}^{[k_{l}]} means a consecutive ordered block of klk_{l} copies of A^l\hat{A}_{l} with empty blocks being omitted, and we introduced shorthand notation in the last line. For instance:

𝒞ρ​(A^1[2],A^4[3])≡𝒞ρ​(A^1,A^1,A^4,A^4,A^4).\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{A}_{1}^{[2]},\hat{A}_{4}^{[3]})\equiv\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{A}_{1},\hat{A}_{1},\hat{A}_{4},\hat{A}_{4},\hat{A}_{4}). (465)

We also define that when kl=0k_{l}=0, ∀l\forall l, the empty cumulant is zero: 𝒞ρ​(empty)≡0\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\text{empty})\equiv 0.

To prove Eq.(464), one may first introduce more independent variables esl​A^l→esl,1​A^l​…​esl,kl​A^le^{s_{l}\hat{A}_{l}}\rightarrow e^{s_{l,1}\hat{A}_{l}}...e^{s_{l,k_{l}}\hat{A}_{l}}. Performing the first derivative for each variable sl,αs_{l,\alpha} once is equivalent to performing klk_{l}-th derivative on sls_{l}, i.e.:

∂s1k1…∂snknG{A^i}({si})|{sl=0}=𝒞ρ(A^1[k1],…,A^n[kn]).\displaystyle\left.\partial_{s_{1}}^{k_{1}}...\partial_{s_{n}}^{k_{n}}G_{\{\hat{A}_{i}\}}(\{s_{i}\})\right|_{\{s_{l}=0\}}=\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{A}_{1}^{[k_{1}]},...,\hat{A}_{n}^{[k_{n}]}). (466)

VI.2.2 Cumulant formulation of PE

Summation notations: We introduce a few useful notations for the summations in the cumulant expansion. The primed summation means the summation of ordered sequences of pairwise distinct electronic orbitals:

∑i1,i2,…​ik′means ​ia≠ib,∀a≠b.\displaystyle\sum^{\prime}_{i_{1},i_{2},...i_{k}}\text{means }i_{a}\neq i_{b},\forall a\neq b. (467)

Here, ordered sequence means that the sequences 2,5,32,5,3 and 3,2,53,2,5 are different and both will appear in the sum. For a subset RR of all electronic orbitals in the system, we denote its complement by RCR^{C}; R∪RCR\cup R^{C} contains all electronic orbitals. We define the primed summation with the superscript ”RR” as the summation of pairwise distinct electronic orbitals all in RR:

∑′Ri1,i2,…​ik≡∑′i1,i2,…​ik∈R.\displaystyle\sum^{\prime R}_{i_{1},i_{2},...i_{k}}\equiv\sum^{\prime}_{i_{1},i_{2},...i_{k}\in R}. (468)

Finally, we define the primed summation with the superscript ”(R)(R)” as the summation of pairwise distinct electronic orbitals in which at least one orbital ∈R\in R:

∑′(R)i1,i2,…​ik≡∑′i1,i2,…​ik−∑′RCi1,i2,…​ik.\displaystyle\sum^{\prime(R)}_{i_{1},i_{2},...i_{k}}\equiv\sum^{\prime}_{i_{1},i_{2},...i_{k}}-\sum^{\prime R^{C}}_{i_{1},i_{2},...i_{k}}. (469)

Static PE: We are now ready to perform the explicit PE calculation. Consider the static PE calculation Eq.(430). To apply the cumulant expansion, we first consider a related quantity:

O~D​(ϵ)≡⟨𝐎^D​(ϵ)​∏i∈DC𝐐^i​(ϵ)⟩ρ⟨∏i∈DC𝐐^i​(ϵ)⟩ρ\displaystyle\widetilde{O}_{D}(\epsilon)\equiv\frac{\langle\hat{\mathbf{O}}_{D}(\epsilon)\prod_{i\in D^{C}}\hat{\mathbf{Q}}_{i}(\epsilon)\rangle_{\rho}}{\langle\prod_{i\in D^{C}}\hat{\mathbf{Q}}_{i}(\epsilon)\rangle_{\rho}} (470)

O~D​(ϵ)\widetilde{O}_{D}(\epsilon) and our goal ⟨O^D⟩​(ϵ)\langle\hat{O}_{D}\rangle(\epsilon) in Eq.(430) differ in their denominators. We then introduce another quantity for any subset RR of all electronic orbitals:

FR​(ϵ)≡log⁡⟨∏i∈R𝐐^i​(ϵ)⟩ρ.\displaystyle F_{R}(\epsilon)\equiv\log\left\langle\prod_{i\in R}\hat{\mathbf{Q}}_{i}(\epsilon)\right\rangle_{\rho}. (471)

Using FDC​(ϵ)F_{D^{C}}(\epsilon) and Fall−orb.​(ϵ)F_{\rm all-orb.}(\epsilon), we have

⟨O^D⟩​(ϵ)=O~D​(ϵ)​exp⁡(−ΔD​(ϵ)),\displaystyle\langle\hat{O}_{D}\rangle(\epsilon)=\widetilde{O}_{D}(\epsilon)\exp(-\Delta_{D}(\epsilon)),
