VI.2.3 PE is a local expansion

Here we comment on the limitation of PE at finite orders. Due to the cumulant-bound Eq.(459), the physical picture of the PE should be viewed as a local expansion. Therefore, for any short-range property, we expect finite-order PE to perform well. These include the energy density of a short-range Hamiltonian, Berry’s phase calculation for quasiparticles and finite-momentum collective modes, etc. On the other hand, many long-range properties are not expected to be well-captured by finite-order PE. These include the long-range tail of correlation functions, the Berry’s phase calculation in the momentum →0\rightarrow 0 limit, etc. These limitations will be shown in our demonstrations in the next subsection. Nevertheless, since PE is a conserving approximation, both statically and dynamically, leading to exact Ward identities in VMPI, the inaccuracy at small momentum is not expected to qualitatively change the physics.

For example, suppose one wants to compute the PE for the static connected density-density correlation function between electronic orbitals: a,ba,b: ⟨n^a(e)​n^b(e)⟩−⟨n^a(e)⟩​⟨n^b(e)⟩\langle\hat{n}^{(e)}_{a}\hat{n}^{(e)}_{b}\rangle-\langle\hat{n}^{(e)}_{a}\rangle\langle\hat{n}^{(e)}_{b}\rangle, according to Eq.(475,478), the PE corrections to the mean-field result (i.e. zeroth order PE result) come in via the insertion of the 𝒒^i,(m)\hat{\bm{q}}_{i,(m)} operators in the ordered-cumulants. Let’s visualize each 𝒒^i,(m)\hat{\bm{q}}_{i,(m)} operator as a dot located at electronic orbital-ii. When the aa and bb orbitals are far apart, there needs to be at least a sequence of dots forming a bridge-like line connecting aa and bb with the dots separating from their nearest neighbors by ∼ξ\sim\xi (see Fig.6). The longer-range correlation will then need a higher-order PE to capture.

VI.2.4 Fusion-correlation-matrix and fusion-channel-space algorithm

In practice, since PE is defined in terms of operators acting on the parton mean-field state, the cumulants can be computed using Wick’s theorem. In this subsection, we introduce a practical algorithm to compute the cumulants, which speeds up computation.

To present the algorithm, we consider a generic single-body electronic operator ci†​cjc^{\dagger}_{i}c_{j} and a two-body electronic operator ci†​cj†​ck​clc^{\dagger}_{i}c^{\dagger}_{j}c_{k}c_{l}. Here, cic_{i} can be either fermionic or bosonic, depending on the parity of the number of parton species npn_{\rm p}. The goal is to compute the static expectation values using PE:

Goal: ⟨ci†​cj⟩​(ϵ)\displaystyle\langle c^{\dagger}_{i}c_{j}\rangle(\epsilon) , ⟨ci†​cj†​ck​cl⟩​(ϵ).\displaystyle\langle c^{\dagger}_{i}c^{\dagger}_{j}c_{k}c_{l}\rangle(\epsilon). (485)

To simplify the presentation, we focus on the case that cic_{i} is either a fermion or a hard-core boson, and only briefly comment on the usual boson case at the end of the subsection. Consequently, we assume in ci†​cj†​ck​clc^{\dagger}_{i}c^{\dagger}_{j}c_{k}c_{l}, i≠ji\neq j and k≠lk\neq l (but c†c^{\dagger} and cc operators can be on the same site). In this case, the electron-number-sector decomposition in Eq.(426) truncates to n=0,1n=0,1:

𝐏^i​(ϵ)=𝐏^i,0+γ⁡(ϵ)​𝐏^i,1,\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{i}(\epsilon)=\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{i,0}+\gamma(\epsilon)\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{i,1}, (486)

where 𝐏^i,0\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{i,0} is the local parton vacuum projector:

𝐏^i,0=∏p=1np𝐏^i,0(p),𝐏^i,0(p)≡∏𝐦i(p)(1−fi,𝐦i(p)(p)†fi,𝐦i(p)(p)),\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{i,0}=\prod_{p=1}^{n_{\rm p}}\hat{\mathbf{P}}^{(p)}_{i,0},\;\;\hat{\mathbf{P}}^{(p)}_{i,0}\equiv\prod_{\mathbf{m}_{i}^{(p)}}(1-f^{(p)\dagger}_{i,\mathbf{m}^{(p)}_{i}}f^{(p)}_{i,\mathbf{m}^{(p)}_{i}}), (487)

where we used the formulation introduced in Eq.(84). Next, we introduce a few shorthand notations:

𝐅^i=\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{i}= ci†​∑α=1Rλα​D^i​α, where ​D^i​α≡fi,𝐦α,i(1)(1)​…​fi,𝐦α,i(np)(np),\displaystyle c_{i}^{\dagger}\sum_{\alpha=1}^{R}\lambda_{\alpha}\hat{D}_{i\alpha},\text{ where }\hat{D}_{i\alpha}\equiv f^{(1)}_{i,\mathbf{m}^{(1)}_{\alpha,i}}...f^{(n_{\rm p})}_{i,\mathbf{m}^{(n_{\rm p})}_{\alpha,i}},
𝐧^i≡\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{i}\equiv 𝐏^i,1=∑α,β=1Rλα∗​λβ​D^i,α†​𝐏^i,0​D^i​β,\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{i,1}=\sum_{\alpha,\beta=1}^{R}\lambda^{*}_{\alpha}\lambda_{\beta}\hat{D}^{\dagger}_{i,\alpha}\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{i,0}\hat{D}_{i\beta}, (488)

where, for simplicity of presentation, we assumed the number of fusion channels Ri=RR_{i}=R and the fusion amplitudes λi,α=λα\lambda_{i,\alpha}=\lambda_{\alpha} are independent of the electronic orbital-ii. We have local PE operators defined in Eq.(442):

𝒒^i,(1)=\displaystyle\hat{\bm{q}}_{i,(1)}= 𝐏^i,0−𝟏+γ(0)​𝐧^i,\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{i,0}-\mathbf{1}+\gamma_{(0)}\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{i},
𝒒^i,(m)=\displaystyle\hat{\bm{q}}_{i,(m)}= γ(m−1)​𝐧^i,∀m≥2.\displaystyle\gamma_{(m-1)}\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{i},\;\;\forall m\geq 2. (489)

We now write down the parton operators corresponding to ci†​cjc^{\dagger}_{i}c_{j} and ci†​cj†​ck​clc^{\dagger}_{i}c^{\dagger}_{j}c_{k}c_{l} according to Eq.(424). It is easy to show that:

[𝐜^i†​𝐜^j]​(ϵ)≡∏a∈{i,j}𝐂^a​(ϵ)†⋅ci†​cj⋅∏b∈{i,j}𝐂^b​(ϵ)\displaystyle[\hat{\mathbf{c}}^{\dagger}_{i}\hat{\mathbf{c}}_{j}](\epsilon)\equiv\prod_{a\in\{i,j\}}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{a}(\epsilon)^{\dagger}\cdot c_{i}^{\dagger}c_{j}\cdot\prod_{b\in\{i,j\}}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{b}(\epsilon)
=γ⁡(ϵ)​∑α,β=1Rλα∗​λβ​D^i​α†​𝐏^i,0​𝐏^j,0​D^j​β≡γ⁡(ϵ)​[𝐜^i†​𝐜^j],\displaystyle=\gamma(\epsilon)\sum_{\alpha,\beta=1}^{R}\lambda_{\alpha}^{*}\lambda_{\beta}\hat{D}_{i\alpha}^{\dagger}\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{i,0}\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{j,0}\hat{D}_{j\beta}\equiv\gamma(\epsilon)[\hat{\mathbf{c}}^{\dagger}_{i}\hat{\mathbf{c}}_{j}],
[𝐜^i†​𝐜^j†​𝐜^k​𝐜^l]​(ϵ)≡∏a∈{i,j,k,l}𝐂^a​(ϵ)†⋅ci†​cj†​ck​cl⋅∏b∈{i,j,k,l}𝐂^b​(ϵ)\displaystyle[\hat{\mathbf{c}}^{\dagger}_{i}\hat{\mathbf{c}}^{\dagger}_{j}\hat{\mathbf{c}}_{k}\hat{\mathbf{c}}_{l}](\epsilon)\equiv\prod_{a\in\{i,j,k,l\}}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{a}(\epsilon)^{\dagger}\cdot c_{i}^{\dagger}c_{j}^{\dagger}c_{k}c_{l}\cdot\prod_{b\in\{i,j,k,l\}}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{b}(\epsilon)
=γ​(ϵ)2​∑α,β,δ,η=1Rλα∗​λβ∗​λδ​λη​D^i​α†​D^j​β†​∏a∈{i,j,k,l}𝐏^a,0​D^k​δ​D^l​η\displaystyle=\gamma(\epsilon)^{2}\sum_{\alpha,\beta,\delta,\eta=1}^{R}\lambda_{\alpha}^{*}\lambda^{*}_{\beta}\lambda_{\delta}\lambda_{\eta}\hat{D}_{i\alpha}^{\dagger}\hat{D}_{j\beta}^{\dagger}\prod_{a\in\{i,j,k,l\}}\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{a,0}\hat{D}_{k\delta}\hat{D}_{l\eta}
≡γ​(ϵ)2​[𝐜^i†​𝐜^j†​𝐜^k​𝐜^l],\displaystyle\equiv\gamma(\epsilon)^{2}[\hat{\mathbf{c}}^{\dagger}_{i}\hat{\mathbf{c}}^{\dagger}_{j}\hat{\mathbf{c}}_{k}\hat{\mathbf{c}}_{l}], (490)

where we separate out the ϵ\epsilon-independent operators in [𝐜^i†​𝐜^j][\hat{\mathbf{c}}^{\dagger}_{i}\hat{\mathbf{c}}_{j}] and [𝐜^i†​𝐜^j†​𝐜^k​𝐜^l][\hat{\mathbf{c}}^{\dagger}_{i}\hat{\mathbf{c}}^{\dagger}_{j}\hat{\mathbf{c}}_{k}\hat{\mathbf{c}}_{l}]. Note that when i=ji=j, [𝐜^i†​𝐜^i]=𝐧^i[\hat{\mathbf{c}}^{\dagger}_{i}\hat{\mathbf{c}}_{i}]=\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{i}. Using Eq.(450,476,479), in order to compute the goal Eq.(485), a typical component of a cumulant has a form:

𝖠(m)[q=1]({sn})≡\displaystyle\mathsf{A}^{[q=1]}_{(m)}(\{s_{n}\})\equiv ⟨[𝐜^i†​𝐜^j]​𝐧^s1​…​𝐧^sm⟩ρ,sn∈{i,j}C\displaystyle\langle[\hat{\mathbf{c}}^{\dagger}_{i}\hat{\mathbf{c}}_{j}]\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{s_{1}}...\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{s_{m}}\rangle_{\rho},\;\;s_{n}\in\{i,j\}^{C}
𝖠(m)[q=2]({sn})≡\displaystyle\mathsf{A}^{[q=2]}_{(m)}(\{s_{n}\})\equiv ⟨[𝐜^i†​𝐜^j†​𝐜^k​𝐜^l]​𝐧^s1​…​𝐧^sm⟩ρ,sn∈{i,j,k,l}C.\displaystyle\langle[\hat{\mathbf{c}}^{\dagger}_{i}\hat{\mathbf{c}}^{\dagger}_{j}\hat{\mathbf{c}}_{k}\hat{\mathbf{c}}_{l}]\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{s_{1}}...\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{s_{m}}\rangle_{\rho},\;s_{n}\in\{i,j,k,l\}^{C}. (491)

where the PE electronic orbitals {sn}\{s_{n}\} are pairwise distinct. If one identifies 𝐧^sn\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{s_{n}} as contributed from 𝒒^sn,(1)\hat{\bm{q}}_{s_{n},(1)}, then the subscript (m) in 𝖠(m)[q]\mathsf{A}^{[q]}_{(m)} can be identified as the PE order. The superscript [q] in 𝖠(m)[q]\mathsf{A}^{[q]}_{(m)} denotes whether the goal electronic operator is single-body or two-body.

There are two complexities involved in computing these expectation values:

  1. 1.

    The presence of the onsite parton vacuum projectors 𝐏^a,0\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{a,0}, which makes Wick’s theorem expansion complicated.

  2. 2.

    The summation of the fusion channel indices {α,β,…}\{\alpha,\beta,...\}, which scales as O⁡(R2​(q+m))O(R^{2(q+m)}) for 𝖠(m)[q]\mathsf{A}^{[q]}_{(m)}, making computation costly when RR is sizable. (Note that there is a double summation for fusion channels in each 𝐧^sn\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{s_{n}})

The purpose of this subsection is to introduce algorithms to tackle these two complexities:

  1. 1.

    We will introduce the fusion-correlation-matrix, such that in terms of Wick’s theorem expansion, the onsite parton vacuum projectors 𝐏^a,0\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{a,0} can be effectively replaced by identity: for each set of fixed fusion channels {α,β,…}\{\alpha,\beta,...\}, only one determinant need to be computed for each parton-pp.

  2. 2.

    We will introduce the fusion-channel-space algorithm: the complexity in computing 𝖠(m)[q]\mathsf{A}^{[q]}_{(m)} is reduced to O⁡(Rq+m+1)O(R^{q+m+1}).

Fusion-correlation-matrix: Now let’s pay attention to the operator expressions on the RHS of Eq.(491). Each [𝐜^i†​𝐜^j][\hat{\mathbf{c}}^{\dagger}_{i}\hat{\mathbf{c}}_{j}], [𝐜^i†​𝐜^j†​𝐜^k​𝐜^l][\hat{\mathbf{c}}^{\dagger}_{i}\hat{\mathbf{c}}^{\dagger}_{j}\hat{\mathbf{c}}_{k}\hat{\mathbf{c}}_{l}], and 𝐧^sn\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{s_{n}} operator has a form that the parton creation operators D^†\hat{D}^{\dagger} on the left, annihilation operators D^\hat{D} on the right, and the projectors 𝐏^a,0\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{a,0} in the middle. Notice that the projector 𝐏^a,0\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{a,0} is fermion parity even, they commute with each other and with any parton operator on a distinct electronic orbital. Consequently, in the operator expressions on the RHS of Eq.(491), after including a fixed fermion sign:

σ(m)[q]≡(−1)np⋅[q​m+m⁡(m−1)2],\displaystyle\sigma_{(m)}^{[q]}\equiv(-1)^{n_{\rm p}\cdot[qm+\frac{m(m-1)}{2}]}, (492)

one can safely move all D^†\hat{D}^{\dagger} to the left (but keeping their order), all D^\hat{D} operators to the right (but keeping their order), and all 𝐏^a,0\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{a,0} in the middle. Denoting the combined fusion channel index as the bold-font Greek letter:

𝜶≡\displaystyle\bm{\alpha}\equiv (α1,…,αq+m),\displaystyle(\alpha_{1},...,\alpha_{q+m}), W𝜶≡\displaystyle W_{\bm{\alpha}}\equiv ∏r=1q+mλαr,\displaystyle\prod_{r=1}^{q+m}\lambda_{\alpha_{r}}, (493)

also denoting:

𝐃¯[q=1]𝜶≡\displaystyle\bar{\mathbf{D}}^{[q=1]}_{\bm{\alpha}}\equiv D^i​α1†​D^s1​α2†​…​D^sm​αm+1†,\displaystyle\hat{D}_{i\alpha_{1}}^{\dagger}\hat{D}^{\dagger}_{s_{1}\alpha_{2}}...\hat{D}^{\dagger}_{s_{m}\alpha_{m+1}},
𝐃[q=1]𝜷≡\displaystyle\mathbf{D}^{[q=1]}_{\bm{\beta}}\equiv D^j​β1​D^s1​β2​…​D^sm​βm+1,\displaystyle\hat{D}_{j\beta_{1}}\hat{D}_{s_{1}\beta_{2}}...\hat{D}_{s_{m}\beta_{m+1}},
𝐃¯[q=2]𝜶≡\displaystyle\bar{\mathbf{D}}^{[q=2]}_{\bm{\alpha}}\equiv D^i​α1†​D^j​α2†​D^s1​α3†​…​D^sm​αm+2†,\displaystyle\hat{D}_{i\alpha_{1}}^{\dagger}\hat{D}_{j\alpha_{2}}^{\dagger}\hat{D}_{s_{1}\alpha_{3}}^{\dagger}...\hat{D}_{s_{m}\alpha_{m+2}}^{\dagger},
𝐃[q=2]𝜷≡\displaystyle\mathbf{D}^{[q=2]}_{\bm{\beta}}\equiv D^k​β1​D^l​β2​D^s1​β3​…​D^sm​βm+2,\displaystyle\hat{D}_{k\beta_{1}}\hat{D}_{l\beta_{2}}\hat{D}_{s_{1}\beta_{3}}...\hat{D}_{s_{m}\beta_{m+2}},
𝐏[q]≡\displaystyle\mathbf{P}^{[q]}\equiv ∏p=1np𝐏(p),[q],\displaystyle\prod_{p=1}^{n_{\rm p}}\mathbf{P}^{(p),[q]},
𝐏(p),[q=1]≡\displaystyle\mathbf{P}^{(p),[q=1]}\equiv 𝐏^i,0(p)​𝐏^j,0(p)​𝐏^s1,0(p)​…​𝐏^sm,0(p),\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{P}}^{(p)}_{i,0}\hat{\mathbf{P}}^{(p)}_{j,0}\hat{\mathbf{P}}^{(p)}_{s_{1},0}...\hat{\mathbf{P}}^{(p)}_{s_{m},0},
𝐏(p),[q=2]≡\displaystyle\mathbf{P}^{(p),[q=2]}\equiv 𝐏^i,0(p)​𝐏^j,0(p)​𝐏^k,0(p)​𝐏^l,0(p)​𝐏^s1,0(p)​…​𝐏^sm,0(p),\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{P}}^{(p)}_{i,0}\hat{\mathbf{P}}^{(p)}_{j,0}\hat{\mathbf{P}}^{(p)}_{k,0}\hat{\mathbf{P}}^{(p)}_{l,0}\hat{\mathbf{P}}^{(p)}_{s_{1},0}...\hat{\mathbf{P}}^{(p)}_{s_{m},0}, (494)

we have:

𝖠(m)[q]=σ(m)[q]​∑𝜶,𝜷W𝜶∗​W𝜷​⟨𝐃¯𝜶​𝐏[q]​𝐃𝜷⟩ρ.\displaystyle\mathsf{A}^{[q]}_{(m)}=\sigma_{(m)}^{[q]}\sum_{\bm{\alpha},\bm{\beta}}W_{\bm{\alpha}}^{*}W_{\bm{\beta}}\langle\bar{\mathbf{D}}_{\bm{\alpha}}\mathbf{P}^{[q]}\mathbf{D}_{\bm{\beta}}\rangle_{\rho}. (495)

Defining vectors 𝜶~(p),𝜷~(p)\tilde{\bm{\alpha}}^{(p)},\tilde{\bm{\beta}}^{(p)} of the combined parton orbital indices (i,𝐦(p))(i,\mathbf{m}^{(p)}) of length q+mq+m:

𝜶~(p),[q=1]≡[(i,𝐦α1(p)),(s1,𝐦α2(p)),…,(sm,𝐦αm+1(p))],\displaystyle\tilde{\bm{\alpha}}^{(p),[q=1]}\equiv[(i,\mathbf{m}^{(p)}_{\alpha_{1}}),(s_{1},\mathbf{m}^{(p)}_{\alpha_{2}}),...,(s_{m},\mathbf{m}^{(p)}_{\alpha_{m+1}})],
𝜷~(p),[q=1]≡[(j,𝐦β1(p)),(s1,𝐦β2(p)),…,(sm,𝐦βm+1(p))],\displaystyle\tilde{\bm{\beta}}^{(p),[q=1]}\equiv[(j,\mathbf{m}^{(p)}_{\beta_{1}}),(s_{1},\mathbf{m}^{(p)}_{\beta_{2}}),...,(s_{m},\mathbf{m}^{(p)}_{\beta_{m+1}})],
𝜶~(p),[q=2]\displaystyle\tilde{\bm{\alpha}}^{(p),[q=2]}
≡[(i,𝐦α1(p)),(j,𝐦α2(p)),(s1,𝐦α3(p)),…,(sm,𝐦αm+2(p))],\displaystyle\equiv[(i,\mathbf{m}^{(p)}_{\alpha_{1}}),(j,\mathbf{m}^{(p)}_{\alpha_{2}}),(s_{1},\mathbf{m}^{(p)}_{\alpha_{3}}),...,(s_{m},\mathbf{m}^{(p)}_{\alpha_{m+2}})],
𝜷~(p),[q=2]\displaystyle\tilde{\bm{\beta}}^{(p),[q=2]}
≡[(k,𝐦β1(p)),(l,𝐦β2(p)),(s1,𝐦β3(p)),…,(sm,𝐦βm+2(p))],\displaystyle\equiv[(k,\mathbf{m}^{(p)}_{\beta_{1}}),(l,\mathbf{m}^{(p)}_{\beta_{2}}),(s_{1},\mathbf{m}^{(p)}_{\beta_{3}}),...,(s_{m},\mathbf{m}^{(p)}_{\beta_{m+2}})], (496)

also defining

𝐟¯𝜶(p),[q]≡\displaystyle\bar{\mathbf{f}}^{(p),[q]}_{\bm{\alpha}}\equiv f(p)†𝜶~1(p),[q]…f(p)†𝜶~q+m(p),[q],\displaystyle f^{(p)\dagger}_{\tilde{\bm{\alpha}}^{(p),[q]}_{1}}...f^{(p)\dagger}_{\tilde{\bm{\alpha}}^{(p),[q]}_{q+m}},
𝐟𝜷(p),[q]≡\displaystyle\mathbf{f}^{(p),[q]}_{\bm{\beta}}\equiv f𝜷~1(p),[q](p)​…​f𝜷~q+m(p),[q](p),\displaystyle f^{(p)}_{\tilde{\bm{\beta}}^{(p),[q]}_{1}}...f^{(p)}_{\tilde{\bm{\beta}}^{(p),[q]}_{q+m}}, (497)

we have:

𝖠(m)[q]=\displaystyle\mathsf{A}^{[q]}_{(m)}= σ(m)[q]​∑𝜶,𝜷W𝜶∗​W𝜷​∏p=1np𝖡𝜶​𝜷(p),[q],\displaystyle\sigma_{(m)}^{[q]}\sum_{\bm{\alpha},\bm{\beta}}W_{\bm{\alpha}}^{*}W_{\bm{\beta}}\prod_{p=1}^{n_{\rm p}}\mathsf{B}^{(p),[q]}_{\bm{\alpha}\bm{\beta}},
where: 𝖡(p),[q]𝜶​𝜷≡\displaystyle\text{where: }\mathsf{B}^{(p),[q]}_{\bm{\alpha}\bm{\beta}}\equiv ⟨𝐟¯𝜶(p),[q]​𝐏(p),[q]​𝐟𝜷(p),[q]⟩ρ(p).\displaystyle\langle\bar{\mathbf{f}}^{(p),[q]}_{\bm{\alpha}}\mathbf{P}^{(p),[q]}\mathbf{f}^{(p),[q]}_{\bm{\beta}}\rangle_{\rho^{(p)}}. (498)

Therefore, the calculation for a fixed set of fusion channels 𝜶,𝜷\bm{\alpha},\bm{\beta} boils down to computing 𝖡𝜶​𝜷(p),[q]\mathsf{B}^{(p),[q]}_{\bm{\alpha}\bm{\beta}}. If there were no projector 𝐏(p),[q]\mathbf{P}^{(p),[q]}, this is straightforward: up to the fermion sign:

σ~(m)(p),[q]≡(−1)(q+m)​(q+m−1)2,\displaystyle\tilde{\sigma}^{(p),[q]}_{(m)}\equiv(-1)^{\frac{(q+m)(q+m-1)}{2}}, (499)

one only needs to compute det[ρ𝜷~(p),[q],𝜶~(p),[q](p)]\det[\rho^{(p)}_{\tilde{\bm{\beta}}^{(p),[q]},\tilde{\bm{\alpha}}^{(p),[q]}}], where the (q+m)×(q+m)(q+m)\times(q+m) submatrix ρ𝜷~(p),[q],𝜶~(p),[q](p)\rho^{(p)}_{\tilde{\bm{\beta}}^{(p),[q]},\tilde{\bm{\alpha}}^{(p),[q]}} selects the 𝜷~(p),[q]\tilde{\bm{\beta}}^{(p),[q]}-indexed rows and 𝜶~(p),[q]\tilde{\bm{\alpha}}^{(p),[q]}-indexed columns of the parton RDM: ρb​a(p)≡⟨fa†​fb⟩\rho^{(p)}_{ba}\equiv\langle f_{a}^{\dagger}f_{b}\rangle. But with the projector 𝐏(p),[q]\mathbf{P}^{(p),[q]}, naively, the computation is complicated.

To solve this complexity, we define the fusion-correlation-matrix as follows. First, we denote all parton-pp orbitals associated with the electronic-orbital labels on which 𝐏(p),[q]\mathbf{P}^{(p),[q]} acts as 𝒮(p),[q]\mathcal{S}^{(p),[q]}:

𝒮(p),[q=1]≡\displaystyle\mathcal{S}^{(p),[q=1]}\equiv {(a,𝐦a(p)):a∈{i,j,s1,…sm},∀𝐦a(p)},\displaystyle\{(a,\mathbf{m}^{(p)}_{a}):a\in\{i,j,s_{1},...s_{m}\},\forall\mathbf{m}_{a}^{(p)}\},
𝒮(p),[q=2]≡\displaystyle\mathcal{S}^{(p),[q=2]}\equiv {(a,𝐦a(p)):a∈{i,j,k,l,s1,…sm},∀𝐦a(p)}.\displaystyle\{(a,\mathbf{m}^{(p)}_{a}):a\in\{i,j,k,l,s_{1},...s_{m}\},\forall\mathbf{m}_{a}^{(p)}\}. (500)

Since there may be many parton-pp orbitals per electronic orbital, the number of elements in 𝒮(p),[q]\mathcal{S}^{(p),[q]}: |𝒮(p),[q]||\mathcal{S}^{(p),[q]}| can be much larger than the number of electronic orbitals that 𝐏(p),[q]\mathbf{P}^{(p),[q]} acts on. The fusion-correlation-matrix for parton-pp is defined as:

ρfus(p),[q]≡ρ𝒮(p),[q],𝒮(p),[q](p)⋅[𝟏−ρ𝒮(p),[q],𝒮(p),[q](p)]−1,\displaystyle\rho^{(p),[q]}_{\rm fus}\equiv\rho^{(p)}_{\mathcal{S}^{(p),[q]},\mathcal{S}^{(p),[q]}}\cdot\Big[\mathbf{1}-\rho^{(p)}_{\mathcal{S}^{(p),[q]},\mathcal{S}^{(p),[q]}}\Big]^{-1}, (501)

which is a |𝒮(p),[q]|×|𝒮(p),[q]||\mathcal{S}^{(p),[q]}|\times|\mathcal{S}^{(p),[q]}| matrix.

It turns out that a known property of Gaussian Grassmann state[26] leads to:

𝖡𝜶​𝜷(p),[q]=σ~(m)(p),[q]⋅Z(p),[q]⋅det{[ρfus(p),[q]]𝜷~(p),[q],𝜶~(p),[q]},\displaystyle\mathsf{B}^{(p),[q]}_{\bm{\alpha}\bm{\beta}}=\tilde{\sigma}^{(p),[q]}_{(m)}\cdot Z^{(p),[q]}\cdot\det\Big\{\big[\rho^{(p),[q]}_{\rm fus}\big]_{\tilde{\bm{\beta}}^{(p),[q]},\tilde{\bm{\alpha}}^{(p),[q]}}\Big\}, (502)

where the (q+m)×(q+m)(q+m)\times(q+m) submatrix of ρfus(p),[q]\rho^{(p),[q]}_{\rm fus} appears inside the determinant, and Z(p),[q]Z^{(p),[q]} is a factor independent of fusion channels:

Z(p),[q]≡det[𝟏−ρ𝒮(p),[q],𝒮(p),[q](p)].\displaystyle Z^{(p),[q]}\equiv\det\Big[\mathbf{1}-\rho^{(p)}_{\mathcal{S}^{(p),[q]},\mathcal{S}^{(p),[q]}}\Big]. (503)

Namely, using the fusion-correlation-matrix, even with the projector 𝐏(p),[q]\mathbf{P}^{(p),[q]}, one still only needs to compute one determinant per fixed set of fusion channels 𝜶,𝜷\bm{\alpha},\bm{\beta}. In particular, for low-order PE, q+mq+m is small (e.g., for a single-body term, 2nd-order PE needs q+m=3q+m=3).

Typically, the determinant is not computed numerically using the permutation-group-based definition, whose complexity scales exponentially with matrix size. Instead, it is usually computed using Gaussian elimination and is applicable to large matrices. However, for the small matrices relevant for PE, both the Gaussian-elimination-based algorithm and the definition-based algorithm give comparable speed for a single determinant. We will shortly see that using the definition-based algorithm will significantly reduce the computation cost for the summation of fusion channels 𝜶,𝜷\bm{\alpha},\bm{\beta}.

Fusion-channel-space algorithm: We still need to sum over the fusion channels 𝜶,𝜷\bm{\alpha},\bm{\beta} to compute 𝖠(m)[q]\mathsf{A}^{[q]}_{(m)}, whose computation cost naively scales as O⁡(R2​(q+m))O(R^{2(q+m)}). We will show that using the definition-based algorithm for the determinant reduces this cost to O⁡(Rq+m+1)O(R^{q+m+1}). To facilitate the discussion, we introduce some notations. First, we collect all the fermion signs

σ[q]≡σ(m)[q]​∏p=1npσ~(m)(p),[q]=(−1)q⁡(q−1)2⋅np,\displaystyle\sigma^{[q]}\equiv\sigma^{[q]}_{(m)}\prod_{p=1}^{n_{\rm p}}\tilde{\sigma}^{(p),[q]}_{(m)}=(-1)^{\frac{q(q-1)}{2}\cdot n_{\rm p}}, (504)

which is independent of mm. Second, we collect all the factors Z(p),[q]Z^{(p),[q]}:

𝖹[q]≡∏p=1npZ(p),[q].\displaystyle\mathsf{Z}^{[q]}\equiv\prod_{p=1}^{n_{\rm p}}Z^{(p),[q]}. (505)

Third, we introduce a shorthand notation for the matrix [ρfus(p),[q]]𝜷~(p),[q],𝜶~(p),[q]\big[\rho^{(p),[q]}_{\rm fus}\big]_{\tilde{\bm{\beta}}^{(p),[q]},\tilde{\bm{\alpha}}^{(p),[q]}}:

[K𝜷​𝜶(p),[q]]b,a≡[ρfus(p),[q]]𝜷~b(p),[q],𝜶~a(p),[q],a,b=1,…,q+m.\displaystyle[K^{(p),[q]}_{\bm{\beta}\bm{\alpha}}]_{b,a}\equiv\big[\rho^{(p),[q]}_{\rm fus}\big]_{\tilde{\bm{\beta}}_{b}^{(p),[q]},\tilde{\bm{\alpha}}_{a}^{(p),[q]}},\;\;a,b=1,...,q+m. (506)

Crucially, for fixed a,ba,b, [K𝜷​𝜶(p),[q]]b​a[K^{(p),[q]}_{\bm{\beta}\bm{\alpha}}]_{ba} depends on 𝜶,𝜷\bm{\alpha},\bm{\beta} only via αa\alpha_{a} and βb\beta_{b} as indicated in Eq.(496). This fact allows us to define, for each pair of a,b∈1,…,q+ma,b\in 1,...,q+m, an R×RR\times R fusion-channel-space matrix Lb,a(p),[q]L^{(p),[q]}_{b,a}:

[K𝜷​𝜶(p),[q]]b,a≡[Lb,a(p),[q]]βb,αa.\displaystyle[K^{(p),[q]}_{\bm{\beta}\bm{\alpha}}]_{b,a}\equiv\big[L^{(p),[q]}_{b,a}\big]_{\beta_{b},\alpha_{a}}. (507)

Altogether, based on Eq.(498), we have:

𝖠(m)[q]=σ[q]​𝖹[q]​∑𝜶​𝜷W𝜶∗​W𝜷​∏p=1npdetK𝜷​𝜶(p),[q]\displaystyle\mathsf{A}^{[q]}_{(m)}=\sigma^{[q]}\mathsf{Z}^{[q]}\sum_{\bm{\alpha}\bm{\beta}}W^{*}_{\bm{\alpha}}W_{\bm{\beta}}\prod_{p=1}^{n_{\rm p}}\det K^{(p),[q]}_{\bm{\beta}\bm{\alpha}} (508)

Now use the definition of determinants, denoting:

∑π1∈Sq+m∑π2∈Sq+m…∑πnp∈Sq+m≡∑𝝅,\displaystyle\sum_{\pi_{1}\in S_{q+m}}\sum_{\pi_{2}\in S_{q+m}}...\sum_{\pi_{n_{\rm p}}\in S_{q+m}}\equiv\sum_{\bm{\pi}},
𝝅≡(π1,…​πnp),(−1)𝝅≡∏p=1np(−1)πp,\displaystyle\bm{\pi}\equiv(\pi_{1},...\pi_{n_{\rm p}}),\;\;(-1)^{\bm{\pi}}\equiv\prod_{p=1}^{n_{\rm p}}(-1)^{\pi_{p}}, (509)

we have

∏p=1npdetK𝜷​𝜶(p),[q]=∑𝝅(−1)𝝅​∏b=1q+m∏p=1np[K𝜷​𝜶(p),[q]]b,πp​(b)\displaystyle\prod_{p=1}^{n_{\rm p}}\det K^{(p),[q]}_{\bm{\beta}\bm{\alpha}}=\sum_{\bm{\pi}}(-1)^{\bm{\pi}}\prod_{b=1}^{q+m}\prod_{p=1}^{n_{\rm p}}[K^{(p),[q]}_{\bm{\beta}\bm{\alpha}}]_{b,\pi_{p}(b)}
=\displaystyle= ∑𝝅(−1)𝝅​∏b=1q+m∏p=1np[Lb,πp​(b)(p),[q]]βb​απp​(b),\displaystyle\sum_{\bm{\pi}}(-1)^{\bm{\pi}}\prod_{b=1}^{q+m}\prod_{p=1}^{n_{\rm p}}\big[L^{(p),[q]}_{b,\pi_{p}(b)}\big]_{\beta_{b}\alpha_{\pi_{p}(b)}}, (510)

where we used Eq.(507). The consequence is that, for fixed 𝜶\bm{\alpha} and 𝝅\bm{\pi}, the 𝜷\bm{\beta}-summation in Eq.(508) factorizes:

𝖢(m)[q]​(𝜶,𝝅)≡∑𝜷W𝜷​∏b=1q+m∏p=1np[Lb,πp​(b)(p),[q]]βb​απp​(b)\displaystyle\mathsf{C}^{[q]}_{(m)}(\bm{\alpha};\bm{\pi})\equiv\sum_{\bm{\beta}}W_{\bm{\beta}}\prod_{b=1}^{q+m}\prod_{p=1}^{n_{\rm p}}\big[L^{(p),[q]}_{b,\pi_{p}(b)}\big]_{\beta_{b}\alpha_{\pi_{p}(b)}}
=\displaystyle= ∏b=1q+m[∑β=1Rλβ​∏p=1np[Lb,πp​(b)(p),[q]]β,απp​(b)],\displaystyle\prod_{b=1}^{q+m}\Big[\sum_{\beta=1}^{R}\lambda_{\beta}\prod_{p=1}^{n_{\rm p}}\big[L^{(p),[q]}_{b,\pi_{p}(b)}\big]_{\beta,\alpha_{\pi_{p}(b)}}\Big], (511)

whose computational complexity is O⁡(R)O(R). And finally:

𝖠(m)[q]=σ[q]​𝖹[q]​∑𝜶W𝜶∗​∑𝝅(−1)𝝅​𝖢(m)[q]​(𝜶,𝝅),\displaystyle\mathsf{A}^{[q]}_{(m)}=\sigma^{[q]}\mathsf{Z}^{[q]}\sum_{\bm{\alpha}}W^{*}_{\bm{\alpha}}\sum_{\bm{\pi}}(-1)^{\bm{\pi}}\mathsf{C}^{[q]}_{(m)}(\bm{\alpha};\bm{\pi}), (512)

where the 𝜶\bm{\alpha} summation contributes another factor of Rq+mR^{q+m} in complexity. If one accounts for all other contributions to the complexity, this fusion-channel-space algorithm to compute 𝖠(m)[q]\mathsf{A}^{[q]}_{(m)} has complexity O⁡([(q+m)!]np​(q+m)​np​Rq+m+1)O\Big(\big[(q+m)!\big]^{n_{\rm p}}(q+m)n_{\rm p}R^{q+m+1}\Big), while the naive algorithm using Gaussian-elimination-based determinant algorithm gives O⁡(np​(q+m)3​R2​(q+m))O\big(n_{\rm p}(q+m)^{3}R^{2(q+m)}\big). For practical low-order PE, when the number of fusion channels RR becomes sizable, the fusion-channel-space algorithm has an advantage.

Finally, we briefly remark on the situation that the electron is a usual boson instead of a hard-core boson, where the truncation to n=0,1n=0,1 in Eq.(486) must be generalized:

𝐏^i​(ϵ)=𝐏^i,0+γ⁡(ϵ)​𝐏^i,1+…+γ​(ϵ)nmax​𝐏^i,nmax,\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{i}(\epsilon)=\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{i,0}+\gamma(\epsilon)\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{i,1}+...+\gamma(\epsilon)^{n_{\rm max}}\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{i,n_{\rm max}}, (513)

where nmaxn_{\rm max} is the maximal boson number allowed by the fusion gate from fermionic partons. For example, consider the n=2n=2 sector 𝐏^i,2\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{i,2}, which involves 𝐂^i,2\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{i,2} according to Eq.(422). 𝐂^i,2\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{i,2} will involve two summation of fusion channels ∑α,β\sum_{\alpha,\beta} and associated fusion operators: D^i​α​D^i​β\hat{D}_{i\alpha}\hat{D}_{i\beta} defined in Eq.(488). Roughly speaking, the n=2n=2 sector 𝐏^i,2\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{i,2} can be treated as two separate n=1n=1 sectors in terms of the current fusion-channel-space algorithm. Generally, the complexity w.r.t. the PE order mm will increase from O⁡(Rm)O(R^{m}) in the hard-core case to O⁡(Rm​nmax)O(R^{mn_{\rm max}}).

VI.3 Benchmarking results

In this subsection, we will start with one of the simplest Hdet states, the bosonic Laughlin ν=12\nu=\frac{1}{2} FQH state with only one local fusion channel R=1R=1, and test the PE for both static properties and the quantum geometric tensor. The advantage of this pedagogical example is that the exact results are available via Monte Carlo, since R=1R=1. In addition, the PE calculation can be performed analytically, yielding simple closed-form results. We then move on to the static properties of the fermionic ν=13\nu=\frac{1}{3} Laughlin state and Jain’s ν=25\nu=\frac{2}{5} FQH state. As mentioned before, Jain’s ν=25\nu=\frac{2}{5} FQH state already has 4 local fusion channels R=4R=4, and cannot be exactly simulated by Monte Carlo for large systems. In these examples, we will test PE up to the second order.

In all the FQH examples mentioned above, the saddle points ρ¯\bar{\rho} for Hdet states are known: partons filling LLs. Finally, we study the FCI model systems, where the saddle points ρ¯\bar{\rho} must be found self-consistently. In principle, one can improve ρ¯\bar{\rho} order by order using PE. But as a benchmark test, we will only apply PE at the zeroth order (i.e., mean-field level) and find the zeroth-order-PE saddle point ρ¯(0)\bar{\rho}_{(0)}, as well as the effective parton Hamiltonian 𝗁^(p)​(𝐤,ρ¯(0))\hat{\mathsf{h}}^{(p)}(\mathbf{k};\bar{\rho}_{(0)}) as in Eq.(413). In particular, we aim to test PE in physical regimes far from the FQH regime. We will show that the static saddle-point results already give reasonable energetics. When limited to a small-sized system where exact diagonalization(ED) can be performed, the exact Hdet wavefunctions based on ρ¯(0)\bar{\rho}_{(0)} can be directly compared with the ED wavefunctions, showing much improved overlap.

Although the examples presented in this subsection belong to the Type-(B) models defined in Sec.IV, PE is generally applicable to both type-(A) and type-(B) models.

VI.3.1 Bosonic Laughlin’s ν=12\nu=\frac{1}{2} state

We fix the unit so that the electron’s magnetic length l(e)=1l^{(e)}=1 throughout this subsection. Since q(1)=q(2)=12q^{(1)}=q^{(2)}=\frac{1}{2}:

(l(1))2=(l(2))2=2​(l(e))2=2.\displaystyle(l^{(1)})^{2}=(l^{(2)})^{2}=2(l^{(e)})^{2}=2. (514)

To set up the PE calculation, we will use the discrete-coherent-state basis for both electrons and partons on the Fine-Grid on a torus sample with Ns(e)N_{s}^{(e)} magnetic flux quanta, as introduced in Sec.III.2.1. Namely, the Fine-Grid is a lattice of Ns(e)×Ns(e)N_{s}^{(e)}\times N_{s}^{(e)} sites: {z;z∈Fine-Grid}\{z;z\in\text{Fine-Grid}\}, whose real-space lattice basis vectors are the minimally allowed electronic magnetic translation vectors. On every Fine-Grid site-zz, there is also a coherent state for each parton species in their LLL. The relevant local quantum states on site-zz are labeled as |z(e)⟩,|z(1)⟩,|z(2)⟩|z^{(e)}\rangle,|z^{(1)}\rangle,|z^{(2)}\rangle, whose corresponding second-quantized operators are denoted as bz,fz(1),fz(2)b_{z},f_{z}^{(1)},f_{z}^{(2)}. Recall the change of viewpoint in Sec.III.2.2, the coherent states on different sites are treated as orthonormal, for both electrons and partons.

The local fusion gate is:

𝐂^z​(ϵ)=|0(e)⟩​⟨0(all ​p)|+γ​(ϵ)12​bz†|0(e)⟩​⟨0(all ​p)|​fz(1)​fz(2),\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{z}(\epsilon)=|0^{(e)}\rangle\langle 0^{(\text{all }p)}|+\gamma(\epsilon)^{\frac{1}{2}}b_{z}^{\dagger}|0^{(e)}\rangle\langle 0^{(\text{all }p)}|f^{(1)}_{z}f^{(2)}_{z}, (515)

The local projection operator in Eq.(424) is:

𝐏^z​(ϵ)=\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{P}}_{z}(\epsilon)= |0(all ​p)⟩​⟨0(all ​p)|+γ⁡(ϵ)​n^z(1)​n^z(2)\displaystyle|0^{(\text{all }p)}\rangle\langle 0^{(\text{all }p)}|+\gamma(\epsilon)\hat{n}_{z}^{(1)}\hat{n}_{z}^{(2)}
=\displaystyle= (𝟏^−n^z(1))​(𝟏^−n^z(2))+γ⁡(ϵ)​n^z(1)​n^z(2)\displaystyle(\hat{\mathbf{1}}-\hat{n}_{z}^{(1)})(\hat{\mathbf{1}}-\hat{n}_{z}^{(2)})+\gamma(\epsilon)\hat{n}_{z}^{(1)}\hat{n}_{z}^{(2)}
=\displaystyle= 𝟏^−n^z(1)−n^z(2)+(1+γ⁡(ϵ))​n^z(1)​n^z(2)\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{1}}-\hat{n}_{z}^{(1)}-\hat{n}_{z}^{(2)}+\big(1+\gamma(\epsilon)\big)\hat{n}_{z}^{(1)}\hat{n}_{z}^{(2)} (516)

where n^z(p)≡f(p)†zf(p)z\hat{n}_{z}^{(p)}\equiv f^{(p)\dagger}_{z}f^{(p)}_{z}, leading to the local PE operator in Eq.(429):

𝐐^z​(ϵ)=\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{Q}}_{z}(\epsilon)= 𝟏^+ϵ⁡(−n^z(1)−n^z(2)+(1+γ⁡(ϵ))​n^z(1)​n^z(2))\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{1}}+\epsilon\Big(-\hat{n}_{z}^{(1)}-\hat{n}_{z}^{(2)}+\big(1+\gamma(\epsilon)\big)\hat{n}_{z}^{(1)}\hat{n}_{z}^{(2)}\Big)
=\displaystyle= 𝟏^+ϵ​𝒒^z,(1)+ϵ2​𝒒^z,(2)+O⁡(ϵ3),\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{1}}+\epsilon\hat{\bm{q}}_{z,(1)}+\epsilon^{2}\hat{\bm{q}}_{z,(2)}+O(\epsilon^{3}), (517)

where the expansion defined in Eq.(442) is

𝒒^z,(1)=\displaystyle\hat{\bm{q}}_{z,(1)}= −n^z(1)−n^z(2)+(1+γ(0))​n^z(1)​n^z(2),\displaystyle-\hat{n}_{z}^{(1)}-\hat{n}_{z}^{(2)}+\big(1+\gamma_{(0)}\big)\hat{n}_{z}^{(1)}\hat{n}_{z}^{(2)},
𝒒^z,(2)=\displaystyle\hat{\bm{q}}_{z,(2)}= γ(1)​n^z(1)​n^z(2).\displaystyle\gamma_{(1)}\hat{n}_{z}^{(1)}\hat{n}_{z}^{(2)}. (518)

When computing PE, the parton number sum rule will be repeatedly used as an operator identity:

∑zn^z(p)=Ne⋅𝟏^\displaystyle\sum_{z}\hat{n}_{z}^{(p)}=N_{e}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{1}} (519)

All higher-order cumulants satisfy:

∑z𝒞ρ(…,n^z(p),….)=Ne𝒞ρ(…,𝟏^,….)=0,\displaystyle\sum_{z}\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(...,\hat{n}_{z}^{(p)},....)=N_{e}\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(...,\hat{\mathbf{1}},....)=0, (520)

except for ∑z𝒞ρ​(n^z(p))=Ne\sum_{z}\mathcal{C}_{\rho}(\hat{n}_{z}^{(p)})=N_{e}.

Static PE, Preparation: Our goal here is to compute the pair-correlation function in the Hdet state |Φ⁡(ρ¯)⟩|\Phi(\bar{\rho})\rangle in the thermodynamic limit using low order PE:

Goal: g[m](|z−w|)≡limNe→∞1n¯2⟨Φ(ρ¯)|n^z(e)n^w(e)|Φ(ρ¯)⟩[m],\displaystyle\textbf{Goal: }g_{[m]}(|z-w|)\equiv\lim_{N_{e}\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{\bar{n}^{2}}\langle\Phi(\bar{\rho})|\hat{n}_{z}^{(e)}\hat{n}_{w}^{(e)}|\Phi(\bar{\rho})\rangle_{[m]}, (521)

Fortunately, due to R=1R=1, the exact Hdet state can be efficiently simulated by Monte Carlo, so that the PE results g[m]​(r)g_{[m]}(r) with m=0,1,2m=0,1,2 can be directly compared with the exact pair correlation function g⁡(r)g(r). Here, the electron density per site is:

n¯≡n¯(e)=⟨Φ⁡(ρ¯)|n^z(e)|Φ⁡(ρ¯)⟩=Ne(Ns(e))2=12​Ns(e).\displaystyle\bar{n}\equiv\bar{n}^{(e)}=\langle\Phi(\bar{\rho})|\hat{n}_{z}^{(e)}|\Phi(\bar{\rho})\rangle=\frac{N_{e}}{(N_{s}^{(e)})^{2}}=\frac{1}{2N^{(e)}_{s}}. (522)

Note ν=NeNs(e)=12\nu=\frac{N_{e}}{N_{s}^{(e)}}=\frac{1}{2}. Since the parton number of each species equals the electron number, we also have:

n¯(e)=n¯(1)=n¯(2)=n¯.\displaystyle\bar{n}^{(e)}=\bar{n}^{(1)}=\bar{n}^{(2)}=\bar{n}. (523)

We will soon apply Wick’s theorem to compute the expectation values ⟨…⟩ρ¯\langle...\rangle_{\bar{\rho}}. According to Eq.(79), the fundamental expectation value is (z,w∈Fine-Grid)(z,w\in\text{Fine-Grid}):

⟨fw(p)†fz(p)⟩ρ¯=n¯(p)⟨z(p)|w(p)⟩0​L​L=n¯e−|w|2+|z|24​(l(p))2+w¯​z2​(l(p))2,\displaystyle\langle f^{(p)\dagger}_{w}f^{(p)}_{z}\rangle_{\bar{\rho}}=\bar{n}^{(p)}\langle z^{(p)}|w^{(p)}\rangle_{0LL}=\bar{n}\;e^{-\frac{|w|^{2}+|z|^{2}}{4(l^{(p)})^{2}}+\frac{\bar{w}z}{2(l^{(p)})^{2}}}, (524)

where we used the overlap between two coherent states for parton-pp (p=1,2.p=1,2.) before the change of viewpoint in Eq.(51). Although Eq.(51) is obtained for the disk geometry, in the thermodynamic limit, the result for the torus sample is the same, provided care is taken to choose the z,wz,w torus image positions to be the closest pair.

We define a dimensionless operator:

d^z≡n^z(1)​n^z(2)n¯2.\displaystyle\hat{d}_{z}\equiv\frac{\hat{n}_{z}^{(1)}\hat{n}_{z}^{(2)}}{\bar{n}^{2}}. (525)

For any pairwise distinct set of sites: Z≡{z1,…,zN}∈Fine-GridZ\equiv\{z_{1},...,z_{N}\}\in\text{Fine-Grid}, define:

d^Z=d^{z1,…,zN}≡∏i=1Nd^zi,\displaystyle\hat{d}_{Z}=\hat{d}_{\{z_{1},...,z_{N}\}}\equiv\prod_{i=1}^{N}\hat{d}_{z_{i}}, (526)

Wick’s theorem leads to:

⟨d^Z⟩ρ¯=[det𝖬Z]2,\displaystyle\left\langle\hat{d}_{Z}\right\rangle_{\bar{\rho}}=[\det\mathsf{M}_{Z}]^{2}, (527)

where the N×NN\times N matrix 𝖬Z\mathsf{M}_{Z} is defined as:

[𝖬Z]i​j≡e−|zi|2+|zj|24​(l(p))2+z¯i​zj2​(l(p))2,(l(p))2=2.\displaystyle[\mathsf{M}_{Z}]_{ij}\equiv e^{-\frac{|z_{i}|^{2}+|z_{j}|^{2}}{4(l^{(p)})^{2}}+\frac{\bar{z}_{i}z_{j}}{2(l^{(p)})^{2}}},\;\;(l^{(p)})^{2}=2. (528)

The pair correlation function (z≠wz\neq w) of the parton mean-field state is nothing but:

g(p)​(|z−w|)=1n¯2​⟨n^z(p)​n^w(p)⟩ρ¯=det𝖬{z,w},\displaystyle g^{(p)}(|z-w|)=\frac{1}{\bar{n}^{2}}\langle\hat{n}^{(p)}_{z}\hat{n}^{(p)}_{w}\rangle_{\bar{\rho}}=\det\mathsf{M}_{\{z,w\}}, (529)

giving the well-known result in the thermodynamic limit:

g(p)​(r)=1−e−r22​(l(p))2=1−e−r24.\displaystyle g^{(p)}(r)=1-e^{-\frac{r^{2}}{2(l^{(p)})^{2}}}=1-e^{-\frac{r^{2}}{4}}. (530)

For later purposes, we also define the connected parton mean-field pair-correlation function (z≠wz\neq w):

h(p)​(|z−w|)=1n¯2​𝒞ρ¯​(n^z(p),n^w(p)),\displaystyle h^{(p)}(|z-w|)=\frac{1}{\bar{n}^{2}}\mathcal{C}_{\bar{\rho}}(\hat{n}^{(p)}_{z},\hat{n}^{(p)}_{w}), (531)

in the thermodynamic limit:

h(p)​(r)=g(p)​(r)−1=−e−r24.\displaystyle h^{(p)}(r)=g^{(p)}(r)-1=-e^{-\frac{r^{2}}{4}}. (532)

Assuming z,w,x,yz,w,x,y are pairwise distinct, we list a few useful ordered-cumulants involving d^z\hat{d}_{z}:

𝒞ρ¯​(d^z)=\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\bar{\rho}}(\hat{d}_{z})= 1\displaystyle 1
𝒞ρ¯​(d^z,d^x)=\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\bar{\rho}}(\hat{d}_{z},\hat{d}_{x})= [det𝖬{z,x}]2−1\displaystyle[\det\mathsf{M}_{\{z,x\}}]^{2}-1
𝒞ρ¯​(d^z,d^x,d^y)=\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\bar{\rho}}(\hat{d}_{z},\hat{d}_{x},\hat{d}_{y})= [det𝖬{z,x,y}]2−[det𝖬{z,x}]2\displaystyle[\det\mathsf{M}_{\{z,x,y\}}]^{2}-[\det\mathsf{M}_{\{z,x\}}]^{2}
−\displaystyle- [det𝖬{z,y}]2−[det𝖬{x,y}]2+2,\displaystyle[\det\mathsf{M}_{\{z,y\}}]^{2}-[\det\mathsf{M}_{\{x,y\}}]^{2}+2, (533)

and a few ordered cumulants involving d^{z,w}\hat{d}_{\{z,w\}}:

𝒞ρ¯​(d^{z,w})=\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\bar{\rho}}(\hat{d}_{\{z,w\}})= [det𝖬{z,w}]2\displaystyle[\det\mathsf{M}_{\{z,w\}}]^{2}
𝒞ρ¯​(d^{z,w},d^x)=\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\bar{\rho}}(\hat{d}_{\{z,w\}},\hat{d}_{x})= [det𝖬{z,w,x}]2−[det𝖬{z,w}]2\displaystyle[\det\mathsf{M}_{\{z,w,x\}}]^{2}-[\det\mathsf{M}_{\{z,w\}}]^{2}
𝒞ρ¯​(d^{z,w},d^x,d^y)=\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\bar{\rho}}(\hat{d}_{\{z,w\}},\hat{d}_{x},\hat{d}_{y})= [det𝖬{z,w,x,y}]2−[det𝖬{z,w,x}]2\displaystyle[\det\mathsf{M}_{\{z,w,x,y\}}]^{2}-[\det\mathsf{M}_{\{z,w,x\}}]^{2}
−\displaystyle- [det𝖬{z,w,y}]2+2​[det𝖬{z,w}]2\displaystyle[\det\mathsf{M}_{\{z,w,y\}}]^{2}+2[\det\mathsf{M}_{\{z,w\}}]^{2}
−\displaystyle- [det𝖬{z,w}]2​[det𝖬{x,y}]2.\displaystyle[\det\mathsf{M}_{\{z,w\}}]^{2}[\det\mathsf{M}_{\{x,y\}}]^{2}. (534)

For the purpose of computing g⁡(r)g(r), let’s write down the relevant 𝐎^D​(ϵ)\hat{\mathbf{O}}_{D}(\epsilon) operators for the single-site electron density O^D(e)=n^z(e)\hat{O}^{(e)}_{D}=\hat{n}_{z}^{(e)} and electron’s pair-density O^D(e)=n^z(e)​n^w(e)\hat{O}^{(e)}_{D}=\hat{n}_{z}^{(e)}\hat{n}_{w}^{(e)} (z≠wz\neq w). Following the definition Eq.(424), we have:

𝐧^z​(ϵ)=\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{z}(\epsilon)= γ⁡(ϵ)​n^z(1)​n^z(2)=n¯2​γ​(ϵ)​d^z,\displaystyle\gamma(\epsilon)\hat{n}_{z}^{(1)}\hat{n}_{z}^{(2)}=\bar{n}^{2}\gamma(\epsilon)\hat{d}_{z},
[𝐧^z​𝐧^w]​(ϵ)=\displaystyle[\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{z}\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{w}](\epsilon)= 𝐧^z​(ϵ)​𝐧^w​(ϵ)=n¯4​γ​(ϵ)2​d^{z,w}.\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{z}(\epsilon)\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{w}(\epsilon)=\bar{n}^{4}\gamma(\epsilon)^{2}\hat{d}_{\{z,w\}}. (535)

For reasons that will become clear soon, we write γ⁡(ϵ)\gamma(\epsilon) in terms of γ~​(ϵ)\tilde{\gamma}(\epsilon), defined as:

γ~​(ϵ)≡n¯​γ​(ϵ).\displaystyle\tilde{\gamma}(\epsilon)\equiv\bar{n}\gamma(\epsilon). (536)

To the first few orders:

𝐧^z,(0)=\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{z,(0)}= n¯​γ~(0)​d^z,\displaystyle\bar{n}\tilde{\gamma}_{(0)}\hat{d}_{z},
𝐧^z,(1)=\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{z,(1)}= n¯​γ~(1)​d^z,\displaystyle\bar{n}\tilde{\gamma}_{(1)}\hat{d}_{z},
𝐧^z,(2)=\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{z,(2)}= n¯​γ~(2)​d^z,\displaystyle\bar{n}\tilde{\gamma}_{(2)}\hat{d}_{z},
[𝐧^z​𝐧^w](0)=\displaystyle[\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{z}\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{w}]_{(0)}= n¯2​γ~(0)2​d^{z,w},\displaystyle\bar{n}^{2}\tilde{\gamma}_{(0)}^{2}\hat{d}_{\{z,w\}},
[𝐧^z​𝐧^w](1)=\displaystyle[\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{z}\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{w}]_{(1)}= n¯2⋅2​γ~(0)​γ~(1)​d^{z,w},\displaystyle\bar{n}^{2}\cdot 2\tilde{\gamma}_{(0)}\tilde{\gamma}_{(1)}\hat{d}_{\{z,w\}},
[𝐧^z​𝐧^w](2)=\displaystyle[\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{z}\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{w}]_{(2)}= n¯2⋅[2​γ~(0)​γ~(2)+γ~(1)2]​d^{z,w}.\displaystyle\bar{n}^{2}\cdot[2\tilde{\gamma}_{(0)}\tilde{\gamma}_{(2)}+\tilde{\gamma}_{(1)}^{2}]\hat{d}_{\{z,w\}}. (537)

Computing γ~(m)\tilde{\gamma}_{(m)}: Let’s first compute γ(0)\gamma_{(0)} using the sum-rule Eq.(432). Using magnetic translation symmetry, to the zeroth-order, Eq.(476,479,481,537) lead to:

n¯=⟨n^z(e)⟩(0)=n~z,(0)=n¯​γ(0)​𝒞ρ¯​(d^z)=γ~(0)​n¯.\displaystyle\bar{n}=\langle\hat{n}^{(e)}_{z}\rangle_{(0)}=\widetilde{n}_{z,(0)}=\bar{n}\gamma_{(0)}\mathcal{C}_{\bar{\rho}}(\hat{d}_{z})=\tilde{\gamma}_{(0)}\bar{n}. (538)

Namely:

γ~(0)=1.\displaystyle\tilde{\gamma}_{(0)}=1. (539)

In fact, we will see soon that to all orders, γ(m)\gamma_{(m)} scales as γ(m)∼1n¯\gamma_{(m)}\sim\frac{1}{\bar{n}}, justifying the normalized γ~​(ϵ)\tilde{\gamma}(\epsilon). This scaling also simplifies the calculation in the thermodynamic limit: one can safely replace the (1+γ(0))(1+\gamma_{(0)}) by γ(0)\gamma_{(0)} in Eq.(518):

𝒒^z,(1)=\displaystyle\hat{\bm{q}}_{z,(1)}= −n^z(1)−n^z(2)+n¯​γ~(0)​d^z+O⁡(n¯2),\displaystyle-\hat{n}_{z}^{(1)}-\hat{n}_{z}^{(2)}+\bar{n}\tilde{\gamma}_{(0)}\hat{d}_{z}+O(\bar{n}^{2}),
𝒒^z,(2)=\displaystyle\hat{\bm{q}}_{z,(2)}= n¯​γ~(1)​d^z.\displaystyle\bar{n}\tilde{\gamma}_{(1)}\hat{d}_{z}. (540)

Basically, all 𝐪^z,(m)\hat{\bm{q}}_{z,(m)} and 𝐧^z,(m)\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{z,(m)} scale as n¯\bar{n}, and [𝐧^z​𝐧^w](m)[\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{z}\hat{\mathbf{n}}_{w}]_{(m)} scales as n¯2\bar{n}^{2}. We will ignore the O⁡(n¯2)O(\bar{n}^{2}) term in 𝒒^z,(1)\hat{\bm{q}}_{z,(1)} below since it does not contribute in the thermodynamic limit.

Next, we fix γ~(1)\tilde{\gamma}_{(1)}. The sum-rule Eq.(432) requires ⟨n^z(e)⟩(1)=0\langle\hat{n}^{(e)}_{z}\rangle_{(1)}=0. Eq.(481) demands us to compute n~z,(1)\widetilde{n}_{z,(1)} and Δz,(1)\Delta_{z,(1)}. According to Eq.(476,537,540), we have:

n~z,(1)\displaystyle\widetilde{n}_{z,(1)} =𝒞ρ¯​(n¯​γ~(1)​d^z)\displaystyle=\mathcal{C}_{\bar{\rho}}(\bar{n}\tilde{\gamma}_{(1)}\hat{d}_{z})
+∑w≠z𝒞ρ¯(n¯γ~(0)d^z,−n^w(1)−n^w(2)+n¯γ~(0)d^w)\displaystyle+\sum_{w\neq z}\mathcal{C}_{\bar{\rho}}(\bar{n}\tilde{\gamma}_{(0)}\hat{d}_{z},-\hat{n}_{w}^{(1)}-\hat{n}_{w}^{(2)}+\bar{n}\tilde{\gamma}_{(0)}\hat{d}_{w})
=\displaystyle= n¯​γ~(1)+n¯​𝒞ρ¯​(d^z,n^z(1)+n^z(2))+n¯2​∑w≠z𝒞ρ¯​(d^z,d^w),\displaystyle\bar{n}\tilde{\gamma}_{(1)}+\bar{n}\mathcal{C}_{\bar{\rho}}(\hat{d}_{z},\hat{n}_{z}^{(1)}+\hat{n}_{z}^{(2)})+\bar{n}^{2}\sum_{w\neq z}\mathcal{C}_{\bar{\rho}}(\hat{d}_{z},\hat{d}_{w}), (541)

where the exact sum rule Eq.(520) is used.

Because d^z​n^z(p)=d^z\hat{d}_{z}\hat{n}_{z}^{(p)}=\hat{d}_{z}, using Eq.(457):

𝒞ρ¯​(d^z,n^z(p))=(1−⟨n^z(p)⟩ρ¯)​⟨d^z⟩ρ¯=1−n¯=1+O⁡(n¯).\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\bar{\rho}}(\hat{d}_{z},\hat{n}_{z}^{(p)})=(1-\langle\hat{n}^{(p)}_{z}\rangle_{\bar{\rho}})\langle\hat{d}_{z}\rangle_{\bar{\rho}}=1-\bar{n}=1+O(\bar{n}). (542)

In the thermodynamic limit, it is safe to ignore the O⁡(n¯)O(\bar{n})-term above, and 𝖦(1)≡n¯​∑w≠z𝒞ρ¯​(d^z,d^w)\mathsf{G}_{(1)}\equiv\bar{n}\sum_{w\neq z}\mathcal{C}_{\bar{\rho}}(\hat{d}_{z},\hat{d}_{w}) can be converted into a continuum integral: n¯∑w≠z→12∫d2​w2​π\bar{n}\sum_{w\neq z}\rightarrow\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{d^{2}w}{2\pi}, where the factor 12\frac{1}{2} is from the filling fraction ν\nu. Using Eq.(533), this integral can be computed analytically:

𝖦(1)=∫d2​w4​π​[[det𝖬{z,w}]2−1]=−32.\displaystyle\mathsf{G}_{(1)}=\int\frac{d^{2}w}{4\pi}\Big[[\det\mathsf{M}_{\{z,w\}}]^{2}-1\Big]=-\frac{3}{2}. (543)

We arrive at:

n~z,(1)\displaystyle\widetilde{n}_{z,(1)} =n¯​[γ~(1)+2]+n¯​𝖦(1)\displaystyle=\bar{n}[\tilde{\gamma}_{(1)}+2]+\bar{n}\mathsf{G}_{(1)}
=n¯​[γ~(1)+12].\displaystyle=\bar{n}[\tilde{\gamma}_{(1)}+\frac{1}{2}]. (544)

Next we compute Δz,(1)\Delta_{z,(1)}, based on Eq.(479):

Δz,(1)=𝒞ρ¯​(𝒒^z,(1))=O⁡(n¯).\displaystyle\Delta_{z,(1)}=\mathcal{C}_{\bar{\rho}}(\hat{\bm{q}}_{z,(1)})=O(\bar{n}). (545)

In fact, it is easy to see that to any order ΔD,(m)=O⁡(n¯)\Delta_{D,(m)}=O(\bar{n}) for any finite operator support DD. But only the O⁡(n¯0)O(\bar{n}^{0}) order of ΔD\Delta_{D} can contribute in the thermodynamic limit due to Eq.(481). Therefore, in the thermodynamic limit, in the present Fine-Grid calculation, we can safely set ΔD​(ϵ)=0\Delta_{D}(\epsilon)=0, and consequently:

⟨n^z(e)⟩(m)=\displaystyle\langle\hat{n}^{(e)}_{z}\rangle_{(m)}= n~z,(m),\displaystyle\widetilde{n}_{z,(m)}, ⟨n^z(e)​n^w(e)⟩(m)=\displaystyle\langle\hat{n}^{(e)}_{z}\hat{n}^{(e)}_{w}\rangle_{(m)}= nz​nw~(m),∀m.\displaystyle\widetilde{n_{z}n_{w}}_{(m)},\;\;\forall m. (546)

The sum-rule Eq.(432) then dictates:

γ~(1)=−12.\displaystyle\tilde{\gamma}_{(1)}=-\frac{1}{2}. (547)

We move on to compute γ~(2)\tilde{\gamma}_{(2)}. We only need to compute n~z,(2)=0\widetilde{n}_{z,(2)}=0. According to Eq.(476,537,540), we have:

n~z,(2)=n¯​γ~(2)+∑w≠z𝒞ρ¯​(n¯​γ~(1)​d^z,−n^w(1)−n^w(2)+n¯​d^w)\displaystyle\widetilde{n}_{z,(2)}=\bar{n}\tilde{\gamma}_{(2)}+\sum_{w\neq z}\mathcal{C}_{\bar{\rho}}(\bar{n}\tilde{\gamma}_{(1)}\hat{d}_{z},-\hat{n}_{w}^{(1)}-\hat{n}_{w}^{(2)}+\bar{n}\hat{d}_{w})
+∑w≠z𝒞ρ¯(n¯d^z,n¯γ~(1)d^w)\displaystyle+\sum_{w\neq z}\mathcal{C}_{\bar{\rho}}(\bar{n}\hat{d}_{z},\bar{n}\tilde{\gamma}_{(1)}\hat{d}_{w})
+12∑w,x′zC𝒞ρ¯(n¯d^z,−n^w(1)−n^w(2)+n¯d^w,−n^x(1)−n^x(2)+n¯d^x)\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2}\sum^{\prime z^{C}}_{w,x}\mathcal{C}_{\bar{\rho}}(\bar{n}\hat{d}_{z},-\hat{n}_{w}^{(1)}-\hat{n}_{w}^{(2)}+\bar{n}\hat{d}_{w},-\hat{n}_{x}^{(1)}-\hat{n}_{x}^{(2)}+\bar{n}\hat{d}_{x})
−∑w≠z𝒞ρ¯(n¯d^z,−n^w(1)−n^w(2)+n¯d^w)𝒞ρ¯(−n^w(1)−n^w(2)+n¯d^w)\displaystyle-\sum_{w\neq z}\mathcal{C}_{\bar{\rho}}(\bar{n}\hat{d}_{z},-\hat{n}_{w}^{(1)}-\hat{n}_{w}^{(2)}+\bar{n}\hat{d}_{w})\mathcal{C}_{\bar{\rho}}(-\hat{n}_{w}^{(1)}-\hat{n}_{w}^{(2)}+\bar{n}\hat{d}_{w}) (548)

The second and third terms have the same form as the term computed before in n~z,(1)\widetilde{n}_{z,(1)}, we do not repeat the calculation. The last term ∝n¯2\propto\bar{n}^{2} can be safely ignored in the thermodynamic limit. Let’s focus on the fourth term:

12​∑w,x′zC𝒞ρ¯​(n¯​d^z,−n^w(1)−n^w(2)+n¯​d^w,−n^x(1)−n^x(2)+n¯​d^x)\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\sum^{\prime z^{C}}_{w,x}\mathcal{C}_{\bar{\rho}}(\bar{n}\hat{d}_{z},-\hat{n}_{w}^{(1)}-\hat{n}_{w}^{(2)}+\bar{n}\hat{d}_{w},-\hat{n}_{x}^{(1)}-\hat{n}_{x}^{(2)}+\bar{n}\hat{d}_{x})
=\displaystyle= ∑w,x′zC[n¯𝒞ρ¯(d^z,n^w(1),n^x(1))+n¯𝒞ρ¯(d^z,n^w(1),n^x(2))\displaystyle\sum^{\prime z^{C}}_{w,x}\Big[\bar{n}\mathcal{C}_{\bar{\rho}}(\hat{d}_{z},\hat{n}_{w}^{(1)},\hat{n}_{x}^{(1)})+\bar{n}\mathcal{C}_{\bar{\rho}}(\hat{d}_{z},\hat{n}_{w}^{(1)},\hat{n}_{x}^{(2)})
−2n¯2𝒞ρ¯(d^z,d^w,n^x(1))+12n¯3𝒞ρ¯(d^z,d^w,d^x)]\displaystyle-2\bar{n}^{2}\mathcal{C}_{\bar{\rho}}(\hat{d}_{z},\hat{d}_{w},\hat{n}_{x}^{(1)})+\frac{1}{2}\bar{n}^{3}\mathcal{C}_{\bar{\rho}}(\hat{d}_{z},\hat{d}_{w},\hat{d}_{x})\Big]
≡\displaystyle\equiv Az+Bz+Cz+Dz,\displaystyle A_{z}+B_{z}+C_{z}+D_{z}, (549)

where we used the parton-species permutation symmetry for the Laughlin state and the invariance of cumulants under the rearrangement of adjacent commuting operators.

We plot these PE pair correlation functions, together with the previously published Monte Carlo(MC) result (Ne=196N_{e}=196)[27] in Fig.7. Clearly, as the PE order increases, the pair correlation becomes very accurate for the short-range part, while the longer-range part is still not fully captured. This is expected since PE is a local expansion. In fact, the integral of g⁡(r)g(r) should satisfy the exact electron-number sum rule:

S≡12​∫d2​z2​π​[g⁡(|z|)−1]=−1.\displaystyle S\equiv\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{d^{2}z}{2\pi}[g(|z|)-1]=-1. (569)

which follows from Eq.(455). The results are:

S[0]=\displaystyle S_{[0]}= −32,\displaystyle-\frac{3}{2}, S[1]=\displaystyle S_{[1]}= −56,\displaystyle-\frac{5}{6}, S[2]=\displaystyle S_{[2]}= −3130.\displaystyle-\frac{31}{30}. (572)

As the order increases, the sum-rule is better and better approximated. This violation of the electron-number sum rule suggests that the long-range Coulomb interaction may be challenging to simulate well using PE, which we will explore shortly in Sec.VI.3.3.

PE for quantum geometric tensors, Preparation: When computing the quantum geometric tensor 𝒬a​b\mathcal{Q}_{ab} for general tangent vectors X^a,X^b\hat{X}_{a},\hat{X}_{b}, one would go outside the LLL of partons, and R>1R>1 fusion channels will be present. In this simple benchmark test, we avoid this technical complication by focusing on specific tangent vectors on the mean-field saddle point: X^a\hat{X}_{a} and X^b\hat{X}_{b} are generators of the pure gauge transformation.

Since the U⁡(1)U(1) gauge charges of the two partons are q(1)=1{\rm q}^{(1)}=1, q(2)=−1{\rm q}^{(2)}=-1, we define the gauge charge density:

n^zg≡n^z(1)−n^z(2).\displaystyle\hat{n}^{g}_{z}\equiv\hat{n}^{(1)}_{z}-\hat{n}^{(2)}_{z}. (573)

The pure gauge generator at momentum 𝐩\mathbf{p} is:

G^𝐩≡1Ns(e)​∑zei​𝐩⋅𝐫z​n^zg,\displaystyle\hat{G}_{\mathbf{p}}\equiv\frac{1}{\sqrt{N^{(e)}_{s}}}\sum_{z}e^{i\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{z}}\hat{n}^{g}_{z}, (574)

where 𝐫z≡(Re​[z],Im​[z])\mathbf{r}_{z}\equiv(\text{Re}[z],\text{Im}[z]). G^𝐩=G^−𝐩†\hat{G}_{\mathbf{p}}=\hat{G}^{\dagger}_{-\mathbf{p}} generates a pure gauge transformation as a unitary rotation:

|ΨM​F(ρ¯)⟩→e−i∑𝐩θ𝐩G^𝐩|ΨM​F(ρ¯)⟩,\displaystyle|\Psi^{MF}(\bar{\rho})\rangle\rightarrow e^{-i\sum_{\mathbf{p}}\theta_{\mathbf{p}}\hat{G}_{\mathbf{p}}}|\Psi^{MF}(\bar{\rho})\rangle, (575)

where Hermiticity requires θ𝐩=θ−𝐩∗\theta_{\mathbf{p}}=\theta^{*}_{-\mathbf{p}}. If we choose parameters a=Re⁡[θ𝐩]a={\rm Re}[\theta_{\mathbf{p}}], b=Im⁡[θ𝐩]b={\rm Im}[\theta_{\mathbf{p}}], the parton bilinear operators defined in Eq.(438) are X^a​(𝐩)=(−i)​[G^𝐩+G^−𝐩],X^b​(𝐩)=G^𝐩−G^−𝐩\hat{X}_{a}(\mathbf{p})=(-i)[\hat{G}_{\mathbf{p}}+\hat{G}_{-\mathbf{p}}],\hat{X}_{b}(\mathbf{p})=\hat{G}_{\mathbf{p}}-\hat{G}_{-\mathbf{p}}. Due to magnetic translation symmetry, apart from isolated 𝐩\mathbf{p} points satisfying −𝐩=𝐩-\mathbf{p}=\mathbf{p}, it is easy to show that 𝒬a​b​(ϵ)\mathcal{Q}_{ab}(\epsilon) has the form:

𝒬a​b​(ϵ)=2​𝒬𝐩​(ϵ)​δa​b,\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}_{ab}(\epsilon)=2\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{p}}(\epsilon)\delta_{ab}, (576)

where the real quantity 𝒬𝐩​(ϵ)\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{p}}(\epsilon) can be computed by considering

𝖷^a=𝖷^b=G^𝐩.\displaystyle\hat{\mathsf{X}}_{a}=\hat{\mathsf{X}}_{b}=\hat{G}_{\mathbf{p}}. (577)

Namely, 𝒬𝐩​(ϵ)\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{p}}(\epsilon) determines the quantum metric of the Hdet tangent states of pure gauge transformations.

The advantage of this benchmark test is that, since the exact Hdet states are not changed by a pure gauge transformation, we know the exact result at ϵ=1\epsilon=1:

Exact result: 𝒬𝐩=0,∀𝐩\displaystyle\text{Exact result: }\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{p}}=0,\;\;\forall\mathbf{p} (578)

The goal of this calculation is the low-order PE results in the thermodynamic-limit:

Goal: limNe→∞𝒬𝐩,[m].\displaystyle\textbf{Goal: }\lim_{N_{e}\rightarrow\infty}\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{p},[m]}. (579)

Using the general PE formula Eq.(439,484), we need to compute:

𝒬𝐩,(0)=\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{p},(0)}= 𝒞ρ¯​(G^−𝐩,G^𝐩),\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\bar{\rho}}(\hat{G}_{-\mathbf{p}},\hat{G}_{\mathbf{p}}),
𝒬𝐩,(1)=\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{p},(1)}= ∑x𝒞ρ¯​(G^−𝐩,𝒒^x,(1),G^𝐩),\displaystyle\sum_{x}\mathcal{C}_{\bar{\rho}}(\hat{G}_{-\mathbf{p}},\hat{\bm{q}}_{x,(1)},\hat{G}_{\mathbf{p}}),
𝒬𝐩,(2)=\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}_{\mathbf{p},(2)}= ∑x𝒞ρ¯​(G^−𝐩,𝒒^x,(2),G^𝐩)\displaystyle\sum_{x}\mathcal{C}_{\bar{\rho}}(\hat{G}_{-\mathbf{p}},\hat{\bm{q}}_{x,(2)},\hat{G}_{\mathbf{p}})
+12∑x≠y𝒞ρ¯(G^−𝐩,𝒒^x,(1),𝒒^y,(1),G^𝐩)\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{x\neq y}\mathcal{C}_{\bar{\rho}}(\hat{G}_{-\mathbf{p}},\hat{\bm{q}}_{x,(1)},\hat{\bm{q}}_{y,(1)},\hat{G}_{\mathbf{p}})

−∑x𝒞ρ¯(G^−𝐩,𝒒^x,(1))𝒞ρ¯(𝒒^x,(1),G^𝐩)\displaystyle-\sum_{x}\mathcal{C}_{\bar{\rho}}(\hat{G}_{-\mathbf{p}},\hat{\bm{q}}_{x,(1)})\mathcal{C}_{\bar{\rho}}(\hat{\bm{q}}_{x,(1)},\hat{G}_{\mathbf{p}}) (580)

These calculations will be performed in the real space: we write:

G^𝐩=\displaystyle\hat{G}_{\mathbf{p}}= 1Ns(e)​∑zei​𝐩⋅𝐫z​(n^z(1)−n^z(2))\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{N^{(e)}_{s}}}\sum_{z}e^{i\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{z}}(\hat{n}^{(1)}_{z}-\hat{n}^{(2)}_{z})
G^−𝐩=\displaystyle\hat{G}_{-\mathbf{p}}= 1Ns(e)∑we−i𝐩⋅𝐫w(n^w(1)−n^w(2)).\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{N^{(e)}_{s}}}\sum_{w}e^{-i\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{w}}(\hat{n}^{(1)}_{w}-\hat{n}^{(2)}_{w}). (581)

Note that, unlike the static PE calculation, we now have contact terms at z=wz=w or x=zx=z, etc. Only the PE operator sites are pairwise distinct, e.g., x≠yx\neq y.

VI.3.2 Fermionic Laughlin’s ν=13\nu=\frac{1}{3} state and Jain’s ν=25\nu=\frac{2}{5} state

Jain’s ν=25\nu=\frac{2}{5} state: pair correlation function. As the first benchmark example with R>1R>1, here we have the number of fusion channels R=4R=4, whose Hdet locality structure is given in Sec.III.2.4. The scaling γ(m)∝1n¯2\gamma_{(m)}\propto\frac{1}{\bar{n}^{2}} remains true, where n¯≡n¯(e)=Ne(Ns(e))2=25​Ns(e)\bar{n}\equiv\bar{n}^{(e)}=\frac{N_{e}}{(N_{s}^{(e)})^{2}}=\frac{2}{5N_{s}^{(e)}}. Since there are more than one parton-orbitals 𝐦(p)\mathbf{m}^{(p)} per site, we define the parton total density:
