which is used repeatedly to simplify the cumulants. In the thermodynamic limit, the relevant PE operators are:

𝒒^z,(1)=−s^z+n¯γ~0d^z,𝒒^z,(m)=n¯γ~(m−1)d^z,(m≥2).\displaystyle\hat{\bm{q}}_{z,(1)}=-\hat{s}_{z}+\bar{n}\tilde{\gamma}_{0}\hat{d}_{z},\;\;\hat{\bm{q}}_{z,(m)}=\bar{n}\tilde{\gamma}_{(m-1)}\hat{d}_{z},(m\geq 2). (605)

At this point, one could proceed with the PE process in the same fashion as the previous R=1R=1 examples, given the fusion channels/amplitudes in Eq.(75) and the parton RDM in Eq.(79). The only challenge is that the most cumulant integrals are complicated to evaluate analytically, but the numerical evaluation is still straightforward.

Uniform-parton-orbitals prescription: However, one PE-related technical issue needs to be addressed. In Eq.(79), where we defined the parton RDM after the change of viewpoint, one finds that there is a normalization factor 1Ncoh(p),a​L​L\frac{1}{N^{(p)}_{\rm coh},aLL}–the number of parton orbitals per site per LL. If one literally follows the parton orbital construction in Eq.(75), one would find for parton p=3p=3, per Fine-Grid site, the 0​L​L0LL has only one orbital: Ncoh,0​L​L(p)=1N^{(p)}_{{\rm coh},0LL}=1, while two orbitals are present for 1​L​L1LL: Ncoh,1​L​L(p)=2N^{(p)}_{{\rm coh},1LL}=2; Namely, the RDM for the coherent states in the 1​L​L1LL is effectively smaller by a factor of 2 compared with the 0​L​L0LL. A more natural way to define the parton RDM is to introduce parton orbitals so that 1N~coh,a​L​L(p)=1N~coh(p)\frac{1}{\tilde{N}^{(p)}_{{\rm coh},aLL}}=\frac{1}{\tilde{N}^{(p)}_{\rm coh}}, independent of the LL index-aa. Practically, it means that we can choose:

N~coh(p)=maxa∈𝖫(p)⁡[Ncoh,a​L​L(p)],\displaystyle\tilde{N}^{(p)}_{\rm coh}=\max_{a\in\mathsf{L}^{(p)}}[N^{(p)}_{{\rm coh},aLL}], (606)

where we introduced 𝖫(p)\mathsf{L}^{(p)} for the collection of LL indices for parton-pp: 𝖫(3)={0,1}\mathsf{L}^{(3)}=\{0,1\}. In the present example, N~coh,0​L​L(3)=N~coh,1​L​L(3)=2\tilde{N}^{(3)}_{{\rm coh},0LL}=\tilde{N}^{(3)}_{{\rm coh},1LL}=2, and the parton-RDM for the 0​L​L0LL and 1​L​L1LL are on the same footing. Despite letting 0​L​L0LL have two orbitals per site: {|z(0)(3)⟩0​L​L,|z(1)(3)⟩0​L​L}\{|z_{(0)}^{(3)}\rangle_{0LL},|z_{(1)}^{(3)}\rangle_{0LL}\}, only |z(0)(3)⟩0​L​L|z_{(0)}^{(3)}\rangle_{0LL} participates in the fusion as Eq.(75). Note that, although |z(1)(3)⟩0​L​L|z_{(1)}^{(3)}\rangle_{0LL} is unused in fusion, it still participates in the exact parton-number sum-rule Eq.(604). We call this prescription uniform-parton-orbitals.

This uniform-parton-orbitals prescription is immaterial if one performs a full projection, since it only gives an overall constant factor for the exact Hdet wavefunction. But, for the low-order PE calculation, this prescription matters. Both calculations, with or without the prescription, lead to the same ϵ→1\epsilon\rightarrow 1 exact result. But for PE, they give different expansion coefficients.

Normalized-fusion-amplitude prescription: A related issue is about the fusion amplitudes. We have computed these fusion amplitudes in Eq.(75), based on the real-space prescription result Eq.(53,55). For fixed (a,b,c)(a,b,c) LL indices of parton-(1,2,3)(1,2,3), we have argued that the general form of the fusion amplitude Eq.(53) can be fixed by the Galilean invariance (see discussions near Eq.(51)), up to an overall factor, which we denote as M(a​b​c)M_{(abc)} here. If we write down the two relevant fusion operators for (a,b,c)=(0,0,0)(a,b,c)=(0,0,0) and (a,b,c)=(0,0,1)(a,b,c)=(0,0,1), using Eq.(76), we have 𝐅^z=𝐅^z,(0,0,0)+𝐅^z,(0,0,1)\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{z}=\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{z,(0,0,0)}+\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{z,(0,0,1)}, where

𝐅^z,(0,0,0)=\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{z,(0,0,0)}= cz†​fz,1(1)​fz,1(2)​fz,1(3)≡cz†​D^z,(0,0,0),\displaystyle c_{z}^{\dagger}f^{(1)}_{z,1}f^{(2)}_{z,1}f^{(3)}_{z,1}\equiv c_{z}^{\dagger}\hat{D}_{z,(0,0,0)},
𝐅^z,(0,0,1)=\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{z,(0,0,1)}= cz†[25fz,2(1)fz,1(2)fz,2(3)+25fz,1(1)fz,2(2)fz,2(3)\displaystyle c_{z}^{\dagger}\Big[\frac{\sqrt{2}}{5}f^{(1)}_{z,2}f^{(2)}_{z,1}f^{(3)}_{z,2}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{5}f^{(1)}_{z,1}f^{(2)}_{z,2}f^{(3)}_{z,2}
−45fz,1(1)fz,1(2)fz,3(3)]≡cz†D^z,(0,0,1).\displaystyle-\frac{4}{5}f^{(1)}_{z,1}f^{(2)}_{z,1}f^{(3)}_{z,3}\Big]\equiv c_{z}^{\dagger}\hat{D}_{z,(0,0,1)}. (607)

As mentioned before, one way to understand the locality structure is to view the fusion as the map from the electronic Hilbert space to the parton Hilbert space (see discussion below Eq.(50)). The parton operators D^z,(a,b,c)\hat{D}_{z,(a,b,c)} introduced above can be viewed as the ”parton-image-state” of the electron in the parton’s (a,b,c)(a,b,c)-LL sector. Note that, as parton many-body states, D^z,(0,0,0)\hat{D}_{z,(0,0,0)} is normalized, but D^z,(0,0,1)\hat{D}_{z,(0,0,1)} is not (norm=25=\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}). Namely, the norm of the parton-image-state depends on the LL-indices (a,b,c)(a,b,c).

Again, a more natural way to define the parton-image-state is to tune the overall factor M(a​b​c)M_{(abc)} so that, the parton-image-state is always normalized independent of (a,b,c)(a,b,c). After this is done, we have the following fusion operators: 𝐅~^z=𝐅~^z,(0,0,0)+𝐅~^z,(0,0,1)\hat{\widetilde{\mathbf{F}}}_{z}=\hat{\widetilde{\mathbf{F}}}_{z,(0,0,0)}+\hat{\widetilde{\mathbf{F}}}_{z,(0,0,1)}, where:

𝐅~z,(0,0,0)=\displaystyle{\widetilde{\mathbf{F}}}_{z,(0,0,0)}= cz†​fz,1(1)​fz,1(2)​fz,1(3)≡cz†​D~^z,(0,0,0),\displaystyle c_{z}^{\dagger}f^{(1)}_{z,1}f^{(2)}_{z,1}f^{(3)}_{z,1}\equiv c_{z}^{\dagger}\hat{\widetilde{D}}_{z,(0,0,0)},
𝐅~z,(0,0,1)=\displaystyle{\widetilde{\mathbf{F}}}_{z,(0,0,1)}= cz†[110fz,2(1)fz,1(2)fz,2(3)+110fz,1(1)fz,2(2)fz,2(3)\displaystyle c_{z}^{\dagger}\Big[\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}f^{(1)}_{z,2}f^{(2)}_{z,1}f^{(3)}_{z,2}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}f^{(1)}_{z,1}f^{(2)}_{z,2}f^{(3)}_{z,2}
−25fz,1(1)fz,1(2)fz,3(3)]≡cz†D~^z,(0,0,1).\displaystyle-\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}f^{(1)}_{z,1}f^{(2)}_{z,1}f^{(3)}_{z,3}\Big]\equiv c_{z}^{\dagger}\hat{\widetilde{D}}_{z,(0,0,1)}. (608)

D~^z,(0,0,1)=52​D^z,(0,0,1)\hat{\widetilde{D}}_{z,(0,0,1)}=\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}\hat{D}_{z,(0,0,1)} is now normalized. We call this procedure normalized-fusion-amplitude prescription.

Similarly, the normalized-fusion-amplitude prescription is immaterial for Jain’s sequence if one performs the full projection, since it only gives an overall constant factor for the exact Hdet state. But for the low-order PE analysis, this prescription matters.

Pair correlation results: We have applied both uniform-parton-orbitals and normalized-fusion-amplitude prescriptions. Performing the numerical integral for the cumulant expansion, we find:

γ~(0)=8,γ~(1)≈−9.837,γ~(2)≈2.118,\displaystyle\tilde{\gamma}_{(0)}=8,\qquad\tilde{\gamma}_{(1)}\approx-9.837,\qquad\tilde{\gamma}_{(2)}\approx 2.118, (609)

and we plot the thermodynamic-limit PE pair correlation function up to the second order in Fig.10. Note that due to R=4R=4, a large-size exact Monte Carlo (MC) simulation result is not available for comparison. On the other hand, Jain-Kamilla[67] developed a method to simulate the ν=25\nu=\frac{2}{5} FQH state, by writing it as a determinant with many-body coordinate-dependent entries, enabling a large-scale MC. Precisely speaking, the Jain-Kamilla ν=25\nu=\frac{2}{5} state is not the original Jain’s state, which we have shown to be an Hdet wavefunction with R=4R=4. Therefore, our PE simulation for the original Jain’s state should not be directly compared with the Jain-Kamilla state. Nevertheless, since the MC (extrapolated to the thermodynamic limit) result for the pair correlation of the Jain-Kamilla state is available in the literature[37], we also present it in the same figure, as a reference.

Noticeably, the pair correlation of the 2nd order PE is slightly higher than the Jain-Kamilla state at short-range r≲2r\lesssim 2 (it is worth mentioning that Ref[37] pointed out that their thermodynamic-limit extrapolation is not smooth in the small-rr regime), where the PE is supposed to be most accurate; while in the mid-range 2≲r≲42\lesssim r\lesssim 4, the 2nd order PE curve is slightly lower. Overall, the trend of the PE results and the Jain-Kamilla state’s published result broadly agree in the short- to mid-range. In the longer range, low-order PE is not expected to be accurate since it is a local expansion.

VI.3.3 Fermionic FCI models at ν=13\nu=\frac{1}{3}: zeroth-order PE saddle-point solutions and parton band structures

Models: We start by introducing the two type-(B) FCI models inside the LLL in the present benchmark test: the Haldane-V1V_{1} model and the bare-Coulomb model. The many-body electron Hamiltonian of both models can be written in the following form:

H^=λ⋅K^+U^,\displaystyle\hat{H}=\lambda\cdot\hat{K}+\hat{U}, (610)

where λ\lambda is a real parameter, K^\hat{K} is a single-body kinetic energy term, and U^\hat{U} is a normal-ordered two-body interaction term.

The difference between the two models only lies in the interaction term: for the Haldane-V1V_{1} model, U^V1\hat{U}_{V_{1}} describes the Haldane-pseudopotential interactions inside the LLL with V1=1V_{1}=1 and all other pseudopotential components being zero, a short-range interaction model; while for the bare-Coulomb model, U^Coul.\hat{U}_{\rm Coul.} describes the long-range bare Coulomb interaction in the LLL. Namely, when λ=0\lambda=0, these FCI systems go back to the well-studied FQH systems. We focus on ν=13\nu=\frac{1}{3}-filling: U^V1\hat{U}_{V_{1}} has Laughlin’s state as the exact zero energy ground state.

The FCI physics is turned on when λ≠0\lambda\neq 0. The kinetic energy term K^\hat{K}, which is the same for both models, describes a square periodic potential projected into the electron’s LLL:

K^≡∑u=x,y[𝝆¯​(𝐪u)+𝝆¯​(−𝐪u)]​e−|𝐪u|2​le24,\displaystyle\hat{K}\equiv\sum_{u=x,y}[\bar{\bm{\rho}}(\mathbf{q}_{u})+\bar{\bm{\rho}}(-\mathbf{q}_{u})]e^{-\frac{|\mathbf{q}_{u}|^{2}l_{e}^{2}}{4}}, (611)

where

𝐪x≡(2​πa,0),𝐪y≡(0,2​πa),a≡2​π⋅le.\displaystyle\mathbf{q}_{x}\equiv(\frac{2\pi}{a},0),\;\;\mathbf{q}_{y}\equiv(0,\frac{2\pi}{a}),\;\;a\equiv\sqrt{2\pi}\cdot l_{e}. (612)

Here e−|𝐪u|2​le24e^{-\frac{|\mathbf{q}_{u}|^{2}l_{e}^{2}}{4}} is the LLL form factor, and 𝝆¯​(𝐪)\bar{\bm{\rho}}(\mathbf{q}) is the Girvin-MacDonald-Platzman (GMP) density operator satisfying the magnetic translation algebra[41]. aa is the unit cell linear size of the square potential, satisfying one flux per unit cell.

At λ=0\lambda=0, the partons fill their LLL. λ≠0\lambda\neq 0 breaks the electron’s magnetic translation group in a FQH system down to the commuting magnetic translations of multiples of aa (denoted as square-potential-translation group). Consequently, the parton LLs will hybridize, and the saddle-point parton state (within the FCI phase) will fill a Chern band, which is a linear superposition of the parton LLs. One goal of the calculation is to find those superposition coefficients An,𝐤(p)A^{(p)}_{n,\mathbf{k}} in Eq.(100), where nn is the parton LL index. Here, as mentioned in Sec.IV.2, the detailed analysis of the fractionalized translation and rotation symmetry analysis – the projective symmetry group (PSG)[136] of partons becomes important: only PSG-allowed parton LL hybridization is present. We have implemented the full square-potential-translation and C4C_{4} rotation PSG into the present PE numerical study.

Simulation Details: At low energy, we expect only the lowest few parton LLs to contribute significantly to the saddle point Chern band. In the present benchmark test, we have kept parton-LL index from 00 up to 44. Namely, there are 5 parton LLs per parton species in our simulation. If we label the parton LL indices as (a,b,c)(a,b,c) for the three parton species: a,b,c=0,1,..4.a,b,c=0,1,..4.. The choice of 00 up to 44 LL indices is motivated by the C4C_{4} symmetry in the present models: on a C4C_{4}-symmetric sample, PSG analysis shows that the high-symmetry parton-𝐤\mathbf{k} points (e.g., the Γ\Gamma-point) will only hybridize LLs whose indices are the same mod 44. 00 up to 44 LLs allows nontrivial LL hybridization for all parton-𝐤\mathbf{k} points for the filled band.

Note that, if one keeps all the fusion channels according to Eq.(53), based on Eq.(57), the total number of fusion channels R=3875R=3875 would be too large. In our calculation, we keep only the fusion channels with (a,b,c)(a,b,c) of the form (3,0,0),(0,2,0),(0,0,4)(3,0,0),(0,2,0),(0,0,4), etc. Namely, among (a,b,c)(a,b,c), two are zeros. This reduces R=103R=103. This RR-reduction practice is motivated by two facts. First, note that this effectively means we set the factor M(a​b​c)M_{(abc)} to zero for any (a,b,c)(a,b,c) that contains more than one nonzero value – deviating from the literal real-space fusion prescription Eq.(53). However, this exercise is perfectly sound mathematically, because as long as the fusion amplitude is given by Eq.(53) up to an overall constant M(a​b​c)M_{(abc)}, the fusion for the overcomplete electron’s discrete-coherent-states on the Fine-Grid is self-consistent. Despite setting many M(a​b​c)=0M_{(abc)}=0, the Hdet’s full fusion tensor Ti​j​k​lT_{ijkl} is perfectly well-defined, giving a well-defined physical wavefunction inside the LLL. Second, as confirmed in our simulation, the dominant superposition weight in the filled parton Chern band is in the LLL: throughout the regimes in our simulation, the saddle point |An=0,𝐤(p)|2>0.95|A^{(p)}_{n=0,\mathbf{k}}|^{2}>0.95. Therefore, the fusion involving two or more nonzero parton LLs is a small effect anyway.

With this reduced R=103R=103, our PE calculation is performed with both uniform-parton-orbitals and normalized-fusion-amplitude prescriptions, and we utilized the fusion-channel-space algorithm in Sec.VI.2.4. Before proceeding, we emphasize again that the rather large RR is a technical complexity induced by insisting on working within a Chern band (i.e., as a Type-(B) model introduced in Sec.IV), which may not be physically necessary. If one works outside the topological band as in a Type-(A) model, the physically necessary RR describing the parton entanglement may not be as large.

On a finite torus, we apply the zeroth-order PE to approximately compute the Fine-Grid expectation values ⟨Φ⁡(ρ)|n^z(e)|Φ⁡(ρ)⟩\langle\Phi(\rho)|\hat{n}_{z}^{(e)}|\Phi(\rho)\rangle and ⟨Φ⁡(ρ)|n^z(e)​n^w(e)|Φ⁡(ρ)⟩\langle\Phi(\rho)|\hat{n}_{z}^{(e)}\hat{n}_{w}^{(e)}|\Phi(\rho)\rangle (z,w∈Fine−Gridz,w\in{\rm Fine-Grid}). Following the prescription of Wang et.al.[129] Eq.(417), both ⟨Φ⁡(ρ)|K^|Φ⁡(ρ)⟩\langle\Phi(\rho)|\hat{K}|\Phi(\rho)\rangle and ⟨Φ⁡(ρ)|U^|Φ⁡(ρ)⟩\langle\Phi(\rho)|\hat{U}|\Phi(\rho)\rangle can be computed, so is the variational energy E⁡(ρ)E(\rho).

To find the saddle |Φ⁡(ρ¯)⟩|\Phi(\bar{\rho})\rangle, in terms of the general algorithm, one starts with some initial parton RDM ρ1\rho_{1}. By computing the derivative of E⁡(ρ1)E(\rho_{1}), the effective single-body Hamiltonian h^​(ρ1)\hat{h}(\rho_{1}) can be found as in Eq.(296). The RDM of the ground state of h^​(ρ1)\hat{h}(\rho_{1}) will be denoted as ρ2\rho_{2}, and the process continues until the self-consistent condition is achieved – the ground state of h^​(ρ¯)\hat{h}(\bar{\rho}) is also ρ¯\bar{\rho}. For the stability of the algorithm, we have applied a standard linear mixing parameter β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1): instead of ρn\rho_{n}, we use ρ~n\tilde{\rho}_{n} defined as the McWeeny purification[89] of ρn−1+β⁡(ρn−ρn−1)\rho_{n-1}+\beta(\rho_{n}-\rho_{n-1}). Here, since we are dealing with a type-(B) model, following Eq.(413), ρi\rho_{i} in this iteration should be understood as ρm,n;𝟎​(𝐤)\rho_{m,n;\mathbf{0}}(\mathbf{k}) in the parton’s LL basis, and the effective single-body Hamiltonian should be understood as 𝗁^​(𝐤)\hat{\mathsf{h}}(\mathbf{k}) in Eq.(413).

Varying λ\lambda, we find the zeroth-order PE optimal states on the 12x12 unit-cell sample with 4848 electrons, utilizing the full square-potential-translation and C4C_{4} symmetry (i.e., PSG for partons). Each optimal state is labeled by {ρ¯m,n;𝟎​(𝐤)}\{\bar{\rho}_{m,n;\mathbf{0}}(\mathbf{k})\} at 4848 parton-𝐤\mathbf{k} points (Recall that due to the fractionalization of translation, the unit cell of partons is three times as large as that of electrons). They are PSG-related, forming 6 PSG-independent groups of 𝐤\mathbf{k} points.

Within the Hdet construction, we expect the saddle point satisfies I​G​G=U​(1)a×U​(1)bIGG=U(1)_{a}\times U(1)_{b}, corresponding to gauge changes: qa(1)=1,qa(2)=−1,qa(3)=0{\rm q}_{a}^{(1)}=1,{\rm q}_{a}^{(2)}=-1,{\rm q}_{a}^{(3)}=0, and qb(1)=1,qb(2)=0,qb(3)=−1{\rm q}_{b}^{(1)}=1,{\rm q}_{b}^{(2)}=0,{\rm q}_{b}^{(3)}=-1. However, throughout the regimes studied, We find that, the saddle states satisfy ρ¯(1)=ρ¯(2)=ρ¯(3)\bar{\rho}^{(1)}=\bar{\rho}^{(2)}=\bar{\rho}^{(3)}, implying a larger I​G​GIGG in a generalized construction (see discussion below).

We then compare the Hdet wavefunction constructed from these (zeroth-order PE approximated) saddle points with wavefunctions obtained from exact diagonalization (ED) on the 6x4 sample with 8 electrons. In order to perform this comparison, we choose the 8 parton-𝐤\mathbf{k} points from the 12x12 sample matching the 6x4 system(see Fig.11 for the illustration), and use the corresponding saddle-point {ρ¯m,n;𝟎​(𝐤)}\{\bar{\rho}_{m,n;\mathbf{0}}(\mathbf{k})\} to construct the full fusion tensor Ti​j​k​lT_{ijkl} as in Eq.(14) based on the local fusion gate 𝐂^z\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{z}. The overlaps between the Hdet saddle-point wavefunctions |Φ⁡(ρ¯)⟩|\Phi(\bar{\rho})\rangle and the ED ground states are then computed exactly by fully computing the many-body wavefunction |Φ⁡(ρ¯)⟩|\Phi(\bar{\rho})\rangle in the electrons’ Bloch basis in the LLL.

Results from exact diagonalization: We first present the 6x4 ED results for both models as a preparation for the comparison with PE. Throughout the FCI phase, the 3-fold ground states in both models have center-of-mass (COM) momenta KC​O​M=(0,0),(2,0),(4,0)K_{COM}=(0,0),(2,0),(4,0) due to sample-size quantization. When λ=0\lambda=0, the many-body gaps from the 3-fold ground state sector to the first excited state are 0.390.39 (Haldane-V1V_{1}) and 0.0520.052 (bare-Coulomb) (in unit l(e)=1l^{(e)}=1), consistent with previously reported values[72, 109]. This many-body gap is due to the charge-neutral collective mode: it is the magnetoroton gap, instead of the quasiparticle-quasihole continuum gap (denoted as PH gap). The nice feature of the FQH λ=0\lambda=0 limit is that there is an existing prescription by Haldane[52] to clearly isolate the magnetoroton excitation branch from the PH continuum, which we show in Fig.12. From this prescription, we find the PH gap to be ΔPHED=0.70\Delta^{\rm ED}_{\rm PH}=0.70 (Haldane-V1V_{1}) and ΔPHED=0.113\Delta^{\rm ED}_{\rm PH}=0.113(bare-Coulomb) at λ=0\lambda=0. As λ\lambda increases, the many-body gap decreases and closes at λc≈0.72\lambda_{c}\approx 0.72 (Haldane-V1V_{1}) and λc≈0.115\lambda_{c}\approx 0.115 (bare-Coulomb) for the two models. (See Fig.16 for details). As a benchmark test, we do not attempt to investigate the nature of the phase transition and the nature of the phase realized at λ>λc\lambda>\lambda_{c}. Instead, we focus on the FCI phase 0≤λ<λc0\leq\lambda<\lambda_{c}.

When λ≠0\lambda\neq 0, we are not aware of direct methods to sharply isolate the PH gap from the magnetoroton spectrum. To this end, we perform a calculation to adiabatically track the magnetoroton modes: we slowly increase λ\lambda step by step from 00. For each λ\lambda, we compute the overlap of the many-body eigenstates with the previous λ\lambda eigenstates. Precisely, we choose the step Δ​λ=0.025\Delta\lambda=0.025 (Δ​λ=0.0025\Delta\lambda=0.0025) for the Haldane-V1V_{1} model (bare-Coulomb model). First, the eigenstate at step-(n+1)(n+1) with the maximal overlap with a magnetoroton mode at step-nn is marked as a ”would-be magnetoroton” mode for the moment, unless that maximal overlap is below a threshold Om​i​n=0.9O_{min}=0.9. Second, the remaining modes are labeled as nonroton modes, whose lowest excitation energy from the top of the 3-fold ground-state sector is defined as ΔPHED\Delta^{\rm ED}_{\rm PH}. Finally, any ”would-be magnetoroton” modes below ΔPHED\Delta^{\rm ED}_{\rm PH} are marked as true magnetoroton modes for step-(n+1)(n+1), while those above ΔPHED\Delta^{\rm ED}_{\rm PH} are marked as nonroton modes, since they are already inside the PH continuum. And the process continues iteratively. In this fashion, we obtain the magnetoroton modes and ΔPHED\Delta^{\rm ED}_{\rm PH} in the range 0≤λ<λc0\leq\lambda<\lambda_{c}. This calculation clearly shows that the magnetoroton gap ΔrotonED\Delta^{\rm ED}_{\rm roton} closes at λc\lambda_{c} in both models, while the PH gap ΔPHED\Delta^{\rm ED}_{\rm PH} remains finite (see Fig.16 for details). We plot the representative many-body spectra in Fig.13,14, in which E0E_{0} is defined to be the top of the three-fold ground state sector.

Results from PE: Parton band structures: Consider the band structure obtained from diagonalizing the 5×55\times 5 𝗁^(p)​(𝐤)\hat{\mathsf{h}}^{(p)}(\mathbf{k}) at the saddle point. This is the direct generalization of the static Hartree-Fock band structure to partons of Hdet states. When λ=0\lambda=0, partons fill their LLL, with higher LLs all empty. Throughout the regime 0≤λ<λc0\leq\lambda<\lambda_{c}, despite hybridization of the parton LLs leading to dispersion of the parton bands, we find that the band gap between the filled C=1C=1 parton-band and higher energy bands does not close, for both models. We have plotted the representative parton band structures for the two models in Fig.15. Note that, since ρ¯(1)=ρ¯(2)=ρ¯(3)\bar{\rho}^{(1)}=\bar{\rho}^{(2)}=\bar{\rho}^{(3)} throughout the range 0≤λ<λc0\leq\lambda<\lambda_{c}, the parton band structure is species-independent.

This parton band structure is not expected to capture the collective modes like the magnetorotons, similar to the fact that static Hartree-Fock cannot capture the collective modes. To capture magnetorotons, we should perform a dynamical PE calculation following VMPI as outlined in Sec.VI.1.3. Namely, one should compute the full dynamical kernel as in Eq.(337) by computing the matrices ℱ^,𝒢^,𝒦^\hat{\mathcal{F}},\hat{\mathcal{G}},\hat{\mathcal{K}} in the tangent space Tρ¯T_{\bar{\rho}} (in the parton LL basis ρm,n;𝐪(p)\rho^{(p)}_{m,n;\mathbf{q}}, see Sec.V.3.8), whose eigenspectrum contains the magnetoroton collective modes. Although this dynamical calculation is already well-defined, due to the scope of this paper, we leave it as a future project. On the other hand, we do expect that this parton band structure can capture the PH continuum in the many-body excitation spectrum (at least when the PE order increases, and assuming the Berry curvature superoperator ℱ^\hat{\mathcal{F}} for these PH excitations can be well approximated by its mean-field value ℱ^[0]\hat{\mathcal{F}}_{[0]}.). This motivates us to plot the PH gap ΔPHED\Delta^{\rm ED}_{\rm PH} from the ED together with the parton indirect band gap ΔpartonPE\Delta^{\rm PE}_{\rm parton} from the parton band structure as a function of λ\lambda in Fig.16 (We have checked that the parton band gap is independent of whether one uses the 4x12-𝐤\mathbf{k}-points from the 12x12 sample or the 2x4-𝐤\mathbf{k}-points from the 6x4 sample).

We find that the trend of ΔpartonPE\Delta^{\rm PE}_{\rm parton} follows ΔPHED\Delta^{\rm ED}_{\rm PH} in both models: as λ\lambda increases Δ\Delta decreases. In addition, in Haldane-V1V_{1} model, ΔpartonPE\Delta^{\rm PE}_{\rm parton} and ΔPHED\Delta^{\rm ED}_{\rm PH} are quantitatively close to each other. In bare-Coulomb model, ΔpartonPE\Delta^{\rm PE}_{\rm parton} is shifted to higher energy by about ∼0.1\sim 0.1 from ΔPHED\Delta^{\rm ED}_{\rm PH}. Since we are performing the zeroth-order PE, this inaccuracy is expected: as a local expansion, the long-range Coulomb interaction requires a higher-order PE.

Overlaps between the ED ground states and the saddle Hdet states: One of the goals for this benchmark section is to test the performance of PE and the associated Hdet saddle-point states far from the FQH regime. For this purpose, we compute the overlap between the Hdet state |Φ⁡(ρ¯)⟩|\Phi(\bar{\rho})\rangle with the ED ground states |ΨGSED⟩|\Psi^{\rm ED}_{\rm GS}\rangle in the three COM sectors as a function of λ\lambda, as shown in Fig.17. One important detail is that, based on the 12x12 sample PE saddle-point, given λ\lambda, we only construct one |Φ⁡(ρ¯)⟩|\Phi(\bar{\rho})\rangle on the 6x4 sample from one fusion tensor Ti​j​k​lT_{ijkl}. Due to the 6x4 sample size, the parton PSG for square-potential-translation is partially broken. Consequently, based on detailed PSG analysis, we know that |Φ⁡(ρ¯)⟩|\Phi(\bar{\rho})\rangle is a simultaneous eigenstate of T3​𝐚1T_{3\mathbf{a}_{1}} and T𝐚2T_{\mathbf{a}_{2}}: the translation operators of the three-time enlarged unit cell. |Φ⁡(ρ¯)⟩|\Phi(\bar{\rho})\rangle is really a linear superposition of the KC​O​M=(0,0)K_{COM}=(0,0), (2,0)(2,0) and (4,0)(4,0) COM sectors. When we present the overlap |⟨ΨGSED|Φ⁡(ρ¯)⟩||\langle\Psi^{\rm ED}_{\rm GS}|\Phi(\bar{\rho})\rangle| in each COM sector, we first project the Hdet state |Φ⁡(ρ¯)⟩|\Phi(\bar{\rho})\rangle into that COM sector and normalize the projection image. As a comparison, we also present the overlap between the ED ground states and the Laughlin states |⟨ΨGSED|ΦLaughlin⟩||\langle\Psi^{\rm ED}_{\rm GS}|\Phi_{\rm Laughlin}\rangle| in the three COM sectors. The Laughlin state contains no tunable variational parameter.

Not surprisingly, the overlap |⟨ΨGSED|ΦLaughlin⟩||\langle\Psi^{\rm ED}_{\rm GS}|\Phi_{\rm Laughlin}\rangle| becomes quite poor when λ\lambda is larger and near λc\lambda_{c} (∼70%\sim 70\% for both models), in both models – a signature of strong deviation from the FQH regime. However, the Hdet saddle states optimized by the zeroth-order PE show much improved overlap: |⟨ΨGSED|Φ⁡(ρ¯)⟩||\langle\Psi^{\rm ED}_{\rm GS}|\Phi(\bar{\rho})\rangle| ∼90%\sim 90\% even near λc\lambda_{c}, in both models. This result indicates that the Hdet wavefunctions together with PE can capture microscopic physics in FCI systems, even far from the FQH regime.

Results from PE: I​G​G=S​U​(3)IGG=SU(3) vs. I​G​G=U​(1)2IGG=U(1)^{2} As mentioned, we find throughout the regime 0≤λ<λc0\leq\lambda<\lambda_{c}, in both models, the saddle-point satisfies ρ¯(1)=ρ¯(2)=ρ¯(3)\bar{\rho}^{(1)}=\bar{\rho}^{(2)}=\bar{\rho}^{(3)}: the parton mean-field states at the saddle satisfy the parton-permutation symmetry. One can further show that the R=103R=103 fusion gate 𝐂^z\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{z} in the present study features the S​U​(3)SU(3) invariance in the parton species space. (In fact, as long as one keeps the parton LLs (a,b,c)(a,b,c) in an S3S_{3} permutation symmetric fashion in 𝐂^z\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{z} for q(1)=q(2)=q(3)=13q^{(1)}=q^{(2)}=q^{(3)}=\frac{1}{3}, 𝐂^z\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{z} is S​U​(3)SU(3) invariant.)

As discussed near Eq.(253), this indicates that the I​G​G=S​U​(3)IGG=SU(3) for the saddle-point in the generalized Hpfaffian construction, whose low-energy effective theory is described by a fluctuating S​U​(3)SU(3) gauge field coupled to fermionic partons filling C=1C=1 bands. After integrating out the matter fields, the S​U​(3)SU(3) level-1 Chern-Simons theory is obtained. The I​G​G=U​(1)2IGG=U(1)^{2} within the Hdet construction may be viewed as a limitation of the formulation, which cannot capture the hybridization between parton species.

VII Discussions and fused Gaussian States

We have introduced a framework to microscopically investigate correlated quantum systems based on Hdet wavefunctions. After the original proposal for the Hdet wavefunction in Ref[62] involving some of us, many puzzles have been resolved (at least to a large extent) in the present paper: the locality structure, the effective theories (variational manifold path integral, VMPI), and practical simulation methods (projective-expansion, PE). In fact, both VMPI and PE are developed as general techniques, whose applications are not limited to Hdet states.

There are many future directions one may explore immediately. For example, we have primarily tested the projective expansion in benchmarking examples of type-(B) models, partially because there are many well-documented results in the FQH context. It would be interesting to also apply PE in examples of type-(A) models to test its performance. In addition, we have not yet demonstrated VMPI’s full capabilities in concrete Hdet simulations, which requires full dynamical PE calculations and can capture collective-mode excitations. The algorithms for these calculations are already well-defined. For instance, we look forward to testing dynamical PE in future calculations, demonstrating the magnetorotons in the context of FQH and FCI or the gauge photons in the context of QSL. In addition, we plan to test the performance of the present framework in exotic states with gapless matter, such as the composite Fermi liquid[53], or the Dirac spin liquid[3, 136, 104, 59].

The Hdet states generalize the previously known fermionic parton constructions[15, 3, 133, 137, 80]. In terms of conceptual progress, the main new physics captured by Hdet states with a locality structure is the entanglement between the partons. In terms of the language used in this paper, this is described by the number of local fusion channels RR. Instead of R=1R=1 in many traditional parton constructions, we have shown that there are important quantum states that necessarily require R>1R>1 (e.g., R=4R=4 in ν=25\nu=\frac{2}{5} Jain’s state). Intuitively, compared with R=1R=1, the R>1R>1 Hdet state can capture more sophisticated local entanglement in the physical electronic wavefunction. For generic microscopic models, we believe that allowing R>1R>1 is crucial to improve energetics and microscopics.

In terms of practical simulations, although we believe PE is a useful method for approximately simulating Hdet states and provides reliable energetics, at least for short-range models, it is interesting to ask whether there are other numerical methods to systematically investigate Hdet wavefunctions. As long as those methods are statically and dynamically conserving as PE (see Eq.(252,253) for definitions), they can be combined with VMPI to produce microscopic effective theories. For example, at least when the partons are not filling topological bands (avoiding the known obstructions in the tensor-network formalism[32, 107]), the Gaussian Grassmann tensor-network[46, 77] describing the parton mean-field state together with local fusion gates (see Fig.4) may be a natural way to simulate Hdet states, possibly accurately. Compared with generic Grassmann tensor-network methods[28, 46, 94], the advantage of using a Gaussian tensor-network with local fusion gates is that, due to VMPI, it immediately provides intuitive, mean-field-like pictures and direct access to fractionalized d.o.f. (i.e., partons). We look forward to combining tensor-network simulation techniques with the present framework to investigate correlated quantum states.

Finally, we remark that the Hdet states with a locality structure, the central topic of this paper, belong to a larger class of variational wavefunctions, which we coin the fused Gaussian states (FGS). Similar to Hdet in Eq.(84,85,III.2.5), FGS is defined by applying the local fusion operator 𝐅^i\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{i}, or equivalently the corresponding local fusion gate 𝐂^i\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{i} on a Gaussian mean-field parton state |ΨM​F⟩|\Psi^{MF}\rangle:

|Ψ(e)⟩=∏i𝐂^i​|ΨM​F⟩.\displaystyle|\Psi^{(e)}\rangle=\prod_{i}\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{i}|\Psi^{MF}\rangle. (613)

Here, the fusion gate 𝐂^i\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{i} in FGS may not have the form Eq.(III.2.5) as in an Hdet state. Instead, 𝐂^i\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{i} should be understood as a general linear map between the local Fock space of electrons and that of the partons, preserving fermion parity. In FGS, one also does not require all partons to be fermionic. For example, the Schwinger-boson construction for 𝐒=12\mathbf{S}=\frac{1}{2} QSL[8, 114, 106, 123], and the slave-boson[75, 80] or the slave-fermion[73, 11] constructions for unconventional superconductivity[7], involving bosonic partons, can also be viewed as FGS-constructions when the parton mean-field states are Gaussian. Finally, |ΨM​F⟩|\Psi^{MF}\rangle does not need to be a tensor product of decoupled parton species. Instead, any Gaussian state which may or may not involve hybridization and/or pairing of partons is allowed for |ΨM​F⟩|\Psi^{MF}\rangle.

The key new ingredient emphasized here is about the fusion gate 𝐂^i\hat{\mathbf{C}}_{i}: as a linear map, it may map one local electronic state to an entangled many-body state (the parton-image state) in the local parton Fock space, resulting in the number of fusion channels R>1R>1. This generalizes most traditional parton constructions where R=1R=1. Again, we believe that allowing R>1R>1 is important for capturing the microscopics in correlated electronic systems. Many of the techniques developed in this paper, particularly VMPI and PE, can be applied to general FGS after minor revisions, leading to computable, microscopic effective theories.

We expect the FGS-based framework to find even broader applications, including nonabelian states in FCI (e.g., the FQAH analog of the ν=52\nu=\frac{5}{2} FQH state [90, 43]) and unconventional superconductivity. For instance, we already mentioned in Sec.VI.3.3, the saddle-points for the FCI benchmarking models are found to be described by the S​U​(3)1SU(3)_{1} effective theory in an Hpfaffian construction (see discussion near Eq.(253) for definition), where different parton species are allowed to hybridize and can be viewed as a FGS-construction. Furthermore, in Sec.IV.1, we explained that the Zhang-Sachdev ancilla construction[147] in the undoped case is secretly a Hdet construction. In the presence of doping, it is easy to show that Zhang-Sachdev ancilla construction can be viewed as an FGS-construction. Precisely, in the formalism developed in Sec.IV.1, introducing three fermionic partons u,v,wu,v,w per site, the fusion gate is:

𝐂^𝐫ZS=∑n∈{0,↑,↓,↑↓}|n𝐫(e)⟩⟨(↑𝐫,u↓𝐫,v−↓𝐫,u↑𝐫,v)⋅n𝐫(w)|,\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{C}}^{\rm ZS}_{\mathbf{r}}=\sum_{n\in\{0,\uparrow,\downarrow,\uparrow\downarrow\}}|n_{\mathbf{r}}^{(e)}\rangle\langle\big(\uparrow_{\mathbf{r},u}\downarrow_{\mathbf{r},v}-\downarrow_{\mathbf{r},u}\uparrow_{\mathbf{r},v}\big)\cdot n_{\mathbf{r}}^{(w)}|, (614)

which generalizes Eq.(92) to the doped case. Here R=2R=2 due to the spin-singlet of u,vu,v partons in the fusion gate.

Appendix A VMPI dictionary: half-filled antiferromagnet

In the application of VMPI to Slater determinants in Sec.V.2 and Hdet states in Sec.V.3, to keep the discussion general, we have introduced a collection of abstract mathematical objects: e.g., the superoperator 𝒦^\hat{\mathcal{K}}, the bilinear form \llangle.,.\rrangle\llangle.,.\rrangle, Hubbard-Stratonovich subspace VHS​(𝐪)V_{\rm HS}(\mathbf{q}), the bond tensor basis {wA​(𝐪)}\{w^{A}(\mathbf{q})\}, etc. The sole purpose of this appendix is to concretely demonstrate these abstract objects in a textbook time-dependent Hartree-Fock (TDHF) calculation, which may help readers to follow those general discussions.

Consider the one-band Hubbard model on the square lattice at half-filling:

H=−t∑⟨𝐫,𝐫′⟩,σ(c𝐫​σ†c𝐫′​σ+c𝐫′​σ†c𝐫​σ)+U∑𝐫n𝐫↑n𝐫↓,\displaystyle H=-t\sum_{\langle\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\rangle,\sigma}\left(c_{\mathbf{r}\sigma}^{\dagger}c_{\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\sigma}+c_{\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\sigma}^{\dagger}c_{\mathbf{r}\sigma}\right)+U\sum_{\mathbf{r}}n_{\mathbf{r}\uparrow}n_{\mathbf{r}\downarrow}, (615)

where 𝐫,𝐫′\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime} label lattice sites, σ=↑,↓\sigma=\uparrow,\downarrow, n𝐫​σ=c𝐫​σ†​c𝐫​σn_{\mathbf{r}\sigma}=c_{\mathbf{r}\sigma}^{\dagger}c_{\mathbf{r}\sigma}, and ⟨𝐫,𝐫′⟩\langle\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\rangle denotes nearest-neighbor pairs.

For a Slater determinant, define the one-body reduced density matrix by

ρ𝐫​α,𝐫′​β≡⟨c𝐫′​β†c𝐫​α⟩,α,β∈{↑,↓}.\displaystyle\rho_{\mathbf{r}\alpha,\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\beta}\equiv\langle c_{\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\beta}^{\dagger}c_{\mathbf{r}\alpha}\rangle,\qquad\alpha,\beta\in\{\uparrow,\downarrow\}. (616)

The local spin-density matrix at site 𝐫\mathbf{r} is the 2×22\times 2 matrix

(ρ𝐫)α​β≡ρ𝐫​α,𝐫​β=⟨c𝐫​β†​c𝐫​α⟩.\displaystyle(\rho_{\mathbf{r}})_{\alpha\beta}\equiv\rho_{\mathbf{r}\alpha,\mathbf{r}\beta}=\langle c_{\mathbf{r}\beta}^{\dagger}c_{\mathbf{r}\alpha}\rangle. (617)

Define the local charge density and spin-density vector by

n𝐫≡trσρ𝐫,m𝐫a≡trσ(ρ𝐫σa),a=x,y,z,\displaystyle n_{\mathbf{r}}\equiv\operatorname{tr}_{\sigma}\rho_{\mathbf{r}},\qquad m_{\mathbf{r}}^{a}\equiv\operatorname{tr}_{\sigma}(\rho_{\mathbf{r}}\sigma^{a}),\qquad a=x,y,z, (618)

where trσ\operatorname{tr}_{\sigma} is the trace over the two spin indices and σa\sigma^{a} are Pauli matrices. Then

ρ𝐫=12​(n𝐫​𝟏+𝐦𝐫⋅𝝈).\displaystyle\rho_{\mathbf{r}}=\frac{1}{2}\left(n_{\mathbf{r}}\mathbf{1}+\mathbf{m}_{\mathbf{r}}\cdot\bm{\sigma}\right). (619)

Using Wick’s theorem in a Slater determinant, it is easy to show that the Hubbard interaction energy is

EU​(ρ)=U​∑𝐫⟨n𝐫↑​n𝐫↓⟩=U4​∑𝐫(n𝐫2−|𝐦𝐫|2).\displaystyle E_{U}(\rho)=U\sum_{\mathbf{r}}\langle n_{\mathbf{r}\uparrow}n_{\mathbf{r}\downarrow}\rangle=\frac{U}{4}\sum_{\mathbf{r}}\left(n_{\mathbf{r}}^{2}-|\mathbf{m}_{\mathbf{r}}|^{2}\right). (620)

A.1 The saddle point analysis

The static Hartree–Fock one-body kernel is the derivative of the energy functional, as in Eq. (156). The interaction contribution at site 𝐫\mathbf{r} is

tU,𝐫​(ρ)=U2​(n𝐫​𝟏−𝐦𝐫⋅𝝈).\displaystyle t_{U,\mathbf{r}}(\rho)=\frac{U}{2}\left(n_{\mathbf{r}}\mathbf{1}-\mathbf{m}_{\mathbf{r}}\cdot\bm{\sigma}\right). (621)

We choose the Néel saddle

n¯𝐫=1,𝐦¯𝐫=m​η𝐫​z^,η𝐫=(−1)rx+ry,\displaystyle\bar{n}_{\mathbf{r}}=1,\qquad\bar{\mathbf{m}}_{\mathbf{r}}=m\eta_{\mathbf{r}}\hat{z},\qquad\eta_{\mathbf{r}}=(-1)^{r_{x}+r_{y}}, (622)

and define

Δ≡U​m2.\displaystyle\Delta\equiv\frac{Um}{2}. (623)

The self-consistent real-space kernel is then

t​(ρ¯)𝐫​α,𝐫′​β=\displaystyle t(\bar{\rho})_{\mathbf{r}\alpha,\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\beta}= −t​δ⟨𝐫,𝐫′⟩​δα​β+δ𝐫𝐫′​[U2​δα​β−Δ​η𝐫​(σz)α​β].\displaystyle-t\,\delta_{\langle\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\rangle}\delta_{\alpha\beta}+\delta_{\mathbf{r}\mathbf{r}^{\prime}}\left[\frac{U}{2}\delta_{\alpha\beta}-\Delta\eta_{\mathbf{r}}(\sigma^{z})_{\alpha\beta}\right]. (624)

The term U/2U/2 is a uniform chemical-potential shift at half filling and will be omitted in the band Hamiltonian below.

Using the doubled magnetic unit cell with sublattices s=A,Bs=A,B, introducing Pauli matrices τa\tau^{a} that act on the sublattice index, in the magnetic Brillouin zone (BZ), the saddle Hamiltonian is

h¯𝐤=ϵ𝐤​τx−Δ​τz​σz,ϵ𝐤=−2​t​(cos⁡kx+cos⁡ky),\displaystyle\bar{h}_{\mathbf{k}}=\epsilon_{\mathbf{k}}\tau^{x}-\Delta\tau^{z}\sigma^{z},\qquad\epsilon_{\mathbf{k}}=-2t(\cos k_{x}+\cos k_{y}), (625)

with single-particle energies

ε𝐤,±=±E𝐤,E𝐤=ϵ𝐤2+Δ2.\displaystyle\varepsilon_{\mathbf{k},\pm}=\pm E_{\mathbf{k}},\qquad E_{\mathbf{k}}=\sqrt{\epsilon_{\mathbf{k}}^{2}+\Delta^{2}}. (626)

At half filling, the two negative-energy bands are filled. The self-consistency condition may be written as

1=U2​Nuc​∑𝐤∈BZ1E𝐤,\displaystyle 1=\frac{U}{2N_{\rm uc}}\sum_{\mathbf{k}\in{\rm BZ}}\frac{1}{E_{\mathbf{k}}}, (627)

where NucN_{\rm uc} is the number of magnetic unit cells.

Now define the Hessian superoperator as in Eq. (158). Let MhM_{\rm h} be the real vector space of Hermitian one-body matrices, equipped with the bilinear form

\llangle​X,Y​\rrangle≡∑𝐫​α,𝐫′​βX𝐫​α,𝐫′​β​Y𝐫′​β,𝐫​α.\displaystyle\llangle X,Y\rrangle\equiv\sum_{\mathbf{r}\alpha,\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\beta}X_{\mathbf{r}\alpha,\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\beta}Y_{\mathbf{r}^{\prime}\beta,\mathbf{r}\alpha}. (628)

For an onsite fluctuation X𝐫X_{\mathbf{r}} at site 𝐫\mathbf{r}, define

δ​n𝐫​[X]≡trσ⁡X𝐫,δ​m𝐫a​[X]≡trσ⁡(X𝐫​σa).\displaystyle\delta n_{\mathbf{r}}[X]\equiv\operatorname{tr}_{\sigma}X_{\mathbf{r}},\qquad\delta m_{\mathbf{r}}^{a}[X]\equiv\operatorname{tr}_{\sigma}(X_{\mathbf{r}}\sigma^{a}). (629)

Expanding Eq. (620) to second order gives

δ2​EU​[X]=U4​∑𝐫[δ​n𝐫​[X]2−∑a=x,y,zδ​m𝐫a​[X]2].\displaystyle\delta^{2}E_{U}[X]=\frac{U}{4}\sum_{\mathbf{r}}\left[\delta n_{\mathbf{r}}[X]^{2}-\sum_{a=x,y,z}\delta m_{\mathbf{r}}^{a}[X]^{2}\right]. (630)

By definition,

δ2​EU​[X]=12​\llangle​X,𝒦^​X​\rrangle.\displaystyle\delta^{2}E_{U}[X]=\frac{1}{2}\llangle X,\hat{\mathcal{K}}X\rrangle. (631)

The unique onsite Hermitian matrix [𝒦^​X]𝐫[\hat{\mathcal{K}}X]_{\mathbf{r}} that reproduces Eq. (630) for all X𝐫X_{\mathbf{r}} is

[𝒦^​X]𝐫=U2​[trσ⁡(X𝐫)​𝟏−∑a=x,y,ztrσ⁡(X𝐫​σa)​σa].\displaystyle[\hat{\mathcal{K}}X]_{\mathbf{r}}=\frac{U}{2}\left[\operatorname{tr}_{\sigma}(X_{\mathbf{r}})\mathbf{1}-\sum_{a=x,y,z}\operatorname{tr}_{\sigma}(X_{\mathbf{r}}\sigma^{a})\sigma^{a}\right]. (632)

If we denote

X𝐫=x𝐫0​𝟏+𝐱𝐫⋅𝝈\displaystyle X_{\mathbf{r}}=x_{\mathbf{r}}^{0}\mathbf{1}+\mathbf{x}_{\mathbf{r}}\cdot\bm{\sigma} (633)

then Eq. (632) becomes

[𝒦^​X]𝐫=U​x𝐫0​𝟏−U​∑ax𝐫a​σa.\displaystyle[\hat{\mathcal{K}}X]_{\mathbf{r}}=Ux_{\mathbf{r}}^{0}\mathbf{1}-U\sum_{a}x_{\mathbf{r}}^{a}\sigma^{a}. (634)

Consequently, as matrices in MhM_{\rm h}, the onsite charge component x𝐫0​𝟏x_{\mathbf{r}}^{0}\mathbf{1} has eigenvalue +U+U, while each onsite spin component x𝐫a​σax_{\mathbf{r}}^{a}\sigma^{a} has eigenvalue −U-U. Now the full HS space VHS⊂MhV_{\rm HS}\subset M_{\rm h} in Eq. (177) is simple: it is spanned by those x𝐫0​𝟏x_{\mathbf{r}}^{0}\mathbf{1}, x𝐫a​σax_{\mathbf{r}}^{a}\sigma^{a}, four matrices per site-𝐫\mathbf{r}. The superoperator 𝒦^HS−1\hat{\mathcal{K}}_{\rm HS}^{-1} is simply

𝒦^HS−1​[x𝐫0​𝟏]=1U​[x𝐫0​𝟏]𝒦^HS−1​[x𝐫a​σa]=−1U​[x𝐫a​σa]\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{K}}_{\rm HS}^{-1}[x_{\mathbf{r}}^{0}\mathbf{1}]=\frac{1}{U}[x_{\mathbf{r}}^{0}\mathbf{1}]\qquad\hat{\mathcal{K}}_{\rm HS}^{-1}[x_{\mathbf{r}}^{a}\sigma^{a}]=-\frac{1}{U}[x_{\mathbf{r}}^{a}\sigma^{a}] (635)

A.2 Goldstone subspace

The broken spin generators are

Q^x=12​∑𝐫c𝐫†​σx​c𝐫,Q^y=12​∑𝐫c𝐫†​σy​c𝐫.\displaystyle\hat{Q}_{x}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\mathbf{r}}c_{\mathbf{r}}^{\dagger}\sigma^{x}c_{\mathbf{r}},\qquad\hat{Q}_{y}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\mathbf{r}}c_{\mathbf{r}}^{\dagger}\sigma^{y}c_{\mathbf{r}}. (636)

Their single-body matrices are Qx=σx/2Q_{x}=\sigma^{x}/2 and Qy=σy/2Q_{y}=\sigma^{y}/2. Following Eq. (191), introduce the infinitesimal angles θx,θy\theta_{x},\theta_{y} and define

δρQa≡iθa[Qa,ρ¯],a=x,y.\displaystyle\delta\rho_{Q_{a}}\equiv\mathrm{i}\theta_{a}[Q_{a},\bar{\rho}],\qquad a=x,y. (637)

The onsite saddle-point RDM is

ρ¯𝐫=12​(𝟏+m​η𝐫​σz).\displaystyle\bar{\rho}_{\mathbf{r}}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\mathbf{1}+m\eta_{\mathbf{r}}\sigma^{z}\right). (638)

Therefore

(δ​ρQx)𝐫\displaystyle(\delta\rho_{Q_{x}})_{\mathbf{r}} =θx​m​η𝐫2​σy,\displaystyle=\theta_{x}\frac{m\eta_{\mathbf{r}}}{2}\sigma^{y}, (δ​ρQy)𝐫\displaystyle(\delta\rho_{Q_{y}})_{\mathbf{r}} =−θy​m​η𝐫2​σx.\displaystyle=-\theta_{y}\frac{m\eta_{\mathbf{r}}}{2}\sigma^{x}. (639)

Similarly, following Eq. (192) and Eq. (193),

χQa=i​θa​[Qa,t⁡(ρ¯)]=𝒦^​δ​ρQa.\displaystyle\chi_{Q_{a}}=\mathrm{i}\theta_{a}[Q_{a},t(\bar{\rho})]=\hat{\mathcal{K}}\delta\rho_{Q_{a}}. (640)

Using Eq. (624),

χQx\displaystyle\chi_{Q_{x}} =−θx​Δ​τz​σy,\displaystyle=-\theta_{x}\Delta\tau^{z}\sigma^{y}, χQy\displaystyle\chi_{Q_{y}} =+θy​Δ​τz​σx,\displaystyle=+\theta_{y}\Delta\tau^{z}\sigma^{x}, (641)

where we use the sublattice space τz\tau^{z} to replace the staggered sign η𝐫\eta_{\mathbf{r}}.

Using the magnetic unit cell and the corresponding Brillouin Zone (BZ), we now choose the bond tensor {wA​(𝐪)}\{w^{A}(\mathbf{q})\} basis of VHS​(𝐪)V_{\rm HS}(\mathbf{q}) (see Eq.(211)) so that the first two vectors span the Goldstone subspace. Note that, since there are two sites per magnetic unit cell, VHS​(𝐪)V_{\rm HS}(\mathbf{q}) is 8-dimensional. A convenient choice is

w1\displaystyle w^{1} =−Δ​τz​σy,\displaystyle=-\Delta\tau^{z}\sigma^{y}, w2\displaystyle w^{2} =+Δ​τz​σx,\displaystyle=+\Delta\tau^{z}\sigma^{x},
w3\displaystyle w^{3} =−Δ​σy,\displaystyle=-\Delta\sigma^{y}, w4\displaystyle w^{4} =+Δ​σx,\displaystyle=+\Delta\sigma^{x},
w5\displaystyle w^{5} =𝟏,\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}, w6\displaystyle w^{6} =τz,\displaystyle=\tau^{z},
w7\displaystyle w^{7} =σz,\displaystyle=\sigma^{z}, w8\displaystyle w^{8} =τz​σz.\displaystyle=\tau^{z}\sigma^{z}. (642)

Note these are the tensor values for {wA​(𝐪)}\{w^{A}(\mathbf{q})\}, and are 𝐪\mathbf{q}-independent. The physical meaning of 𝐪\mathbf{q} in {wA​(𝐪)}\{w^{A}(\mathbf{q})\} is carried in Eq.(205). In the language of (𝐑,𝛂)(\mathbf{R},\bm{\upalpha}), these w𝛂​𝛃;𝜹Aw^{A}_{\bm{\upalpha}\bm{\upbeta};\bm{\delta}} correspond to 𝜹=𝟎\bm{\delta}=\mathbf{0}, and 𝛂\bm{\upalpha}(𝛃\bm{\upbeta}) labels the spin and the sublattice within one magnetic unit cell (a 4-dimensional index). The 4×44\times 4 matrix w𝛂​𝛃;𝜹=𝟎Aw^{A}_{\bm{\upalpha}\bm{\upbeta};\bm{\delta}=\mathbf{0}} is written as the tensor product of τ\tau and σ\sigma matrices above. We then have, as in Eq.(216):

χQx=θx​w1​(𝐪=0),χQy=θy​w2​(𝐪=0).\displaystyle\chi_{Q_{x}}=\theta_{x}w^{1}(\mathbf{q}=0),\qquad\chi_{Q_{y}}=\theta_{y}w^{2}(\mathbf{q}=0). (643)

Following the discussion below Eq. (216),

VG​(𝐪)=span⁡{w1​(𝐪),w2​(𝐪)},\displaystyle V_{\rm G}(\mathbf{q})=\operatorname{span}\{w^{1}(\mathbf{q}),w^{2}(\mathbf{q})\}, (644)

and the complement subspace is

V⟂​(𝐪)=span⁡{w3​(𝐪),w4​(𝐪),w5​(𝐪),w6​(𝐪),w7​(𝐪),w8​(𝐪)},\displaystyle V_{\perp}(\mathbf{q})=\operatorname{span}\{w^{3}(\mathbf{q}),w^{4}(\mathbf{q}),w^{5}(\mathbf{q}),w^{6}(\mathbf{q}),w^{7}(\mathbf{q}),w^{8}(\mathbf{q})\}, (645)

satisfying VHS​(𝐪)=VG​(𝐪)⊕V⟂​(𝐪)V_{\rm HS}(\mathbf{q})=V_{\rm G}(\mathbf{q})\oplus V_{\perp}(\mathbf{q})

A.3 Full kernel DD, reduced kernel Π\Pi, and long-wavelength analysis

Following Eq.(218), we expand the χ\chi-field as

χ⁡(𝐪,ω)=∑a=12ϕa​(𝐪,ω)​wa​(𝐪)+∑B=38ηB​(𝐪,ω)​wB​(𝐪).\displaystyle\chi(\mathbf{q},\omega)=\sum_{a=1}^{2}\phi_{a}(\mathbf{q},\omega)w^{a}(\mathbf{q})+\sum_{B=3}^{8}\eta_{B}(\mathbf{q},\omega)w^{B}(\mathbf{q}). (646)

The action has the form of Eq. (219).

Now separate the six-dimensional V⟂V_{\perp} into the transverse uniform spin sector

Vη​(𝐪)=span​{w3​(𝐪),w4​(𝐪)},\displaystyle V_{\eta}(\mathbf{q})=\text{span}\{w^{3}(\mathbf{q}),w^{4}(\mathbf{q})\}, (647)

and the charge/longitudinal sector

VL​(𝐪)=span​{w5​(𝐪),w6​(𝐪),w7​(𝐪),w8​(𝐪)}.\displaystyle V_{L}(\mathbf{q})=\text{span}\{w^{5}(\mathbf{q}),w^{6}(\mathbf{q}),w^{7}(\mathbf{q}),w^{8}(\mathbf{q})\}. (648)

Since the saddle preserves the U⁡(1)U(1) spin rotation generated by SzS^{z}, the quadratic kernel can only mix VGV_{\rm G} with VηV_{\eta}, but VLV_{L} cannot mix with either VGV_{\rm G} or VηV_{\eta}. Consequently the kernel DD in Eq.(220) has the form

D⁡(𝐪,ω)=(DGGDG​η0Dη​GDη​η000DL​L),\displaystyle D(\mathbf{q},\omega)=\begin{pmatrix}D_{\rm GG}&D_{{\rm G}\eta}&0\\ D_{\eta{\rm G}}&D_{\eta\eta}&0\\ 0&0&D_{LL}\end{pmatrix}, (649)

with respect to VG⊕Vη⊕VLV_{\rm G}\oplus V_{\eta}\oplus V_{L}. The Schur complement for the reduced kernel Π\Pi in Eq. (227) is

Π\displaystyle\Pi =DGG−(DG​η0)​(Dη​η00DL​L)−1​(Dη​G0)\displaystyle=D_{\rm GG}-\begin{pmatrix}D_{{\rm G}\eta}&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}D_{\eta\eta}&0\\ 0&D_{LL}\end{pmatrix}^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}D_{\eta{\rm G}}\\ 0\end{pmatrix}
=DGG−DG​η​Dη​η−1​Dη​G.\displaystyle=D_{\rm GG}-D_{{\rm G}\eta}D_{\eta\eta}^{-1}D_{\eta{\rm G}}. (650)

For small 𝐪\mathbf{q} and ω\omega, direct evaluation of Eq.(220) gives the Goldstone block

DGG​(𝐪,ω)\displaystyle D_{\rm GG}(\mathbf{q},\omega) =CAFM​ω2​𝟏2+∑u,v𝐪u​𝐪v​GAFMu​v​𝟏2+O3,\displaystyle=C_{\rm AFM}\omega^{2}\mathbf{1}_{2}+\sum_{u,v}\mathbf{q}_{u}\mathbf{q}_{v}G^{uv}_{\rm AFM}\mathbf{1}_{2}+O_{3}, (651)

the Goldstone–transverse block

DG​η​(𝐪,ω)\displaystyle D_{{\rm G}\eta}(\mathbf{q},\omega) =i​ω​MAFM​ϵ+O2,\displaystyle=\mathrm{i}\omega M_{\rm AFM}\bm{\epsilon}+O_{2}, (652)

and the transverse non-Goldstone block

Dη​η​(𝐪,ω)\displaystyle D_{\eta\eta}(\mathbf{q},\omega) =−Ωη⋅𝟏2+O1.\displaystyle=-\Omega_{\eta}\cdot\mathbf{1}_{2}+O_{1}. (653)

Here OnO_{n} means up to a nn-th order polynomial of |𝐪|,ω|\mathbf{q}|,\omega, and ϵ12=−ϵ21=1,ϵ11=ϵ22=0\bm{\epsilon}_{12}=-\bm{\epsilon}_{21}=1,\bm{\epsilon}_{11}=\bm{\epsilon}_{22}=0 is the fully antisymmetric tensor.

The coefficients appearing in Eqs. (651)– (653) are

Ωη=2​Δ2Nuc​∑𝐤∈BZϵ𝐤2E𝐤3,MAFM=Δ3Nuc​∑𝐤∈BZ1E𝐤3,\displaystyle\Omega_{\eta}=\frac{2\Delta^{2}}{N_{\rm uc}}\sum_{\mathbf{k}\in{\rm BZ}}\frac{\epsilon_{\mathbf{k}}^{2}}{E_{\mathbf{k}}^{3}},\;\;\;\;\;M_{\rm AFM}=\frac{\Delta^{3}}{N_{\rm uc}}\sum_{\mathbf{k}\in{\rm BZ}}\frac{1}{E_{\mathbf{k}}^{3}},
CAFM=Δ22​Nuc​∑𝐤∈BZ1E𝐤3,\displaystyle C_{\rm AFM}=\frac{\Delta^{2}}{2N_{\rm uc}}\sum_{\mathbf{k}\in{\rm BZ}}\frac{1}{E_{\mathbf{k}}^{3}},
GAFMu​v=−Δ22​Nuc∑𝐤∈BZ[ϵ𝐤​∂ku∂kvϵ𝐤E𝐤3\displaystyle G^{uv}_{\rm AFM}=\frac{-\Delta^{2}}{2N_{\rm uc}}\sum_{\mathbf{k}\in{\rm BZ}}\Bigg[\frac{\epsilon_{\mathbf{k}}\,\partial_{k_{u}}\partial_{k_{v}}\epsilon_{\mathbf{k}}}{E_{\mathbf{k}}^{3}}
+(2​Δ2−ϵ𝐤2)​(∂kuϵ𝐤)​(∂kvϵ𝐤)E𝐤5].\displaystyle\quad+\frac{(2\Delta^{2}-\epsilon_{\mathbf{k}}^{2})(\partial_{k_{u}}\epsilon_{\mathbf{k}})(\partial_{k_{v}}\epsilon_{\mathbf{k}})}{E_{\mathbf{k}}^{5}}\Bigg]. (654)

Substituting Eqs. (651)–(653) into the full Schur complement Eq. (650) gives

Πa​b​(𝐪,ω)=ω2​𝖢a​bAFM+∑u,v𝐪u​𝐪v​𝖦a​bu​v,AFM+O3,\displaystyle\Pi_{ab}(\mathbf{q},\omega)=\omega^{2}\mathsf{C}^{\rm AFM}_{ab}+\sum_{u,v}\mathbf{q}_{u}\mathbf{q}_{v}\mathsf{G}^{{uv},{\rm AFM}}_{ab}+O_{3}, (655)

where

𝖢a​bAFM=(CAFM+MAFM2Ωη)​δa​b,𝖦a​bu​v,AFM=GAFMu​v​δa​b.\displaystyle\mathsf{C}^{\rm AFM}_{ab}=\Big(C_{\rm AFM}+\frac{M_{\rm AFM}^{2}}{\Omega_{\eta}}\Big)\delta_{ab},\;\;\mathsf{G}^{{uv},{\rm AFM}}_{ab}=G^{uv}_{\rm AFM}\delta_{ab}. (656)

In the strong-coupling limit Δ≫t\Delta\gg t, one can show:

Ωη=\displaystyle\Omega_{\eta}= 8​t2Δ+O⁡(t4Δ3),\displaystyle\frac{8t^{2}}{\Delta}+O(\frac{t^{4}}{\Delta^{3}}), MAFM\displaystyle M_{\rm AFM} =1+O⁡(t2Δ2),\displaystyle=1+O(\frac{t^{2}}{\Delta^{2}}),
CAFM=\displaystyle C_{\rm AFM}= 12​Δ+O⁡(t2Δ3)\displaystyle\frac{1}{2\Delta}+O(\frac{t^{2}}{\Delta^{3}}) GAFMu​v=\displaystyle G^{uv}_{\rm AFM}= −δu​v​t2Δ+O⁡(t4Δ3).\displaystyle-\delta_{uv}\frac{t^{2}}{\Delta}+O(\frac{t^{4}}{\Delta^{3}}). (657)

Putting together, Eqs. (656) leads to

𝖢a​bAFM=δa​b​Δ8​t2+O⁡(1Δ).\displaystyle\mathsf{C}^{\rm AFM}_{ab}=\delta_{ab}\frac{\Delta}{8t^{2}}+O(\frac{1}{\Delta}). (658)

The Goldstone modes from kernel-Π\Pi is then described by the velocity cAFMc_{\rm AFM} at long wavelength, to the leading order of tΔ\frac{t}{\Delta}-expansion:

ω𝐪AFM=cAFM​|𝐪|+O⁡(q2),cAFM2=−GAFMx​x𝖢11AFM≃8​t4Δ2≃2​J2,\displaystyle\omega_{\mathbf{q}}^{\rm AFM}=c_{\rm AFM}|\mathbf{q}|+O(q^{2}),\;\;c_{\rm AFM}^{2}=-\frac{G^{xx}_{\rm AFM}}{\mathsf{C}^{\rm AFM}_{11}}\simeq\frac{8t^{4}}{\Delta^{2}}\simeq 2J^{2}, (659)

with J≡4​t2/UJ\equiv 4t^{2}/U after using Δ≃U/2\Delta\simeq U/2 at strong coupling. cAFM=2​Jc_{\rm AFM}=\sqrt{2}J is consistent with the usual linear spin-wave analysis for the Heisenberg model.
